case|( There are three grammatical values that comprise the category of “case” in Kagayanen Referring Phrases. These are absolutive absolutive, ergative/genitive genitive ergative and oblique oblique. These cases are expressed by prenominal case markers (CM), or zero. The reason we consider these forms to express case is that, in their usual usages, they reflect a grammatical relationship between the RP and the main predicator in their clause. A traditional grammar would say that the predicator (usually a verb) governs government, syntactic the appearance of these prenominal markers. For our purposes, we do not take a stand on whether the inflected Verb inflected verbs governs the prenominal case marker (including zero), or whether the choice of nominal category as expressed by prenominal case markers governs the form of the verb---the directionality of the relationship is not crucial. What is crucial is that particular arrangements of categories expressed by prenominal case markers correlate with particular verb forms. Thus we say that there is a structural link or “grammatical relation” grammatical relations between the two. In chap:voice we discuss the system of organizing grammatical relations in more detail. In this section we describe the case forms, and illustrate their usages from the text corpus.

prenominal case markers|( For basic Referring Phrases (those not headed by personal names), ergative/genitive and oblique cases are isomorphic (identical in form), expressed by the prenominal case marker ta, while absolutive case is zero-marked. For RPs headed by personal names (names referring to people), absolutive and ergative/genitive are isomorphic (zero-marked), and oblique case is marked by the prenominal case marker ki. Justification for these terms is provided in more detail in chap:voice, sec:grammaticalrelations. Personal and demonstrative pronouns also appear in absolutive, and non-absolutive forms (see sec:pronouns, tab:personalpronouns ). Personal pronouns functioning in Oblique roles are the same as the absolutive pronouns, but are preceded by the oblique marker ki (see tab:personalpronouns in sec:personalpronouns for the complete paradigm of personal pronouns). tab:prenominalcasemarkers above displays the prenominal case markers, repeated in tab:prenominalcasemarkingparticles for convenience.

The following examples illustrate the uses of the three cases in various contexts:

ta marking non-absolutive common nouns \\
Daw dili pa gusto ta mga ginikanan, mama i masirbi anay ta baļay ta bai. \\
Daw dili pa gusto ta mga ginikanan, mama i ma-sirbi anay ta baļay ta bai. \\
if/when neg.ir inc want nabs pl parent male def.n a.hap.ir -serve first nabs house nabs woman \\
`If the parents (RP ergative) still do not want (their children to marry each other), the man will serve in the house (RP oblique) of the woman (RP genitive).’ [DBOE-C-01 1.6]

… gaimes ta sidda sawa din an na bai. \\
… ga-imes ta sidda sawa din an na bai. \\
i.r -prepare nabs fish spouse 3 s.gen def.m lk woman \\
‘(When he came home having fished already,) his wife prepared the/some fish (RP oblique).’ [CBON-C-02 2.3] \\

Pasaway a ta bai na duma nay… \\
Pa-saway a ta bai na duma nay… \\
t.r -correct 1 s.abs nabs woman lk companion 1 p.excl.gen \\
‘ The woman (RP ergative) who was our companion corrected me…’ [CBWN-C-10 4.14]

ki marking oblique personal names \\
Nabaton nay imo na suļat na padaļa no ki Maria ta pitsa 23 ta Oct. \\
Na-baton nay imo na suļat na -pa-daļa no ki Maria ta pitsa 23 ta Oct. \\
a.hap.r -receive 1 p.excl. erg 2 gen lk letter lk t.r-caus- carry 2serg obl.p Maria nabs date 23 nabs October \\
This example is from a letter, and reflects what the writer actually wrote, for example, “23 ta Oct.”.
`We received your letter that you sent with Maria (RP oblique) on the date of the 23 rd in October.' [PBWL-C-04 3.1]

ki marking third person oblique pronoun \\
… danen i Papa daw Mama gatagad ki kanen na uļa pa kuļi. \\
… danen i Papa daw Mama ga-tagad ki kanen na uļa pa ka-uļi. \\
3 p.abs def.n Papa and Mama i.r -wait obl.p 3s lk neg.r inc i.exm -go.home \\
`Papa and Mama were waiting for him (RP oblique) when he had not yet come home.’ [CBWN-C-18 4.1]

The absolutive case is unmarked for common nouns and personal names. Since both the actor ( ergative ) personal name and the absolutive undergoer are unmarked, when both occur in one clause, their roles are distinguished only by order ( bkm:Ref329345305 )---the Actor is always first and the Undergoer second.

Zero marking on absolutive actor common noun \\
Lugay gaambaļ mga ittaw an, “Sunog! Sunog!” \\
Lugay ga-ambaļ mga ittaw an, “Sunog! Sunog!” \\
long.time i.r -say abs pl person def.m burn burn \\
‘Then the people said, “Fire! Fire!”' [RZWN-T-02 2.5]

Zero marking on absolutive undergoer common noun \\
Pagkita ko ta ittaw ya, paanggat ko bata i ta tag-iya ta lansa na manaog. \\
Pag-kita ko ta ittaw ya, pa-anggat ko bata i ta tag-iya ta lansa na m-panaog. \\
nr.act -see 1 s.gen nabs person def.m t.r -ask.to.accompany 1 s.erg abs child def.n nabs owner nabs launch lk i.v.ir -go.down \\
`When/after I saw the person, I asked the child of the owner of the motorized launch to accompany me to go down (off the boat).’ [DBWN-T-23 9.2]

Zero marking on absolutive location/recipient common noun (applicative construction) \\
Tapos paatagan din mama ya ta buļak … \\
Tapos pa-atag-an din mama ya ta buļak … \\
then t.r -give- apl 3 s.erg abs man def.f nabs flower \\
`Then she gave the man a flower.'

Zero marking on absolutive location common noun (applicative construction) \\
… daw pailingan danen yo na lungag …. \\
… daw pa-iling-an danen yo na lungag …. \\
and t.r -go- apl 3 p.erg abs d4abs lk hole \\
‘…and they went to that hole …’ [ETON-C-07 5.1]
summary: Kagayanen Referring Phrases have three case values: absolutive, ergative/genitive, and oblique, expressed by prenominal case markers or by zero. For common nouns, ergative/genitive and oblique are both marked by **ta** while absolutive is zero-marked; for personal names, absolutive and ergative/genitive are zero-marked while oblique is marked by **ki**, and personal pronouns use absolutive forms with **ki** for oblique roles. The passage explains that these markers correlate with grammatical relations to the predicator, and gives examples showing zero-marked absolutive actors and undergoers, as well as oblique uses in common nouns, personal names, and pronouns.

text:
Zero marking on absolutive actor personal name \\
Mugtaw kaw tak guli Maria i. \\
M-bugtaw kaw tak ga-uli Maria i. \\
i.v.ir -wake.up 2 s.abs because i.r -go.home abs.p Maria def.n \\
‘Wake up because Maria came home.’ [CBWN-C-19 5.2]

Zero marking on absolutive undergoer personal name \\
Nuļog Pedro ya. \\
Na-uļog Pedro ya. \\
a.hap.r -fall abs.p Pedro def.f \\
‘ Pedro fell (off a carabao).’ [RCON-L-02 2.15]

… pakapkap din Maria an. \\
… pa-kapkap din Maria an. \\
t.r -feel 3 s.erg abs.p Maria def.m \\
‘… he felt Maria.’ [LGON-L-01 7.12]

Zero marking on absolutive location personal name (applicative construction) \\
… na nakamang din bayo ta Pedro, pasuot din daw ilingan dya Maria i ta selled din ya. \\
… na na-kamang din bayo ta Pedro, pa-suot din daw...-iling-an dya Maria i ta selled din ya. \\
when a.hap.r - get 3 s.erg clothes nabs Pedro t.r -wear 3 s.erg and t.r -go- apl d4loc abs.p Maria def.n nabs inside 3 s.gen def.f \\
Sometimes after the conjunction daw the prefix of the following verb drops off. In this example the verb pa-iling-an, which is realis, becomes iling-an which looks like the irrealis form of the same verb. The initial vowel also may drop off, as in this example, leaving lingan as the surface form. This tendency to drop affixes is described in chap:verbstructure, sec:omissionofprefixes.
`… when he had gotten the clothes of Pedro, he put them on and went there to Maria in her room.’ [LGON-L-01 7.3]

Zero marking on ergative personal name \\
… daw papayapunan man Manang kanen an. \\
… daw pa-pa-yapun-an man Manang kanen an. \\
and t.r-caus -supper- apl too erg.p older.sister 3 s.abs def.m \\
‘… and Manang fed him supper.’ [CBWN-C-18 3.1]

Zero marking on genitive personal name \\
Pagsabat ko namatian ko kagi Manang … na gainsa ki yaken daw kamusta a kon. \\
Pag-sabat ko na-mati-an ko kagi Manang … na ga-insa ki yaken daw kamusta a kon. \\
nr.act -answer 1 s.erg a.hap.r -hear- apl 1 s.erg voice gen.p older.sister lk i.r -ask obl.p 1s if/when greet 1 s.abs hsy \\
`When I answered (the telephone) I heard the voice of Manang … asking me how I am.’ [CBWN-C-22 2.8]

Zero marking on ergative and absolutive personal names \\
Pasugo Manang Pedro an na mandok. \\
Pa-sugo Manang Pedro an na m-sandok. \\
t.r -order erg.p older.sister abs.p Pedro def.m lk i.v.ir -carry.water \\
‘ Older-sister ordered Pedro to carry water.’

Though there are no case markers preceding either of the core arguments in bkm:Ref329345305, the interpretation is unambiguous as to who is ordering whom to carry water. First, there is a strong preference for ergative arguments to precede other arguments, especially when proper names are involved. Second, the demonstrative determiner an, though not required, reinforces the idea that Pedro is the absolutive argument, therefore the Patient/Causee. Third, pragmatically a younger person (Pedro) could not conceivably order his older sister to do something.

Personal pronouns personal pronouns and enclitics also distinguish all three cases. The demonstratives demonstrative pronouns only distinguish absolutive and non-absolutive cases. See sec:pronouns for a description and exemplification of the cases of the various types of pronouns. case|)
summary: The passage shows that personal names in the language can appear with zero case marking in absolutive, ergative, and genitive roles, as well as in some locative applicative constructions. Even when both core arguments lack overt case markers, word order, optional determiners, and pragmatic knowledge usually make the grammatical roles clear. It also notes that pronouns distinguish case differently: personal pronouns and enclitics mark all three cases, while demonstratives distinguish only absolutive from non-absolutive.

number|( Referring Phrases are optionally marked for plural depending on what type of noun functions as the Head. Common nouns are optionally marked for plural with the particle mga. Example ex:bata describes a marriage arranged by the parents. Note that the fathers and mothers are marked as plural with mga in the first clause, but the fathers and mothers are not marked as plural in the second clause. In this context, it is understood that each child has a mother and a father and these are the ones referred to in the second clause. Including mga in the second instance of “fathers and mothers” would seem redundant.

Plural marker with common noun \\
… mga tatay daw nanay may kasugtanan na darwa na bata magsawaay danen daw may idad en na usto. Piro, tatay daw nanay ta mga bata na darwa may kundisyunis. \\
… mga tatay daw nanay may kasugtanan na darwa na bata mag-sawa-ay danen daw may idad en na usto. Piro, tatay daw nanay ta mga bata na darwa may kundisyunis. \\
pl father and mother ext.in agreeement lk two lk child i.ir -spouse- rec 3 p.abs if/when ext.in age cm lk proper/sufficient but father and mother nabs pl child lk two ext.in qualifications \\
` Fathers and mother s have an agreement that two children will marry each other when the age is sufficient. But the fathers and mothers of the two children had qualifications.’ [HCOE-J-02 3.2-3]

In conversation the plural marker is often left out, especially when plurality is obvious. For example, in bkm:Ref447720182 the RP ittaw i na malain ‘people who are bad’ has no plural marker but it is obvious that this is plural from the 3 rd person plural pronoun danen after the verb referring to the same people.

Tapos na gakilem en ittaw i na malain gapanaik danen ta isya na baļay … \\
Tapos na ga-kilem en ittaw i na ma-lain ga-panaik danen ta isya na baļay … \\
then lk i.r -night cm person def.n lk abs -bad
i.r -go.up 3 p.abs nabs one lk house \\
The ma- prefix here is identical to the irrealis happenstantial prefix. However, this is not the happenstantial prefix. See the discussion in chap:modification, sec:ma-derivation on the use of the prefix ma - to mark property concept words that refer to permanent or inherent properties.
`Then when it became night the people who are bad they went up to one house…' [BCWN-C-02 3.5]

Personal names can be marked for plural with plural pronouns, in which case the RP refers to the person named and some group of associates, for example, danen Maria `Maria and them/family/companions/associates', danen Papa `Dad and them/family/companions/associates' (see sec:referringphrasesheadedbypersonalnames, examples bkm:Ref53060834 and bkm:Ref343578640 ). Referring Phrases can also be pluralized with numerals, quantifiers, collective nouns, and with two adjectives that have specialized plural forms – sise/siset ‘small’, derse/derset ‘small. pl ’ ( bkm:Ref447720514 ), and bakod ‘big’, darko ‘big. pl ’ (examples bkm:Ref447720545 and bkm:Ref447720547 ). Collections or groups can also be specified morphologically, for example, bata ‘child’, bataan ‘group of children usually with the same parents’ kabataan ‘groups or many children usually having different parents’ (see sec:ka-an above). The plural marker mga is optional when there is a plural form of a numeral, quantifier or adjective:

Plural form of an adjective \\
Tapos lungagan ta derset na lungag para makasingngaw daw magsikaļ waig an. \\
Tapos -lungag-an ta derset na lungag para maka-singngaw daw mag-sikaļ waig an. \\
then t.ir -hole- apl nabs small. pl lk hole purp i.caus.hap.ir -evaporate if/when i.ir -boil water def.m \\
`Then make small holes (in the can) for the purpose of the water evaporating out when boiling.’ [ETOP-C-11 1.7]

… dili pa kuļi tenged ta biskeg na angin daw darko na mga baļed. \\
… dili pa ka-uļi tenged ta biskeg na angin daw darko na mga baļed. \\
neg.ir inc i.exm -go.home because nabs strong lk wind and big. pl lk pl wave \\
`… (they) cannot go home because of strong wind and big waves.’ [VPWE-T-01 2.8]

Unsi bilog na darko na sidda igo nang layungan ta appat na bataan. \\
Unsi bilog na darko na sidda igo nang -layung-an ta appat na bata-an. \\
eleven round lk big. pl lk fish right just t.ir -carry.on.pole- apl nabs four lk child- nr \\
`Eleven big fish is just right for four children to carry between them (on a pole over the shoulders).’ [EFWN-T-11 16.3]

Numeral \\
Sampuļo daw annem na bļangay naan man dya. \\
Sampuļo daw annem na bļangay naan man dya. \\
ten and six lk 2.mast.boat spat.def too d 4 loc \\
‘ Ten and six (sixteen) two-masted boats were there too.’ [VAWN-T-18 3.2]

Quantifier \\
May bandilyo na tanan na ittaw magpaindyiksyon naan ta Health Center. \\
May bandilyo na tanan na ittaw mag-pa-indyiksyon naan ta Health Center. \\
ext.in public.announcement lk all lk person i.ir - caus -injection
spat.def nabs Health Center \\
`There was a public announcement that all people will have themselves injected at the Health Center.’ [JCWN-T-21 7.2]

Collective noun \\
Daw may saļa ka na dili matuman iran na kasuguan may bunaļ … \\
Daw may saļa ka na dili ma-tuman iran na ka-sugu-an may bunaļ … \\
if/when ext.in mistake/wrong 2 s.abs lk neg.ir a.hap.ir -fulfill/obey

summary:
Referring phrases are optionally marked for plural, depending on the head noun. Common nouns may take the plural marker **mga**, but it is often omitted in conversation when plurality is already clear, and personal names can be pluralized by plural pronouns to mean the named person plus associates.  

Plural reference can also be expressed through numerals, quantifiers, collective nouns, and special plural adjective forms; in these cases, **mga** is optional. The passage also notes morphological devices for group reference, such as **bataan** for groups of children and **kabataan** for many children, usually with different parents.

Kagayanen has three demonstrative determiners i, an, and ya that occur in the RP as part of the enclitic complex we designate as “Є” (see the template in example ex:rptemplate, and tab:rptemplate ). If the Head is a common noun, the determiners indicate that it is definite, in a specific Kagayanen sense, Terms such as ``definite" and ``identifiable" as they are commonly used for Indo-European languages do not correspond directly to the pragmatic function of these determiners in Kagayanen. describes their functions in detail from a discourse perspective. For the purposes of this grammar, however, we consider ``definite" to reasonably evoke the pragmatic sense that these determiners impart. and specify its location in space and/or time. The determiner i ` def.n ’ indicates that the referent is close to the speaker or current in time, an ` def.m ’ indicates it is nearby in the area and/or further away in time, and ya ` def.f ’ indicates that it is far away, out of sight or more distant in time.
Absolutive nouns frequently occur with a determiner, but not obligatorily. RPs in all other roles can also occur with these forms. In other words, these are not case markers (contra ). The demonstrative determiners can also occur on genitive and oblique common nouns ( ex:prison - ex:night ). Any common noun that occurs clause finally preferentially takes a determiner (see example bkm:Ref447721085 and many others below). The ergative element is usually already introduced into the story and so does not need to be marked with a definite marker. However, sometimes a definite marker does occur in an ergative RP ( ex:woman - ex:snake ). There are also discourse functions for i, an, and ya that involve staging of participants. They cannot occur with other demonstrative elements in the same RP.

In addition to their usages in RPs headed by common nouns, the demonstrative determiners also occur when the Head is an absolutive proper name or absolutive free personal pronoun. When the RP head is a proper name or personal pronoun, the three determiners do not indicate definiteness since these are already definite. Rather they indicate only the location in space and time (see examples bkm:Ref447721085, and bkm:Ref447721088 - bkm:Ref447721090 ).

Phonologically, the demonstrative determiners are enclitics, and thus exhibit initially geminate transition consonants in certain environments (see chap:phonology, sec:gemination ). provides extensive discussion of the discourse functions of the demonstrative determiners in Kagayanen. In this chapter we discuss the very general communicative function of modification modification|(. Modification is a function that can be performed within any construction type, and contrasts with other functions such as syntactic headship, heads, syntactic predication predication, participant reference reference, and complementation complementation.

We define modification as the function of any “optional” substantive element By “substantive element” substantive element we mean words or phrases that express semantically rich meanings. Such elements contrast with grammatical functors grammatical functors functors, grammatical, such as pronouns, articles, deictic elements, and affixes, which tend to express limited and relatively precise grammatical meanings. This distinction was probably first proposed by, and has been largely assumed in subsequent linguistic research. See, for example,. that clarifies or adds detail to the discourse scene discourse scenes|( scenes|( evoked by a particular grammatical construction, without changing the construction’s basic propositional meaning. This definition is based on the metaphor of communication as a “stage” on which communicators depict and interpret scenes being communicated. The scenes evoked by individual lexical items and basic constructions tend to be sparse and schematic schematic (characteristic of discourse scenes). Sometimes the communication situation invites speakers to enrich the discourse scene in order to develop a more explicit picture of the idea being expressed. For example, consider the following imaginary English utterances:

We had dinner. \\

Honestly, we had the best dinner at a new Italian restaurant last night.

Example bkm:Ref441656793-a is a complete, grammatical sentence that is likely to evoke a certain scene in the minds of English speakers. However, the scene depicted is very vague and, frankly, uninteresting. In a Western context there may be a table and chairs, at least two diners and some unspecified food, but little else “on stage”. On the other hand, a construction like bkm:Ref441656793-b evokes a much more enriched version of possibly the same scene. Now we have a better idea of what kind and quality of food may be present, something about the surroundings, the presence of servers, money, the approximate time that this event is alleged to have occurred, and also the speaker’s attitude toward this scene (“honestly”). The scene is still vague, to be sure. We don’t know, for example, how many other diners were present, exactly what menu items were ordered, and so on. Nevertheless, bkm:Ref441656793-b is much more explicit and communicative than bkm:Ref441656793-a.

The difference between bkm:Ref441656793-a and bkm:Ref441656793-b is mostly modification. First there is modification of the noun “dinner”. This very general notion has been restricted to a certain class of dinners, those portrayed by the speaker as “the best”, “new” and``Italian” similarly enrich the scene by modifying the noun “restaurant”. Then there are modifying elements that restrict the scene to a place (“at a new Italian restaurant”) and a time (“last night”). Finally, there is one modifying element that specifies the speaker’s attitude toward the speech act itself (“honestly”). None of this information is technically required by the grammar, but all of it enriches and clarifies the scene in ways that make it more consistent with the communicative intentions of the speaker. discourse scenes|) scenes|)

In Kagayanen, modifying elements occur in many construction types. In this chapter we describe elements and constructions that serve as modifiers within the Referring Phrase ( bkm:Ref422117197 - bkm:Ref52774536 ), the Modifier Phrase ( bkm:Ref418142991 ), the Predicate ( bkm:Ref420904083 ), and the Clause ( bkm:Ref441599506 and bkm:Ref481473714 ). modification|)
summary:
The passage defines modification as the function of an optional substantive element that clarifies or adds detail to the discourse scene evoked by a construction, without changing its basic propositional meaning. It contrasts substantive elements, which carry rich semantic content, with grammatical functors, which express limited grammatical meanings.

Using English examples, the passage shows how modifiers can enrich a scene by restricting nouns, adding place and time information, and indicating the speaker’s attitude. It also notes that in Kagayanen, modifiers occur in several construction types, including the referring phrase, modifier phrase, predicate, and clause.

adjectives|(

Adjectives are a grammatically distinct class of words that express property concepts|( “property concepts”, i.e., semantic notions that describe the properties of items. categorizes the semantic properties that tend to underlie the word class of adjectives in any language into core types and peripheral types as follows:

Core semantic property types often expressed by adjectives: \\
Dimension: big, small, long, tall, short, wide, deep, etc. \\
Age: new, young, old, etc. \\
Value: good, bad, lovely, atrocious, perfect, proper/real, odd, strange, curious, necessary, crucial, important, lucky, etc. \\
Color: black, white, red, etc.

Peripheral semantic property types often expressed by adjectives: \\
Human propensity - jealous, happy, kind, clever, generous, cruel, proud, ashamed, eager, etc. \\
Physical property: hard, soft, heavy, wet, strong, clean, hot, sour, etc. And a subclass referring to corporeal properties: well, sick, dead, absent. \\
Speed: fast, quick, slow, etc.

Because the notion of “property concept” is semantic (it has to do with the ideas being expressed in language), its boundaries are “fuzzy” and not necessarily comparable from one language to the next. For this reason, we must look at language-internal evidence in order to identify adjectives, rather than simply assume that words that translate as adjectives in one language (say, English) will necessarily be expressed with a distinct category that can be called “adjectives” in another language.

contends that every language does have a grammatically distinct class of forms whose prototypical function is to refer to property concepts, though the morphosyntactic criteria for distinguishing this class may be subtle, and are different from one language to the next. shows that in some languages property concept words are grammatically similar to referring words (“nouns”), while in other languages they are similar to predicating words (“verbs”). Still other languages express property concepts in a more noun-like way when they are used attributively attributive!use of property concept words (i.e., within a Referring Phrase to modify the head noun---“the red barn”), but in a more verb-like way when used predicatively predicative!use of property concept words (i.e., to assert a property of some item---“the barn is red ”).

The grammar of Kagayanen treats adjectives and nouns similarly, in both the attributive and predicative usages. For example, the bare forms of prototypical nouns nouns!prototypical, like baļay ‘house’, and prototypical property concept words, like bakod ‘big’, can both function as the Head of a Referring Phrase (examples in ex:bighouse, and as the main predicator in a non-verbal predication predicative!use of nouns (examples in bkm:Ref422575828; see also chap:non-verbalclauses ):

bakod na baļay / baļay na bakod \\
big lk house \\
‘a big house’

bakod nai \\
big d1adj \\
‘this big (one)’

Baļay ni. \\
house d1abs \\
‘This is a house.’

Bakod na baļay ni. / Baļay na bakod ni. \\
‘This is a big house.’

Bakod ni. \\
‘This is big/a big one.’

Despite these important grammatical similarities, there are subtle ways in which property concept words are treated differently than nouns. First, while property concept words can always function as Heads heads, syntactic or Modifiers in Referring Phrases, not all nouns can freely function as attributive Modifiers attributive!use of nouns:

Examples bkm:Ref422580186-a and bkm:Ref422580189-a show that the nouns kaoy ‘wood’ and kawayan ‘bamboo’ may not function as modifiers of the head baļay. bkm:Ref422580186-b, bkm:Ref422575828-b and bkm:Ref422575828-c show that kaoy and kawayan may function predicatively predicative!use of nouns to express a material composition. However, a relative clause structure more commonly expresses the idea of ‘house made of wood’ bkm:Ref422580186-c. Some other “material composition” words may directly modify the head of an RP, as shown in bkm:Ref422580415:

property concepts|)

The exact patterns of which nouns can modify which other nouns seem to be lexically determined. Perhaps some noun-noun pairs in which one noun modifies the other are compound words ( bkm:Ref422581440 ). However, we have no independent reason for calling these compounds. They exhibit the same intonational characteristics and variability as Referring Phrases, and their meanings are as compositional and transparent as those of ordinary RPs. Furthermore, the fact that the order of elements may be reversed, as in most modifier+noun constructions, is an argument against the analysis of these noun-noun pairs as lexicalized compounds. The point of these illustrations, however, is to show that property concept words can always be Modifiers or Heads of RPs, while referring words (nouns) can always be Heads, but only sometimes Modifiers of RPs. This is one subtle grammatical property that distinguishes adjectives and nouns.

A second grammatical property that distinguishes adjectives as a class is their ability to be modified by the degree adverbs sikad ‘very’, segeng ‘extremely’, gid ‘really’, tise (nang) ‘a little bit’ and midyo ‘somewhat’. The following are a few examples. Additional examples from the text corpus are found in bkm:Ref418142991 below.
summary: The passage argues that adjectives are a distinct word class whose prototypical function is to express property concepts, such as dimension, age, value, and color, though these concepts vary semantically across languages and must be identified by language-internal evidence. It notes that in Kagayanen, property-concept words and nouns behave similarly in attributive and predicative positions, but adjectives differ in that they can always modify or head referring phrases and can be modified by degree adverbs, whereas nouns can only sometimes function as modifiers.

tise nang gisi na bayo \\

*tise nang bayo na gisi The word tise as a noun modifier means small in number or size. As a modifier of a gradable quality, such as spoiled, red or smelly, it means slightly. As a modifier of an activity it means almost (see bkm:Ref480610640 ). The word sise means small in size. But sometimes Kagayanen speakers use these two words interchangeably. When the word tise means small in number (‘a few’), or a little bit of a quality, as in example bkm:Ref441658460, then it is always followed by nang. In its other usages, nang is optional. The form tise (nang), like most adverbial elements, may also function as a noun modifier. However, in that case the linker na is required: tise nang na bayo ‘a few clothes’, ‘small clothes’. This usage, however, is far less common than the usage as a degree adverb.

tise nang baļ-es na kan-en \\
little just spoiled lk cooked.rice \\
‘slightly spoiled cooked rice’

sikad bakod na baļay \\
very big lk house \\
‘a very big house’

baļay na sikad bakod \\
house lk very big \\
‘a very big house’ \\

*sikad baļay na bakod \\
*sikad siminto na baļay \\

etc.

‘a really very attractive young woman’

This property of course only applies to gradable property concepts, like bakod ‘big’, gwapa ‘attractive’ and the others illustrated in these examples. In fact, we may say that all true adjectives in Kagayanen express gradable property concepts property concepts!gradable. Non-gradable concepts property concepts!non-gradable such as mama ‘male’ and bai ‘female’ exhibit no properties that distinguish them from nouns:

mama na bata / bata na mama \\
male lk child \\
`male child’

bai na bata / bata na bai \\

mama na ingkantado / ingkantado na mama ‘male fairy’ \\

There are a few words in Kagayanen, all borrowings from Spanish, which reflect a masculine/feminine distinction. In each such pair, - o expresses the masculine and - a the feminine gender, as in Spanish.

Finally, the last morphosyntactic property that may be said to distinguish a word class of adjectives is that this class can be the target of certain word-forming patterns. The resulting forms may function as Heads of RPs, Modifiers of RPs, or as non-verbal Predicators. Furthermore, most of them may occur with intensity and degree adverbs (examples in bkm:Ref422804351 ), and so may be considered true adjectives. In the following subsections we describe ten adjective-forming processes that occur in the corpus for this study. adjectives|)
summary: The passage explains that Kagayanen words like *tise* and *sise* can function as degree adverbs and noun modifiers, but their behavior depends on meaning: *tise* means “small in number” or “slightly” with gradable qualities, and when it means “a few” or “a little bit,” it must be followed by *nang*; as a noun modifier it requires the linker *na*. It also shows that true adjectives in Kagayanen are gradable, can appear with intensifiers like *sikad* and *segeng*, and can serve as modifiers or predicates, whereas non-gradable words such as *mama* ‘male’ and *bai* ‘female’ behave like nouns. A few Spanish loanwords also preserve masculine/feminine endings (*-o*, *-a*), and the class of adjectives is further identified by productive word-forming processes.

In this section we describe several regular morphological patterns that derive gradable property concept words (or``adjectives"). Some of these patterns also have roles in nominal and verbal derivations. In this section we concentrate on morphology that derives adjectives, making note of similarities to other derivational categories where applicable.

ma - derivation

-én/-ón derivation

Certain roots employ the suffix - én (with the allomorph - ón ) to express property concepts based on the root concept. Since this suffix is stressed, we write the stress in the following examples, even though it is not written in the official orthography. Stress distinguishes this derivation from the transitive irrealis verbal suffix - en (see chap:verbstructure, sec:transitiveirrealis ). It is similar to the nominalizing suffix - én/-ón that creates future patient nouns (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:en ), though there is no futurity associated with the adjective-forming usage. The allomorph - ón occurs when the last vowel in the root is /u/.

ka- … -én/-ón derivation

Ka - … - én/-ón occurs on a few verbal roots, notably tanuga ‘sleep’, kaan ‘eat’, agaļ ‘cry’ and other body activity verbs. The meaning of the resultant adjective is the property of feeling like one is about to verb or has the urge to verb: This is very similar to the nominalizing affix having the same form ka - … - én/-ón. It attracts the main stress of the word, and it is pronounced as ka - … -ón when the vowel of the final syllable of the root is /u/ (see chap:referringexpressions sec:ka-en ).

summary:
The passage describes several productive morphological patterns that derive adjective-like property concept words. These include ma- derivation, suffixation with -én/-ón, combined ma-…-én forms for permanent characteristics, and ka-…-én/-ón forms on certain verbal roots expressing an urge or feeling of being about to perform an action.

It also notes that these forms behave like adjectives because they can co-occur with intensity and degree adverbs. In addition, the text points out similarities between some adjective-forming patterns and related nominal or verbal derivations, while distinguishing them by stress and meaning.

text:
As with most adjective-forming derivational affixes, the forms ka - and - én are also related to inflectional verb affixes ( chap:verbstructure ). ka - is a happenstantial mood prefix, while - en (without stress) is a dynamic mood, transitive, irrealis suffix. As verb affixes, these forms are distinct members of the same paradigm, and can never simultaneously inflect the same root. Therefore, the functions of these forms as adjectivizers are clearly distinct from their uses as verbal inflectional affixes. The following are some additional examples of ka- … -én formations used as adjectives:

Katanugaén kanen ya na ittaw. \\
Ka-tanuga-én kanen ya na ittaw. \\
adj -sleep- adj 3 s.abs def.f lk person \\
The Predicate in this construction is katanugaén na ittaw ‘a sleepy person’. The absolutive argument, kanen ya ‘s/he (far away)’ is in the position after the first element in the predicate. We describe this phenomenon as “pronoun intrusion” in chap:non-verbalclauses and beyond.
‘S/he is a sleepy person.’ (‘S/he is a person who often has the urge to sleep’)

Kanen ya sikad katanugaén na ittaw. \\
Kanen ya sikad ka-tanuga-én na ittaw. \\
3 s.abs def.f very adj -sleep- adj lk person \\
‘S/he is a very sleepy person.’

Pirmi a nang gabatyag ta kiién daw paryo a man ta kindisén. \\
Pirmi a nang ga-batyag ta kiién daw paryo a man ta ka-indis-én. \\
always 1 s.abs just i.r -feel nabs adj -urinate- adj and same 1 s.abs also nabs adj -defecate- adj \\
`I kept feeling the urge to urinate and it was like I had the urge to defecate.’ (This is a story of a man who had a severe asthma attack and almost died) [JCWN-T-22 3.10].

Na yaken i naan ta annem na taon, yaken may inagian asta anduni daw mademdeman ko paryo a pa kagaļén. \\
Na yaken i naan ta annem na taon, yaken may <in>agi-an asta anduni daw ma-demdem-an ko paryo a pa ka-agaļ-én. \\
when 1 s.abs def.n spat.def nabs six lk year 1 s.abs ext.in
< nr.res >pass- nr until now/today if/when a.hap.ir -remember- apl 1 s.erg same 1 s.abs inc adj -cry- adj \\
`When I was six years old, I had an experience that until now when I remember it, it is like I still feel like crying.’ [HBWN-T-01 1.1]

Katawaén waļeng din an. \\
Ka-tawa-én waļeng din an. \\
adj -laugh/smile- adj face 3 s.gen def.m \\
‘His face (looks like he) has the urge to laugh.’ This sentence was used in a conversation to refer to a picture depicting several people. It is marginally acceptable out of context. Usually a person would be the Head of the RP modified by a ka-…-én adjective, but in this case it is the person’s face.

The complex prefix pinaka - may derive the superlative form of some adjectives:

‘This is the most fearsome sickness that arrived on Cagayancillo.’ [JCWN-T-21 20.1]

3 s.abs int superl -attractive nabs 3 p.gen lk place \\

Pinakamadali ta pagkamang ta sidda bungbong. \\

superl - adj -quick/easy nabs nr.act -get nabs fish dynamite \\

3 p.abs int superl -last go.home lk spat.def nabs graveyard \\

ka- … -an derivation – absolute extent

For other adjectives, the prefix-suffix combination ka- … -an forms an adjective or noun (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:ka-an ) that refers to the greatest possible extent of a quality. Sometimes words so derived may be interpreted as superlative adjectives, as in bkm:Ref52463441:

Ake na kamaguļangan na bata na bai nagatapos unduni ta sais grado. \\
Ake na ka-maguļang-an na bata na bai naga-tapos unduni ta sais grado. \\
1 s.gen lk nr -older.sibling- nr lk child lk female i.r -finish now/today
nabs six grade \\
The prefix naga - on this word is code switching from Ilonggo. The Kagayanen form would be gatapos.
`My oldest daughter is now finishing grade six.’ [VPWL-T-04 76.5]

Other times, the ka- … -an derivation forms a comparative nominalization, as described in chap:referringexpressions sec:ka-an. For example katumanan ‘the absolute end point or boundary’, katapusan `absolute end', kaumpisaan ‘absolute beginning place’ and kaunaan ‘very first place’, and example bkm:Ref113278812 from the corpus:

U-yi na isturya ni ka-matuod-an gid. \\
emph-d 1 abs lk story d 1 pr nr -true- nr int \\
‘This very story is the absolute truth.’ [MBON-T-07 61.-2]

pala - derivation

The prefix pala- on verbal roots derives an adjective that refers to the property of always liking to do the action described by the verb. This is not a common derivation, and no examples of it occur in the text corpus. All the following examples come from conversation or elicitation. Words derived with pala - are clearly adjectives as evidenced by the fact that they may occur with degree adverbs ( bkm:Ref439853390 ):

tabbing

ingaw ‘drunk’ \> palaingaw ‘likes to always get drunk’ \\
kaan ‘to eat’ \> palakaan ‘likes to always eat’ \\
butaļ ‘to fight/argue’ \> palabutaļ ‘likes to always fight/argue’ \\
sayaw ‘to dance’ \> palasayaw ‘likes to always dance’
tabbing

Sikad palabutaļ na bai nan. \\
Sikad pala-butaļ na bai nan. \\
very likes.always-fight/argue lk woman d 3 abs \\
‘That one is a woman who really likes to fight/argue.’
summary: The passage explains that the forms **ka-** and **-én** function both as adjective-forming affixes and as inflectional verb affixes, but these uses are distinct: as verb affixes they belong to the same paradigm and cannot co-occur on the same root. In adjectival use, **ka-…-én** formations can describe a person characterized by a tendency or urge, and related patterns include **pinaka-** for superlative adjectives and **ka-…-an** for expressions of greatest extent or absolute endpoints. It also notes a rarer **pala-** derivation, which forms adjectives meaning someone who always likes to perform the action named by the verb.

maka - derivation

The prefix maka- on verbal roots describes the quality of allowing, enabling or causing the activity described by the verb. This is also a relatively uncommon derivation occurring only eight times in the text corpus ( bkm:Ref125305525 ):

tabbing
4cm \=
adlek ‘to fear/be afraid’ \> makaadlek ‘scary/frightening’ \\
patay ‘to die/be dead’ \> makapatay ‘deadly, able to kill’ \\
luoy ‘pity/compassion’ \> makaluluoy ‘pitiful’ \\

sablag ‘to disturb’ \> makasablag ‘able to disturb’ \\
tabang ‘to help’ \> makatabang ‘helpful’ \\
biskeg ‘strong’ \> makabiskeg ‘strengthening’
tabbing

The meaning of maka - as an adjectivizer is clearly related to its meaning as a verbal inflectional prefix as described in chap:verbstructure, sec:ambitransitivehappenstantialirrealis as happenstantial, often abilitative modality. Unlike the inflectional verbal prefix, however, this usage of maka - does not express irrealis modality. Examples bkm:Ref117581373 through bkm:Ref117580692 illustrate additional examples of maka - from the corpus:

Makaadlek na Masakit. Masakit na kulira makaadlek. \\
Maka-adlek na Masakit. Masakit na kulira maka-adlek. \\
adj -afraid lk sickness sickness lk cholera adj -afraid \\
‘Frightening Sickness (the title of the text). The sickness cholera is frightening.' (first sentence of the same text) [JCWN-T-21 1.1-2]

… agian din na bilang sikad makaadlek \\
… agi-an din na bilang sikad maka-adlek \\
pass- nr 3 s.erg lk as very adj -afraid \\
‘…his/her experience that was as (something) very scary’ [JCOE-T-06 2.5]

Yi makailo ig gapanipis ta langgit ta lima no na gapalot ka. \\
Yi maka-ilo ig ga-pa-nipis ta langgit ta lima no na ga-palot ka. \\
d 1 abs adj -poison and i.r - caus -thin nabs skin nabs hand 2 s.gen
lk i.r -peel 2 s.abs \\
The use of ig as a conjunction is code-switching from Cuyonon. The Kagayanen form here would be daw. We will not mention this in subsequent examples, as it is very frequent in conversation and in writing.
`This is poisonous and causes the skin of your hand to become thin when you are peeling (it).’ (This is about a kind of root crop called kallot that is poisonous before it is processed the right way). [JCWE-L-32 5.8]
summary: The prefix **maka-** on verbal roots forms adjectives meaning ‘allowing,’ ‘enabling,’ or ‘causing’ the action expressed by the verb, and it is relatively rare in the corpus, occurring only eight times. Its adjectival use is closely related to its verbal inflectional use with abilitative/happenstantial meaning, but unlike the verbal prefix it does not mark irrealis modality.

Complete or partial root reduplication may derive downtoning adjectives from other adjectives, similar to the adjective suffix - ish in English ( greenish, smallish, etc.). It may also express a slight comparative degree (see example bkm:Ref117581975 ). For partial reduplication, the first consonant and vowel are reduplicated, and if the root ends in a consonant, the final consonant is also reduplicated. All roots that reduplicate allow complete reduplication, but not all allow partial reduplication. In particular, roots with closed initial syllables do not allow partial reduplication, for example, darko, derse, tambek and sagbak (see bkm:Ref481477458 below).

Partial Reduplication, C-final root: C 1 V 1 XC 2 # → C 1 V 1 C 2 XC 2 # \\

di - derivation

The prefix di - is probably borrowed from Spanish de ‘of’. The meaning of the resulting form is ‘of a certain kind’. Occasionally, the resulting form can function as a Modifier, as in examples bkm:Ref481478039- bkm:Ref481478100:

Ta una na timpo naan ta banwa Cagayancillo uļa anay mga sakayan na dimakina. \\

nabs first/for.awhile lk time spat.def nabs town/country Cagayancillo neg.r for.a.while pl ride- nr lk adj -motor/machine \\
`In the earliest times in the town of Cagayancillo there were at first no motorized vehicles.’ [VPWN-T-06 1.3]

Napalit din ki kami tenga sako na beggas daw mga dilata na sid-anan. \\
Na-palit din ki kami tenga sako na beggas daw mga di-lata na sid-anan. \\
a.hap.r -buy 3 s.erg obl.p 1 p.exc half sack lk milled.rice
and pl adj -can lk viand \\
‘Viand’ is a word in Philippine English that refers to any meat, fish or vegetable dish served over rice. It comes from French, through 19 th -20 th century English, and came to be used in the Philippines during the American colonial period (1898--1946).
`He bought for us half a sack of rice and some canned viand.’ [DBWN-T-22 7.13]

Labi na gid ta dipamilya rispunsibilidad… \\

‘Especially the family kind of responsibility…' [TTOB-L-03 9.12]

`There they knew that Pedro was truly the kind of person who is a servant of God.’ [TTOB-L-03 7.25]

The di - prefix occurs mostly with roots borrowed from Spanish (as in bkm:Ref481478039 - bkm:Ref117583999 ), but may occur on original Kagayanen roots, as in bkm:Ref113279533:

‘They rode a sail kind of outrigger canoe.’

summary:
The passage describes two adjective-forming patterns in Kagayanen: root reduplication and the prefix di-. Complete or partial reduplication can form downtoning adjectives meaning ‘kind of X’ or express a slight comparative, with partial reduplication following specific phonological rules but being blocked for roots with closed initial syllables.  

It also notes that some reduplicated forms, especially tanan ‘all’ and matuod ‘true,’ can have superlative meanings like ‘absolutely X,’ and that reduplicated adjectives may appear in comparative constructions. The prefix di-, probably borrowed from Spanish de, means ‘of a certain kind’ and is used mostly with Spanish loan roots, though it can also attach to native roots.

text:
numbers|(

The second type of modification in the Referring Phrase that we will discuss is the numbers---one, two, three; first, second, third, and so on. As with most Philippine languages, numbers in Kagayanen are complicated by the fact that there are two number systems---the original Austronesian-based Kagayanen numbers and the Spanish-based numbers numbers!Spanish-based, spelled according to the Kagayanen pronunciations. Furthermore, since math is taught mostly in English, English numbers are also quite common. However, in this grammar, we will discuss only the Austronesian and Spanish-based number systems. While both systems are decimal (base ten), they differ in their structure and use.

The Kagayanen numbers numbers!Austronesian are either cardinal with no affixes ( bkm:Ref479572983 ), ordinal bkm:Ref479339690, or distributive bkm:Ref479572999. Ordinal ordinal numbers numbers!ordinal and distributive numbers distributive numbers numbers!distributive above one are derived by affixation from the cardinals, as described in bkm:Ref479339690 and bkm:Ref479572999. Numbers normally occur in the pre-Head (MOD 1 ) position in the Referring Phrase, though they may appear following the Head (in MOD 2 ). See bkm:Ref418107822 below for a detailed description of Number Phrases (NumPs):

darwa na adlaw \\
darwa na adlaw \\
two lk day \\
`two days'

pangarwa na adlaw \\
pang-darwa na adlaw \\
ord -two lk day \\
‘second day’

Like other modifying elements, numbers and Number Phrases may also function as predicates of non-verbal clauses ( bkm:Ref329087374 ). See also chap:non-verbalclauses on non-verbal clauses):

Darwa nang ame na bata. \\
Darwa nang ame na bata. \\
two only 1 p.excl.gen lk child \\
‘We have only two children.’ (lit. ‘Our children are only two.’)
summary: Kagayanen has two decimal number systems: an original Austronesian-based system and a Spanish-based system, though the grammar discusses only these two rather than the also-common English numbers. In the Austronesian system, numbers can be cardinal, ordinal, or distributive, with ordinals and distributives above one formed by affixation from cardinals. Numbers usually appear before the head in the referring phrase, but they can also follow it, and number phrases may serve as predicates in non-verbal clauses.

cardinal numbers|( numbers!cardinal|(

The original Kagayanen cardinal numbers are used for counting, especially up to ten. After ten the Spanish-based number Spanish-based numbers numbers!Spanish-based set is more common, probably because the names of Spanish numbers are shorter. For counting money and for clock time, the Spanish-based numbers are usually used.

For time expressions, Kagayanen numbers can modify nouns for periods like “month” or “year,” with the linker often omitted, but they do not occur with certain time-of-day terms such as “morning” or “afternoon.” The plural marker mga before a number or time phrase can indicate approximation, as in ‘approximately two weeks’ or ‘approximately ten o’clock.’

text:
ordinal numbers|( numbers!ordinal|(

There are two sets of ordinal numbers in Kagayanen, both based on Austronesian cardinal number numbers!Austronesian roots above the first ordinal. One type is formed with the prefix pang - and the other is formed with the prefix ka -. The first ordinal for both types is borrowed from Spanish numbers!Spanish-based (exx. bkm:Ref479573487 and bkm:Ref479573710 ).

pang - general ordinal

The pang - ordinals are unspecified for the kind of order such as order in space, in time or in importance. The ordinal referring to ‘first’ in this system is the Spanish cardinal number una (exx. ex:unmarkedordinal and bkm:Ref479573487 ). For the numbers darwa ‘two’, tallo ‘three’, and those beginning with a glottal stop (orthographic vowel-initial roots), the root-initial consonant is omitted following pang - (see the examples in ex:unmarkedordinal ). The initial consonant is not omitted with limma ‘five’, pitto ‘seven’, waļļo ‘eight’, and sampuļo ‘ten’.

Since the instrumental nominalizer pang - ( chap:referringexpressions, sec:pang ) may also occur with number roots, we include examples of these constructs in ex:unmarkedordinal to illustrate the contrast between these two stem-forming prefixes. As mentioned in chap:referringexpressions, the instrumental pang - prefix never causes root-initial consonant omission:

ka - temporal ordinal

Ordinals derived with ka - have a more specific function, referring only to order in time. For example, kadarwa na gira ‘the second war.’ Also katallo na bukid ‘the third mountain (that someone came upon)’. It can also mean the first, second, and so on in a series of actions bkm:Ref479574197. The first ordinal for the ka - derivation set is borrowed from Spanish ‘primero’ (exx. ex:temporalordinals and bkm:Ref479573710 ). For the second to tenth ordinals, the Kagayanen numbers are used, but after the tenth, the Spanish-based numbers are used as in example bkm:Ref481151157. The second ordinal in this set sometimes reduces to karwa (exx. ex:temporalordinals and bkm:Ref479574075 ).

text:
distributive numbers|( numbers!distributive|(

The distributive numbers describe the distribution of numbers of items in groups. They usually function as clause-level adverbial modifiers. There are two types of distributive numbers in Kagayanen---those involving reduplication alone, and those involving the prefix tag -/ tig -. Each type has its own function, as described in the following paragraphs.
summary: Distributive numbers in Kagayanen express the distribution of quantities across groups and usually function as clause-level adverbial modifiers. There are two types: one formed by reduplication alone and another using the prefix **tag-/tig-**, and each type has its own distinct function.

numbers!reduplication distributive|(

The original Kagayanen numbers numbers!Austronesian may be completely reduplicated, indicating groups of N participants in an action. For example, isya-isya ‘one by one’ or ‘one at a time’ and darwa-darwa ‘two by two’ or ‘two at a time’.

The prefix tag - or tig - occurs with the original Kagayanen numbers!Austronesian cardinal numbers to indicate how many items go into each group. summary: Kagayanen can express distributive number meanings in two main ways. First, full reduplication of cardinal numbers, such as *isya-isya* ‘one by one’ and *darwa-darwa* ‘two by two,’ indicates groups of participants or items, and *isya-isya* can also mean ‘each and every one’ when modifying a noun phrase. Second, the prefixes *tag-* or *tig-* attach to numeral forms to mean ‘X each’ or the number of items per group, with *tag-isya/tagsaļa* both meaning ‘one each’ and *tag-* also used with Spanish-based numerals for prices like *tagdyis* ‘ten pesos each.’

Non-numeral quantifiers in Kagayanen can only occur in the pre-head position (MOD 1 ) in the Referring Phrase. They may occur as predicates of clauses, but they do not take affixes. Only tanan ‘all’ and tama ‘many’ can take complete reduplication; tanan-tanan, meaning ‘absolutely all’ and tama-tama ‘quite a few’. All the non-numeral quantifiers are listed in bkm:Ref424336114:

The forms tise and sise are idiolectal variants in this context. We suspect interference from the adjective sise meaning ‘small (sg.) in size’. The variant forms tiset and siset also occur, parallel to the variants derse and derset for the adjective meaning ‘small (pl.)’. Both of these forms are also predicate adverbs indicating ‘almost do X’ (see bkm:Ref420904083 ).

The non-numeral quantifiers tama ‘many’, tise ‘few’ and pila ‘few’ can occur with degree/intensity adverbs, and so qualify as adjectives bkm:Ref425171721- bkm:Ref479341772.
