summary:
Non-numeral quantifiers in Kagayanen occur only in pre-head position in referring phrases and may also function as clause predicates, but they do not take affixes. Only *tanan* ‘all’ and *tama* ‘many’ can reduplicate, and some quantifiers such as *tama*, *tise*, and *pila* can combine with degree/intensity adverbs, behaving like adjectives.

The passage lists several quantifiers and their meanings, including *kada* ‘each/every,’ *duma* ‘some/other,’ *bilog* ‘whole,’ *tama* ‘many/much,’ and *tise/sise* or *pila* ‘few.’ It also notes that *duma* is especially multifunctional, and that in known contexts most non-numeral quantifiers except *kada* can serve as the head of a referring phrase.

text:
Modifier Phrases|(

We refer to syntactic constructions headed by Modifiers as Modifier Phrases (MPs). There are three situations in which MPs may function in Kagayanen clauses:

enumerate
Attributively attributive use of Modifier Phrases Modifier Phrases!attributive use in Referring Phrases" ( the very thick rain)
Predicatively predicative!use of Modifier Phrases Modifier Phrases!predicative use as non-verbal Predicates ( The rain is very thick.)
Adverbially adverbial use of Modifier Phrases as clause-level Modifiers ( It is raining very thickly.)
enumerate

In this section, we will describe the internal structure of MPs serving each of these three major functions. The distribution of MPs in their larger contexts will be described in other sections: attributive functions of MPs are discussed in chap:referringexpressions; predicative functions are discussed in chap:non-verbalclauses; and adverbial functions are discussed in bkm:Ref420904083 below.

Modifier Phrases (MP) consist minimally of a Head, which may be a lexical adjective, a derived adjective, a noun, a precategorial root, a numeral, one of a small set of quantifiers, a genitive case RP, or a relative clause. We argue that when MPs function predicatively or adverbially they are nominalized (see bkm:Ref418108091 ).

The basic template for Modifier Phrases is given in bkm:Ref343768497:

MP = (ADV1 degree ) (ADV2 intensity/aspect ) Head

As shown in bkm:Ref343768497, there are generally two groups of adverbial elements (ADV) that may occur within a Modifier Phrase. Group one, degree adverbs degree adverbs adverbs!degree, always precede the head. Group two, intensity intensity adverbs adverbs!intensity and aspect adverbs aspect adverbs adverbs!aspectual, are second-position enclitics. They occur following the first major constituent in the phrase. Thus, if no degree adverb occurs, any intensity/aspect adverbs follow the Head (exx. bkm:Ref479575080, and bkm:Ref479575151 ):

sikad gid tama na ittaw \\

ADV1 ADV2 HEAD \\
[ sikad gid tama ] na ittaw \\
very int many lk people \\
‘very many people’

dani nang man na baryo \\

Head ADV2 \\
[ dani nang ] man na baryo \\
close only too lk barrio \\
‘a very close barrio too’ [DDWN-C-01 3.6]

dayad gid na ittaw \\

Head ADV2 \\
[ dayad gid ] na ittaw \\
good int lk person \\
‘a really good person’ [JCOE-T-06 1.1]

The intensity adverb gid and the aspectual adverbs may occur after the Head even if a degree adverb appears before the head. This suggests a “tighter” link between the ADV1 and the HEAD, as indicated by the bracketing in examples bkm:Ref439938209 and bkm:Ref425605536. Such special constructions indicate higher intensity, as indicated by upper case in the free translations:

sikad tama gid na ittaw \\

ADV1 Head ADV2 \\
[ [ sikad tama ] gid ] na ittaw \\
very many int lk people \\
‘really very many people’

sikad lawig pa na iksplikar \\

ADV1 Head ADV2 \\
[ [ sikad lawig ] pa ] na iksplikar \\
very long.time inc lk explanation \\
‘very long explanation’ [SBWL-C-03 6.4]

The central degree adverbs are sikad ‘very’, segeng ‘extremely’ and tise (nang) ‘slightly/a little bit/almost’. A fourth degree adverb, midyo ‘kind of/sort of’ may also be included in this set, though it has slightly different syntactic properties, as discussed below.

Intensity adverbs include the intensifier gid ‘truly’, and the downtoner nang ‘just/only’ (see examples bkm:Ref425250007 - bkm:Ref424739679 below). What we are calling “aspectual” adverbs are pa ‘incompletely’ or ‘still’ (exx. bkm:Ref424739679, bkm:Ref424800529 ) and en ‘completely’ ( bkm:Ref425694314 ). Tagalog also employs a particle pa with senses comparable to the same particle in Kagayanen. The en adverb is comparable to Tagalog na, and is sometimes represented in the free translations as “already” or “now”.

-1.3ptIn the following sections we will describe MPs functioning attributively ( bkm:Ref424719800 ), predicatively ( bkm:Ref418108091 ), and adverbially ( bkm:Ref439924168 ). Following this, we will describe two subtypes of MPs---MPs headed by numbers (NumP) and non-numeral quantifiers ( bkm:Ref439924202 ).
distributive numbers|) numbers!distributive|)
summary:
Modifier Phrases (MPs) in Kagayanen are constructions headed by a modifier and can be used attributively, predicatively, or adverbially. Their head may be an adjective, noun, root, numeral, quantifier, genitive RP, or relative clause, and when used predicatively or adverbially they are analyzed as nominalized.

The basic MP structure is optional degree adverb before the head, followed by optional second-position intensity or aspect adverbs. Degree adverbs such as *sikad* ‘very’ and *segeng* ‘extremely’ precede the head, while intensifiers and aspectual particles such as *gid*, *nang*, *pa*, and *en* follow the first major constituent.

text:
ordinal numbers|(

As mentioned above, MPs consist minimally of a single modifying element. Several examples of minimal MPs in MOD 1 and MOD 2 positions are presented in bkm:Ref422117197 above. Examples bkm:Ref417997093- bkm:Ref425250007 illustrate slightly more complex MPs functioning attributively in the MOD 1 position in an RP. In these examples the MP is indicated in brackets:

sikad dakmeļ na mga lamunon \\

ADV1 6ptHead \\
[ sikad dakmeļ ] na mga lamon-én \\
very thick lk pl to.weed- nr \\
‘very thick weeds’ [PBWN-C-13 10.2]

segeng bao na tangkaļ ta baboy \\

ADV1 24ptHead \\
[ segeng bao ] na tangkaļ ta baboy \\
extremely odor lk pen nabs pig \\
‘extremely smelly pen of the pig’

midyo inog na nangka \\

ADV1 14ptHead \\
[ midyo inog ] na nangka \\
kind.of ripe lk jackfruit \\
‘kind of ripe jackfruit’

tise nang bao na tangkaļ ta baboy \\

ADV1 16ptADV2 16ptHead \\
[ tise nang bao ] na tangkaļ ta baboy \\
slightly just/only odor lk pen nabs pig \\
‘just slightly smelly pen of the pig’

Examples bkm:Ref425694314- bkm:Ref424739679 illustrate MPs with intensity/aspect adverbs in the ADV2 position.

subļa en na dikstros. \\

Head 24ptADV2 \\
[ subļa en ] na dikstros. \\
too.much cm lk dextrose \\
‘too much dextrose now’ [JCWN-T-21 17.3]

bugtong nang na bata \\

Head 20ptADV2 \\
[ bugtong nang ] na bata \\
sole only lk child \\
‘one and only child’ [CBWN-C-17 2.2]

sikad gid tama na mga pilak na dayad \\

ADV1 ADV2 Head \\
[ sikad gid tama ] na mga pilak na dayad \\
very int many lk pl silver lk good \\
‘really very much silver that is good’ [AGWN-L-01 5.8]

sikad tama gid na mga pilak na dayad \\

12ptADV1 Head 12ptADV2 \\
[ [ sikad tama ] gid ] na mga pilak na dayad \\
very many int lk pl silver lk good \\
We have used multiple brackets in this example to illustrate the tight syntactic relationship between sikad and the following Head. This is mentioned above, and in the following discussion.
‘really very MUCH silver that is good’

sikad pa lawig na iksplikar \\

ADV1 ADV2 Head \\
[ sikad pa lawig ] na iksplikar \\
very inc long.time lk explanation \\
‘a very long explanation’

The following examples illustrate an aspectual plus an intensity adverb following the HEAD bkm:Ref424800529 and preceding the HEAD bkm:Ref481481587. The combinations pa gid ‘truly very’ and pa man ‘very (emphatic)’ may be lexicalized compounds. They are quite common, while other combinations of aspectual and intensity adverbs do not occur:

matama pa gid na ambaļanen \\

6ptHead 18ptADV2 ADV2 \\
[ ma-tama pa gid ] na ambaļ-anen \\
adj -many inc int lk say- nr \\
‘really many more sayings’ [SFOB-L-02 4.5]

sikad pa man gwapa na bata \\

ADV1 ADV2 ADV2 Head \\
[ sikad pa man gwapa ] na bata \\
very inc emph attractive lk child \\
‘a very attractive child’ [CBOE-C-01 1.9]

As mentioned above, and illustrated in bkm:Ref418078036-- bkm:Ref425326439, in general when a degree adverb occurs in an MP, the intensity and aspectual adverbs occur after the degree adverb or after the Head of the MP. However, the downtoner nang is an exception. It only occurs after the degree adverb tise. If there is no degree adverb, nang may appear after the Head, but it does not occur with any degree adverb other than tise. For this reason we sometimes consider tise nang, ‘just a little bit’, to be a fixed compound adverbial expression (see bkm:Ref425693139 ).

As is the case at all levels of Kagayanen syntax, various “intrusive” elements may occur after the first syntactic element in the MP. These may be clause-level enclitic pronouns or clausal adverbial particles. Examples bkm:Ref401111978 through bkm:Ref422823012 illustrate MPs with an intrusive clausal attitude marker, pronoun and/or clause-level enclitic (bolded).

sikad ya tama na sagbetan \\
[ sikad ya tama ] na sagbet-an \\
very att many lk weeds/trash- nr \\
‘the very many weeds (far away, out of sight)’

mataļem kaw man na maistro daw maistra \\
[ ma-taļem kaw man ] na maistro daw maistra \\
adj -sharp 2 p.abs emph lk teacher. m and teacher. f \\
‘ also you (will be) skillful teachers (male) and teachers (female)’ [SFOB-L-01 8.7]…

sikad kon gwapa na dļaga \\
[ sikad kon gwapa ] na dļaga \\
very hsy attractive lk single.woman \\
‘a very, they say, attractive young woman’ [PBWN-C-12 15.3]

… sikad ka kon miad na dļaga. \\
[ … sikad ka kon miad ] na dļaga. \\
very 2 s.abs hsy kind lk single.woman \\
‘… they say you are a very kind single woman.’ [PBWN-C-12 15.3]

sikad man kon tama na kwarta … \\
[ sikad man kon tama ] na kwarta … \\
very emph hsy many lk money \\
‘ it is said (there was) very much money …' [PBWN-C-13 14.2]

As mentioned in chap:referringexpressions, sec:basicreferringphrases there is an element we’ve termed “Є" that consists of a genitive enclitic and/or a deictic determiner. The genitive enclitic occurs in the second position in the Referring Phrase. Of course, if the MP is in MOD 1, and consists of a single word, the genitive enclitic follows that word. However, if the MP is complex, the genitive enclitic intrudes after the first element of the MP. Examples bkm:Ref418078298 and bkm:Ref418078380 illustrate MPs with such intrusive genitive enclitic pronouns.

tallo ko nang na mga mangngod na mga dirset \\
[ tallo ko nang ] na mga mangngod na mga dirset \\
three 1 s.gen only lk pl younger.sib lk pl small. pl \\
‘just my three small younger siblings’ [ETOP-C-08 4.1]

ta tanan-tanan no gid na pamilya \\
ta [ tanan -tanan no gid ] na pamilya \\
nabs red all 2 s.gen int lk family \\
‘truly all your family’ [ETOP-C-08]
summary: The passage describes how modifying phrases (MPs) in Kagayanen can be simple or complex, with modifiers appearing in specific positions such as MOD 1 and ADV2. It shows that degree, intensity, and aspectual adverbs usually follow the degree adjective or the head, with some common lexicalized combinations like *pa gid* and *pa man*, while the downtoner *nang* is highly restricted and mainly occurs after *tise*. It also notes that intrusive elements such as enclitic pronouns, clausal particles, and genitive enclitics can appear after the first element of a complex MP.

text:
As mentioned above, the degree adverbs seem to be more tightly bound syntactically to the following Head than other modifiers, since genitive enclitics may not intrude between them and the Head of the MP. Instead the only possible order in this case is for the genitive enclitic to follow the Head of the MP, thus indicating that sikad bakod in example bkm:Ref52474400 is treated as a unitary substantive element for purposes of Є placement:

sikad bakod no na baļay ‘your very big house’ \\
*sikad no bakod na baļay

Interestingly, this restriction only applies to genitive enclitics. Clausal pronouns, attitude markers and adverbs may intrude between sikad and the Head of the MP (exx. bkm:Ref424739555, bkm:Ref424739557, and bkm:Ref422823012 ). Also, intensity/aspectual clausal adverbs may occur after sikad (exx. bkm:Ref418078036 and bkm:Ref424739679 ).
summary: Degree adverbs are more tightly bound to the following head than other modifiers, because genitive enclitics cannot come between them and the head of the MP; instead, the enclitic must follow the head, showing that sequences like *sikad bakod* are treated as a single unit for enclitic placement. However, this restriction applies only to genitive enclitics: clausal pronouns, attitude markers, adverbs, and even intensity/aspectual clausal adverbs may intervene between *sikad* and the MP head.

text:
Every language has ways of predicating concepts referring to properties. For example, in English one can say “she is very tall” or “he is taller than his father”. The predicates in these sentences are sometimes called “adjectival predicates” or “predicate adjective phrases”. Such adjectival predicates have much in common with Modifier Phrases within Referring Phrases, but they are not exactly the same. For example, in English one can use “very tall” attributively, “A very tall woman”, or predicatively “the woman is very tall”. However “taller than his father” can only be used predicatively. The attributive use is not allowed - “*A taller than his father boy”. Even some individual modifiers may be used attributively but not predicatively, and vice versa:

tabbing
5.5cm \=
Attributive use \> Predicative use \\
The dolphin is a marine mammal. \> *Some mammals are marine. \\
They caught the serial killer. \> *That killer is serial. \\ \\
*An ablaze house \> The house was ablaze. \\
*An ashamed teacher \> I am ashamed.
tabbing

For this reason, the notion of “Adjective Phrase” in English needs to be qualified as to whether it is the type of phrase that may be used attributively, predicatively or both.

Something similar is true in Kagayanen as well. We propose that MPs functioning as Predicates are actually nominalizations, and that therefore there is no essential difference between nominal predicates and adjectival predicates. Furthermore, there is a reasonable functional explanation for this fact.

To illustrate, compare examples bkm:Ref417997171 and bkm:Ref113343326 with bkm:Ref417997093 and bkm:Ref418000563 (repeated here as bkm:Ref479412653 and bkm:Ref418087692 ):

Predicative use of modifier phrases: \\
Sikad na dakmeļ mga lamunon. \\
[ Sikad na dakmeļ ] mga lamon-én. \\
very lk thick pl to.weed- - nr \\
‘The weeds are very thick.’ Or ‘Very thick ones are the weeds.’

Segeng na bao tangkaļ ta baboy. \\
[ Segeng na bao ] tangkaļ ta baboy. \\
extremely lk odor pen nabs pig \\
‘The pig pen is extremely smelly.’

Attributive use of modifier phrases: \\
sikad dakmeļ na mga lamunon \\
[ sikad dakmeļ ] na mga lamunon \\
very thick lk pl weeds \\
‘very thick weeds’ [PBWN-C-13 10.2]

segeng bao na tangkaļ ta baboy \\
[ segeng bao ] na tangkaļ ta baboy \\
extremely odor lk pen nabs pig \\
‘extremely smelly pig pen’

Note that the only overt indication of the distinction between the predicative versus attributive functions is the position of the linker, na. This generalization is true in careful speech. In relaxed speech, all linkers are subject to omission, thus potentially obscuring the grammatical distinction between Clause and RP. However, in context speakers are easily able to replace the dropped linkers, thus disambiguating the structures in exactly the manner described in this section. In the predicative use (exx. bkm:Ref417997171 and bkm:Ref113343326 ), the linker occurs inside the Modifier Phrase, whereas in the attributive use (exx. bkm:Ref479412653 and bkm:Ref418087692 ), the linker occurs between the Modifier Phrase and the Head of the nominal predicate RP. This is entirely parallel to simple predicate nominal constructions in which a modified RP functions as a predicate:

Layen gid na bata Pedro ya. \\

Predicate 70pt Absolutive \\
Layen gid na bata Pedro ya. \\
mischievious int lk child Pedro def.f \\
‘Pedro is really a mischievous child.’

Beet na ittaw kanen an. \\

Predicate 40pt Absolutive \\
Beet na ittaw kanen an. \\
behaved lk person 3 s.abs def.m \\
‘S/he is a well-behaved person.’

Thus if we consider modifier phrases functioning as predicates as being nominalizations (e.g. “very thick ones” in bkm:Ref418088532, and “extremely smelly one” in bkm:Ref113343326, there is no need to posit an “optional” linker that only shows up when the phrase functions as a predicate. These modifying predicates are just RPs with a property concept word as the Head and the degree adverbs in the MOD 1 position. The RP structure explains the presence of the linker.

A reasonable functional explanation for this fact is simply that, if the predicating modifiers were not nominalized, there would be no structural distinction between attribution and predication, for example sikad dakmeļ mga lamunon would mean both “the very thick weeds" and “the weeds are very thick”.

Just as illustrated in English above, in Kagayanen certain modifying expressions may occur attributively, but not predicatively. This is the difference between midyo ‘kind of/sort of’ and the other degree adverbs, sikad ‘very’ segeng ‘extremely’ and tise (nang) ‘a little bit’. As illustrated in example bkm:Ref418000663, repeated here as bkm:Ref418089153, midyo may function to modify a property concept word such as inog ‘ripe’.

midyo inog na nangka \\
[ midyo inog ] na nangka \\
kind.of ripe lk jackfruit \\
‘kind of ripe jackfruit’

However, midyo by itself may not appear in a predicate modifier:

[ * Midyo na inog ] nangka an. \\
(‘The jackfruit is kind of ripe.’)

The other degree adverbs may freely function in either context (see exx. bkm:Ref418088532 through bkm:Ref418087692 ). For this reason, we say that midyo is a non-central member of the class of degree adverbs. Of course this may be because it is a recently borrowed word, coming originally from Spanish medio ‘half/partly’.

Similar to attributive MPs when MPs occur as predicates, an enclitic pronoun referring to the absolutive argument of the clause may intrude in second position. In example bkm:Ref418091763, the second clause, “we were very tired” consists of a predicate modifier sikad gid bellay ‘very tired’, with the linker na dropped out before the word bellay. The absolutive argument of this predicate is kay ‘we’ which appears in second position in the clause:

Mam, ta ame na pag-uli di [ sikad kay gid bellay … \\
Mam, ta ame na pag-uli di [ sikad kay gid bellay ] … \\
ma’am nabs 1 p.excl.gen lk nr.act -go.home d 1 loc very 1 p.excl.abs int tired \\
`Ma’am, when we went home here, we were really very tired…' [AFWL-L-01]
summary: The passage argues that in English and Kagayanen, modifier/adjective phrases can function either attributively or predicatively, but these uses are not always identical and must be distinguished. In Kagayanen, predicative modifier phrases are analyzed as nominalizations, with the linker *na* marking the structural difference between attributive and predicative uses; some items like *midyo* occur only attributively, while others such as *sikad*, *segeng*, and *tise* can occur in both contexts.

text:
The second clause of example bkm:Ref418091763, with pronoun intrusion, is the most normal way of expressing this type of clause. The “non-intrusive” version is used in unusual situations, such as excited speech bkm:Ref422836404 (see chap:non-verbalclauses ):

Sikad gid (na) bellay kami i. \\
Sikad gid (na) bellay kami i. \\
very int lk tired 1 p.excl.abs def.n \\
‘We were very tired (excitedly).’

As mentioned above, the linker na often drops out in relaxed speech. However, there is no apparent communicative function for this omission of na.

Similarly, in example bkm:Ref418091931, the predicate is sikad (na) sadya ‘very happy.’ In this case both the absolutive enclitic pronoun and a clause-level adverbial particle appear after the degree adverbial:

Sikad kaw taan sadya. \\
[ Sikad kaw taan sadya. ] \\
very 2 p.abs perhaps happy \\
‘Y’all are perhaps very happy.’ [SBWL-C-01 4.2]

Finally, bkm:Ref418092305 illustrates two coordinate predicate modifier clauses. In the second clause, the absolutive enclitic kay ‘we exclusive’ intrudes in the MP functioning as the predicate.

Sikad tama ame na kaoy daw sikad kay na teggeb. \\
Sikad tama ame na kaoy daw [ sikad kay na teggeb. ] \\
very many 1 p.excl.gen lk wood and very 1 p.excl.abs lk overloaded \\
‘Our wood was very much and we were very overloaded…’ (This is a story about riding in an outrigger canoe.) [CBWN-C-11 2.6]
summary: The passage says that pronoun intrusion in the second clause is the normal way to express this kind of clause, while the non-intrusive form appears only in unusual contexts such as excited speech. It also notes that the linker **na** often drops in relaxed speech without any clear communicative function, and gives further examples where enclitic pronouns and clause-level particles follow degree adverbials in predicate modifier clauses.

text:
MPs functioning as clause-level modifiers mostly occur with a non-absolutive marker ta preceding them, and there is usually no linker between any degree adverb and the Head. Examples bkm:Ref113345573 and bkm:Ref113345575 illustrate basic MPs in this function, with both degree and intensity/aspectual adverbs:

Guran ta sikad gid dakmeļ. \\
Ga-uran ta sikad gid dakmeļ. \\
i.r -rain nabs very int thick \\
‘It is/was really raining very thickly.’

Bukasan din ta tise nang. \\
-Bukas-an din ta tise nang. \\
t.r -open- apl 3 s.erg nabs little.bit only/just \\
‘S/he opened it just a little bit.’

Examples bkm:Ref52476459 through bkm:Ref479413467 from the corpus illustrate MPs of various compositions functioning as clause-level modifiers:

Sikad gatingaļa gid ta bakod mga ittaw an man-o tak ittaw i gatallog. \\
Sikad ga-tingaļa gid ta bakod mga ittaw an man-o tak ittaw i ga-tallog. \\
very i.r -wonder int nabs big pl person def.m why because person def.n i.r -egg \\
‘People really were wondering greatly (lit. big) why a person was laying eggs.’ [MBON-T-07 10:7]

Dayon kon papakang buļag tamboļ ya ta sikad tudo. \\
Dayon kon pa-pakang buļag tamboļ ya ta sikad tudo. \\
right.away hsy t.r -hit blind drum def.f nabs very intense \\
‘Right away the blind one hit the drum very hard.’ [CBWN-C-10 7.12]

Ta buļan ta Abril gulpi nang uran ta sikad dakmeļ. \\
Ta buļan ta Abril gulpi nang uran ta sikad dakmeļ. \\
nabs month/moon nabs April suddenly only/just rain nabs very thick \\
‘In the month of April (it) suddenly rains very heavily.’ [JCWE-T-14 3.5]

Kada adlaw mag-istudyo ta iran na liksyon ta miad. \\
Kada adlaw mag-istudyo ta iran na liksyon ta miad. \\
each day i.ir -study nabs 3 p.gen lk lessson nabs well/good \\
‘Each day (they) studied their lessson well.’ [CFWE-T-01 2.7]

Mga kan-en na sinama dapat na takļeban ta usto. \\
Mga kan-en na s<in>ama dapat na -takļeb-an ta usto. \\
pl cooked.rice lk < nr.res >leftover must lk t.ir -cover- apl nabs well \\
‘Leftover rice must be covered well.’ [JCWN-T-21 12.6]

Sometimes in relaxed speech the non-absolutive marker drops out (as in bkm:Ref479413467 ).

Tenged ta adlek din, gadļagan tudo kabaw ya. \\
Tenged ta adlek din, ga-dļagan tudo kabaw ya. \\
because nabs afraid 3 s.gen i.r -run intense carabao def.f \\
‘Because of his (the rider of the carabao) fear, the carabao ran intensely.’ [RCON-L-02 2.13]
summary: Clause-level modifier particles (MPs) usually appear with the non-absolutive marker **ta** before them, and there is typically no linker between a degree adverb and the head. The examples show MPs used with degree and intensity/aspectual meanings, such as ‘really,’ ‘very,’ ‘just a little bit,’ ‘well,’ and ‘hard.’ In relaxed speech, the **ta** marker may sometimes be omitted.

subsection: MPs headed by numbers and quantifiers
text:
Number Phrases (NumP) are a subtype of Modifier Phrases. They may function as RP modifiers in MOD 1 or MOD 2 position, or as non-verbal predicates. However, they have a slightly different structural template than other Modifier Phrases, and so we are treating them distinctly. A Numeral Phrase may consist of just a numeral, a numeral accompanied by adverbs, and/or an optional classifier or measure word. Unlike other MPs, only one adverbial particle can precede the numeral, namely the indefinite plural adverbial mga. The basic structure of the NumP is given in bkm:Ref343924122:

NumP = (PL) NUM (ADV2) (\CLASS/MEASURE\)

The Numeral Phrase consists of an optional adverb mga (glossed PL, as it is identical to the plural marker at the RP level) indicating “approximately”, followed by the cardinal or ordinal numeral. Following the numeral are optional intensity and aspectual adverbs as in the MP. Following the adverb(s), an optional noun classifier, such as buok ‘piece’, bilog ‘round’, panid ‘flat sheet’, puon ‘stem’, naet ‘strand’, or an optional measurement, such as akep ‘handful’, kilo ‘kilogram, litsi ‘8oz.can’, gantang ‘ganta’ A ganta is a dry measure in the Philippines mostly for rice that equals about 3 quarts., pungpong ‘cluster’, begkes ‘bundle’, baso ‘glass’ and many others.

Mga ‘approximately’ and the measurement/classifier words do not occur with ordinal numbers in the text corpus, but do occur in conversation ( bkm:Ref365610460 and bkm:Ref365610463 ). When the numeral phrase includes mga ‘approximately’ before the numeral, there is usually no mga plural marker immediately before the Head of the larger RP, though it sometimes does occur. Examples bkm:Ref117598318 through bkm:Ref343776670 illustrate a few Number Phrases occurring in the text corpus:

NumP in attributive function: \\
tallo i na mag-arey \\
tallo i na mag-arey \\
three def.n lk rel -friend \\
‘the three friends’ [CBWN-C-10 2.2]

kapitto ya na bukid \\
ka-pitto ya na bukid \\
ord- seven def.f lk mountain \\
‘the seventh mountain’ [PBWN-C-12 11.7]

isya nang panid na daon \\
isya nang panid na daon \\
one only sheet lk leaf \\
‘only one leaf’ [MBON-T-07 13.4]

isya nang litsi na ummay na may passi pa \\
isya nang litsi na ummay na may passi pa \\
one only 8oz.can lk unmilled.rice lk ext.in husk still \\
‘just one can of rice still with the husks’ [PBWN-C-12 8.2]

mga pangappat na adlaw \\
mga pang-appat na adlaw \\
pl ord -fourth lk day \\
‘approximately the fourth day’

panglimma bilog na baboy \\
pang-limma bilog na baboy \\
ord -five piece lk pig \\
‘the fifth pig’

NumP in predicate function: \\
Mga tallo nang en duminggo ame na klasi bag-o eman magbakasyon. \\
Mga tallo nang en duminggo ame na klasi bag-o eman mag-bakasyon. \\
pl three only cm week 1 p.excl.gen lk class
before again.as.before i.ir -vacation \\
Notice the absence of linker na before the Head of the RP, duminggo. Speakers report that such time-setting phrases are more natural without the linker. This example is a nominal predicate that sets the time frame for a main assertion.
` Only about three weeks was before our vacation again.’ [JBWL-J-03 3.4]

… riliyon kon i danen dili kon una gid na riliyon ta kalibutan. \\
… riliyon kon i danen dili kon una gid na riliyon ta kalibutan. \\
religion hsy def.n 3 p.gen neg.ir hsy
first int lk religion nabs world \\
‘…their religion is not, they say, the very first religion in the world.’ [JCOE-C-04 8.7]

Isya nang en na layag ame na palayag. \\
Isya nang en na layag ame na pa-layag. \\
one only cm lk sail 1 p.excl.gen lk t.r -sail \\
‘ Only one sail now was what we were sailing with.’ [VAWN-T-18 5.2]

As shown in the RP template given in chap:referringexpressions, sec:basicreferringphrases, an Є element (enclitic genitive pronoun and/or enclitic demonstrative determiner) may follow any MOD 1 element, though it is less common after NumPs bkm:Ref342658638- bkm:Ref343529548 than after other types of modifiers. Like other modifier phrases in MOD 1 position, no examples were found in texts of a Numeral Phrase with a numeral and an adverb in MOD 1 as well as an Є element. In the following examples the NumP is in brackets and the Є element is bolded.

darwa ko ya na mga utod \\
[ darwa ] ko ya na mga utod \\
two 1 s.gen def.f lk pl sibling \\
`my two siblings’ [PBWN-C-13 8.3]

katallo din ya na uyok \\
[ ka-tallo ] din ya na uyok \\
ord -three 3 s.gen def.f lk whistle \\
‘his/her third whistle’ [CBWN-C-20 6.5]

As with Modifier Phrases, the genitive enclitic of the referring phrase follows the first substantive word in a Numeral Phrase. This means that when a Numeral Phrase consists of more than one word, the genitive enclitic intrudes inside the phrase:

tallo ko nang na mga mangngod na mga dirset \\
[ tallo ko nang ] na mga mangngod na mga dirset \\
three 1 s.gen only lk pl younger.sibling lk pl small. pl \\
‘only my three younger siblings who are small’ [ETON-C-07 1.3]

tenga sako na beggas \\

summary:
Number Phrases (NumP) are a type of Modifier Phrase, but they have their own structure: an optional plural adverb mga, a numeral, optional adverbs, and optional classifier or measure words. They can function as modifiers or as non-verbal predicates, and unlike other Modifier Phrases, only mga may precede the numeral; ordinal forms, classifiers, and measure words also show some restrictions in distribution.

The passage also notes how NumPs interact with enclitic genitive pronouns and demonstratives: the genitive enclitic follows the first substantive word inside the phrase, while the demonstrative determiner follows the whole numeral phrase. Finally, it observes that the fraction tenga ‘half’ appears before the noun when it is the only numeral, but after the noun when another numeral is present.

adverbs|(

Adverbs are general-purpose modifiers. They are words or lexicalized multiword expressions that qualify properties, actions or states within a clause, or express epistemic, modal or evidential value for an entire speech act.

We recognize six main groups of adverbs in Kagayanen. It must be kept in mind, however, that, except for locative adverbs ( bkm:Ref52477189 ), these groups are not lexical subclasses of the lexical category “adverb”. The first four types are adverbial “positions” in a clause, that may be filled by any number of lexical adverbs. Which adverb goes into which position or positions is a matter of lexical semantics in combination with a specific communicative situation and the creativity of the speaker. Often the semantic or discourse-pragmatic contribution of a particular lexical adverb varies depending on which position it occurs in, as will be seen in the following discussion. The fifth type, prepositional adverbs, is defined by the presence of the non-absolutive case marker ta appearing before any lexical adverb. Finally, locational adverbs are a distinct lexical class that have much in common with demonstrative pronouns and adjectives ( chap:referringexpressions, sec:deicticpronouns ). In this section, we will describe the six groups, and will illustrate adverbs commonly occurring in each group.

Disjunct adverbs disjunct adverbs adverbs!disjunct ( bkm:Ref441599506 ) are those that occur preverbally outside the clause and normally express the speaker’s attitude or evaluation of the proposition expressed in the clause. Canonical adjunct adverbs canonical adjunct adverbs adverbs!canonical adjunct occur inside the clause. They may be in clause-initial position preceding the predicating word, second position following all other second-position clitics, or they may occur at any major constituent boundary, including clause-finally ( bkm:Ref52688127 ). Non-canonical adjunct adverbs non-canonical adjunct adverbs adverbs!non-canonical adjunct also occur inside a clause, but they normally occur in clause-initial position, though a few may occur immediately post-verbally. When occurring in clause-initial position, these adverbs impose formal restrictions on the form of the main verb ( bkm:Ref480610640 ). The fourth group, second-position adverbs second-position adverbs adverbs!second-position, always occur after the first major constituent of the clause, be it a verb, an adjunct adverb, or some other fronted clause constituent ( bkm:Ref479858962 ). The fifth group, prepositional adverbs prepositional adverbs adverbs!prepositional, always follow the non-absolutive case marker, ta ( bkm:Ref480640397 ), and distribute like canonical adjunct adverbs except they do not occur clause-initially. The disjunct adverb, second-position adverb, and prepositional adverb positions are filled by small and relatively well-defined sets of lexical items. Both types of adjunct adverbs constitute large, and semantically heterogeneous classes. However, as mentioned above, just about any lexical adverb may function in just about any position, depending on the communicative needs and creativity of the speaker. Finally, locative adverbs locative adverbs adverbs!locative are deictic forms referring to places, such as here and there in English ( bkm:Ref52477189 ). This is the most restricted and lexically well-defined set of adverbs.
summary: Kagayanen adverbs are general-purpose modifiers that can qualify properties, actions, states, or the speaker’s epistemic, modal, or evidential stance toward a speech act. The passage distinguishes six groups: four clause-based adverb positions (disjunct, canonical adjunct, non-canonical adjunct, and second-position), plus prepositional adverbs marked by ta and a separate lexical class of locative adverbs. It also notes that most of these are positional rather than lexical subclasses, and that the same lexical adverb can function differently depending on its position and context.

disjunct adverbs
Disjunct adverbs disjunct adverbs|( adverbs!disjunct|( are syntactically outside of, or “disjoined”, from the clause (see, e.g., on this term as applied to English). Evidence for this in Kagayanen is that disjunct adverbs occur before the predicating word, are potentially followed by a pause, and do not attract the second-position enclitic pronouns and adverbs. Furthermore, verbal predicates that follow a disjunct adverb are fully finite---they may appear in any inflectional form. Disjunct adverbs mostly express the speaker’s attitude or confidence in the truth of the whole utterance. The canonical lexical adverbs that often function in this position are sigurado ‘surely’, siguro ‘perhaps’, basi ‘maybe’, ti / ta ‘so’, inta ‘(I) wish/wishfully’ (glossed opt for`optative mood'), lugay/lugar/tapos ‘then’ and dason ‘next’. Sigurado ‘surely’, siguro ‘perhaps’, and tapos can also function as inflected complement-taking predicates (see chap:clausecombining, sec:nominalizationsasdirectcomplementclauses, and sec:subjunctivecomplementclauses ). But basi, ti / ta, inta, and lugay/lugar do not function in this way.
Inta can also occur as a second-position adverbs adverbs!second-position second-position adverb (see bkm:Ref441599628 below). Other adverbs may also appear in the disjunct position, but we consider the eight mentioned above as canonical disjunct adverbs canonical disjunct adverbs adverbs!canonical disjunct, because they are far more common and frequent than any of the others.

The following are some examples of disjunct adverbs in context:

Sigurado ‘surely’ \\
Sigurado, muli danen anduni tak linaw en. \\
Sigurado, m-uli danen anduni tak linaw en. \\
surely i.v.ir -go.home 3 p.abs now/today because calm cm \\
‘ Surely, they will come home now because (winds and/or waves are) calm.’

In example bkm:Ref441903321, if the adverb sigurado were a clause constituent, the absolutive enclitic danen would occur immediately following it. Furthermore, there is a noticeable pause after sigurado, as signaled by the comma. The following are a few more examples of disjunct adverbs from the corpus:

However, in other positions, it expresses the idea that a significant length of time has passed between clauses. In other environments it is a noun that means `place' (as in Spanish).
‘ Then, he said, “Friend, you are kind only if/when there is food.”' [RBWN-T-02 5.3]

summary:
Disjunct adverbs in Kagayanen are syntactically outside the clause: they occur before the predicate, may be followed by a pause, and do not attract second-position enclitic pronouns or adverbs. Predicates following them remain fully finite, and these adverbs mostly express the speaker’s attitude, certainty, or a narrative relation such as resumption, new development, or sequence.

The canonical disjunct adverbs listed are sigurado ‘surely,’ siguro ‘perhaps,’ basi ‘maybe,’ ti/ta ‘so,’ inta ‘wishfully,’ lugay/lugar ‘then/long time,’ and tapos ‘after/finish,’ with some of them also able to function as complement-taking predicates or in other positions. Examples show that these forms often mark the speaker’s confidence level or signal movement in the discourse, such as a new event or a return to the main story line.

canonical adjunct adverbs|( adverbs!canonical adjunct|(

Canonical adjunct adverbs usually precede the predicating word. They may occur in second position following all other second-position clitics, or they may occur at any major syntactic boundary later in the clause, including clause-final position. When they appear before the predicating word, they are not followed by a pause, and they do attract the enclitic pronouns and adverbs. For these reasons, it is clear that adjunct adverbs are syntactically adjoined to the clause. Canonical adjunct adverbs canonical adjunct adverbs tend to express temporal notions, and all have Austronesian etymologies. A selection of adverbs that tend to function as canonical adjunct adverbs is given in bkm:Ref479947563:

There are clearly different nuances associated with these adverbs depending on whether they appear preverbally, in second position, or in clause-final position. A thorough study of the use of adverbs in discourse will be necessary to tease apart all such nuances and variable usages.

The following are examples from the corpus of adjunct adverbs in context. Example bkm:Ref480191239 illustrates kani appearing clause-initially:

Nasugid na gakumpanyar an ta paglebbeng, kani kanen en man ilebbeng. \\

Note that in bkm:Ref480191239 the enclitics kanen, en and man follow kani. This shows that kani is adjoined to the clause (i.e. it is the first element inside the clause boundary). This is the property that distinguishes adjunct adverbs from disjunct adverbs, which do not attract any second-position elements.

In bkm:Ref481496721 kani appears following the main predicating word, which is in second position in this clause ( daw and the other conjunctions are outside the clause boundary, and therefore do not attract second position elements):

summary:
Canonical adjunct adverbs usually precede the predicating word, but they can also occur in second position after other clitics or at later major clause boundaries, including clause-final position. When preposed, they do not take a pause and they attract enclitic pronouns and adverbs, which shows that they are syntactically adjoined to the clause rather than disjuncts.

These adverbs often express temporal meanings and have Austronesian etymologies. The passage argues that their exact nuance varies by position in the clause, and it gives corpus examples especially with *kani* to illustrate clause-initial, second-position, fronted, and clause-final uses.

text:
Daw gamiten no sundang Tatay, magilek kanen ki kaon kani. \\
Daw gamit-en no sundang Tatay, ma-gilek kanen ki kaon kani. \\

‘If you use Father’s machete, he will be angry with you later.’

Any canonical adjunct adverb must occur in the clause it is modifying and not after dependent clauses or RPs containing relative clauses bkm:Ref329779114.

Apiten din nang en kani bata an na gatagad naan ta inyo. \\

stop.off -t.ir 3 s.erg just cm later child def.m lk i.r -wait spat.def nabs 2 p.gen \\
‘S/he will stop off later for the child who is waiting at your (place).’

In examples bkm:Ref329779247 and bkm:Ref329779234, the adverb anduni ‘now/today’ occurs clause-initially. However, the function of this adverb in each of the two examples is very different because they illustrate two distinct constructions. In bkm:Ref329779247 the adverb is in a clause with a verb that has an exclamatory suffix (see chap:stemformingprocesses sec:exclamatory ). The adverb is very closely tied to the clause itself and it modifies the whole clause. In contrast the adverb in bkm:Ref329779234 is set off from the clause by a slight pause. Also, it is functioning at a higher, discourse level, as a disjunct adverb (see bkm:Ref441599506 above). In this case, the speaker is providing a setting for this clause and those that follow.

Anduni din nang nļami na kapasar kanen ta board exam! \\
Anduni din nang na-aļam-i na ka-pasar kanen ta board exam! \\
now/today 3 s.erg just/only a.hap.r -know- xc.apl lk i.exm -pass 3 s.abs
nabs board exam \\
`Only now/today s/he knows that s/he passed the board exam!’

Anduni, nļaman din en na kapasar kanen ta board exam. \\

nabs board exam \\

In fact all canonical adjunct adverbs may function in the disjunct adverb position with varying semantic scope effects. Such constructions are rather unusual, however, and a thorough study of their usages will have to await future research.
adverbs!canonical adjunct|) canonical adjunct adverbs|)
summary:
The passage explains that canonical adjunct adverbs normally occur in the clause they modify and not after dependent clauses or relative clauses. It also shows that the adverb *anduni* ‘now/today’ can appear clause-initially in two different constructions: as a true clause modifier with exclamatory force, or as a higher-level discourse disjunct that sets the scene for the following clauses.

It further notes that all canonical adjunct adverbs can also appear in this disjunct position, though with different scope effects. Such uses are described as unusual and in need of further study.

text:
non-canonical adjunct adverbs|( adverbs!non-canonical adjunct|(

There exists a group of words in Kagayanen that exhibit many properties of adjunct adverbs, but differ in three important ways:

enumerate
They only appear in pre-predicate position.
When a non-canonical adjunct adverb is present, the form of the following verb is restricted in some way. Some require nominalized verbs, others bare-form or irrealis verbs. Others permit bare forms, but also allow other forms.
More than one-third of non-canonical adjunct adverbs are from Spanish (perhaps via other Philippine languages). This is in clear contrast with the class of canonical adjunct adverbs, none of which are from Spanish (see bkm:Ref479947563 ). This suggests that the non-canonical adverb position itself may be a recent innovation.
enumerate

Non-canonical adverbs tend to express manner, modal, aspectual or epistemic notions. One may argue that non-canonical adjunct adverbs are somewhere on a continuum between adverb and auxiliary for the following reasons:

enumerate
It is common in the world’s languages for auxiliaries to “govern”, or impose grammatical restrictions on the semantically main verb in the construction.
Aspectual, modal, and epistemic notions are the sort likely to be expressed by auxiliaries universally.
Preverbal position is the most likely location for auxiliaries in a VO language (; ).
enumerate

Though non-canonical adjunct adverbs exhibit these properties known to hold of auxiliaries in other languages, there are also arguments against this analysis. First, there is little to no evidence that these elements are basically verbs (though some may be used as verbs in other constructions, as can most lexical roots in Kagayanen). As adverbs, they do not take verbal inflection. Second, there is no well-established and uncontroversial auxiliary position in Kagayanen that may serve as the target for grammaticalization of these adverbs. Further research may reveal additional arguments for and against the auxiliary hypothesis for non-canonical adjunct adverbs.

Words that commonly occur in this category are listed in bkm:Ref441309176, sub-classified according to the restrictions they impose on the following verb. For the most part, these formal sub-classes seem to have semantic motivations. Our general impressions of the semantics of each class are given in parentheses, though these characterizations are not meant to be absolute.

The word bag-o is a multi-purpose word that can function as an adjective meaning ‘new’, and as a subordinate clause introducer that means ‘before doing X’, as in galangoy kay ta isya na oras bag-o megbeng naan ta ebes ‘We bathed for one hour before going down below.’ With this meaning it always precedes an irrealis verb. The ungrammatical examples illustrate syntactic positions that these adverbs may not appear in, thus demonstrating their grammatical distinctness from canonical adjunct adverbs.

The speaker left this ta out, which is common in conversation. However, it is clear that kayaran is non-absolutive because the verb is marked as intransitive, and the actor, kiten, is in the absolutive case.
`… each and every one of us must give goodness to our fellow humans.’ (The meaning of give goodness is to do good things.) [JCOB-L-02 10.4] \\
summary:
Kagayanen has a set of non-canonical adjunct adverbs that behave like adjunct adverbs in many respects but differ in that they occur only before the predicate and restrict the form of the following verb. Many of them express modal, aspectual, epistemic, manner, or related meanings, and over a third are borrowed from Spanish, unlike canonical adjunct adverbs, which are not Spanish-derived.

The passage suggests these forms may lie on a continuum between adverbs and auxiliaries because they can impose grammatical restrictions and tend to occur in preverbal position, but it also notes problems with analyzing them as auxiliaries. The adverbs are further divided into subtypes based on the verb forms they require or allow, such as irrealis, bare, nominalized, or inflected verbs.

summary:
The passage illustrates the placement of several kinds of adverbs in the language, showing that their position is constrained relative to the verb and other clause elements. It distinguishes classes such as punctuality adverbs, durational manner adverbs, velocity adverbs, and general adverbs, with examples showing which word orders are grammatical and which are not.

It also notes that some forms behave as compound adverbs, such as *sali ta* ‘persistently,’ which normally appears before an unaffixed verb stem. Overall, the examples show that adverb position is tightly regulated and differs by adverb class.

Most non-canonical adjunct adverbs in classes b through e occur in two constructions. One construction is illustrated in examples bkm:Ref480616181-- bkm:Ref113431626 the adverb occurs clause-initially and is followed by the main verb that is often unaffixed. Any second-position elements, such as enclitic pronouns and adverbs, are attracted to the position after the adverb. Referring Phrases remain in their post-verbal positions in their normal Absolutive/Ergative case roles, depending on the transitivity of the verb. In this construction, the main verb describes an event that is on the main storyline of a narrative.

In the second construction, the pre-verbal adverb is followed by a nominalized clause. The nominalized verb is usually unaffixed, but may take the pag - action nominalization prefix (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:pag and sec:actionnominalizations ). It is clear that the verb is nominalized because a genitive pronoun, enclitic or full RP refers to the Actor, whether the verb is transitive or not. Also, in examples such as bkm:Ref329771116 a genitive pronoun precedes the verb with the linker na intervening, which is a common structure for RPs with possessors. This construction is illustrated in exx. bkm:Ref113431770- bkm:Ref481732330 and bkm:Ref329771116 through bkm:Ref481737967:

summary: Most non-canonical adjunct adverbs in classes b through e appear in two main constructions: either clause-initial before an often unaffixed main verb, with second-position elements following the adverb, or before a nominalized clause whose verb may be unaffixed or marked with pag-. The second type is identified by genitive marking on the Actor and is used more often in background, descriptive material. A possible third construction places a linker between the preverbal adverb and the verb, apparently for slowed, emphatic speech, and this is attested with dapat, kinanglan, and sigi.

text:
The third group of adverbs consists of those that appear after the first major constituent in the clause. They are mostly monosyllabic, and all have Austronesian etymologies. Up to three of these adverbs may “stack” in second position, in which case there is a fairly strict order in which they may occur (see tab:orderofsecondpositionadverbs below). All second-position adverbs follow any second-position pronominal enclitics. Semantically, second-position adverbs tend to express aspectual and modal notions. Some of the English “translations” are impressionistic. Different speakers use them in different ways, and contextual factors often interact with their lexical meanings to produce nuances that are difficult to describe in a concise English gloss.

This looks like the yes/no question particle in Tagalog and many other Philippine languages. Kagayanen marks yes/no questions with intonation (see chap:pragmaticallymarkedstructures, sec:yesnoquestions ), and does not use a question particle. However, this form is used as a marker of rhetorical irony, as discussed further below and in chap:pragmaticallymarkedstructures, sec:rhetoricalconfirmation.
These second-position adverbs are homophonous with the demonstrative determiners that occur in Referring Phrases (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:definiteness ). As second-position adverbs, they express various strong emotions, such as ‘wow!’, ‘oh man!’, ‘what the heck?’ etc. See below for more explanation.

summary:
The third group of adverbs consists of monosyllabic, Austronesian-derived forms that occur in second position after the first major constituent of the clause. Up to three may stack in a fixed order, and they always follow any second-position pronominal enclitics; semantically, they mainly express aspectual and modal meanings, though their English glosses are often only approximate and vary by speaker and context.

The passage also notes that these forms are homophonous with demonstrative determiners, but in adverbial use they can convey strong emotions, irony, hearsay, emphasis, or related meanings. Examples show their use with meanings such as intensifier, “only,” “first,” “ahead of time,” and “momentarily.”

-4.1ptThe adverbs anay and tuo indicate politeness. As mentioned earlier, anay means `first' or `for a while'. This meaning is extended to politeness in requests and commands because it expresses the idea that the request is`only for a while'. However, in context anay expresses many of the nuances of ‘please’ in English. Tuo also indicates politeness, but is used more in statements. Tuo may be somewhat archaic.

Mamati kaw anay ki kanen na mambaļ ta Kagayanen. \\
Ma-mati kaw anay ki kanen na m-ambaļ ta Kagayanen. \\
a.hap.ir -hear 2 p.abs please obl.p 3s lk i.v.ir -say nabs Kagayanen \\
‘Listen please to her speaking Kagayanen.’ [JCOE-T-06 17.2]

Unso ki tuo mag-isturya. \\
Unso ki tuo mag-isturya. \\
d 4 loc.pr 1 p.incl.abs please i.ir -talk \\
‘Over there can we talk please.’ (This is grammatically a statement---not a question or imperative. The politeness adverb tuo makes it a request rather than the literal “Over there we will talk,” which would be considered rude.)

summary: The passage describes several adverbs and particles used for emphasis, repetition, evidentiality, and politeness. It notes that **kon** marks hearsay, while **man**, **isab**, **gyapon**, **inta**, **en**, and **eman** add meanings such as emphasis, “again,” “just the same,” unrealized intention, completion, and repetition. It also explains that **imo** is used for excitement, intensity, or as an attention-getter, **anay** and **tuo** express politeness, **taan** means “perhaps” based on evidence, and **gani** means “truly/in fact,” often correcting a mistaken understanding.

Example bkm:Ref113434139 is from a conversation in which the previous speaker asked where the people from Cagayan Sulu were headed, assuming they had a definite destination in mind. But the truth was they fled without really having any specific place they were trying to get to. So the speaker of this sentence is correcting a mistaken assumption.

Example bkm:Ref113434330 is from a story about a race between a sea turtle and a hermit crab. The hermit crab is giving instructions to his fellow hermit crabs to distribute themselves along the race course. His instructions are interrupted by a digression about how proud the sea turtle is about being so fast. After the digression when he returns to his instructions about what his fellow crabs will do, he uses the word ‘ gani ’ in order to get their attention focused back to the main point of what he is saying which is what they will do during the race to help him win.

In example bkm:Ref441345768, abi functions as ‘for instance’, but in examples bkm:Ref441345813- bkm:Ref441514069 it functions to soften a request for another person to do something. It can also indicate what other people might be thinking as in bkm:Ref441514118.

The second-position adverb ba is used as a marker of rhetorical irony (see chap:pragmaticallymarkedstructures, sec:rhetoricalconfirmation rhetoricalconfirmation. In Kagayanen, ba implies the speaker is trying to get the addressee to react somehow by gently teasing or joking. It can express irony and sarcasm---saying one thing but meaning the opposite. Sikad dayaw ba. ‘Wow how beautiful!’ (teasing). It can also imply real or false admiration.

Bellay ba bag-o utod buok din an. \\
Bellay ba bag-o utod buok din an. \\
difficult irn newly cut hair 3 s.gen def.m \\
‘Oh so difficult, his/her hair is newly cut.’ (The speaker is referring to the hearer’s hair. Many times in irony the third person is used in place of second person.)

The second-position adverbs i, an, and ya express intensity of attitude and emotion of the speaker, and give emphasis as exclamations bkm:Ref441519758- bkm:Ref441519766. They are homophonous with the demonstrative determiners, but distribute as second-position adverbs (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:definiteness on the demonstrative determiners). They seem to retain the deictic properties of the determiners, however, insofar as i ‘near’ is used to describe situations close to the speaker bkm:Ref441519758- bkm:Ref52607199, whereas an bkm:Ref52607927- bkm:Ref52607929 and ya describe situations more distant from the speaker bkm:Ref52607977- bkm:Ref52607980:

Sakit man i gettek ko i a! \\
Sakit man i gettek ko i a! \\
continual emph att stomach 1 s.gen def.n inj \\
‘Oh, my stomach is continual!’ [PBON-T-01 3.8]

Miling a i ta pari ko ya! \\
M-iling a i ta pari ko ya! \\
i.v.ir -go 1 s.abs att nabs friend 1 s.gen def.f \\
‘Man, I am going to my friend!’ [RBWN-T-02 5.1]

Example bkm:Ref52607199 expresses strong emotion because the speaker’s friend did not help him when he really needed help. So he is going to his friend to break the friendship. Just as the English interjections ‘man’ or ‘oh!’ are used to express strong emotion, i, an, and ya as second-position adverbs in Kagayanen express similar, but generic, strong emotions.

Daw sikad man an inog nangka i, lugay makamang iya an na bao. \\
Daw sikad man an inog nangka i, lugay ma-kamang iya an na bao. \\

a.hap.ir -remove 3 s.gen def.m lk odor \\

int att a.hap.ir- write \\
`Like for instance “winnowing basket”, previously that one, oh man, really could not be written!’ (The word kaļaw was hard to write since it has the Kagayanen interdental approximant /ð̞/ which has no symbol in the major Philippine languages or in English.) [MOOE-C-01 33.1]
summary: The passage describes several second-position particles in Kagayanen and their discourse functions. *Gani* is used to redirect attention back to the main point after an interruption, *abi* can mean “for instance” or soften requests and indicate others’ thoughts, and *ba* marks rhetorical irony, teasing, or sarcasm. It also notes that *i, an,* and *ya* express strong speaker emotion and emphasis, functioning like exclamations while retaining a deictic contrast between near and more distant situations.

The second-position adverb paran ‘perhaps’ occurs in questions to indicate that the speaker is not sure about what he is asking about and wants the addressee to give her opinion bkm:Ref441522128. It is also used in rhetorical questions when trying to get the addressee to think about something bkm:Ref441522154. When it occurs with the irrealis negator dili in the phrase dili paran, it is asking ‘won’t this perhaps be right?’ bkm:Ref441522272. This adverb is not used widely and may be borrowed from Tagalog or Hiligaynon.

[ROOB-T-01 9.8]

The second-position adverb pļa indicates something that is unexpected or surprising to the participants in the story or to the speaker herself bkm:Ref441348269.

`His younger sibling was wondering because his older sibling said, “That person surprisingly is a wild pig.”' (This is a story about a brother who leads his younger brother to believe that he killed a person on the mountain just to see how he reacts. When they go to the mountain the younger brother sees that the older brother killed a wild pig, not a person.) [RBWN-T-02 4.2]

More than one post-verbal adverb may co-occur. In general, the order is first the intensity adverbs nang ‘only/just’, gid ‘really/truly’, pa ‘even/still’; second the clausal adverbs, such as kon or man; and third the aspect adverbs pa ‘incompletive’ or en ‘completive’ bkm:Ref329776500- bkm:Ref329776503. tab:orderofsecondpositionadverbs displays the order of second-position adverbs. Their glosses are given in bkm:Ref113436041 above, but are repeated in tab:orderofsecondpositionadverbs for convenience. Text examples of multiple second-position adverbs follow.

Inta is a clause-level optative adverb, and as such may appear in the disjunct (clause-initial) position. It has roughly the same meaning in its clause-internal usage as a second-position adverb. We normally gloss it as opt for `optative mood'.

just emph cm Pedro def.n \\

summary: The passage describes several second-position adverbs in the language and their discourse functions. It notes that *paran* ‘perhaps’ is used in questions and rhetorical questions to show uncertainty or to prompt the addressee’s opinion, while *pļa* marks something unexpected or surprising to the speaker or participants. It also explains that multiple post-verbal adverbs can co-occur in a fairly fixed order, and that *inta* is an optative adverb that can occur clause-initially or internally with the meaning ‘optative mood.’

The two adverbs pirmi ‘always’ and dayon ‘immediately’ may occur either preverbally as the first constituent in the clause, or in second position. Their unmarked position is second, but they occur in first position at heightened, intense, or climactic sections of a narrative.

When dayon ‘immediately’ occurs clause-initially, it has the discourse function of marking new developments in the story, especially those that are exciting, lead to the climax, or are the climax itself (examples bkm:Ref425603569 - bkm:Ref425607917 ). In these cases, it is glossed as ‘right away’. When in second position, dayon expresses manner of action bkm:Ref425607938- bkm:Ref425607965, in which case it is glossed as ‘immediately’.

Pre-verbal dayon \\
Nakita din ake na mangngod na nalemmes. Dayon din kamangen daw duaļ din ta baybay daw ilingan nanay ko daw tatay na bata nyo nalemmes. \\

When clause-initial, especially *dayon*, they signal heightened or climactic narrative developments and are glossed as ‘right away’; in second position, *dayon* instead expresses the manner of action and is glossed as ‘immediately’.

The word teyep is a special word for ‘blow’ meaning what a shaman does with the ginger as part of diagnosing an illness. The usual word for ‘blow’ is eyep.

`When a pregnant woman has a continual pregnancy, her stomach hurts her. Call immediately the midwife and shaman in order to blow ginger on the woman with a continual pregnancy.’ [VAOE-J-05 1.4]

Similarly, when pirmi ‘always’ occurs initially in the clause it usually is at places that have heightened tension in the story ( bkm:Ref441602096 ). The unmarked position is second in the clause bkm:Ref441602112.

Pre-verbal pirmi \\

The adverb inta ‘ optative /wish/intention’ can occur pre-verbally outside the clause (as a disjunct adverb, as described in bkm:Ref441599506 ), or in second position in the clause, in which case it describes an unfulfilled intention sometimes idiomatically translated as ‘should have’. Examples bkm:Ref443721187 and bkm:Ref443721212 illustrate inta in second position:

Mļagan man kon inta mga ittaw tak nakita danen en na manigir danen napatay. \\
M-dļagan man kon inta mga ittaw tak na-kita danen en na manigir danen na-patay. \\
i.v.ir -run emph hsy opt pl person because a.hap.r -see 3 p.erg cm lk manager 3 p.gen a.hap.r -dead \\
`The people should have/intended to run (intention not fulfilled) because they saw that their manager died.’ [MBON-T-04 12.10]

Yi na manakem uļa inta kanen napatay tak kanen gatago naan ta kasilyas ya. \\

d 1 adj lk older neg.r opt 3 s.abs a.hap.r -dead because
3 s.abs i.r -hide spat.def nabs restroom def.f \\
`This older person should not have died (but he was shot when running back to the house to get some money) because he hid in the restroom.’ [BCWN-C-04 6.7]

Some adverbs such as sigurado ‘surely’, siguro ‘perhaps’, basi ‘maybe’, dapat ‘must/ought’ and kinangļan ‘necessary’ besides their modification of the verb or clause, can also function as uninflected complement-taking predicates. See the discussion of complement clause constructions in chap:clausecombining, sec:na-complementclauses.
summary:
The passage describes the meanings and clause positions of several adverbs. It notes that *teyep* is a special verb meaning a shaman’s act of blowing ginger in diagnosis, while the usual word for ‘blow’ is *eyep*; it also shows that *pirmi* ‘always’ can occur clause-initially, in second position, or clause-finally, with the initial and final positions drawing special attention, and that *inta* can occur preverbally or in second position, where it expresses an unfulfilled intention, often translated as ‘should have.’  

It also states that some adverbs such as *sigurado*, *siguro*, *basi*, *dapat*, and *kinangļan* can function not only as modifiers but also as uninflected predicates that take complements.

prepositional adverbs adverbs!prepositional

Clause-level modifiers following the non-absolutive prepositional marker ta are described in bkm:Ref439924168. In this section we briefly describe and exemplify adverbs that appear in this construction. Adverbs following ta never occur before the main verb of the sentence, as allowed for locative oblique elements. Also, unlike other oblique elements these structures never occur with a complex preposition---the marker is always and only ta. These prepositional adverbs prepositional adverbs tend to express the extent, degree or value of the action, as listed in bkm:Ref441309255.

summary: The passage describes a class of clause-level modifiers that follow the non-absolutive prepositional marker **ta**. These prepositional adverbs must appear after the main verb, never before it, and unlike other oblique elements they always use **ta** alone rather than a complex preposition. They typically express extent, degree, or value of the action, with examples such as **ta miad** ‘well’ and **ta usto** ‘completely/well/properly.’

text:
Locative adverbs locative adverbs adverbs!locative are words that refer specifically to locations, such as here and there in English. Some other grammars of Philippine languages call these kinds of words “deictics” or “deictic pronouns”. We prefer the term locative adverb because these words distribute in sentences like adverbs, and are not distinguished by case. However, there are certain similarities between locative adverbs and demonstrative pronouns. First, locative adverbs exhibit the same four spatial distinctions as demonstrative pronouns, and, except for D4, the forms are clearly parallel to the non-absolutive demonstrative pronouns (see chap:referringexpressions, tab:demonstrativepronounsadjectives ). Second, locative adverbs have general and precise forms. Finally, the precise forms occur in long and short variants. We have yet to discern any meaningful difference between the long and the short forms of precise locative adverbs.

The following are some examples of locative adverbs in context:

Lugay munta baybay, Manang, tak untan pugya baļay daen. \\
Lugay m-punta baybay, Manang, tak untan pugya baļay daen. \\
long.time i.v.ir -go beach older.sister because d3loc.pr long.ago
house 3 p.gen \\
‘Some time past (she) was going to the beach, Older Sister, because right there long ago was their house.’ [CBON-T-03]

Yaan ta Iloilo tama don buļag na gapangayo. \\
Yaan ta Iloilo tama don buļag na ga-pangayo. \\
spat.def nabs Iloilo many d3loc blind lk i.r -request \\
‘In Iloilo there are many blind there who ask for things.’ [TTOB-L-03 10.10]

The unmarked position for locative adverbs is post-verbal, either before or after the first noun phrase ( bkm:Ref52348615 - bkm:Ref113439285 ). Personal pronouns and shorter adverbs occur before the locative adverb. An oblique location phrase with the definite spatial marker naan and a noun can occur clause-finally further specifying the location ( bkm:Ref52439592 ).

Tukad danen dya. Padaļa din utod din dya. \\
Tukad danen dya. Pa-daļa din utod din dya. \\
go.uphill 3 p.abs d 4 loc t.r -carry 3 s.erg sibling 3 s.gen d 4 loc \\
‘They went up there. He took his sibling there.’ [RBON-T-01 6.8]

Padaļa nay dya a kabaong ta ake na bayaw naan ta simbaan ta mga sundaļo. \\
Pa-daļa nay dya a kabaong ta ake na bayaw naan ta simba-an ta mga sundaļo. \\
t.r -carry 1 p.excl.erg d 4 loc inj coffin nabs 1 s.gen lk sibling-in-law
spat.def nabs worship- nr nabs pl soldier \\
`We took the coffin of my brother-in-law there to the church of the soldiers.’ [VAWN-T-15 3.2]

Nabatyagan ko gid dya na uļa gid man en gasakit. \\
Na-batyag-an ko gid dya na uļa gid man en ga-sakit. \\
a.hap.r- feel- apl 1 s.erg int d 4 loc lk neg.r int also cm i.r -pain \\
‘I really felt there that there was no more pain.’ [JCWN-T-22 8.13]

Locative adverbs and the definite spatial oblique marker naan sometimes occur together, for example, naan dya. However, when a general locative adverb is in the pragmatically marked pre-verbal position, then naan must occur before it (exx. bkm:Ref52439592 - bkm:Ref52439595 ). When the spatial marker and the locative adverb are pre-verbal, any clitic pronouns and clitic adverbs must also occur in pre-verbal position ( bkm:Ref52439592 ).

Naan kay dya gakitaay kay, kami Maria daw Neneng naan Gaisano. \\
Naan kay dya ga-kita-ay kay, kami Maria daw Neneng naan Gaisano. \\
spat.def 1 p.lexcl.abs d4loc i.r -see- rec 1 p.excl.abs 1 p.excl.abs
Maria and Neneng spat.def Gaisano \\
‘(It was) there we met each other, I and Maria and Neneng, in Gaisano.’ [BMON-C-05 10.2]

The following orders are also possible:

a. Naan dya kami gakitaay. \\
b. Naan kay/kami dya gakitaay. \\

But the following are impossible:

a. * Naan dya kay gakitaay. \\
b. * Naan dya gakitaay kay. \\
c. * Naan dya gakitaay kami.

Example bkm:Ref52439955 illustrates a precise locative pronoun.

Nļaman no na kaselled aren ta ubra unti nang man ta ame i na munisipyo, naan ta upisina i ta trisurer. \\
Na-aļam-an no na ka-selled aren ta ubra unti nang man ta ame i na munisipyo, naan ta upisina i ta trisurer. \\
a.hap.r -know- apl 2serg lk i.exm -go.inside 1 s.abs+cm nabs work d1loc.pr only also nabs 1 p.incl.gen def.n lk town.hall spat.def nabs office def.n nabs treasurer \\
`You know that I got to go to work just right here in our town hall, in the office of the treasurer.’ [DBWL-T-20 8.5]

One difference between the distribution of general and precise locative adverbs is that with the precise forms the definite spatial oblique marker naan is optional when in preverbal position and usually does not occur. Compare the following to examples bkm:Ref52439592 and bkm:Ref52439595:

Unti ko man nakita isya na waig na pasaļok nang ta kabo daw mandok ka. \\
Unti ko man na-kita isya na waig na pa-saļok nang ta kabo daw m-sandok ka. \\
d1loc.pr 1 s.erg also a.hap.r -see one lk water lk t.r -dip only nabs dipper if/when i.v.ir -fetch.water 2 s.abs \\
`(It was) right here I even saw one (source of) water that is just dipped out with a dipper when you fetch water.' [DBWN-L-21 2.10]

Naan unti gabetang en simbaan ta ebes i. Piro naan unso datas na simbaan. \\
Naan unti ga-betang en simba-an ta ebes i. Piro naan unso datas na simba-an. \\
spat.def d 1 loc.pr i.r -placed cm worship- nr nabs down def.n but
spat.def d 4 loc.pr high lk worship- nr \\
`(It is) right here the church was placed below (the hill). But (it is) right there (on the hill) is the high church.’
adverbs|)
summary:
Locative adverbs are words that refer specifically to locations, and the author prefers this term over “deictics” because these forms behave like adverbs in sentences and are not case-marked. They share four spatial distinctions with demonstrative pronouns, along with general and precise forms, and the precise forms have both long and short variants, though no clear difference between those variants has yet been identified.

Their normal position is post-verbal, with personal pronouns and shorter adverbs appearing before them, and a spatial oblique phrase with naan can further specify location. When locative adverbs occur pre-verbally, especially the general forms, naan must precede them and any clitic pronouns or clitic adverbs must also appear in pre-verbal position; for precise locative adverbs, naan is usually optional in preverbal position.

Prepositional Phrases|(

In this section we will treat prepositional phrases (non-absolutive constituents expressing oblique elements) as optional clause-level modifiers, similar to adjunct adverbs adverbs!adjunct. Prepositional phrases consist minimally of an oblique case-marked RP, that is, an RP with one of the oblique case particles, ki for personal names or ta for all other head nouns (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:caseinreferringexpressions ). Spatial prepositional phrases spatial Prepositional Phrases Prepositional Phrases!spatial may also contain the spatial definite particle naan (variants yaan, nyaan, or an ), and an optional spatial preposition prepositions!spatial|( (PREP) before the RP. The template for prepositional phrases is given in bkm:Ref479920100, and some examples are presented in bkm:Ref117667676:

naan (PREP) RP obl

a. naan dani ta apoy ‘near to the fire’ [AGWN-L-01 3.18] \\
b. naan dani (ki) Pedro ‘near Pedro' (elicited) \\
c. naan tengnged ta bai na gamasakit ‘next to the woman who was sick’ [EDWN-T-03 2.17] \\
d. naan apaw ta iya na mata ‘above his/her eye’ [EDWN-T-03 2.21] \\
e. madyo ta duma na banwa ‘far from other towns/countries’ [JCWL-T-19 4.2] \\
f. tengnged ta baļay danen ‘next to their house’ [BMON-C-05 3.22] \\
g. naan ta Manila ‘in/at Manila’ [BMON-C-05 3.3] \\
h naan ta Cagayancillo ‘on Cagayancillo’ [VAWN-T-15 5.5] \\
I naan Cagayancillo ‘on Cagayancillo’ [LTOE-C-01 1.3] \\
j ta Cagayancillo ‘on Cagayancillo’ [JCWN-L-33 2.1]

Nearly all the spatial prepositions (listed in bkm:Ref329066261 ) transparently derive from relational nouns, that is, nouns that specify a relational term, such as top, bottom, side, inside, outside, and so on. These spatial prepositions indicate the location or direction of the following RP in relation to the proposition expressed in the clause. They also may indicate certain logical relations.

As prepositions, these forms usually follow the definite spatial marker naan.

Tapos, gapungko kay naan dani ta apoy agod may pagdangga. \\

then i.r -sit.down 1 p.excl.abs spat.def near nabs fire so.that
ext.in nr.act -hot \\
`Then we sat close to the fire so that there was (something) to warm (us) up.’ [AGWN-L-01 3.19]

Ta iya na pagpanaw nakaagi kanen ta mga tindaan naan kilid ta daļan. \\
Ta iya na pag-panaw naka-agi kanen ta mga tinda-an naan kilid ta daļan. \\
nabs 3 s.gen lk nr.act -go/walk i.hap.r -pass 3 s.abs nabs pl sell- nr
spat.def side nabs road \\
`During his walking, he happened to pass some stores on the side of the road.’ [VPWN-T-05 2.4]

Eviok isya man na lugar naan dapit ta Mamaan. \\
Eviok isya man na lugar naan dapit ta Mamaan. \\
Eviok one too lk place spat.def towards nabs Mamaan \\
‘Eviok (is) a place too that (is) towards Mamaan.’ [EFWN-T-11 9.6]

The definite demonstrative naan can also occur without a spatial preposition, in which case the meaning is general location---‘in’, ‘at’, or ‘on’. In such cases, the non-absolutive marker ta or ki often drops out, suggesting that naan is almost grammaticalized as a third oblique case marker oblique case markers (exx. bkm:Ref480787107 - bkm:Ref52441569 ). If a place is very familiar, then it seems more often the non-absolutive case marker drops out.

Gamasyar a naan ta baļay danen. \\
Ga-ng-pasyar a naan ta baļay danen. \\
i.r - pl -visit 1 s.abs spat.def nabs house 3 p.gen \\

‘The boat anchored at Anini-y.’ [VAWN-T-18 6.1]

Gapit kay pa naan Duļļo. \\
Ga-apit kay pa naan Duļļo. \\
i.r -stop.off 1 p.excl.abs inc spat.def Duļļo \\
‘We still stopped off at Dullo.’ [DBON-C-06 4.8] \\
( ta has dropped out of naan ta Duļļo ).

Piro uļa ka gambaļ naan yaken na nadayaran ka sa asta nang en gapudpod. \\

lk a.hap.r -good- apl
2 s.abs d 4 nabs until just cm i.r -crumble.apart \\

( ki dropped out of naan ki yaken ).

The following examples illustrate these prepositions in their usages as relational nouns nouns!relational.

Naan ta apaw tallo na kanyon gabatang ta atubangan ta Lipot. \\
Naan ta apaw tallo na kanyon ga-batang ta atubangan ta Lipot. \\

‘ On the top (of a hill) three canons were positioned in front of Lipot (community).’ [JCWN-T-24 5.3]

Lugay ambaļ gid mangngod ko mag-angad kay kon naan ta apaw tak naan dya galin kanta ya. \\

summary: Prepositional phrases in this language are optional clause-level modifiers that minimally consist of an oblique-case RP, with spatial PPs optionally including the definite spatial particle naan and a spatial preposition before the RP. Most spatial prepositions are historically derived from relational nouns and express location, direction, or other logical relations. The particle naan can also appear alone to mark general location, and in such cases the usual oblique marker ta or ki often drops, suggesting that naan is becoming a third oblique case marker.

summary:
The passage describes the behavior of spatial and directional prepositions in the language. Spatial prepositions occur with the definite spatial marker **naan** (and variants), while directional prepositions like **munta**, **asta**, and **keteb** generally do not; both types are followed by a non-absolutive case marker and a referring phrase, though the case marker may sometimes drop, especially before proper names.  

It also notes that relational nouns can be modified by genitive case RPs, and that two directional prepositional phrases can appear in one sentence if they express different directions.
