text:
Every language has constructions that express classification classification proper inclusion, equation equative clauses, attribution attributive clauses attribution, location location, existence existence and possession predicative!possession possession!predicative (defined below). In Kagayanen these functions are typically expressed in clauses that do not involve an Inflected verb. Instead, the predicate in such constructions is a Basic Referring Phrase, a Modifier Phrase, a Genitive Referring Phrase, a Locative adverbial element (either a location word or a prepositional phrase), an Existential element, or a Manner adverbial. Consistent with the general typology of the language, non-verbal predicates normally precede their single argument, and optional adverbial or oblique elements. Example 1 illustrates the basic template for most non-verbal clauses. Existential and possessive constructions are also non-verbal, however many of them are represented by a slightly different template described in sec:existentialconstructions and sec:predicativepossession:

Predicate + Argument (Oblique)

In Kagayanen there is no copula or “coupling element” that intervenes between the predicate and the argument. Time adverbs, such as gibii ‘yesterday’, kisyem ‘yesterday,’ gina ‘earlier’, kani ‘later’, or basi ‘maybe’, are used to express the time and/or modal status of the situation if necessary (see examples below). As is generally true for all clause types, the basic Predicate+Argument order may be inverted for a variety of discourse functions, including emphasis, new topic topicalization topic, or focal prominence focus (see chap:pragmaticallymarkedstructures, sec:constituentordervariation for a discussion of these concepts).

Constructions that belong to the family of non-verbal predicates are described below as predicate Nominals ( sec:predicatenominals ), predicate Modifiers ( sec:predicatemodifiers ), Locational Clauses ( sec:locationalclauses ), Existential Constructions ( sec:existentialconstructions ), Possessive Clauses ( sec:predicativepossession ), Manner Clauses ( sec:mannerclauses ), and Comparative and superlative constructions ( sec:comparativesuperlativeclauses ).
summary: Kagayanen uses non-verbal clauses to express classification, equation, attribution, location, existence, possession, and related meanings, usually without an inflected verb. In these constructions the predicate is typically a basic referring phrase, modifier phrase, genitive referring phrase, locative adverbial, existential element, or manner adverbial, and the normal order is Predicate + Argument, with no copula between them. This order can be inverted for discourse purposes such as emphasis, topicalization, or focus, and existential and possessive constructions sometimes use a slightly different template.

text:
predicate nominals|(
The basic functions of predicate nominals are to express classification classification|( proper inclusion and equation. Classification is the idea that a particular argument is properly included within a set of things, for example, “Pedro is a teacher,” or “the earth is a planet.” These propositions express the ideas that Pedro is a member of the class of teachers, and the earth is a member of the class of planets, respectively. Classification may be expressed with a “proper subset sign”: X$ $Y (X is included within Y) in mathematical notation. Equation equation is the idea that the argument is equated, or identified with some specific item, for example, “Pedro is the teacher” or “the earth is the planet I live on”. In these cases, the predicate and argument can be related with an “equals sign”: X=Y (X and Y are identical). The following are some basic examples in Kagayanen. In these examples, the argument is bracketed:

Classification (Our vehicle $ $ two masted ship) \\
Bļangay ame na sakayan. \\
Predicate.8cm Argument \\
Bļangay [ ame na sakay-an ]. \\
2.masted.boat 1 p.excl.gen lk ride -nr \\
‘Our vehicle is a two masted boat.’
classification|)

equation|(
Equation (Pedro = my cousin) \\
Katagsa ko Pedro an. \\
Predicate.8cm Argument \\
Katagsa ko [ Pedro an ]. \\
cousin 1 s.gen Pedro def.m \\
‘Pedro is my cousin.’

In the case of equative clauses, it is often difficult or impossible to determine which element is the argument and which is the predicate, since of course the equality relationship is symmetric. In general we can say that the argument is likely to be the discourse topic (see, e.g., ), and the predicate is a comment on that topic. For example, if the topic of conversation is “Pedro,” then a sentence like bkm:Ref442630001 would be a Predicate+Argument structure. On the other hand, if the topic of conversation were “my cousin”, the same sentence would have the pragmatically marked Argument+Predicate structure ‘As for my cousin (he) is Pedro.’ This would likely be used if the speaker wished to contrast the equality of Pedro and the cousin with a different idea held by the hearer, for example, ‘Pedro is my brother,’ or ‘Juan is my cousin.’ equation|)

Note that when the argument is an enclitic pronoun enclitic pronouns, it occurs after the first element in the predicate. This means that if the predicate includes more than one word, the pronominal argument “intrudes” pronoun intrusion within the predicate phrase, as in examples bkm:Ref442631395 and bkm:Ref428962681:... sawa a no. \\
Predicate Arg..1cm Predicate \\... sawa [ a ] no. \\
spouse 1 s.abs 2 s.gen \\
‘... I am your spouse.’ [PBON-T-01 2.23]

Example bkm:Ref428962681 contains a phrase, ta highschool, “of high school” modifying the RP that functions as the predicate. Thus “high school teachers” is the set, and the clause asserts that “s/he” is a member of that set:

Maistro ta highschool kanen an. \\
Predicate 2.7cmArgument \\
Maistro ta highschool [ kanen an 3pt]. \\
teacher nabs highschool 3 s.abs def.m \\
‘S/he is a high school teacher.’

While example bkm:Ref428962681 is grammatical, the more common order when the argument is instantiated as a pronoun is for the pronoun to occur after the first major constituent of the predicate, as in example bkm:Ref428962810. As mentioned in chap:modification, sec:attributivemps, such “ intrusive pronouns ” pronoun intrusion are formally second-position enclitics enclitics!second-position, and as such do not usually take demonstrative determiners:

Maistro kanen ta highschool. \\
Predicate Arg..5cm Predicate \\
Maistro [ kanen ] ta highschool. \\
teacher 3 s.abs nabs high.school \\
‘S/he is a highschool teacher.’

Any difference in meaning between bkm:Ref428962681 and bkm:Ref428962810 is subtle, and is not usually pertinent in conversation---the two may be considered paraphrases of one another, though bkm:Ref428962810 is clearly preferred.

A predicate nominal construction may contain a location phrase, as in the following.

Maistro kanen ta highschool naan ta Puerto. \\
Predicate Arg..5cmPredicate 1.2cm Location \\
Maistro [ kanen ] ta highschool naan ta Puerto. \\
teacher 3 s.abs nabs high.school spat.def nabs Puerto \\
‘S/he is a high school teacher in Puerto.’ or ‘S/he is a teacher in the high school in Puerto.’

As mentioned above, the order of predicate and argument may be inverted for various pragmatic purposes. This is consistent with the function of argument fronting throughout the language (see chap:pragmaticallymarkedstructures, sec:constituentordervariation ). Small capitalization is used in free English translations of the following examples to approximate the contrastive sense of these marked constructions:

Kanen an maistro ta highschool. \\.2cmArgument.8cm Predicate \\
[ Kanen an ] maistro ta highschool. \\
3 s.abs def.m teacher nabs high.school \\
‘ s/he is a highschool teacher.’

Yi en inyo na apo. \\.2cmArg..6cm Predicate \\
[ Yi ] en inyo na apo. \\
d1abs cm 2 p.gen lk descendant \\
‘ this now is your descendant.’ [JCWE-T-15 5.1]
summary: Predicate nominal clauses are used to express either classification, where an argument is included in a class (e.g. “Pedro is a teacher”), or equation, where an argument is identified with a specific item (e.g. “Pedro is my cousin”). In equative clauses, the argument is often the discourse topic and the predicate comments on it, so word order can vary pragmatically. The passage also shows that in Kagayanen, pronominal arguments may appear as enclitics after the first element of the predicate, and that predicate nominals can include modifiers or location phrases.

‘Lion fish is the type of fish that has many prickles on his/her body.’ [VAWE-T-10 9.1]

summary: When the predicate is especially “heavy,” as when it contains a long modifying clause, the normal order can be inverted so that the argument comes before the predicate. In such cases, this inversion is expected and does not necessarily mark contrastive focus.

text:
predicate modifiers|( predicative!modification

The basic function of predicate modifiers is to assert an attribute attributive predicates or property of some argument. The predicate of a predicate modifier clause is a Modifier Phrase (see chap:modification, sec:modifierphrases ), examples bkm:Ref329869322, bkm:Ref428973739, and bkm:Ref428973723, or a Referring Phrase (RP) with a modifier, as in bkm:Ref445618532. The argument can be any definite RP, as in bkm:Ref329869322 and bkm:Ref428973723, or a nominalized clause as in bkm:Ref428973739. In the examples in this section, the argument will be surrounded by square brackets:

Piro mga salingan nay sikad gid dessen iran na tagipusuon. \\
Piro mga salingan nay sikad gid dessen [ iran na tagipusuon ]. \\
but pl neighbor 1 p.excl.gen very int hard 3 p.gen lk heart \\
‘But as for our neighbors their hearts are very hard.’ [ETON-C-07 2.9]

Sikad gid tudo iran na pag-dļagan. \\
Sikad gid tudo [ iran na pag-dļagan ]. \\
very int intense 3 p.gen lk nr.act -run \\
‘Their running was really very intense.’

Miad mga Kagayanen an. \\
Miad [ mga Kagayanen an ]. \\
kind pl Kagayanen def.m \\
‘The Kagayanen (people) are kind.’

Kagayanen miad na mga ittaw. \\
[ Kagayanen ] miad na mga ittaw. \\
Kagayanen kind lk pl person \\
‘Kagayanens are kind people.’ [JCWN-T-24 4.2]

As with predicate nominals, if the argument is a pronoun, it usually intrudes pronoun intrusion after the first element of the predicate, creating a discontinuous predicate. Example bkm:Ref428973688 would be more likely in daily conversation than bkm:Ref442632390:

Sikad kanen kon miad na dļaga. \\
Sikad [ kanen ] kon miad na dļaga. \\
very 3 s.abs hsy kind lk single.woman \\
‘She is a very kind single woman, they say.’ [EMWL-T-04 5.1]

Sikad kon miad na dļaga kanen an. \\
Sikad kon miad na dļaga [ kanen an ]. \\
very hsy kind lk single.woman 3 s.abs def.m \\
‘She is a very kind single woman, they say.’

As with predicate nominals, the order of predicate and argument may be inverted to express contrastive focus (small capital letters in the free translations of the following examples indicate the sense of contrast):

Kanen an sikad kon miad na dļaga. \\
[ Kanen an ] sikad kon miad na dļaga. \\
3 s.abs def.m very hsy kind lk single.woman \\
‘ she is a very kind single woman they say.’

Example bkm:Ref442632516 is a particularly clear example of Argument+Predicate constructions used for contrastive focus. In this example the speaker uses two predicate modifier constructions in a row to contrast the characters of two brothers.

Mangngod ya a dili maisa. Maguļang ya a maisaen. \\
[ Mangngod ya ] a dili ma-isa. [ Maguļang ya ] a ma-isa-en. \\
younger.sibling def.f ctr neg.ir adj -selfish older.sibing def.f ctr adj -selfish- adj \\
The use of - én in the second part of this contrastive pair of clauses indicates that the older brother had an inherent tendency toward selfishness. In the first part, the same root is used without - én. This is because one can’t have an inherent tendency toward not being selfish---unselfishness is the norm. See chap:modification, sec:adjectiveformingprocesses for a discussion of ma-, versus ma-... -én as adjective-forming processes.
‘ the younger brother was not selfish. the older brother was selfish.’ [MBON-T-04 13.4-5]
predicate modifiers|)
summary:
Predicate modifiers are used to assert an attribute or property of an argument, and their predicate may be a modifier phrase or a referring phrase with a modifier. The argument can be a definite referring phrase or a nominalized clause, and when the argument is a pronoun, pronoun intrusion often creates a discontinuous predicate.  

Like predicate nominals, predicate modifier constructions can invert the order of predicate and argument to mark contrastive focus, and the passage gives examples showing this in everyday speech and in paired clauses contrasting two brothers’ characters.

text:
locational clauses|(

A locational clause functions to express the location of some argument. In Kagayanen, any prepositional phrase may appear in the predicate position, while the located argument normally follows. The preposition is naan (with the idiolectal variants yaan and nyaan ) when the predicate is a definite location, as in bkm:Ref107331810 through bkm:Ref444841001:

Naan ki kanen bata ko ya. \\
Naan ki kanen [ bata ko ya ]. \\
spat.def obl.p 3s child 1 s.gen def.f \\
‘My child is there with her/him.’ \\

Naan ta dagat tama mga sidda. \\
Naan ta dagat [ tama mga sidda ]. \\
spat.def nabs sea many pl fish \\
‘Many fish are in the sea.’ (Even though the quantifier tama appears here, it also has a plural marker possibly because there are many different kinds of fish.) [JCON-L-07 2.4]

Naan ta Guimaras kabatuan man pario ta ate na banwa. \\
Naan ta Guimaras [ ka-bato-an man pario ta ate na banwa ]. \\
spat.def nabs Guimaras nr -rock- nr also like nabs 1pl incl.gen lk town \\
‘Places with many rocks like in our town are in Guimaras.’ [SFOB-L-01 7.22]

Naan ta Manila sawa ko ya. \\
Naan ta Manila [ sawa ko ya ]. \\
spat.def nabs Manila spouse 1 s.gen def.f \\
‘My spouse is in Manila.’

When the argument is a pronoun, the enclitic form normally intrudes pronoun intrusion within the predicate, and the ta prenominal case marker prenominal case markers is optional, as in bkm:Ref429114698 through ex:yourplace.

Naan kanen (ta) Manila. \\
Naan [ kanen ] (ta) Manila. \\
spat.def 3 s.abs nabs Manila \\
‘S/he is in Manila.’

Examples ex:inpuerto and ex:yourplace are from the corpus. In both of these examples, the optional ta is retained.... yaan kay ta Puerto. \\... yaan [ kay ] ta Puerto. \\
spat.def 1 p.excl.abs nabs Puerto \\
‘... we were in Puerto.’ [ETON-C-07 1.2]

Salig danen kani Papa a daw naan ki pa ta inyo ya. \\
Salig danen kani Papa a daw naan [ ki ] pa ta inyo ya. \\
think.wrongly 3 p.erg later papa inj if/when spat.def 1 p.incl.abs inc nabs 2 p.gen def.f \\
‘Our papa and companions will think wrongly later that we are still at your (place).’ [CBWN-C-11 5.20]

As with other non-verbal predicates, the order of predicate and argument may be inverted for contrastive focus:

Kanen ya naan ta Manila. \\
[ Kanen ya ] naan ta Manila. \\
3 s.abs def.f spat.def nabs Manila. \\
‘ s/he is in Manila.’

Examples bkm:Ref442263283 through bkm:Ref444840137 illustrate locational clauses with locational demonstratives in the predicate:

Naan dya Pedro ya. \\
Naan dya [ Pedro ya ]. \\
spat.def d4loc Pedro def.f \\
‘Pedro is over there.’

Uļa pa tagaok manok ya gina nyaan kay di en. \\
Uļa pa tagaok manok ya gina nyaan [ kay ] di en. \\
neg.r inc crow chicken def.f earlier spat.def 1 p.excl.abs d 1 loc cm \\
‘The chicken had not yet crowed earlier and we were here.’ [BGON-L-01 3.17]... nyaan dya iran ya na lugar. \\... nyaan dya [ iran ya na lugar ]. \\
spat.def d 4 loc 3 p.abs def.f lk place \\
‘...their place was there.’ [TTOB-J-01 4.3]

Sir, melled ka. Nyaan ka ti selled i. \\
Sir, m-selled ka. Nyaan [ ka ] ti selled i. \\
Sir i.v.ir -inside 2 s.abs spat.def 2 s.abs d 1 loc.pr inside def.n \\
The form unti often reduces to ti, as in this example and the next.
‘Sir, come inside. You will be right here inside.’ [BGON-L-01 4.11-12]

In example bkm:Ref444840137, the argument (“I”) appears as an enclitic in second position, and then is recapitulated in its full form following the locational demonstrative:

Naan a ti yaken i. \\
Naan [ a ] ti [ yaken i ]. \\
spat.def 1 s.abs d 1 loc.pr 1 s.abs def.n \\
‘I am right here.’ [PBON-T-01 2.26]

This doubling of the argument pronoun is quite common in conversation. It adds an emotional nuance, such as excitement, wonder, happiness, and so on. It may also be a way of attracting the hearer’s attention.

Other prepositions may also occur in the predicate of a locational clause. However, we use the term “locational” in a general way to describe all clauses in which the predicate is a prepositional phrase or locational demonstrative, even if the semantic relation is not, strictly speaking, locational. For example, prepositional phrases with parti or tenged ‘about’ may occur in a non-verbal clause ( bkm:Ref246297918 and ex:fish ). In this case, the marked order Argument+Predicate Argument+Predicate constructions occurs quite frequently since this construction type functions to introduce important participants into the discourse, as in ex:fish and bkm:Ref429136467:

Parti ta sidda yi na libro. \\
Parti ta sidda [ yi na libro ]. \\
about nabs fish d1adj lk book \\
‘This book is about fish.’

Isturya na i tenged a ta mga sidda. \\
[ Isturya na i ] tenged a ta mga sidda. \\
story lk d1abs about inj nabs pl fish \\
‘This story is about fish.’ [JCON-L-07 2.3]

Yi na isturya parti ta darwa na magsawa. \\
[ Yi na isturya ] parti ta darwa na mag-sawa. \\
d1adj lk story about nabs two lk rel -spouse \\
‘This story is about a married couple.’ [PBON-T-01 2.1]
locational clauses|)
summary:
Locational clauses in Kagayanen have a prepositional phrase or locational demonstrative in predicate position, with the located argument normally following. The definite locative preposition is **naan** (with variants **yaan** and **nyaan**), but when the argument is a pronoun it often appears as an enclitic in the predicate, and an optional **ta** case marker may occur; the order can also be inverted for contrastive focus, and pronoun doubling is common in conversation for emphasis.  

The passage also notes that other prepositions may occur in this clause type, including **parti** and **tenged** ‘about,’ so “locational” is used broadly for clauses with a prepositional or locational-demonstrative predicate, even when the relation is not strictly spatial. These constructions often present important discourse participants.

text:
existential constructions|(

Existential constructions predicate the existence of something, usually in some specific location. In Kagayanen, existential constructions normally have three constituents: an existential particle existential particles or particles functioning as the predicate, a Referring Phrase functioning as the argument (the item that exists), and an optional location, as shown in ex:existentialtemplate.

Predicate exist Argument (Location)
summary: Existential constructions in Kagayanen express the existence of something, usually in a specific location. They normally consist of an existential particle functioning as the predicate, a referring phrase as the argument denoting the item that exists, and an optional location.

text:
existential constructions!basic|(

There are two existential particles in Kagayanen which collaborate to define three existential constructions. The two forms are may ‘indefinite existential particle’ indefinite existential particle existential particles!indefinite, and anen, the ‘given existential particle given existential particle existential particles!given ’. May without anen defines the indefinite new indefinite new existential construction existential constructions!indefinite new existential construction bkm:Ref329888024. This construction introduces a participant for the first time into the discourse, “out of the blue” so to speak. Anen without may defines the definite given existential construction definite given existential construction existential constructions!definite given bkm:Ref329888060- bkm:Ref442643960, which asserts the presence of a particular referent that the speaker assumes the hearer can identify, and is probably aware of at the moment of speaking. In addition, may and anen may co-occur to form what we identify as the indefinite given existential construction indefinite given existential construction existential constructions!indefinite given bkm:Ref329888090. This construction is used when the speaker presupposes that the hearer is thinking about, or is aware of some defined group of referents (e.g. ‘men’), but cannot identify the particular referent or subgroup of referents being singled out. In the following examples, the English free translations ‘some N’ or ‘some Ns’ are used to refer to the argument in an indefinite, given construction, though this is not a fully adequate translation. For instance, bkm:Ref329888090 below may be the answer to a question such as “Are there any men here?” The question refers to a set of possible referents, namely ‘men’, and the response implies that one or more of those are present, but the speaker does not think the hearer can identify which specific one or ones might be intended. Note that may and anen are dedicated existential particles. They are not locational demonstratives meaning ‘here’ or ‘there’.

indefinite new existential construction existential constructions!indefinite new
Indefinite, new: May mama di. \\
Predicate Argument (Location) \\
May mama di. \\
ext.in man d 1 loc \\
‘There is a man here.’

Definite, given: Anen a di. \\
Anen a di. \\
ext.g 1 s.abs d 1 loc \\
`I’m here.’

definite given existential construction existential constructions!definite given
Definite, given: Anen di yaken i. \\
Anen di yaken i. \\
ext.g d 1 loc 1 s.abs def.n \\
‘ I’m here.’ (Contrasitive)

Definite, given: Anen di mama an. \\
Anen di mama an. \\
ext.g d 1 loc man def.m \\
‘The man is here.’ (we’ve been expecting a particular man.)

indefinite given existential construction existential constructions!indefinite given
Indefinite, given: May anen mama di. \\
May anen mama di. \\
ext.in ext.g man d 1 loc \\
‘There’s some man/men here.’ (‘Men’ have been mentioned or otherwise presupposed, but the particular man or men have not been identified).

-5.8ptIn the indefinite constructions (i.e., those with may ), the argument is a “stripped” Referring Phrase stripped Referring Phrases in that it takes no demonstrative determiners, genitive pronouns, or demonstratives bkm:Ref329889347- bkm:Ref442938671. Also, it may not be replaced by a pronoun (see on the notion of “noun stripping” and its similarity to noun incorporation). However, it may take quantifiers, relative clauses, and other modifiers. This stripped argument is clearly not absolutive because it does not take determiners, and does not participate in syntactic processes, such as fronting and relativizability, that are allowed for absolutives. While the stripped argument is not absolutive, neither is it Oblique in that it does not take any of the Oblique prepositions (including the non-absolutive case marker ta ) and it may not be fronted, as can Obliques. Thus the indefinite existential constructions are among the very few constructions in Kagayanen that do not require an absolutive constituent. Another salient characteristic of the two indefinite existential constructions is that they serve as the bases for a type of predicative possession predicative!possession in which the possessed item is the stripped argument, and a possessor occurs as a distinct absolutive referring expression (see sec:predicativepossession below).

The following are examples of the indefinite, new existential construction:
indefinite new existential construction existential constructions!indefinite new

Argument with adjective: \\
May manakem na mama. (Or: May mama na manakem.) \\
May manakem na mama. \\
ext.in older lk man \\
‘There’s an older man.’

Argument with number: \\
May tallo na mama. (*May mama na tallo.) \\
May tallo na mama. \\
ext.in three lk man \\
‘There are three men.’ \\

May tallo buok na mama. Or: May mama na tallo buok. \\
May tallo buok na mama. \\
ext.in three cl lk man \\
‘There are three individual men.’

Argument with location phrase: \\
May manakem na mama naan ta gwa. \\
May manakem na mama naan ta gwa. \\
ext.in older lk man spat.def nabs outside \\
We find no definitive evidence for analyzing this location phrase as being a constituent of the argument (‘a man outside’), or of the larger construct (‘outside is a man.’). However, “bare” indefinite existentials (‘there are men’) are extremely rare, since a location is normally added to such utterances. For this reason, the general template for the existential construction includes the possibility of a construction-level location element, though sometimes evidence for this occurring at the construction or RP level is unclear.
‘There is an older man outside.’

Argument with nominalized (relative) clause: \\
May manakem na gatindeg naan ta gangaan. \\
May manakem na ga-tindeg naan ta gangaan. \\
ext.in older lk i.r -stand spat.def nabs doorway \\
‘There’s an older (one) standing in the doorway.’ [YBWN-T-01 2.15]

The next set of examples are of indefinite, given existential constructs: indefinite given existential construction existential constructions!indefinite given

Argument with adjective: \\
May anen manakem na mama. (Or: May anen mama na manakem.) \\
May anen manakem na mama. \\
ext.in ext.g older lk man \\
‘There’s some older man.’ (The conversation has evoked the notion of “men”, but the speaker assumes the hearer cannot identify
which particular man is meant).
summary:
Kagayanen has two existential particles, **may** and **anen**, which combine to form three existential constructions: **indefinite new** (may alone), **definite given** (anen alone), and **indefinite given** (may + anen). The first introduces a referent for the first time, the second asserts the presence of an identifiable referent already known to the hearer, and the third refers to an unspecified member of a previously evoked or presupposed set.

In the indefinite constructions, the argument is a **stripped referring phrase** that lacks determiners, pronouns, and demonstratives, and it does not behave like an absolutive or oblique constituent. These constructions can also serve as the basis for a type of predicative possession.

text:
Argument with number: \\
May anen tallo na mama. (*May anen mama na tallo.) \\
May anen tallo na mama. \\
ext.in ext.g three lk man \\
‘There are some three men.’

May anen tallo buok na mama. (?May anen mama na tallo buok.) \\
May anen tallo buok na mama. \\
ext.in ext.g three cl lk man \\
‘There are some three individual men.’

Argument with location phrase: \\
May anen manakem naan ta gwa. (*May anen naan ta gwa manakem.) \\
May anen manakem naan ta gwa. \\
ext.in ext.g older spat.def nabs outside \\
‘There’s some older man outside.’ \\

Argument with relative clause: \\
May anen gatindeg na manakem naan ta gangaan. \\
May anen ga-tindeg na manakem naan ta gangaan. \\
ext.in ext.g i.r -stand lk older spat.def nabs doorway \\
‘There’s some older one who is standing in the doorway.’

In the definite given existential construction, the argument may be an absolutive pronoun or Referring Phrase that includes the full range of possible determiners and modifiers ex:definitegivenexistentialwithadjective- bkm:Ref329939931. The following are examples of definite, given existential constructs: definite given existential construction existential constructions!definite given

Argument with adjective: \\
Anen manakem an na mama. (?Anen mama an na manakem.) \\
Anen manakem an na mama. \\
ext.g older def.m lk man \\
‘The older man is present.’ (Or: ‘There’s the older man.’)

Argument with number: \\
Anen tallo an na mama. (*Anen mama an na tallo.) \\
Anen tallo an na mama. \\
ext.g three def.m lk man \\
‘The three men are present.’ (Or: ‘There are the three men.’) \\
Also possible: \\
Anen tallo buok na mama. \\
Anen mama an na tallo buok.

Argument with location phrase: \\
Anen manakem an naan ta gwa. (*Anen naan ta gwa manakem an.) \\
Anen manakem an naan ta gwa. \\
ext.g older def.m spat.def nabs outside \\
‘The older one is present outside.’ \\

Argument with relative clause: \\
Anen gatindeg ya na manakem naan ta gangaan. (Or: Anen manakem ya na gatindeg naan ta gangaan.) \\
Anen ga-tindeg ya na manakem naan ta gangaan. \\
ext.g i.r -stand def.f lk older spat.def nabs outside \\
‘The older one is present who was standing in the doorway.’ \\

Example bkm:Ref329939931 employs the distal deictic determiner deictic determiners ya instead of the intermediate deictic determiner an in the argument RP. This can mean the older man is the one who previously was standing, or the one who previously was far away.
existential constructions!basic|)
summary: The passage shows that in the indefinite existential construction, the argument follows the existential marker and can be a noun phrase with adjectives, numerals, location phrases, or relative clauses, with some restrictions on word order. It then shows that in the definite given existential construction, the argument may be an absolutive pronoun or a referring phrase with the full range of determiners and modifiers, and the order can vary somewhat, including cases with the distal determiner **ya** instead of **an**.

text:
existential constructions!head omission|(

When the argument includes a relative clause relative clauses, the head of the clause can drop out, leaving just a clause or verb. This is a property of relative clauses in general (see chap:clausecombining, sec:relativeclauses ), and not specifically of the existential construction. However, since such omission of the head occurs often in existential contexts, we are including a selection of such examples here.

Example ex:indefinitenewconstruct illustrates an indefinite new existential construct, while ex:indefinitenewconstructwithheadomission illustrates the same construct with omission of the head in the argument Referring Phrase:

May manakem na gatindeg naan ta gangaan. (Or: May gatindeg na manakem naan ta gangaan.) \\
Pred 13ptArgument 58pt Location \\
May manakem na ga-tindeg naan ta gangaan. \\
ext.in older lk i.r -stand spat.def nabs doorway \\
‘There’s an older one standing in the doorway.’

May gatindeg naan ta gangaan. \\
Pred 13ptArgument Location \\
May ga-tindeg naan ta gangaan. \\
ext.in i.r -stand spat.def nabs doorway \\
‘There’s someone standing in the doorway.’

Example ex:indefiniteexistentialclausewithafullrpargument illustrates an indefinite existential clause indefinite existential constructions with a full RP argument:

May nakita na yupan maguļang ko an. \\
Pred 13ptArgument \\
May na-kita na yupan maguļang ko an. \\
ext.in a.hap.r -see lk bird older.sibling 1 s.gen def.m \\
`My older sibling saw a bird.’ (lit. `There was a bird that my older sibling saw')

The head noun may drop out of the RP leaving just the verb:

May nakita maguļang ko an. \\
Pred 13ptArgument \\
May na-kita maguļang ko an. \\
ext.in a.hap.r -see older.sibling 1 s.gen def.m \\
‘My older sibling saw something.’ (lit. ‘There was something my older sibling saw.’)

The following are a few additional examples of head omission in existential clauses:

May anen nabilin. \\
May anen na-bilin. \\
ext.in ext.g a.hap.r -leave \\
‘There is/was some left.’

May anen daļa maguļang ko an. \\
May anen daļa maguļang ko an. \\
ext.in ext.g take/carry older.brother 1 s.gen def.m \\
‘My older sibling has something brought (with him).’

Anen gatindeg ya gina naan ta gangaan. \\
Anen ga-tindeg ya gina naan ta gangaan. \\
ext.g i.r -stand def.f earlier spat.def nabs doorway \\
‘Here’s the one standing earlier in the doorway.’

Anen ki kanen pangita no ya. \\
Anen ki kanen pa-ng-kita no ya. \\
ext.g obl.p 3s t.r - pl -search 2 s.erg def.f \\
The root kita, is glossed `to see' when occuring in happenstantial mode. When occuring in dynamic mode, as in this example, it implies an active process rather than a non-volitional experience of perception. Combined with the pluractional stem-forming prefix, the image evoked is of someone actively ``seeing", that is, looking multiple times in multiple places. As such the English gloss ``search" is more accurate.
‘Something that you are/were searching for is with him/her.’

because ext.in i.r - nr -house \\

The passage emphasizes that this head omission is a general property of relative clauses, but it is especially common in existential contexts, and it illustrates this with several examples from both constructed sentences and corpus data.

subsection: Definite non-specific individuals of a group
text:
existential constructions!definite|(

When talking about definite but non-specific individuals of a group, as in ‘some of us’, ‘some of you’, or ‘some of them’, then may anen is followed by a plural pronoun in the oblique case.

May anen ki kyo na gasunod pa ta mikaw. \\ May anen ki kyo na ga-sunod pa ta mikaw. \\
ext.in ext.g obl.p 2p lk i.r -follow inc nabs food.sacrifice \\
‘There are some of you who still follow food sacrifice.’

Siguro may anen ki kyo dyan na gapati na a bayo nyo an iling tan unduni alin ta kaoy. \\ Siguro may anen ki kyo dyan na ga-pati na a bayo nyo an iling tan unduni alin ta kaoy. \\
perhaps ext.in ext.g obl.p 2p d 2 loc lk i.r -believe lk inj clothes 2 p.gen def.m
like d 3 nabs now/today from nabs tree/wood \\
‘Perhaps, there are some of you there (near addressees) who believe that your clothes like that now are from trees.’ [ROOB-T-01 7.7]

The examples show this construction expressing that some members of the addressed group still hold a belief or practice.

text:
possessive clauses|( predicative!possession|(

described clauses that assert the notion that “X possesses Y” as “predicative posssion” (e.g., I have a book ), as distinct from adnominal possession possession!adnominal (e.g., my book ). In Kagayanen, there are three construction types that express predicative possession, all of which lack an Inflected Verb (see chap:verbstructure ), and therefore belong to the family of non-verbal predicates. The first predicative possession construction is based on the predicate nominals predicate nominal template ( sec:predicativepossession-predicatenominal ), the second is based on the predicate locative template ( sec:predicativepossession-predicatelocative ), and the third is based on the existential existential constructions template ( sec:existentialpossession ).
summary: The passage distinguishes predicative possession, which expresses “X possesses Y” (as in *I have a book*), from adnominal possession, as in *my book*. In Kagayanen, predicative possession is expressed by three construction types, all of which lack an inflected verb and therefore count as non-verbal predicates: one based on predicate nominals, one on predicate locatives, and one on existential constructions.

subsection: Possessive clauses formed on a predicate nominal template
text:
possessive clauses!predicate nominal|(

Perhaps the most common means of expressing predicative possession in Kagayanen is the use of a free genitive pronoun ( bkm:Ref429136651 - bkm:Ref246298287 ) or genitive Referring Phrase bkm:Ref429136604 as the predicate (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:pronouns and sec:caseinreferringexpressions ). This construction normally expresses permanent possession, and is structurally identical to predicate nominals:

Ame yan na baļay. \\
Predicate.5cmArgument \\
Ame yan na baļay. \\
1 p.excl.gen d2abs lk house \\
‘That house is ours.’

Yan na baļay ame. \\
Argument 1cmPredicate \\
Yan na baļay ame. \\
d2abs lk house 1 p.excl. gen \\
‘ That house is ours.’

Iya (ta) maguļang ko yon na baļay. \\
Predicate 3.5cmArgument \\
Iya (ta) maguļang ko yon na baļay. \\
3 s.gen nabs older.sibling 1 s.gen d3abs lk house \\
‘That house is my older sibling’s.’ (lit. ‘His/hers (of) my older sibling is that house.’)

Yi na lugar ni a, iya ta mga patay. \\
Argument 2.9cmPredicate \\
Yi na lugar ni a, iya ta mga patay. \\
d1abs lk place d1pr inj 3 s.gen nabs pl dead \\
‘ This very place is the dead one’s (place).’ [PBON-T-01 2.15]

This type of construction is not considered to be predicative possession by, because it is simply one usage of the predicate nominal template. In other words, there is no evidence that it is a dedicated possessive construction. However, it is very common in Kagayanen as a means of expressing permanent possession, and so warrents mention in this section of the grammar.
possessive clauses!predicate nominal|)
summary:
In Kagayanen, predicative possession is commonly expressed by placing a free genitive pronoun or genitive referring phrase in predicate position, and this construction is structurally identical to ordinary predicate nominals. It typically conveys permanent possession, as in examples meaning “That house is ours” or “That house is my older sibling’s.”  

The text argues that this is not a dedicated possessive construction, but rather one use of the general predicate nominal template, with no evidence for a special possessive clause type.

subsection: Possessive clauses formed on a predicate locative template
text:
possessive clauses!locative|(

The locational non-verbal construction serves as the basis for the second type of predicative possession. This is an instance of the “locational possessive” locational possessive constructions type, which is the most common type exhibited in the languages in Stassen’s sample. In Kagayanen, the locational possessive construction normally expresses temporary possession. The predicate of this construction consists of a locative phrase initiated by the spatial demonstrative naan, with idiolectical variants yaan and nyaan ( bkm:Ref251934246 - ex:elementaryschool ). Naan is the most common variant of the spatial demonstrative, followed by yaan, and then nyaan. There are no examples of nyaan in locational possessive constructions in the corpus. All variants are equivalent in meaning and can be substituted for one another in the following examples. A thorough study is needed to determine any sociolinguistic or topolectical patterns to their usages.

Naan ki kanen kalaw no an. \\
Predicate 2.2cmArgument \\
Naan ki kanen kalaw no an. \\
spat.def obl.p 3s winnow.basket 2 s.gen def.m \\
‘S/he has your winnowing basket.’ (lit. ‘Your winnowing basket is with/on/at him/her.’)

Kaļaw no an naan ki kanen. \\
Argument 3cmPredicate \\
Kaļaw no an naan ki kanen. \\
winnow.basket 2 s.gen def.m spat.def obl.p 3s \\
‘S/he has your winnowing basket.’

Daw tenged ta libro na ambaļ naan ki danen Maria uļa pa danen gapadaļa… \\ Daw tenged ta libro na ambaļ naan ki danen Maria uļa pa danen ga-pa-daļa… \\
and about nabs book lk say spat.def obl.p 3p Maria neg.r inc 3 p.abs
i.r - caus -carry \\
‘And about the book that is said to be with Maria and companions, they have not yet sent (it)….’ [BCWL-C-02 5.1]

Tanan-tanan na mga tudlo yaan ki danen. \\ tanan -tanan na mga tudlo yaan ki
danen. \\
red all lk pl teaching spat.def obl.p 3p \\
`Absolutely all the teaching they have.' (This is from a speech at an elementary school graduation.) [SFOB-L-01 8.3]

Occasionally, naan/yaan/nyaan may be replaced by the given existential particle existential particles!given anen ( ex:winnowingbasket, ex:onethousandpesos ).

Anen ki kanen kaļaw no an. \\
Predicate 1.7cmArgument \\
Anen ki kanen kaļaw no an. \\
ext.g obl.p 3s winnowing.basket 2 s.gen def.m \\
‘S/he has your winnowing basket.’ (lit. ‘Your winnowing basket exists with/on/at him/her.’)

Daw gusto nyo, anen man ki yaken risibo i ta isya libo. \\ Daw gusto nyo, anen man ki yaken risibo i ta isya libo. \\
if/when want 2 p.erg ext.g also obl.p 1s receipt def.n nabs one thousand \\
‘If you want (to get it), there is with me a receipt (I have a receipt) for one thousand (pesos).’ [PBWL-T-06 7.3].

This variant of the locational possessive construction is a “bridge” to the existential possessive constructions described in sec:existentialpossession. However the two constructions differ in their treatment of the possessor and argument. In all locational possessive constructions, including those with anen, the possessor is treated grammatically as a Location, and the possessed item (the argument) is in the absolutive role. Whereas in the existential possessive construction described below, the possessor is presented in the absolutive role and the possessed item is a “stripped” Referring Phrase stripped Referring Phrases (see sec:existentialpossession below).
possessive clauses!locative|)
summary: Kagayanen uses a locational non-verbal construction to express a common type of predicative possession, typically temporary possession, with a locative phrase headed by the spatial demonstrative **naan** (and variants **yaan** and **nyaan**). In this construction, the possessor is grammatically treated as a Location and the possessed item as an absolutive argument, though the existential particle **anen** can sometimes replace the demonstrative phrase. The text notes that this **locational possessive** pattern serves as a bridge to existential possessive constructions, which differ in how possessor and possessed item are grammatically encoded.

text:
possessive clauses!existential|(

A third way of predicating possession in Kagayanen is to use an Existential construction (see sec:existentialconstructions above). In this usage, the possessor is expressed in the absolutive case and the possessed item is a “stripped” Referring Phrase stripped Referring Phrases, that is, a Referring Phrase lacking determiners, case marking and some modifiers as discussed in sec:existentialconstructions. All three subtypes of existential construction mentioned in sec:existentialconstructions may be employed in such possessive constructions, though the definite given existential construction overlaps with the locative template, as discussed in section sec:predicativepossession-predicatelocative above.

Examples ex:manhashouse and ex:manhashouseonbeach illustrate the indefinite new existential construction expressing possession.

May baļay mama an. \\ May baļay mama an. \\
ext.in house man def.m \\
‘The man has a house.’

May baļay mama an naan ta baybay. \\ May baļay mama an naan ta baybay. \\
ext.in house man def.m spat.def nabs beach \\
‘The man has a house on the beach.’

Examples ex:manhassomehouse and ex:manhassomehouseonbeach illustrate the indefinite given existential construction.

May anen baļay mama an. \\ May anen baļay mama an. \\
ext.in ext.g house man def.m \\
‘The man has some house.’

May anen baļay mama an naan ta baybay. \\
May anen baļay mama an naan ta baybay. \\
ext.in ext.g house man def.m spat.def nabs beach \\
‘The man has some house on the beach.’

-0.6ptDefinite, given Existential predicates express temporary possession. These constructs are related to the “locational possessive” locational possessive constructions type identified by, and discussed in sec:predicativepossession-predicatelocative above:

Anen pala no ya ki manong ko. \\ Anen pala no ya ki manong ko. \\
ext.g shovel 2 s.gen def.f obl.p older.brother 1 s.gen \\
‘ Your shovel is with my older brother.’

In this construction the possessor appears as an oblique argument, rather than as an absolutive RP. This kind of possessive clause is identical to the given existential anen with a location phrase in ex:givendefiniteexistentialwithlocation. It also shares properties with the Locational construction with the spatial demonstrative naan/yaan/nyaan, except that the “location” is animate, usually human.
summary:
Kagayanen can express possession through an existential construction, where the possessor is in the absolutive case and the possessed noun is a stripped referring phrase without determiners or case marking. All three existential subtypes can be used this way: the indefinite new and given existentials express ordinary possession, while the definite given existential can express temporary possession.

The definite given existential possessive is related to locational possessive constructions and uses an oblique possessor instead of an absolutive one. It is structurally identical to a given existential with a location phrase, except that the “location” is typically an animate, usually human, argument.

subsubsection: Constituent orders in existential possessive clauses
text:
constituent orders in existential possessive clauses|( possessive clauses!constituent orders

For possessive existential clauses, the possessor may be fronted before the predicate, but the argument (the possessed item) may not be fronted. This construction resembles the “topic possessive type” topic possessive constructions identified by:

Kami i may (anen) baļay naan ta Cawili. \\ Kami i may (anen) baļay naan ta Cawili. \\
1 p.excl.abs def.n ext.in ext.g house spat.def nabs Cawili \\
‘ as for us, (we) have a/some house on Cawili (island).’

The location may also be fronted:

Naan ta Cawili may (anen) baļay kami i. \\
Naan ta Cawili may (anen) baļay kami i. \\
spat.def nabs Cawili ext.in ext.g house 1 p.excl.abs def.n \\
‘ on cawili (island) we have a/some house.’

Naan ta Cawili may (anen) kay baļay. \\
Naan ta Cawili may (anen) kay baļay. \\
spat.def nabs Cawili ext.in ext.g 1 p.excl.abs house \\
‘ on cawili (island) we have a/some house.’

The ungrammatical examples in bkm:Ref143335735 show that the possessed item may not be fronted. This is consistent with the analysis of the possessed item as a stripped nominal stripped Referring Phrases that has been incorporated into the predicate:

* Baļay naan ta Cawili may (anen) kay/kami i. \\

* Baļay may (anen) naan ta Cawili kami i. \\

* Baļay may (anen) kay naan ta Cawili.

When the possessor RP of an indefinite new existential clause is a pronoun, it can be either the enclitic enclitic pronouns ex:wehavechickens-a or the free free pronouns absolutive ex:wehavechickens-b.

May manok kay. \\
May manok kay. \\
ext.in chicken 1 p.excl.abs \\
‘We have chicken(s).’

May manok kami i. \\
May manok kami i. \\
ext.in chicken 1 p.excl.abs def.n \\
‘WE have chicken(s).’ (Contrastive)

If the RP in the predicate is longer than one word, then the enclitic pronoun intrudes pronoun intrusion inside the predicate ex:wehavefatchickens-a. The free pronoun does not intrude ex:wehavefatchickens-b:

May manok kay na tambek. (Or: May tambek kay na manok.) \\
May manok kay na tambek. \\
ext.in chicken 1 p.excl.abs lk fat \\
‘We have fat chicken(s).’ \\
* May manok na tambek kay.

May manok na tambek kami i. (Or: May tambek na manok kami i.) \\
May manok na tambek kami i. \\
ext.in chicken lk fat 1 p.excl.abs def.n \\
‘WE have fat chicken(s).’ \\
* May manok kami na tambek.

With indefinite given existential possessive clauses, the enclitic or free pronoun that refers to the possessor can occur after the two existential words may anen ex:wehavesomefatchickens. Speakers may make the possessor more prominent by placing the free pronoun, but not the enclitic, clause finally ex:wehavesomefatchickens.

May anen kay manok na tambek. (Or: May anen kay tambek na manok.) \\ May anen kay manok na tambek. \\
ext.in ext.g chicken lk fat \\
‘We have a/some fat chicken(s).’

May anen manok na tambek kami i. (Or: May anen tambek na manok kami i.) \\ May anen manok na tambek kami i. \\
ext.in ext.g chicken lk fat 1 p.excl.abs def.n \\
` we have a/some fat chicken(s).' \\
* May anen manok na tambek kay. \\

With the definite given possessive existential clause, the possessor, whether pronoun or RP, can occur after the existential word ex:shovel-1- ex:shovel-2, but not clause initially.

Anen ki manong ko pala no ya. \\ Anen ki manong ko pala no ya. \\
ext.g obl.p older.brother 1 s.gen shovel 2 s.gen def.f \\
‘Your shovel is with my older brother.’ \\
* Ki manong ko anen pala no an. \\

Anen ki kami pala no ya. \\ Anen ki kami pala no ya. \\
ext.g obl.p 1 p.exc shovel 2 s.gen def.f \\
‘Your shovel is with us.’ \\
* Ki kami anen pala no an.

However, the argument may be fronted as in ex:shovel-3.

Pala no ya anen ki manong ko. \\
Pala no ya anen ki manong ko. \\
shovel 2 s.gen def.f ext.g obl.p older.brother 1 s.gen \\
` your shovel is with my older brother.'
constituent orders in existential possessive clauses|)
summary: In possessive existential clauses, the possessor or location may be fronted, but the possessed item/argument may not be fronted; this supports an analysis in which the possessed noun is incorporated into the predicate. The passage also shows that pronominal possessors can appear as enclitic or free pronouns, but the free pronoun can be placed more prominently, especially clause-finally in longer predicates.

manner clauses|(

Manner clauses have the same Predicate+Argument structure common to other non-verbal predications, except that the argument is a clause nominalized with the action nominalizer pag-, or a bare form ( bkm:Ref246298440 - bkm:Ref429143130 ). The predicate is an adverb that modifies the nominalized clause. For some adverbs, such as dasig ‘quickly’ and tudo `intense/all out effort', it is possible to invert the order of predicate and argument ( bkm:Ref329886574 - bkm:Ref429143130 ).

* Iya na (pag)-agal sikad.

Sikad also functions as a canonical clause level adverb, in which case it expresses the idea of `habitually', and is followed by a clause with an Inflected Verb in irrealis modality, rather than a nominalization:

Sikad kanen manaw. \\ Sikad kanen m-panaw. \\
very 3 s.abs i.v.ir -go/walk \\
‘S/he habitually goes/walks.’ \\

Some adverbs, including sigi ‘continually’, diritso `straight away', inay-inay `slowly' and sali(ta) `persistently', can only occur before the argument. Following these ``durational manner adverbs" (see chap:modification, sec:non-canonicaladjunctadverbs ), the verb root in the argument must be in the bare form ( bkm:Ref329934414 - ex:straightaway ):

Sigi panaw din an. \\ Sigi panaw din an. \\
continually go/walk 3 s.gen def.m \\
`S/he keeps going.’ (‘His/her going is continuous.’)

Sigi iya na panaw. (... *manaw,...*pagpanaw, etc.) \\ Sigi iya na panaw. \\
continually 3 s.gen lk go/walk \\
‘S/he keeps going.’ (‘His/her going is continuous.’)

Diritso kanen panaw. (... *manaw,...*pagpanaw, etc.) \\ Diritso kanen panaw. \\
straightaway 3 s.abs go/walk \\
‘S/he straightaway goes.' (`Her/his going is straightaway.')
manner clauses|)
summary:
Manner clauses have the same predicate-plus-argument structure as other non-verbal predications, with an adverb as predicate and a nominalized clause, or sometimes a bare verb form, as the argument. Some adverbs such as *dasig* ‘quickly’ and *tudo* can appear before or after the nominalized clause, while *sikad* ‘very’ may occur alone in predicate position to express intensity but requires an adjective when postposed; as a clause adverb, it instead means ‘habitually’ and takes an irrealis inflected verb.

Other durational manner adverbs, including *sigi* ‘continually’, *diritso* ‘straight away’, *inay-inay* ‘slowly’, and *sali(ta)* ‘persistently’, occur only before the argument, and the verb root in the argument must be in bare form.

Comparative and superlative constructions are built on the non-verbal predicate template. They consist of a non-verbal predicate plus its argument followed by a standard usually expressed in an oblique case. A marker of comparison, kaysa or kis-a, ‘than’, may precede the standard, or the Marker may be a stem-forming morphological process that derives a comparative or superlative adjective. The basic comparative/superlative construction can be diagrammed as follows:

Predicate Argument (Marker) Standard

The predicate in this construction is a predicate modifier (as described in sec:predicatemodifiers ), either a plain, comparative or superlative adjective. It may also be a nominalized clause. In this section we describe comparative and superlative constructions based on predicate modifiers first. Further below we discuss comparative and superlative constructions based on nominalized clauses. Example bkm:Ref107820669 is a simple comparative construct based on the predicate modifier layog ‘be tall’:

Layog kanen kaysa ki yaken. \\
Layog kanen kis-a ki yaken. \\
Layog kanen ki yaken. \\
Pred..2cmArg..4cmMkr. 1.3cm Standard \\
Layog kanen (kaysa/kis-a) ki yaken. \\
tall 3 s.abs than obl.p 1s \\
‘S/he is taller than me.’

Consistent with the pattern for non-verbal constructions in general, the predicate modifier may appear in any of the orders described above in sec:introduction-5, including Argument+Predicate and pronoun intrusion. The following are examples of various orders of elements in comparative constructions from the corpus:

Iya na labbot bakod-bakod pa ta iya na lawa… \\
Argument 1.2cmpredicate 1.6cmStandard \\
Iya na labbot bakod -bakod pa ta iya na lawa… \\
3 s.gen lk bottom red big emph nabs 3 s.gen lk body \\
‘Its bottom is somewhat bigger than its body….’ (This is a description of a coconut crab. Lit: ‘Its bottom is a little bit big to its body.’) [DBWE-T-27 2.3]

Ittaw na gaistar ta baļay ko i mas pa bakod ki yaken. \\
Argument 5.3cmpredicate \\
Ittaw na ga-istar ta baļay ko i mas pa bakod \\
person lk i.r -live nabs house 1 s.gen def.n more emph big \\
Standard \\
ki yaken. \\
obl.p 1s \\
‘The person who lives in my house is bigger than me.’ [CBWN-C-107.14]

In bkm:Ref107822397 the oblique case Standard intrudes between the predicate and the argument:

Datas pa ki kanen ittaw ya na bakod. \\
Predicate.5cmStandard.55cmArgument \\
Datas pa ki kanen ittaw ya na bakod. \\
high emph obl.p 3s person def.f lk big \\
‘The person who was big was taller than him.’ (lit. ‘The big person was tall to him’).

Consistent with the pattern for modifiers in general, when the modifier is completely or partially reduplicated reduplication, the extent of the quality expressed is attenuated, for example, ‘somewhat/a little bit tall’.

Layog-layog kanen ki yaken. \\ Layog -layog kanen (kaysa/kis-a) ki yaken. \\
red tall 3 s.abs than obl.p 1s \\
‘S/he is somewhat taller than me.’ \\

Again, consistent with the pattern for modifiers in general, downtoning downtoning or intensifying adverbial elements may also modify the extent of the comparison ( bkm:Ref107407647 - bkm:Ref107821212 ):

Layog kanen sise ki yaken. \\ Layog kanen sise (kaysa/kis-a) ki yaken. \\
tall 3 s.abs small than obl.p 1s \\
‘S/he is a little taller than me.’

Layog-layog kanen sise ki yaken. \\ Layog -layog kanen sise (kaysa/kis-a) ki yaken. \\
red tall 3 s.abs small than obl.p 1s \\
‘S/he is a very little bit taller than me.’

Sikad pa gid layog kanen ki yaken \\ Sikad (pa) (gid) layog kanen (kaysa/kis-a) ki yaken \\
very emph int tall 3 s.abs than obl.p 1s \\
‘S/he is (really) much taller than me.'

Pandan i a lipo kaysa ta buli. \\
Argument 1.3cmPred. Mkr..3cmStandard \\
Pandan i a lipo kaysa ta buli. \\
pandan def.n ctr short than nabs buri \\
‘Pandan is shorter than buri.' Pandan and buri are types of palms. [EFWE-T-04 19.1]

The second comparative construction includes the word mas ‘more’ (from Spanish) before the predicate. The optional intensifier gid and emphasis particle pa can also occur after mas. The comparee is absolutive and the standard is normally in the oblique case. The markers of comparison marker of comparison kaysa or kis-a ‘than’ may occur before the oblique.

Mas pa gid layog kanen ki yaken. \\
Predicate 2.2cmArg..3cmMkr. 1.2cm Standard \\
Mas (pa) (gid) layog kanen (kaysa/kis-a) ki yaken. \\
more emph int tall 3 s.abs than obl.p 1s \\
‘S/he is (really) (much) taller than me’

Because of semantic incompatibility, the intensifying adverbials mas and sikad cannot occur with a reduplicated adjective.

* Mas laglayog kanen (kaysa/kis-a) ki yaken. \\
* Sikad laglayog kanen (kaysa/kis-a) ki yaken.

The word mas ‘more’ can also be used with an adjective to function as a complement taking predicate.

Piro mas dayad daw legeman buli para dayad lagen. \\
Piro mas dayad daw -legem-an buli para dayad luag-en. \\
but more good if/when t.ir -dye- apl buri purp good look- t.ir \\
‘But (it is) better if the buri leaves are dyed in order that it looks good.’ [BCWE-T-09 2.11]

The following illustrate additional comparative constructions from the corpus. In these complex examples, the comparative constructions are bolded:

Paibitan nay ta timbang mama na duma nay daw muoy piro mama an galeddang daw nadaļa din man kami tak mama i bakod kis-a ki kami. \\ Pa-ibit-an nay ta timbang mama na duma nay daw m-luoy piro mama an ga-leddang daw na-daļa din man kami tak mama i bakod kis-a ki kami. \\
t.r -hold.on- apl 1 p.excl.erg nabs balance man lk companion 1 p.excl.gen
and i.v.ir -swim but man def.m i.r -sink and a.hap.r -take/carry 3 s.erg too
1 p.excl.abs because man def.n big than obl.p 1p \\
‘We held on to both sides of the man that was our companion and swam, but the man was sinking and took us also (down with him) because the man was bigger than us.’ [CBWN-C-11 4.8]
summary: Comparative and superlative constructions are built on the non-verbal predicate template: a predicate plus its argument is followed by a standard in an oblique case, optionally introduced by kaysa or kis-a ‘than’. The predicate may be a plain, comparative, or superlative adjective, or even a nominalized clause, and the construction can appear in several word orders; reduplication and adverbial modifiers can soften or intensify the degree, while the Spanish loan mas ‘more’ can also mark comparison, though it cannot combine with reduplicated adjectives.

inst - red -sun/day 1 p.incl.erg only/just a.hap.r -wear pants def.n ctr
more good int dress because d 3 abs house nabs Lord \\
‘(It is) good if we wear a dress because as for the pants, daily we just wear pants. Dresses are really better because that is the Lord’s house.’ [ETOE-C-04 3.8]

Na kaluoy ta Dios na grasya ta Dios ki kami na mas subļa pa iran na mga pangabuian ki kami. \\ Na ka-luoy ta Dios na grasya ta Dios ki kami na mas subļa pa iran na mga pangabui-an ki kami. \\
lk nr -mercy nabs God lk grace nabs God obl.p 1 p.exc lk more too.much emph 3 p.gen lk pl livelihood- nr obl.p 1 p.exc \\
‘When (it is) the mercy of God that God’s grace is with us, then much more overwhelming will be their (the children’s) livelihood than ours.’ [LTOE-C-01 2.3]

When comparing the modification of two events, the word mas occurs at the beginning before the modifier of the clause that is being compared. Also kis-a/kaysa ‘than’ occurs before the standard, which is expressed as an oblique RP. There are two constructions for this that are similar to the constructions for modifying a clause with an adverb.

The first construction must have an irrealis verb in the clause that is being compared ex:fasterthanme. The ungrammatical example below shows that a verb inflected in realis mode ( gadļagan ) may not occur in this construction.

Mas dasig kanen mļagan kaysa ki yaken. \\
Pred. 1cmArg..4cmPred..9cmMkr..3cmStandard \\
Mas dasig kanen m-dļagan kaysa ki yaken. \\
more fast 3 s.abs i.v.ir -run than obl.p 1s \\
‘S/he runs faster than me.’ \\
* Mas dasig kanen gadļagan kis-a/kaysa ki yaken.

The second comparative construction comparing events involves a nominalized clause. This construction is completely parallel to comparative and superlative constructions involving non-verbal predicates.

Mas dasig pagdļagan din an kaysa ki yaken. \\
Predicate.4cmArg. 3.3cmMkr..2cmStandard \\
Mas dasig pag-dļagan din an kaysa ki yaken. \\
more fast nr.act -run 3 s.erg def.m than obl.p 1s \\
‘S/he runs faster than me.’ (lit. ‘Her running is faster than mine.’)

The following is an example of a comparative construction involving events from the text corpus.

Piro, gineļet nang gid na uļo ta sidda papili nang daen na uļas tak sikad gid en iran na kakulba daw mas dali tuugon uļo an a kaysa ta ikog. \\ Piro, g<in>eļet nang gid na uļo ta sidda pa-pili nang daen na uļas tak sikad gid en iran na ka-kulba daw mas dali tuog-en uļo an a kaysa ta ikog. \\
but < nr.res >cut only/just int lk head nabs fish t.r -choose only/just 3 p.erg
lk share because very int cm 3 p.gen lk nr -fear and
more easy put.through- t.ir head def.m ctr than nabs tail \\
‘But the slices of the head of the fish they chose as (their) share because their fear was really great and (it is) easier to put (a string) through the head than the tail.’ [JPWN-L-01 5.4]

The superlative is formed in two ways. The first way is with the complex prefix pinaka - on an adjective root. The thing being compared is in the absolutive case and usually fronted in the clause. The standard of comparison is again in the oblique case. In this construction, no syntactic marker of comparison (such as kis-a/kaysa ) occurs. Rather, the prefix constitutes the marker of the superlative construction.

Kanen gid pinakalayog ki kami. \\
Argument Mkr-Predicate Standard \\
Kanen gid pinaka-layog ki kami. \\
3 s.abs int superl -tall obl.p 1 p.excl \\
‘ s/he is really the tallest of us.’

The second superlative construction includes an adjective with the nominalizing affixes ka-…-an (See chap:modification sec:ka-an ). With adjective roots this can have a superlative meaning.

Kanen gid kalayugan ta mag-utod. \\
Argument Mkr-Predicate-Mkr Standard \\
Kanen gid ka-luyog-an ta mag--utod. \\
3 s.abs int nr -tall- nr nabs rel -sibling \\
‘ s/he is really the tallest of (his/her) siblings.’

Dondonay kabakeran na puļo. \\ Dondonay ka-baked-an na puļo. \\
Dondonay nr -big- nr lk island \\
‘ Dondonay is the biggest island.’ [LMWO-L-01 31.1]

too 3 s.gen lk last.name week/Sunday Gloria \\
‘Seven siblings, the youngest has a different last name. Sunday Glory (or Easter day).’ (This is a riddle with the answer.) [MRWR-T-01 18.1]

summary:
The passage explains that in event comparisons, *mas* appears before the modifier in the clause being compared, while *kis-a/kaysa* ‘than’ introduces the standard in an oblique phrase. It distinguishes two comparative constructions: one requires an irrealis verb in the compared clause, and the other uses a nominalized clause and is parallel to nominal comparative and superlative constructions.

It also describes two ways to form the superlative: with the prefix *pinaka-* on an adjective root, or with the nominalizing affixes *ka-…-an* on an adjective root, which can also yield a superlative meaning. In both superlative constructions, the item compared is typically in the absolutive case, and the standard of comparison is oblique.

text: While Referring Phrases mention people and things that are involved in a situation being communicated ( chap:referringexpressions ), the predicating word, or predicate, predicate is the part of the clause that describes the situation itself. In Kagayanen discourse, the most frequent clause types begin with a predicating word, usually an inflected verb inflected verbs. In addition to functioning as predicates in basic clauses, verb-like elements also function in nominalization s ( chap:referringexpressions ), and various types of dependent clause constructions dependent clauses ( chap:clausecombining ). In chap:non-verbalclauses we discussed predicates that are not based on verbs. In this chapter we will discuss the general structure of verbal predicates. We argue for a major distinction between inflectional morphology inflectional morphology and stem-forming morphology stem-forming morphology, and describe the inflectional paradigm. In chap:stemformingprocesses we describe and exemplify eight stem-forming morphological processes. In chap:verbclasses-1 we identify several morphosyntactically distinct verb classes verb classes, and attempt to describe their usages in terms of the parameters of situation type situation type, volitionality volitionality and semantic transitivity semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic. In chap:verbclasses-2, we take a semantics prior approach to several other verb classes, all of which exhibit specialized morphosyntactic behavior.
summary: The passage explains that while referring phrases identify participants in a situation, the predicate describes the situation itself, and in Kagayanen the most common clause types begin with a predicating word, usually an inflected verb. It notes that verb-like elements also appear in nominalizations and dependent clauses, and outlines the chapter’s focus on verbal predicates, including the distinction between inflectional and stem-forming morphology, the inflectional paradigm, stem-forming processes, and several verb classes analyzed by morphosyntactic and semantic properties.

text:
inflection|(

There are two classes of morphological processes in Kagayanen verbs which we describe as inflectional inflectional and stem-forming processes stem-forming. We use the term “(morphological) process” morphological processes as a cover term for prefixation, suffixation, infixation, and reduplication. Reduplication does not play a role in inflection in Kagayanen, therefore we can refer to the set of inflections as “ inflectional affixes ” (see tab:inflectionalaffixes ). However, the stem-forming group includes two types of reduplication, so the group as a whole can only accurately be described as “processes”. The difference between these two classes is that inflectional processes are strictly paradigmatic, whereas stem-forming processes are not. To clarify this important distinction, we need to introduce the difference between a paradigm paradigm and a word family word family (following a long tradition in linguistics, summarized nicely in ). We will do this using the verb forms of English.

The inflectional paradigm of English verbs consists of exactly five forms:

Paradigm for the English verb “do”. \\
Past tense: did \\
Present participle: doing \\
Past participle: done \\
“S-form” (3 rd person singular, present): does \\
Bare form: do

Whenever the verb “do” is used in discourse, it must occur in one of these five forms. Notice that the bare form, sometimes called the “zero form”, is a member of this paradigm. This is because English speakers subconsciously know that any verb must embody one of these values, therefore when no overt marker (- d, - ing, - n, or - s ) occurs, it leaves a “conspicuous absense”. This conspicuous absense is then available as the marker (or exponent exponent ) of a particular value in the list. A zero is as strong a “marker” of a member of a paradigm as any overt affix.

Contrast the paradigm in bkm:Ref59175832 with a family of words also based on the root do:

Word family based on the root “do”: \\
Reiterative: redo \\
Reversative: undo \\
Abilitative: doable \\
Reiterative abilitative: redoable \\
Reversative abilitative: undoable \\...

The forms in bkm:Ref59176157 can be thought of as a partial word family because they are all based on the same root. However, they are not a paradigm. There are several reasons this list of forms is not a paradigm. First, they do not vary according to any coherent semantic dimension – their meanings are logically independent of one another: reversative, reiterative, ability, etc. Second, the meaning elements they express may combine with one another, for example undoable combines the notions of reversative and ability; redoable combines reiteration with ability. Forms such as un-redo, re-undo, and re-undoable, though perhaps odd-sounding out of context, are also conceivable members of this family. Third, none of the affixes that define a word family are required for the root to be used in discourse. Fourth, these forms do not have analogies for every English verb. For example forms like * resee, * unremember, * bleedable and many others are extremely difficult to find appropriate communicative contexts for. Finally, the forms undo and redo are verbs, just like the root do. As such, they also occur in the five possible inflectional forms for English verbs: undid, redoing, undone, redoes, undo, and so on. In other words, the affixes that define the word family may occur with each other, and with the inflectional forms in the paradigm.

In contrast, the inflections, as given in bkm:Ref59175832, are mutually exclusive – a form cannot logically express present tense and past tense at the same time; 3 rd person singular and non-3 rd person singular at the same time, and so on. Thus forms with multiple inflections are impossible: * diding, * doinged, * done-ing, * dids, * dones, etc. Note that these forms are strictly uninterpretable; they do not just “sound odd out of context” the way un-redo and re-undo might.

Dictionary makers usually consider members of a word family to be different words: do, redo, and undo probably have their own entries in a reasonably complete dictionary of English (with possible cross-references to one-another). The forms in a paradigm, on the other hand, are not considered different dictionary entries. They are versions of the same lexical item. You might say the members of a paradigm are like one person wearing different sets of clothing, whereas the members of a word family are like different people with a family resemblance to one another.

Paradigms and word families occur in many languages of the world; language communities everywhere seem to find groups similar to these useful for expressing meanings. Philippine languages, and Kagayanen in particular, have much richer and more powerful paradigms paradigm and word families than English does. Because English has relatively simple morphology, it is easier to show the difference between paradigmatic and non-paradigmatic morphological values in English than it is in Kagayanen, though the distinction is still very relevant to Kagayanen. The principles we have just outlined apply equally to paradigms and word families in Kagayanen.

inflectional affixes inflectional affixes in Kagayanen define a paradigm. There are exactly twelve possible inflectional forms for every verb (recall that English has only five). One and only one of these forms is required in order for a word to function as a verbal predicate in a main, independent clause. Furthermore, the inflectional affixes express points on two well-defined and intersecting dimensions: grammatical transitivity and modality (see bkm:Ref58564378 ). The meaning of each affix in the inflectional paradigm logically excludes the others: A verb cannot be both realis and irrealis in modality; grammatically transitive and simultaneously grammatically intransitive, and so on. Furthermore, a zero form is not simply the lack of inflection, but rather it expresses very specific inflectional values, namely transitive and irrealis. The thirteen possible inflectional forms of any verb may be compared to the different clothes that one person might wear (see tab:inflectionalaffixes ).
summary:
Kagayanen verbs have two kinds of morphological processes: inflectional processes and stem-forming processes. Inflectional affixes are paradigmatic and mutually exclusive, with exactly twelve possible verbal forms that express combinations of grammatical transitivity and modality; one of these forms is required for a verb to function as a main-clause predicate, and the zero form specifically marks transitive irrealis.

By contrast, stem-forming processes are like an English word family rather than a paradigm: they are not organized along one coherent semantic dimension, can combine with one another, are not required for use in discourse, and may occur together with inflection. The passage uses English examples such as do, redo, undo, and doable to illustrate the difference between paradigms and word families.

text:
Stem-forming processes stem-forming processes, on the other hand, are non-paradigmatic—they may combine with one another to form complex meaningful stems that are then available for inflection. They also express meaning elements that are logically independent of one another, such as causative, applicative, pluraction, reciprocity and aspect. Roots with stem-forming affixes can be compared to members of a family, all of whom resemble one another, but who are clearly different people. For example, consider a family of words based on the root atag ‘to give.’

“Family” of stems based on the root -atag: \\
tabbing
4cm \= 2.4cm \=
bare root: \> - atag \> ‘give’ \\
causative: \> - paatag \> ‘cause/let give’ \\
applicative: \> - atagan /- tagan \> ‘give to s.o.’ \\
pluraction: \> - ngatag \> ‘give together/several times’ \\
continuative: \> - atag-atag \> ‘keep on giving’ \\
distributive: \> - tagtag \> ‘give to several/distribute’ \\
reciprocal: \> - atagay \> ‘give to each other’ \\
causative+applicative: \> - paatagan \> ‘cause/let give to s.o.’ \\
causative+continuative: \> - paatag-atag \> ‘cause/let keep on giving’ \\
continuative+reciprocal: \> - atag-atagay \> ‘to keep giving to each other’ \\...
tabbing

The Kagayanen words in bkm:Ref59345903 are all verb stems, ready to be inflected with one of the possible inflectional affixes (indicated by the dash in front of each form). They all have different, though related, meanings. Note that the morphological processes that give rise to these forms ( pa -, ng -, - an, - ay and reduplication) may combine with one another to produce even more complex forms, as illustrated in the last three examples in bkm:Ref59345903. These stem-forming morphological processes stem-forming morphology, and others, are a rich resource available to Kagayanen speakers to create complex and nuanced meanings.

We hope this discussion has clarified the important distinction between inflectional and stem-forming morphological processes. In the rest of this chapter, we will describe how inflectional and stem-forming processes contribute to the structure of verbal predicates, including preliminary examples in tab:someexamplesofverbalpredicates. In bkm:Ref62720957 we discuss overall verb structure. In bkm:Ref59351027 we briefly describe roots in Kagayanen. In bkm:Ref59351065 we discuss and exemplify inflectional affixes, and in bkm:Ref119308716 we describe certain discourse conditions under which inflectional prefixes may be omitted.

In the Kagayanen examples based on *atag* ‘give,’ different stem-forming affixes and reduplication express related but independent meanings such as causative, applicative, pluraction, reciprocity, and aspect, and these processes can combine to produce even more complex forms.

roots|(
A root root is the main element that expresses the general situation described in a verbal clause. It is the “foundation” on which speakers build complex and nuanced discourse scenes scenes. Substantive roots are two or more syllables in length. Roots with more than two syllables are sometimes borrowings, or involve archaic stem-forming processes that are not used productively to accomplish communicative work by modern speakers. In chap:stemformingprocesses we describe stem-forming processes that are still “live”, and productive.

Most lexical roots in Kagayanen are “precategorial” precategoriality in that they are not absolutely categorized as verbs, nouns, adjectives, and so on. Rather they function as predicators (verbs), Referring Expressions (nouns), or modifiers (adjectives/adverbs) as they are integrated into grammatical constructions. Because of their meanings, some roots are more likely to function as Referring Expressions, others as Modifiers, others as predicators, and so on, but in few cases is such categorization absolute.

For convenience, we will use the term “verb" verbs to refer to roots that typically function as predicators, though this must be understood as a descriptive convenience-substantive lexical items are not inherently categorized as verbs, nouns or modifiers (see for discourse-based argumentation for a similar claim in Waray Waray language, another Philippine language).
roots|)
summary: The passage explains that roots are the main elements expressing the general situation in a verbal clause, and that substantive roots are at least two syllables long; longer roots may be borrowings or come from older, nonproductive stem-forming processes. It also states that most lexical roots in Kagayanen are precategorial, meaning they are not fixed as verbs, nouns, or adjectives but can function as predicators, referring expressions, or modifiers depending on the grammatical construction.

inflection|(
Inflectional affixes inflectional affixes consist of a set of prefixes, and one suffix, - en (sometimes realized as - on or zero). These affixes simultaneously express two major dimensions, which we term grammatical transitivity ( transitive, intransitive, and ambitransitive ) and modality ( realis modality!realis and irrealis modality!irrealis, dynamic dynamic modality modality!dynamic, happenstantial modality modality!happenstantial, external motivation modality!external motivation, and deontic modality modality!deontic ) as displayed in tab:inflectionalaffixes. All other morphological processes in verbs, including two kinds of reduplication, other prefixes and suffixes, and one infix belong to the stem-forming group. These are described in chap:stemformingprocesses.

As discussed in the introduction to this chapter, the inflectional affixes constitute a paradigm ---a finite set of affixes, one and only one of which is required for a form to function as the main predicator in an independent verbal clause. A discusssion of the terms in tab:inflectionalaffixes immediately follows. In bkm:Ref124921711 through bkm:Ref64362346, examples of each of these affixes in context are provided.
summary: The passage says that the verb inflectional affixes are a small set of prefixes plus one suffix, **-en** (sometimes **-on** or zero), and that they jointly mark two dimensions: **grammatical transitivity** and **modality**. It also states that these affixes form a **paradigm**, meaning that one and only one of them is required for a verb to serve as the main predicator in an independent clause, while other verbal morphological processes are treated separately as stem-forming processes.
