grammatical transitivity|( transitivity!grammatical|(

There is a difference between semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic and grammatical transitivity. Semantic transitivity has to do with situations being communicated, whereas grammatical transitivity has to do with grammatical structures used to depict those situations. The two types of transitivity do not necessarily coincide. For example, English constructions such as she already ate, or he drank of the water of bitterness present semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic situations (someone eating or drinking something) in grammatically intransitive constructions (there is no direct object). Something similar occurs in Kagayanen. Situations that seem to require an Undergoer and a distinct Controller may be expressed in an intransitive construction, with the Undergoer simply omitted or presented in the non-absolutive case, preceded by ta or ki. We describe such constructions as detransitive detransitive constructions. Such constructions are used when there is an Undergoer, but it is less salient in the communicative situation than the Actor in some way. The Actor is presented as the most affected participant, and the Undergoer, if present at all, is presented as less central in some way, either by being indefinite, non-specific, incompletely affected, and so on. Of course, the big difference between English and Kagayanen is that English does not mark grammatical transitivity on the verb, whereas Kagayanen does. The verb eat is the same whether it occurs in a transitive (SUBJ eats OBJ) or intransitive (SUBJ eats ) frame. In Kagayanen, however, the verb in a detransitive construction is explicitly marked as intransitive. Examples bkm:Ref118364790 and bkm:Ref125017724 illustrate detransitive constructions from the corpus. Additional examples are found throughout this grammar.

Pagtapos nay igma, gatan-aw kay ta sini. \\

Pag-tapos nay igma, ga-tan-aw kay ta sini. \\
nr.act -finish 1pexcl.gen lunch t.r -look 1pexcl.abs nabs movie \\
‘After finishing our lunch, we watched a movie.’ [AGWN-L-01 5.5]

Piro tama man na mga inay na galuag man ta kaanlao... \\

Piro tama man na mga inay na ga-luag man ta kaanlao... \\
but many also lk pl mother lk i.r -watch emph nabs lunar.eclipse \\
‘But there were many mothers who watched a lunar eclipse...’ [JCOE-C-03 5.4]

Example bkm:Ref118364790 is part of a story about what the Actors did. It is not about any particular movie. In terms of, sini, `movie', simply describes the ``range" over which the watching took place; the Actors engaged in ``movie watching". Therefore the Actor is presented as absolutive ( kay `absolutive, first person plural exclusive'), and the verb is inflected as intransitive ( ga - `intransitive, realis'). Similarly, example bkm:Ref125017724 is about the mothers, and not any particular lunar eclipse. In this case, the mothers are the Head of a modifying (relative) clause. As will be discussed in chap:clausecombining, the Head of a relative clause must be the absolutive of that clause. Therefore, the verb inside the relative clause must be in an intransitive form with the Actor understood as the absolutive.

As discussed in chap:voice, Grammatical transitivity in Kagayanen is crucially involved in the expression of voice voice. That is to say, the transitivity values of the inflectional affixes reflect the Grammatical transitivity of the clause depending on the voice being expressed. Since voice is a global property of constructions rather than individual verbs (i.e., in addition to verb marking, voice also involves case marking of Referential Expressions, and is dependent on discourse considerations), we defer a discussion of how Grammatical transitivity is deployed in the voice system until chap:voice.

A macrorole macroroles is a cover term for a group of semantic roles that tends to be treated grammatically in a similar way in a particular language. The macroroles that are most relevant to Kagayanen syntax are the Actor actor (or Starting point starting point ) and the Undergoer undergoer (or Endpoint endpoint ) of the situation described in the predicate. Specific semantic roles included within these macroroles are listed in tab:macrorolesandsemanticroles. However, the precise semantic role of the absolutive and other nominals depends to a large extent on the context and the situation type expressed by the stem. In chap:verbclasses-1 and chap:verbclasses-2, we discuss a range of situation types and the semantic roles that they represent.

transitivity!grammatical|) grammatical transitivity|)
summary: The passage distinguishes semantic transitivity, which concerns the kind of situation being described, from grammatical transitivity, which concerns the structure used to express it; the two do not always match. In Kagayanen, situations with an Actor and Undergoer may be expressed in intransitive, detransitive constructions when the Undergoer is less salient, and the verb is then explicitly marked as intransitive, unlike in English where the verb form does not change. It also notes that grammatical transitivity is important for voice marking and relates to the treatment of macroroles such as Actor and Undergoer.

modality|(

The terms dynamic modality!dynamic, happenstantial modality modality!happenstantial, realis modality!realis, irrealis modality!irrealis, external motivation modality!external motivation and deontic modality!deontic deontic modality refer to particular grammatical values in the inflectional paradigm of Kagayanen (see tab:inflectionalaffixes ). These terms are based on what we see as the most general functions of these values, most of which seem to belong to a category best described as modality, that is, the speaker’s perspective on the truth, likelihood, or necessity of a situation, as well as the speaker’s assessment of responsibility and control exercised by various referents or external forces. This is a very broad characterization of the functions of these values. As will become clear, some specific usages may seem to fall outside these notions, or even outside the domain of “modality” altogether as traditionally defined (see, e.g.,, ). Modality, as with all other components of the verbal system, is used creatively by speakers to create complex and nuanced meanings that sometimes defy categorical analysis by linguists.

As mentioned above, the inflectional values illustrated in tab:inflectionalaffixes sometimes have different effects depending on the situation type being expressed. For example, dynamic modality is the common form for situations involving volitional motion, development, and/or change of state. In these situations, dynamic modality may be understood as perfective perfective aspect in aspect, and in narrative discourse as main storyline (or foreground foreground ) events. Happenstantial modality happenstantial modality|( may be used to express these same situation types, while presenting them as accidental, abilitative, opportunitive or perfect aspect, depending on the context.

On the other hand, happenstantial modality is the common form for situations involving sensory, emotional One apparent emotion verb stands out as an exception to this generalization. The root gilek ‘to get angry’ is usually expressed in dynamic modality, gagilek rather than happenstantial?nagilek. It is possible that gilek is perceived as a volitional reaction to something, rather than an emotion, in which case the English gloss ‘get angry’ may be misleading. or cognitive experience, and intransitive, non-volitional situations ( melt, die, drift off, etc.). In these situations, happenstantial modality may be understood as perfective perfective aspect in aspect, and in narrative discourse as depicting foreground events foreground. Dynamic modality may be used for these same situation types, but presents them as ongoing processes or inchoatives inchoative (with intransitive inflections), or causatives causative (with transitive inflection). tab:Relationshipbetweensituationtypesanddynamicvshappenstantialmodality summarizes the relationship between general situation types and dynamic versus happenstantial modality. Specific examples are provided below. happenstantial modality|)

irrealis modality|( modality!irrealis|( The values described as “irrealis” irrealis have several usages, including future time, imperative imperative modality, optative modality, and others. What the main uses of the irrealis forms have in common is that they describe unrealized situations, therefore irrealis is a reasonable descriptive cover term. irrealis modality|) modality!irrealis|)

For some of the categories in tab:inflectionalaffixes we have made a distinction between “general” general inflectional values and “narrow” narrow inflectional values values. The general values are those that are the default in everyday discourse, and which express the widest range of meanings. The narrow values, while preserving the transitivity and modality values of their general counterparts, zero in on and enforce more precise meanings. Repetitive repetitive, volitional, deontic modality, hypothetical, habitual, and external motivation meanings may be inferred from verbs with the general affixes, but they are directly expressed by verbs with the narrow affixes.

Volitional situations volitional situations are those in which a semantic Agent instigates and controls the situation consciously and with intent, for example, the basic senses of go, come, jump, kneel, grumble, wink, cook, read, etc. Non-volitional situations are those for which there is no controller or initiator, for example, die, melt, come untied, drift off, sink, etc. The prototypical absolutive argument of a non-volitional intransitive verb is a semantic Patient, or a theme (in the sense of ).

Deontic modality deontic modality modality!deontic is a kind of irrealis that asserts that the normally human Agent is compelled by some external force to perform the activity described by the verb. We will use the English modal have to to approximate the meaning of deontic forms cited out of context. Deontic modality receives explicit expression in the dynamic transitive prefix i -. For grammatically intransitive constructions, and happenstantial modality constructions, deontic is not formally distinguished from other irrealis modalities in verbal morphology. When necessary, a deontic sense can be specified for irrealis constructions using adverbials such as kinangļan, ‘necessary/need’, and dapat, ‘must’ (see chap:modification, sec:adverbs ).

It is clear that the dynamic affixes dynamic modality modality!dynamic constitute the most straightforward and easily understood verbal inflections. For this reason, when describing the inflections, we omit mention of modality for the dynamic mode affixes. For example, “transitive irrealis” is a shorthand way of referring to the dynamic, transitive, irrealis inflections -en/-on/-0.

Examples of constructions that employ each of the inflectional affixes are given in the following subsections, with the relevant verb forms bolded. Short explanations are sometimes provided as justification for the terminology chosen. A description of the classes of roots that are distinguished in terms of the way they interact with inflectional morphology is provided in chap:verbclasses-1.
modality|)

Intransitive realis ga -
intransitive realis inflection|(

The inflectional prefix ga - is the most common form for dynamic intransitive events on the storyline in narratives. In this usage, the aspectual interpretation is perfective perfective aspect, as in the first clause of example bkm:Ref396718263:

Gapit kay anay ta dawisan tak ganampara pa mga gurmiti ta sid-anan. \\
Ga-apit kay anay ta dawis-an tak ga-ng-tampara pa mga gurmiti ta sid-anan. \\
i.r -stop.off 1 p.excl.abs first/for.a.while nabs point- nr because i.r-pl -goggles inc pl crew nabs viand \\
`We stopped off first at the point (of the island) because the crew were still spear fishing for viand.’ [VAWN-T-18 2.8]
summary:
The passage explains that Kagayanen verbal inflection includes several modality-related values—such as dynamic, happenstantial, irrealis, and deontic—that reflect speakers’ perspectives on truth, likelihood, necessity, and control. These values interact with situation type: dynamic forms often mark volitional motion or changes of state, while happenstantial forms commonly mark sensory, emotional, or non-volitional events, and both can receive different aspectual interpretations in context.

It also distinguishes “general” from “narrow” inflectional values: general forms are default and cover a wide range of meanings, whereas narrow forms directly encode more specific meanings such as repetitive, habitual, hypothetical, or external motivation. Deontic modality is treated as a kind of irrealis meaning expressing external obligation, and intransitive realis ga- is presented as the common prefix for dynamic intransitive events in narrative foregrounding.

text:
However, predicates inflected with ga - may be understood as imperfective imperfective aspect. For example, the second occurrence of ga- ( ganampara ) in bkm:Ref396718263 is within an adverbial clause expressing a backgrounded, non-storyline event. The imperfective aspect interpretation is reenforced by the use of the incompletive adverbial pa.

Example bkm:Ref396718461 illustrates one use of ga- in which the interpretation may be either inceptive or imperfective. The event of walking is ongoing in the story. After the sentence illustrated in bkm:Ref396718461, the story describes crossing a river on stepping stones and other events that happened on the way to the community of Teresa. Therefore, example bkm:Ref396718461 may be understood as a (perfective) inceptive “we began to walk again” or it could mean “we were walking again.” In either case it does not describe the entire event of walking to Teresa, and therefore is not perfective:

Pag-abot nay ta liyo, gapanaw kay eman munta ta Teresa. \\
Pag-abot nay ta liyo, gapanaw kay eman m-punta ta Teresa. \\
nr.act -arrive 1 p.excl.gen nabs other.side i.r -go/walk 1 p.excl.abs
as.before i.v.ir -go nabs Teresa \\
`When we arrived on the other side (of a river), we were/began walking again as before going to Teresa.’ [BGON-L-01 1.10]

With roots that describe properties or states, ga - expresses the process of entering the state ( inchoative ) inchoative. Examples bkm:Ref119937645 and bkm:Ref416513591 are common greetings, both of which may be considered compliments, or fixed expressions of greeting after long separation:

Gatambek ka. \\
Ga-tambek ka. \\
i.r -fat/healthy 2 s.abs \\
‘You are becoming/became fat/healthy.’

Ganiwang ka. \\
Ga-niwang ka. \\
i.r -skinny 2 s.abs \\
‘You are becoming/became skinny.’

The following are additional examples of inchoative ga - from the corpus:

Daw isya na bai gabagnes dili kanen magpanaw daw kilem. \\
Daw isya na bai ga-bagnes dili kanen mag-panaw daw kilem. \\
if/when one lk woman i.r -pregnant neg.ir 3 s.abs i.ir -go/walk if/when night \\
‘When a woman becomes pregnant, she will not go (anywhere) at night.’ [VAOE-J-05 1.1]

Gabakod yaken i tenged ta iran na pagsupurta, labi na gid ta iran na pagpalangga. \\
Ga-bakod yaken i tenged ta iran na pag-supurta, labi na gid ta iran na pag-palangga. \\
i.r -big 1 s.abs def.n because nabs 3 p.gen lk nr.act -support
especially lk int nabs 3 p.gen lk nr.act -love/affection \\
`I grew up (became big over time) because of their support, especially their love/affection.’ [JBON-J-01 1.11]

These examples illustrate why we consider that ga - primarily expresses realis modality, and dynamicity, rather than aspect or tense. It is used when the situation expressed involves a change in state, completed or in process, currently relevant or in the past.
intransitive realis inflection|)

Transitive realis pa -
transitive realis inflection|(

The inflectional prefix pa- is the basic form for dynamic, grammatically transitive clauses on the storyline of narratives. There is also a stem-forming prefix pa - that is a morphological causative. We provide arguments that there are indeed two distinct pa - prefixes in chap:stemformingprocesses, sec:morphologicalcausative. As such its interpretation is normally perfective perfective aspect in aspect, with no reference to any internal temporal structure:

Pag-abot danen naan ta suba, palubbas danen iran na bayo daw pabatang danen naan ta kilid ta suba daw maglangoy. \\
Pag-abot danen naan ta suba, pa-lubbas danen iran na bayo daw pa-batang danen naan ta kilid ta suba daw mag-langoy. \\
nr.act -arrived 3 p.gen spat.def nabs river t.r -undress 3 p.erg 3 p.gen lk
clothes and t.r -put 3 p.erg spat.def nabs side nabs river and i.ir -bathe \\
This is the “culminative” use of irrealis inflection discussed below.
`Arriving at the river, they took off their clothes and put (them) at the side of the river and began to bathe.’ (This is a story about a cow and a water-buffalo who accidentally switch skins that they call clothes.) [CBWN-C-25 5.4]

Paibitan nay ta timbang mama na duma nay. \\
Pa-ibit-an nay ta timbang mama na duma nay. \\
t.r -hold- apl 1 p.excl.erg nabs balance man lk companion 1 p.excl.gen \\
The word duma has several functions, including as a comitative preposition ‘with’. Since it is followed by an enclitic genitive pronoun, nay ‘our’, it has to mean ‘companion’ in this context.
‘We held on both sides to the man who was our companion.’ (CBWN-C-11 4.8]

In rare cases, a verb inflected with pa - may be understood as imperfective imperfective aspect:

Pabunakan din pa mga bayo din. \\
Pa-bunak-an din pa mga bayo din. \\
t.r -wash- apl 3 s.erg inc pl clothes 3 s.gen \\
‘S/he is still washing his/her clothes.’

In this case the adverbial particle pa, ‘still’ (glossed inc for ‘incompletive’ in this context), forces an imperfective interpretation of this clause. Again, we conclude that aspect is secondary to the main function of the inflectional prefix pa-. It always expresses dynamicity (movement or change), grammatical transitivity, and realis modality. This results in a perfective aspect interpretation in most cases, but this strong tendency may at times be overridden by other factors. Like ga -, the main function of pa - is to assert that a dynamic situation described by the verb is actually true in the discourse world. In contrast to ga -, pa - always indicates that the predicate has two core arguments either overtly expressed or strongly understood – an Undergoer, or endpoint, in the absolutive case, and a separate Actor, or starting point, in the ergative case.
transitive realis inflection|)
Realis repetitive ag -
realis repetitive inflection|(
summary: The passage argues that **ga-** mainly marks **realis, dynamic predicates** rather than aspect or tense: with activity roots it can be read as imperfective or inceptive, and with stative roots it expresses entering a state (inchoative). It also shows that **pa-** is the basic marker for **dynamic transitive realis clauses**, usually yielding a perfective interpretation, though in rare contexts it can be read as imperfective when other elements force that reading; in all cases, it signals a transitive event with an Actor and an Undergoer.

text:
The prefix ag - occurs only once in the corpus (example ex:ag below) and is not used often in everyday speech. It may be used in a transitive or intransitive case frame, and therefore may be considered ambitransitive ambitransitive. It expresses the idea that the situation has happened more than one time, a few times, once in a while or occasionally. It neither asserts the occurrence of one particular event, nor a habitual (often/on a regular basis) sense. Here we gloss it as rep.r for “repetitive, realis”. However, further research is needed to determine the precise aspectual or modal range of this relatively uncommon prefix.

Prefix ag- in an intransitive frame: \\
Ag-iling kay ta Cawili. \\
Ag-iling kay ta Cawili. \\
rep.r -go 1 p.excl.abs nabs Cawili \\
‘We have gone at times to Cawili.’

Agsud-o kay ki danen daw uļa ubra. \\
Ag-sud-o kay ki danen daw uļa ubra. \\
rep.r -visit 1 p.excl.abs obl.p 3 p if/when neg.r work \\
‘We visited them if/when there was no work.’

Prefix ag- in a transitive frame (inside a relative clause): \\
Apo Arey isya na manakem na ag-insaan ta mga ittaw. \\
Apo Arey isya na manakem na ag-insa-an ta mga ittaw. \\
ancestor Arey one lk older lk rep.r -ask- apl nabs pl person \\
‘Ancestor Arey is an older person that people asked/requested things of.’ [EFWE-T-06 2.1]

This prefix may be considered “narrow”, since it occurs far less often than the general, or default, forms ga - and pa -, and it expresses a more precise meaning, since a repetitive inference is possible with ga - and pa -, but is enforced with ag -. This distinction between general and narrow dynamic realis prefixes mirrors a similar distinction in the dynamic irrealis prefixes, and happenstantial modalities (see sec:transitiveirrealis and sec:intransitivehappenstantialirrealis ).
realis repetitive inflection|)

Intransitive irrealis mag - and m-
intransitive irrealis inflection|(

The inflectional prefix mag - is the general inflection for most dynamic intransitive irrealis predicates. It neither requires nor excludes volitionality. The prefix m - is the more narrow form, which always indicates volitional events. Most verbs only take mag -, while some allow either mag - or m -. As far as we know, there are no verb roots that take only m -. Both mag - and m - are irrealis counterparts of ga -. Long lists of verb roots that take only mag - versus those that take mag - or m - are provided in chap:verbclasses-1, sec:irrealisinflections. Here we provide a few examples from the corpus.

Example bkm:Ref392932747 illustrates a majority class root, ayad ‘be careful’, in the irrealis form in a construction with a verb in happenstantial modality ( matellek ‘might get stuck’):

Pambaļan ko ake na mga duma na mag-ayad tak basi matellek danen an. \\
Pa-ambaļ-an ko ake na mga duma na mag-ayad tak basi ma-tellek danen an. \\
t.r -say- apl 1 s.erg 1 s.gen lk pl companion lk i.ir -be.careful because perhaps a.hap.ir -stick 3 p.abs def.m \\
`I warned my companions to be careful because maybe they might (happen to) get stuck (by a nail in a piece of wood on the ground).’ [VAWN-T-16 2.10]

For minority class verbs, m - is the unmarked form expressing a relatively likely irrealis, or immediate future situation, while mag - expresses the idea of hypothetical or distant future situations. For example, the form manaw, based on the root panaw ‘to go’, is used in simple future contexts, as when taking leave of someone:

… manaw kay en. \\
… m-panaw kay en. \\
i.v.ir -walk/go 1 p.excl.abs cm \\
‘…we will leave now.’ [RMWN-L-01 3.2]

Manaw ki nang isab kani ta baybay i. \\
M-panaw ki nang isab kani ta baybay i. \\
textsci.v.ir-walk/go 1 p.incl.abs only/just again later nabs beach def.n \\
‘We will just walk again later on the beach.’ [BGON-L-01 12.6]

In contrast, magpanaw expresses a more distant future bkm:Ref63688177, or more hypothetical irrealis action bkm:Ref63688194:

Magpanaw danen magsimba ta Leganes. \\
Mag-panaw danen mag-simba ta Leganes. \\
i.ir -go/walk 3 p.abs i.ir -worship nabs Leganes \\
‘They will go to worship in Leganes.’

Para dili mabao bai i daw gusto din magpanaw daw deļem magdaļa kanen ta uling, asin daw luy-a ugsak ta bulsa ta bai na gabagnes. \\
Para dili ma-bao bai i daw gusto din mag-panaw daw deļem mag-daļa kanen ta uling, asin daw luy-a ugsak ta bulsa ta bai na ga-bagnes. \\
for neg.ir a.hap.ir -painful.pregnancy woman def.n if/when want 3 s.erg
i.ir -go/walk if/when dark i.ir -carry 3 s.abs nabs charcoal salt and
ginger inside nabs pocket nabs woman lk i.r -pregnant \\
There are two words spelled bao in Kagayanen. They are homographs, but not homophones. Bao meaning “painful pregnancy” is stressed on the second syllable and there is a final glottal stop: [baʔóʔ]. Bao meaning ‘odor’ is stressed on the first syllable, and lacks the final glottal stop: [báʔo]. Neither glottal stop nor stress is represented consistently in the writing system, though both are contrastive.
`In order for the woman not to have a painful pregnancy, if she wants to go somewhere when dark, she will carry charcoal, salt, and ginger inside the pocket of the woman who is pregnant.’ [VAOE-J-05 1.7]

In example bkm:Ref392932169 the prefix mag - is used twice on minority class verbs in grammatically intransitive constructions, and the prefix m - is used once on a minority class verb. In this example, the verbs with mag - describe situations that that may or may not happen ( deontic modality in this case, signaled by the adverbial kinangļan ), whereas the verb with m - describes the much more inevitable event that the baby will come out.
summary: The prefix **ag-** is a relatively rare, ambitransitive realis prefix that occurs in both intransitive and transitive frames and expresses repetition or occasionality, without implying a single event or a habitual pattern. It is glossed as **rep.r** (“repetitive, realis”), and the passage notes that it is a narrower form than the more general **ga-** and **pa-**, with a more specific repetitive meaning.

text:
Daw bagnes en isya na nanay kinangļan kanen magkaan ta gulay daw mag-inem kanen ta bitamina agod daw mwa bata an biskeg iya na lawa daw madyo ta masakit. \\
Daw bagnes en isya na nanay kinangļan kanen mag-kaan ta gulay daw mag-inem kanen ta bitamina agod daw m-gwa bata an biskeg iya na lawa daw madyo ta masakit. \\
if/when pregnant cm one lk mother need 3 s.abs i.ir -eat
nabs vegetables and i.ir -drink 3 s.abs nabs vitamins so.that if/when i.v.ir -go.out child def.m strong 3 s.gen lk body and far nabs sick \\
`When a mother is pregnant she should eat vegetables and take (lit. drink) vitamins so that when the baby comes out, his/her body is strong and (s/he) is far from sickness.’ [LBOP-C-03 11.3]

Example bkm:Ref396719550 illustrates what we call the culminative culminative usage of the irrealis mood. Even though the events of walking and returning home are semantically realis in the story, they are presented as the culminating events in a string of main line events that are closely linked. The events previous to this were about chopping wood and preparing it to carry away. The development in example bkm:Ref396719550 is about how the Actor carried the wood home, at which point the story ends. This usage is very common following the conjunction daw, and any of the irrealis affixes may function in this way.

Tapos na pag-ipid din ta iya na apin, papas-an din daw manaw muli. \\
Tapos na pag-ipid din ta iya na apin, pa-pas-an din daw m-panaw muli. \\
then lk nr.act -arrange 3 s.gen nabs 3 s.gen lk protective.cloth
t.r -carry.on.shoulder 3 s.erg and i.v.ir -go/walk i.v.ir -go.home \\
Recall from Chapter 3 that there are both enclitic pronouns that follow their heads, and free pronouns that normally precede their heads. The form din in the first line of this example is the 3 sg.gen enclitic pronoun that follows the nominalized verb pag-ipid ‘folded/folding’, while iya is the 3 sg.gen free pronoun that precedes apin ‘protective cloth,’ with the linker na intervening. The genitive forms are the same as the ergative forms that occur with verbs inflected as transitive, as is the case with the use of din in the second line of example bkm:Ref396719550.
`Then when s/he arranged his/her protective cloth, s/he carried (wood) on his/her shoulders and walked going home.’ (The protective cloth goes on the shoulders under the wood.) [NFWN-T-01 2.21]

Example bkm:Ref395019310 above also includes a verb with mag - in this culminative function: daw maglangoy ‘and began bathing.’ Verbs in the culminative usage definitely express realis events, though they appear in irrealis form. The functional or historical scenario under which this usage could have developed is a topic for future investigation.

Transitive irrealis - en/-on/-0
transitive irrealis inflection|(

The inflectional affix - en and allomorphs - on and - are the basic forms for dynamic irrealis transitive clauses. The occurrence of - en/on versus - depends on the lexical class of the verbal root, and the presense versus absense of an applicative suffix. tab:rootsthattaketwodistincttransitiveirrealisinflections-1 in chap:verbclasses-1 lists a large subset of roots that are distinguished on the basis of the transitive irrealis inflections that they occur with. Here we will describe in prose how these root classes are related.

First, most verbal roots take the - en/-on forms, for example, the second bolded verb in bkm:Ref119939353, and the bolded verb in bkm:Ref119939420. In chap:verbclasses-1 these are designated as ``Class VI" roots. There is also a minority class of roots that always take - as the transitive, irrealis inflection. These are designated as ``Class VII" roots.

Second, whenever a stem-forming suffix (applicative - an or the exclamatory - a, or - i ) appears, the form - en/-on is excluded for all roots, leaving - as the exponent of the transitive, irrealis inflection. Thus one could say that the stem-forming suffixes form a Class VII stem from a Class VI root.

Third, the minority class consists of two subclasses, Class VIa and Class VIIb. Class VIIa roots may or may not take an applicative suffix in a grammatically transitive frame, while Class VIIb roots always take an applicative suffix in a grammatically transitive frame. Semantically, Class VIIa consists mostly of verbs of transfer, for example the first bolded verb in bkm:Ref119939353, while Class VIIb consists of verbs that always take an applicative suffix in their basic, transitive form ( ex:yourthings and ex:yourschooling ). They may occur without the applicative, but only in a grammatically intransitive frame (i.e., detransitive constructions, see example bkm:Ref447101267 further below, and chap:voice, sec:grammaticalrelations ). Semantically, Class VIIb verbs tend strongly to describe activities that involve superficial, incomplete, or invisible effect on the Patient.

Finally, for Class VI roots, the form - on occurs whenever the last vowel in the stem is /u/. Otherwise the default allomorph - en occurs:

… daw pangallo batang no kamuti an na agi asod naan ta kaldiro daw tapos lutuon. \\
… daw pang-tallo - batang no kamuti an na agi asod naan ta kaldiro daw tapos luto-en. \\
and ord -three t.ir -put 2 s.erg cassava def.m lk pass pound spat.def
nabs pot and then cook- t.ir \\
`…and third, put the cassava that has been pounded in the pot and then cook (it).’ [BCWE-T-07 2.9]

Uļa ki nang lugay dya daw lubbasen ta nang bayo ta i aged dili mabasa... \\
Uļa ki nang lugay dya daw lubbas-en ta nang bayo ta i aged dili ma-basa... \\
neg.r 1 p.incl.abs only/just long.time d 4 loc and undress- t.ir 1 p.incl.erg
only/just clothes 1 p.incl.gen def.n so.that neg.ir a.hap.ir -wet \\
`We won’t be long there and we will just take off our clothes so that (they) will not be wet.’ [CBWN-C-25 4.8]
summary:
The passage explains the “culminative” use of irrealis mood, where events that are semantically realis are nevertheless marked irrealis because they function as the culminating actions in a chain of events, often after daw. In this usage, verbs such as walking home or beginning to bathe can appear in irrealis form even though they describe actual events.

It also outlines the transitive irrealis inflection system: the basic forms are -en/-on versus zero, with the choice determined by root class and by whether a stem-forming suffix such as -an, -i, or -a is present. Most roots take -en/-on, while a minority class takes zero; for Class VI roots, -on appears after /u/ and -en is the default elsewhere.

2 p.abs 3 s.erg nabs 2 p.gen lk nr.act -school \\

As mentioned above, for Class VI roots, the applicative - an overrides - en/-on, thus leaving “zero” (a conspicuous absence of affixation) as the indicator of the transitive, irrealis inflection (see chap:stemformingprocesses, sec:applicative-an for further discussion). Thus the applicative suffix forms a stem that belongs to Class VII. This makes some semantic sense since the applicative indicates a superficially, invisibly or partially affected Undergoer (see chap:voice, sec:applicativevoice ), and most verbs in Class VII also involve less than fully affected Patients as Undergoers (see tab:rootsthattaketwodistincttransitiveirrealisinflections-1 in chap:verbclasses-1 ). Example bkm:Ref447101267 illustrates the Class VII root akid, ‘to serve food’, in the basic transitive form (realis modality), and in the irrealis detransitive form:

Ti paakiran din en bataan ya tak ambaļ ta manakem ya, “ Kiran no bataan no. \\
Ti pa-akid-an din en bata-an ya tak ambaļ ta manakem ya, “ - akid-an no bata-an no. \\

nabs older def.f t.ir -serve.food- apl 2 s.erg child- nr 2 s.gen \\
`So she served food to the children because the older woman said, “Serve food to your children.”' [AION-C-01 7.7]

Example bkm:Ref499555402 illustrates the root legem ‘to dye’ that normally takes - en as its transitive, irrealis form, but in this example it occurs with the applicative suffix, which overrides - en, thus leaving - as the exponent of the transitive, irrealis inflection:

Daw gusto no na ikam i na paļaļa no betangan legem, pwidi no legeman ta minog, grin daw violet. \\
Daw gusto no na ikam i na pa-ļaļa no -betang-an legem, pwidi no -legem-an ta minog, grin daw violet. \\

In this example, the non-absolutive ta has dropped out between betangan and legem. This sometimes happens when a nominal has lost its status as absolutive as a result of the applicative derivation. In Relational Grammar terms, this may be a characteristic of “chômeurs.” Speakers agree that ta could be added here, but that it sounds more natural to leave it out.
`If you want to put dye on the mat you wove, you can dye (it) with red, green and violet.’ [DBOP-C-12 1.11]

Note that - an itself cannot be the marker of the transitive, irrealis inflection because it also occurs in realis contexts (see bkm:Ref120012965 and many other examples thoughout this grammar). On the other hand, “zero” as a marker of transitive, irrealis inflection is independently attested for a large lexical class of roots (Class VII, see chap:verbclasses-1, tab:rootsthattaketwodistincttransitiveirrealisinflections-1 ).

The following is an example from the corpus of the culminative use of transitive irrealis inflections:

Lugar na gatago kanen i nakita din iya na maguļang na galebbeng naan ta bļawan daw padakep ta mga ittaw maguļang ya daw gapuson daw patayen. \\
Lugar na ga-tago kanen i na-kita din iya na maguļang na ga-lebbeng naan ta bļawan daw pa-dakep ta mga ittaw maguļang ya daw gapos-en daw patay-en. \\
then comp i.r -hide 3 s.abs def.n a.hap.r -see 3 s.erg 3 s.gen lk elder.sibling
lk i.r -bury spat.def nabs gold and t.r -capture nabs pl person elder.brother def.f and tie- t.ir and kill- t.ir \\
`Then when he hid, he saw his older-brother who was-being-buried in gold and the people captured the older brother and tied (him) up and killed him.’ [CBWN-C-22 12.4]

In addition to the culmination of a series of events, this example also exhibits high tension in this part of the story. When there is higher tension or climax, the culminative usage of irrealis mood tends to be used, as well as fewer nouns and pronouns. A full discourse study is needed to corroborate this observation.

transitive deontic inflection|(
summary: The passage explains that for Class VI roots, the applicative suffix **-an** overrides the usual transitive irrealis markers **-en/-on**, so the irrealis transitive form is marked by **zero affixation**; this zero marking is also independently attested for Class VII roots. It also notes that **-an** cannot itself mark transitive irrealis because it appears in realis contexts, and gives examples where irrealis forms occur in discourse with culminative or high-tension narrative passages, often accompanied by fewer nouns and pronouns.

text:
The prefix i - usually expresses or reports an admonition, telling someone what they should, must or ought to do. We see this deontic deontic modality meaning as related to the ``conveyance", ``instrumental" or ``benefactive" voice meanings that have been ascribed to cognate i- prefixes in other Philippine languages (see, e.g., on Cebuano ). Briefly, a beneficiary, an instrument and a requirement all participate in the instigation of an action in some way. A beneficiary is a motivation for the action, an instrument assists or enables the actor to accomplish the action, and a requirement or necessity acts as an unseen force spurring the actor to action. Our hypothesis is that i - evokes an image in which there is such an external motivating or enabling force in the discourse scene scenes depicted in the clause., in a description of Waray, refer to this motivating force as a ``co-actant". Sometimes the co-actant can be mentioned as the absolutive of the clause, in which case i - expresses a benefactive or instrumental applicative. In Waray, as in Kagayanen, the co-actant need not be overt at all, but remains ``behind the scenes", motivating the activity. In Kagayanen, i - always expresses irrealis modality, and is usually understood as expressing deontic modality. We see its use as an instrumental applicative marker as a reasonable extension of this ``external enablement" meaning (see chap:voice, sec:applicativevoice for further discussion and corpus examples of - i functioning as an instrumental applicative).

Prefixation with i- is possible for some Class VI verbs as displayed in tab:rootsthattaketwodistincttransitiveirrealisinflections-1 in chap:morphosyntacticallydefinedverbclasses and all Class VII verbs. None of the Class VIII verbs (those that take - an in their basic transitive form) can occur with the i - prefix. For a few Class VI verbs, i - functions as an instrumental or benefactive/recipient applicative, in which case deontic modality is a possible, but not necessary, implication (see chap:voice, sec:applicativevoice for a definition of applicative). The prefix i- is not used very often, and when it does occur, the Actor is usually 2 nd person.

Examples bkm:Ref447002651 and bkm:Ref119941331 illustrate the verb beļad ‘to dry X in the sun’. In bkm:Ref447002651 it occurs with the normal transitive irrealis suffix - en and in example bkm:Ref119941331 the same verb occurs with i - and the meaning is that it is necessary to dry the cassava after soaking it so that it does not go bad.

Dayon kamangen sinaksak an na derse daw beļaren. \\
Dayon kamang-en s<in>aksak an na derse daw beļad-en. \\

‘Right away get the chopped parts that are small and dry (them in the sun).’ [JCWE-L-32 6.6]

For this and similar verbs, i- selects the instrument as the absolutive argument (instrumental voice-see chap:voice, sec:instrumentalvoice ), though with -en and the other transitive affixes, this verb selects the theme as the absolutive:
summary:
The passage argues that the prefix **i-** primarily expresses an admonition or deontic modality, meaning something like ‘should,’ ‘must,’ or ‘ought to,’ and links this to related benefactive, instrumental, and conveyance meanings in other Philippine languages. It proposes that **i-** evokes an external motivating or enabling force in the event, sometimes overt as a “co-actant” and sometimes implicit; in Kagayanen it is associated with irrealis and often deontic meaning, though in some verbs it can also mark instrumental or benefactive applicative functions.

The prefix occurs only with certain verb classes: some Class VI verbs and all Class VII verbs, but not Class VIII verbs. It is relatively rare and often appears with second-person actors, and the examples show both clear deontic uses, such as needing to dry cassava or place thorns on a banana plant, and more limited applicative uses where an instrument becomes the absolutive argument.

Instrumental voice (applicative) \\

Similarly, the verb akid ‘to serve food’ strongly implies a specific serving implement, normally a spoon:

The verb akid also describes transfer (‘serve X to Y’). Therefore, for this verb, i - may also select a beneficiary/recipient as the absolutive argument, as illustrated in bkm:Ref447269492:

Beneficiary/recipient voice applicative \\

‘Serve some rice for/to me.’

For verbs that allow both types of applicative (such as akid ), the instrumental versus benefactive meanings can always be distinguished-instruments are inanimate tools, while beneficiaries or recipients are always animate and usually human. There are additional verbs that can occur with the i - instrumental and beneficiary applicative meanings, other than Class VI and VII listed in chap:verbclasses-1, tab:rootsthattaketwodistincttransitiveirrealisinflections-1. Furthermore, some speakers use i - with more verbs than other speakers do, so there is variation in this system. However, the functions of i - are constant: It only occurs in grammatically transitive constructions, and always expresses deontic modality. It can at times occur in an applicative frame, if the constructional context allows it.

The following are a few examples of the i- transitive deontic applicative construction in context:

Ambitransitive happenstantial realis na -
ambitransitive happenstantial realis inflection|(

The term “happenstantial” is sometimes used in descriptions of Philippine languages for a verbal category that describes non-deliberate, abilitative or coincidental situations. This is generally accurate for Kagayanen. However, it must be kept in mind that for some non-volitional intransitive verbs, and transitive experiential verbs (verbs of non-volitional perception, emotion and cognition) the happenstantial prefixes are the basic narrative forms, and as such can be understood as perfective in aspect. For other verb classes, happenstantial modality implies happenstance, for example, they happened to meet, he happened to pass by; ability, we were able/managed to hold on; opportunitive, he got to listen to a story; or perfect aspect, I have been to Manila, he has used up all the rice. The extension of happenstantial modality to perfect aspect may be motivated by the fact that perfect aspect is always non-volitional, since it asserts the state that results from some (volitional or non-volitional) event, and not the event itself. An Actor may carry out an event on purpose, but the resultant state is just a fact of the new condition of the world. This is why English expressions like “She wanted to have seen that movie”, or “I intend to have been to Manila” are pragmaticaly odd at best. Having seen a particular movie is just the expression of a new state of the world that is the result of an event of seeing the movie. It is not something that one can volitionally intend or want to occur.
summary:
The passage describes the Kagayanen **i-** prefix as a transitive deontic marker that can function in instrumental or benefactive/applicative constructions, but its applicative uses are limited and show speaker variation. When both instrumental and benefactive readings are possible, they are distinguished by animacy: instruments are inanimate tools, while beneficiaries/recipients are animate, usually human.

It also notes that only two corpus examples clearly show **i-** in an applicative frame, both with instrumental absolutives, and that one example occurs in a nominalized dependent clause rather than a main clause. The passage then introduces the notion of **happenstantial** realis inflection, explaining that in Kagayanen it can express non-volitional situations, ability, opportunity, and sometimes perfect aspect, especially for some verb classes where it serves as a basic narrative form.

text:
The happenstantial prefixes na- and ma- may occur in grammatically transitive or intransitive frames, but in all cases, except the special hypothetical/polite usage of ma - described in bkm:Ref125306234, the situation is understood as not under the control of the absolutive argument. For this reason, we say these prefixes are “Undergoer oriented” – the absolutive is always an Undergoer. In order to detransitivize a transitive construction in happenstantial modality, the forms naka- or maka - must be employed (see bkm:Ref447381050 and bkm:Ref122761448 ). The following examples illustrate this pattern with the realis, happenstantial na-:

Transitive frame ( ta bata an = ergative) \\
Nasugat a ta bata an. \\
Na-sugat a ta bata an. \\
a.hap.r -meet 1 s.abs nabs child def.m \\
‘The child happened to meet me.’ \\
(Neither ‘*I happened to have met the child’, nor ‘*I hypothetically met the child.’)

Detransitive frame ( ta bata an = downplayed/demoted Undergoer) \\
Nakasugat a ta bata an. \\
Naka-sugat a ta bata an. \\
i.hap.r -meet 1 s.abs nabs child def.m \\
‘I happened to meet the child.’

Intransitive frame ( ta kabaw an = Oblique) \\
Nuļog a ta kabaw an. \\
Na-uļog a ta kabaw an. \\
a.hap.r -fall 1 s.abs nabs carabao def.m \\
‘I fell off the carabao (accidentally).’

Example bkm:Ref392922279 illustrates the happenstantial realis prefix na- in its basic usage on a non-volitional intransitive verb describing an event on the story line of a narrative:

Nuļog a ta kabaw tak gadļagan tudo kabaw an. \\
Na-uļog a ta kabaw tak ga-dļagan tudo kabaw an. \\
a.hap.r -fall 1 s.abs nabs carabao because i.r -run intense carabao def.m. \\
‘I fell off the carabao because the carabao was running hard.’ [RCON-L-02 3.6]

Examples bkm:Ref448318853 and bkm:Ref120012965 illustrate na - in its usage on transitive experiential verbs of perception and cognition on the story line of a narrative:

Nakita din ake na mangngod na nalemmes. \\
Na-kita din ake na mangngod na na-lemmes. \\
a.hap.r -see 3 s.erg 1 s.gen lk younger.sibling lk a.hap.r -drown \\
‘He saw my younger sibling who drowned.’ [LCWN-T-01 2.8]

Nademdeman din arey din Lisga. \\
Na-demdem-an din arey din Lisga. \\
a.hap.r -remember- apl 3 s.erg friend 3 s.gen fire.ant \\
Usually this word is pronounced and spelled lasga, but this author has written Lisga. This may be an error, code mixing, or idiolectal variation.
‘S/he remembered his friend Fire Ant.’ [VBWN-T-01 3.5]

Example bkm:Ref508296047 illustrates an emotion verb in its default usage:

Kanen i nadlek gid tak uļa gid duma. \\
Kanen i na-adlek gid tak uļa gid duma. \\
3 s.abs def.n a.hap.r -aftaid int because neg.r int companion \\
‘He was really afraid because there was no companion.’ [MBON-T-05 3.6]

In example bkm:Ref396387524 the happenstantial na - expresses a realized dynamic event that just happened without anyone intentionally trying to make it happen. This sentence could also express a realized capability, ‘they were able to (intentionally) meet’, but the discourse context makes it clear that the intended meaning is happenstance. It is also not perfect aspect because it asserts the event rather than a state resulting from an earlier event:

Nasugat danen bata i ta iran na maistro na ngaran din Pedro na galin Puerto… \\
Na-sugat danen bata i ta iran na maistro na ngaran din Pedro na ga-alin Puerto… \\
a.hap.r -meet 3 p.erg child def.n nabs 3 p.gen lk teacher lk name
3 s.gen Pedro lk i.r -from Puerto \\
`They happened to meet the son of their teacher whose name is Pedro who came from Puerto.’ [JCWN-T-20 21.2]

In examples bkm:Ref396387548 and bkm:Ref119941722 na - expresses a realized capability: ‘was able to.’ In this case, happenstance is not likely since “catching the ball” and “carrying the child” are not situations that occur without intention. And again, they are not perfect in aspect since they assert events rather than resultant states:

Paglabyog ta pangka ta bula ya, nasaļap dayon ta princesa. \\
Pag-labyog ta pangka ta bula ya, na-saļap dayon ta princesa. \\

summary: The happenstantial prefixes na- and ma- are used in both transitive and intransitive frames, but they consistently present the absolutive argument as an Undergoer and the event as outside the absolutive’s control, except for a special hypothetical/polite use of ma-. In transitive constructions, detransitivization requires naka- or maka-, and the text shows na- also extending to intransitive, experiential, emotional, abilitative, and some perfect-like uses on narratives.

text:
As with the happenstantial realis prefix na -, the prefix ma - occurs in intransitive non-volitional constructions and in certain transitive constructions. In its primary usage it expresses potential non-volitional situations. Like the realis counterpart, na -, ma - normally occurs with Patient-preserving intransitive verbs. In other words, the absolutive argument is a Patient/Undergoer rather than an Actor. If the absolutive is an Actor, either the form maka - occurs, or the construction is understood as the hypothetical/polite usage described in bkm:Ref125306276. The following examples illustrate the usages of ma - versus maka -:

Transitive frame ( ta bata an = ergative) \\
Masugat a ta bata an. \\
Ma-sugat a ta bata an. \\
a.hap.ir -meet 1 s.abs nabs child def.m \\
‘The child will possibly meet me.’ Or ‘The child will be able to meet me.’ (Not ‘*I will possibly/be able to meet the child’)

Detransitive frame ( ta bata an = downplayed/demoted Undergoer) \\
Makasugat a ta bata an. \\
Maka-sugat a ta bata an. \\
i.hap.ir -meet 1 s.abs nabs child def.m \\
‘I will possibly/be able to meet the child.’

Intransitive frame ( ta kabaw an = Oblique) \\
Muļog kanen kani ta kabaw an. \\
Ma-uļog kanen kani ta kabaw an. \\
a.hap.ir -fall 3 s.abs later nabs carabao def.m \\
‘S/he will possibly fall off the carabao (accidentally).’

Mawigit kani kwarta no an ta bulsa no. \\
Ma-wigit kani kwarta no an ta bulsa no. \\
a.hap.ir -fall.unnoticed later money 2 s.gen def.m nabs pocket 2 s.gen \\
‘Your money will later fall unnoticed from your pocket.’

Detransitive frame, polite usage (see bkm:Ref125306312 ) \\
Masugat ka ta bata an. \\
Ma-sugat ka ta bata an. \\
a.hap.ir -meet 2 s.abs nabs child def.m \\
‘You should meet the child (polite).’

Examples bkm:Ref440036963 and bkm:Ref119941820 illustrate intransitive clauses with ma - in its primary usage from the corpus:

Examples bkm:Ref119942002 through bkm:Ref89078422 illustrate what we are calling the hypothetical usage of the prefix ma-. In this usage, predicates inflected with ma - describe situations that may occur from time to time, but no specific actual event. This usage occurs frequently in expository texts.

summary:
The prefix **ma-** occurs in intransitive non-volitional constructions and in some transitive constructions, and its primary meaning is to express **potential, non-volitional situations**. It normally appears with **Patient-preserving intransitive verbs** where the absolutive argument is an Undergoer; if the absolutive is an Actor, either **maka-** is used or the form is interpreted as a hypothetical/polite construction.  

The passage also distinguishes this primary use from a **hypothetical usage**, in which ma- describes situations that may happen from time to time rather than a specific event, a use common in expository texts.

Kan-o na timpo daw malarga mga bļangay o lansa man galiid gid ti na puļo… \\
Kan-o na timpo daw ma-larga mga bļangay o lansa man ga-liid gid ti na puļo… \\

launch also t.r -pass.close.by int d 1 nabs lk island \\
`In previous times, if/when two-masted boats or launches would depart, (they) passed close by this island…’ [VAWN-T-17 3.2]

If the first verb in the construct illustrated in bkm:Ref89078422 were marga, which consists of m - ‘dynamic, intransitive, irrealis’ plus the root larga, then the sentence would imply a more immediate event ‘(the launch) will purposely depart’. The verb form maglarga is the general irrealis form, open to multiple interpretations, or some more distant future event. The form malarga describes events that happened many times in the past. Irrealis modality is appropriate because no particular event is asserted.

The happenstantial realis prefix naka - only occurs in grammatically intransitive constructions in which the controller of the situation is expressed in the absolutive case. Normally naka - and its irrealis counterpart maka - describe animate activity or activity that is “animate-like.” Example bkm:Ref447862310 illustrates naka - expressing perfect aspect (a state resulting from an earlier event). If these two verbs, agi ‘to pass’ and tinir ‘to stay’, were on the storyline they would have the dynamic intransitive prefix ga - instead of naka -. This is a fairly prototypical usage of naka-:

… may gakuyog na Japonis na nakaagi ta dagsa daw nakatinir di ta pila na buļan. \\
… may ga-kuyog na Japonis na naka-agi ta dagsa daw naka-tinir di ta pila na buļan. \\
ext.in i.r -come.with lk Japanese lk i.hap.r -pass nabs shore
and i.hap.r -stay d 1 loc nabs few lk month \\
`…there was a Japanese (person) who came with (someone) who had passed by way of the shore and had stayed here a few months.’ [HEWE-L-02 4.1]

Example bkm:Ref447862310 contrasts with the usage of na- in, for example, bkm:Ref447862443 above in that the events of passing through and staying in bkm:Ref447862310 are volitional---they are something the absolutive participant does, rather than something that “happens to” the absolutive. For this reason, we say that naka - (and maka -) are “Actor-oriented”. Falling off the carabao in bkm:Ref447862443, on the other hand, is “Undergoer-oriented”---it is something that “happens to” the absolutive marked participant. However, in bkm:Ref447862310, neither situation is on the storyline of the narrative. They are both “flashbacks” to earlier events that have relevance to the current narrative, but which do not themselves advance the storyline. For this reason a perfect aspect interpretation is appropriate. Furthermore, bkm:Ref447862310 contrasts with bkm:Ref448318853 through bkm:Ref392922782 in that these earlier examples are in transitive frames, whereas naka - always appears in an intransitive or detransitive frame in which the absolutive refers to the Controller.

Concerning example bkm:Ref448309255, the event expressed by sangga, ‘bump into’, occurred previously in the story expressed with the form nasanggaan ‘happened to bump into’. In that case, the implication is that the fish accidentally bumped into a limestone formation after having swum off quickly without regard to the direction he was going. Then example bkm:Ref448309255 occurs at the end of the story with naka- indicating that the parrot fish had some responsibility for running into the rock because he had so mindlessly swum off. The moral of the story is overtly stated as “think before reacting”. We have attempted to capture this assertion of impulsiveness on the part of the parrot fish in the free translation with the English expression “had gone and banged...”:

A, yon en na anduni tuļ-ungan i daw makita ta naan dagat, takong din an buksoļ, unti, tenged na nakasangga kanen ta manunggoļ. \\
A, yon en na anduni tuļ-ungan i daw ma-kita ta naan dagat, takong din an buksoļ, unti, tenged na naka-sangga kanen ta manunggoļ. \\
inj d 3 abs cm lk now/today parrot.fish def.n if/when a.hap.ir -see 1 p.incl.erg spat.def sea forehead 3 s.gen def.m lump d l loc.pr because lk i.hap.r -bump.into 3 s.abs nabs limestone \\
`Well, that (is the reason) now/today that the parrot fish when we see (it/them) in the sea, his forehead is lumped, here, because he (has gone and) banged into a limestone formation.’ [JCON-L-07 21.1]

In example bkm:Ref392929987 nakabantaw expresses a realized ability: ‘we were able to see’:

Ta seled ta limma na adlaw nakabantaw kay ta isya na bukid ta Panay. \\
Ta seled ta limma na adlaw naka-bantaw kay ta isya na bukid ta Panay. \\

nabs one lk mountain nabs Panay \\
`Within five days we were able/managed to spot far away one mountain on Panay.’ [VPWN-T-06 2.4]

The forms naka - and maka - may be used in some situations in which the central participant is not animate or volitional. For example, the verb abot ‘arrive’ usually takes an animate, volitional Agent as its only required argument. However, it can also be used for typhoons, telegrams, boats, sicknesses, suffering and so on. In such usages, it may take the naka - and maka - prefixes:

Ake na masakit, nakaabot gid isyam na buļan pinitinsya ko. \\
Ake na masakit, naka-abot gid isyam na buļan pinitinsya ko. \\
1 s.gen lk sick i.hap.r -arrive int nine lk month suffering 1 s.gen \\
‘My sickness, my suffering arrived (i.e. lasted) for nine months.’ [PEWN-T-01 2.15]
summary:
The passage explains that **marga/maglarga/malarga** differ in irrealis meaning and temporal interpretation: *marga* would imply a more immediate, purposeful departure, *maglarga* is a general irrealis form, and *malarga* refers to repeated past events. It then describes **naka-** as a happenstantial realis prefix used only in intransitive constructions where the absolutive participant is the controller, often with perfect-aspect or “flashback” readings that present earlier events relevant to the narrative but not advancing it.  

The text also shows that **naka-/maka-** are actor-oriented and can express volitional actions, realized ability, or even non-animate events in some cases, as with *abot* ‘arrive’ used for sickness or other nonhuman phenomena.

text:
The verb idad ‘(person/animal) to age’ (from the Spanish noun edad ‘age’) may also take naka - or maka -, though it is hard to construe “aging” as a volitional process: Perhaps this figure of speech is appropriate in Kagayanen because it takes a lot of effort to age successfully on an isolated island without much in the way of medical help, stores, or other amenities of life. To live to an old age is a highly respected accomplishment on Cagayancillo. In any case, even if ‘to age’ is not intentional, the only argument of this verb is always an animate participant.

Nakaidad a ta 27 na anyos. \\
Naka-idad a ta 27 na anyos. \\
i.hap.r -age 1 s.abs nabs 27 lk years \\
‘I was 27 years old.’ (lit. ‘I had managed to age for 27 years.’)

Finally, some sensory verbs, kita ‘see’, mati ‘hear’, batyag ‘feel’, plamao `smell', and lasa ‘taste’, normally occur with the naka - and maka - prefixes in happenstantial intransitive constructions, though they are clearly experiential rather than volitional.

Busa, ta pagpatay Mambeng, pangaranan na Lungag Mambeng ta iya kadengegan na kanen nakakita ta nyan na lungag. \\
Busa, ta pag-patay Mambeng, pa-ngaran-an na Lungag Mambeng ta iya ka-dengeg-an na kanen naka-kita ta nyan na lungag. \\

nabs 3 s.gen nr -honor- nr lk 3 s.abs i.hap.r -see nabs d3 abs lk hole/cave \\
`So, when Mambeng died, (the cave) was named Cave of Mambeng in his honor for he had found (saw) that cave.’ [SAWE-L-02 4.3]

Nakabatyag a ta ļettem tak uļa a kamaaw. \\
Naka-batyag a ta ļettem tak uļa a ka-maaw. \\
i.hap.r -feel 1 s.abs nabs hunger because neg.r 1 s.abs i.hap -breakfast \\
‘ I felt hungry because I did not eat breakfast.’

Example bkm:Ref447897963 is particularly interesting in that it illustrates the same verb, mati ‘to hear/listen’ both in the dynamic form, and the intransitive happenstantial:

Kami darwa kay Maria gamati ta drama iran Mama. Kami i nakamati kay ta isya na singgit ta isya na bai na ame man na katagsa. \\
Kami darwa kay Maria ga-mati ta drama iran Mama. Kami i naka-mati kay ta isya na singgit ta isya na bai na ame man na katagsa. \\
1 p.excl.abs two 1 p.excl.abs Maria i.r -hear nabs drama 3 p.gen Mother/Aunt
1 p.excl.abs def.n i.hap.r -hear 1 p.excl.abs nabs one lk shout nabs one
lk woman lk 1 p.excl.gen too lk cousin \\
`We both Maria and I were listening to a drama (program on the radio) at the place of Mama (aunt). We heard a shout of a woman who was indeed our cousin.’ [RZWN-T-02 2.2-3]

In the first instance of the verb mati in bkm:Ref447897963, gamati, the dynamic form implies the Actors were intentionally listening to the drama. In the second instance, nakamati, they happened to hear something, not intentionally, but only experientially. English expresses this intentional/non-intentional distinction in the two lexical verbs, listen and hear, whereas Kagayanen accomplishes the same semantic distinction by exploiting the morphological contrast between dynamic and happenstantial modalities. The form namatian would require the Actor to be in the ergative case, and the Undergoer in the absolutive, and since this excerpt is a series of events describing what the main protagonists were doing, the Actor-oriented intransitive form nakamati is more appropriate.

Example bkm:Ref448405038 illustrates the cognition verbs intindi ‘understand’, and sat-em ‘comprehend’ in their normal usages with naka. Other cognition verbs in this group include isip ‘think’, demdem ‘remember’, and lipat ‘forget’:

i.v.ir -say cm immediately where money 2 s.gen def.f \\

Finally, the happenstantial affixes may be used to downplay one’s personal achievements. In the following example, the speaker worked very hard to graduate, but uses the happenstantial, as though it were something that “just happened”:

Kaluoy man ta Dyos nakatapos a man ta elementarya. \\
Kaluoy man ta Dyos naka-tapos a man ta elementarya. \\

‘By the mercy of God I was able to finish elementary school.’ [DDWN-C-01 3.13]

intransitive happenstantial irrealis inflection|(

The prefix maka - is the irrealis counterpart of naka-. It also occurs only in intransitive frames in which the single argument is animate, or an inanimate entity that acts in an animate way. Example bkm:Ref447962976 is a near prototypical example of the use of maka -:

Kanen makabali ta sundang daw iya na makagat. \\
Kanen maka-bali ta sundang daw iya na ma-kagat. \\
3 s.abs i.hap.ir -break nabs machete if/when 3 s.gen lk a.hap.ir -bite \\
‘ he (coconut crab) can break a machete if (it is the thing) he bites.’ [DBWE-T-27 2.5]

If the prefix ma - were used here, it would be extremely awkward, and could only mean “ him the machete broke,” since with ma - the absolutive has to be the Undergoer. To preserve the basic semantics using ma - the argument structure would need to change in order to make it clear that the machete is the Patient. Thus, the first part of bkm:Ref447962976 can be considered a detransitive counterpart of bkm:Ref447963964 (see chap:voice for a discussion of detransitive constructions):

Mabali din sundang an. \\
Ma-bali din sundang an. \\
a.hap.ir -break 3 s.erg machete def.m \\
‘S/he can break the machete.’

summary: The passage explains that Kagayanen uses the intransitive happenstantial prefixes naka- and maka- with verbs whose sole argument is animate, even when the action is not truly volitional, such as aging, sensing, or understanding. In these cases, the morphology distinguishes intentional from non-intentional experience, as with dynamic gamati ‘listen’ versus happenstantial nakamati ‘hear,’ and it can also be used to present achievements modestly as if they “just happened.” The irrealis prefix maka- is the counterpart of naka- and appears in similar intransitive frames, including cases where an inanimate entity behaves like an animate one.

The verb tabang, ‘to help’, is one that requires the applicative suffix in its basic transitive usage (see chap:verbclasses-1, sec:volitionaltransitiveroots ). Since there is no applicative on tabang in bkm:Ref447963006, it must be detransitive, and therefore is the counterpart of the transitive construction illustrated in bkm:Ref448035920. Examples bkm:Ref392930212 and bkm:Ref120014811 illustrate maka - with the experiential verbs kita ‘to see/find’ and singngot ‘to smell s.t.’ With perception and cognition verbs, naka - and maka - are the normal detransitive (or “Actor voice”) forms that correspond to na -/ ma - in a transitive frame: For this reason, the ka component of naka - and maka - may be considered an explicit marker of an antipassive construction. However, we find scant independent evidence that this ka is a separate morpheme, for example, it is not used in any other modalities to express an antipassive (our detransitive) construction..

Examples bkm:Ref447964968 through bkm:Ref120014968 illustrate maka - with semantically intransitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic volitional verb stems. These cannot be considered detransitives, because there is no Undergoer, and no transitive counterpart in which the Actor is ergative. They are semantically intransitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic concepts in which the only participant is an Actor, rather than an Undergoer. The dynamic irrealis affixes for these verbs are m - or mag - as in megbeng/magtegeng, miling/mag-iling, and magbakasyon. In these examples the happenstantial maka - expresses potential ability:

External motivation ka -

external motivation|(

The syllable ka has a number of functions in Kagayanen inflectional and stem-forming morphology. In this section, we describe the inflectional prefix ka -, which we gloss as exm for external motivation external motivation. This is a specialized intransitive happenstantial inflection that expresses the idea that there is some external factor that motivates or enables either the situation expressed by the stem, or the speaker’s knowledge of that situation. This ka - may be considered the specialized counterpart of na -, ma -, naka - and maka - since a) it occurs in realis or irrealis contexts, and b) it occurs in all situation types (recall that naka - and maka - describe situations in which the absolutive argument is in control, whereas na - and ma - describe situations in which the absolutive argument is not in control).

In the external motivation usage, ka - expresses that there is some external factor that motivates, or enables (prevents in the case of negative situations) the controller to carry out the activity. For example, in bkm:Ref389056631 a wooden cane enables the actor to walk, and in bkm:Ref396746244 fear prevents the actor from speaking:

Dayon a kamang ta kaoy na sungkod para kapanaw a. \\
Dayon a...-kamang ta kaoy na sungkod para ka-panaw a. \\
right.away 1 s.abs i.r -get nabs wood lk cane
for i.abl -go/walk 1 s.abs \\
In this sentence, the intransitive, realis prefix ga - has been omitted. This is a common feature of daily conversation, and is discussed in bkm:Ref120017222.
`Then I got a wooden cane so that I could walk.’ [EFWN-T-11 15.2]

Pag-abot nay ta baļay, uļa kambaļ katagsa ko ya tak nakulbaan … \\

because a.hap.r -frightened- apl \\
`When we arrived at the house, my cousin could not speak because of being frightened (of something)...' [CBWN-C-19 8.1]

nabs community Nusa i.hap -catch.fish inc nabs two piece \\
`With much good luck, even when I was beginning to go to the shallow sea (along the shore) of the community of Nusa, I was able to catch two more pieces (fish)...’ [EFWN-T-11 8.1]

all.day.long

`So in their hauling water sometimes they stayed all day long. (They) will not be able to come home (all day until late in the afternoon) because of strong winds and large waves.’ [VPWE-T-01 2.8]

The prefix ka - also has an inferential inferential usage. In the context of example bkm:Ref447986985, a fish sees a ship coming and tells all the other fish to hide. After the fish have hidden, example bkm:Ref447986985 occurs, expressing the inference that the boat most likely has passed by. In the sentence after that, the fish all look up and see that the boat in fact is moving away fast. An enablement interpretation of bkm:Ref447986985 is excluded by native speakers. In this context, the speaker (the fish) infers that the situation expressed by the root is true because of the external fact that much time has passed.

Anduni kalambay en bļangay ya en. \\
Anduni ka-lambay en bļangay ya en. \\
now/today i.hap -pass.by cm 2.masted.boat def.f cm \\
‘Now the boat (must have) passed by.’ (Or ‘Now the boat most-likely/feasibly/predictably has passed by.’) [JCON-L-07 5.1]

With the prefix maka - this construction would express a different meaning, namely that the ship ‘will/can/may possibly pass by’, and naka - would mean it ‘has already passed by.’
summary:
The passage describes the Kagayanen prefix **ka-** as an inflectional marker of **external motivation**, used in intransitive happenstantial contexts to show that some outside factor enables or prevents an action or situation. It occurs in both realis and irrealis contexts and across situation types, including cases where winds, fear, luck, or another person’s absence affect what the controller can do.

The text also notes an **inferential** use of ka-, where the speaker infers that an event has occurred because of external evidence such as the passage of time. In this usage, ka- differs from related forms like **maka-** and **naka-**, which have different meanings of possibility or completed action.

affix omission|(

There is a common tendency in Kagayanen conversation for inflectional prefixes ( pa-, ga-, na-, mag-, ma -, and ka- ) to be omitted in certain “candidate environments”. These are the environments in which prefixes may be omitted:

enumerate

Following adverbs such as tapos ‘after’, ubos ‘all used up’, dayon ‘right away’, diritso ‘straight away,’ listo ‘hastily’, sigi ‘continuously’, tudo ‘with all-out effort’, primi ‘always’, uļa ‘negative, realis’, and perhaps others.

In fast or excited speech.

At peaks of narratives, or other contexts that involve tension.

In relative clauses especially when they occur before the head nominal.

In habitual actions.
enumerate

It is clear that this omission of prefixes is “optional” for two reasons. First, such omission never results in ambiguity—speakers are always able to supply the missing form based on contextual factors. Second, sometimes inflectional prefixes do appear in these contexts, with no apparent variation in meaning. A full discourse study may be needed to determine whether there is a consistent pattern as to when prefixes are omitted versus when they are retained. Since most of the examples in this grammar are from natural texts, many have omitted prefixes. We have not edited or flagged these in any way, unless the omission is important to the point being illustrated in the example. Examples bkm:Ref119307770 and bkm:Ref119307774 illustrate affix omission, with the ellipsis character (…) in place of the omitted affix:

Indi no imo kamanga mga blawan an Pedro? \\
Indi no imo … -kamang-a mga blawan an Pedro? \\
where 2 s.erg emph t.r -get- xc pl gold def.m Pedro \\
‘Where did you get the gold, Pedro!?' [CBWN-C-22 8.3]

The following examples illustrate the root, dala, ‘take/carry’, both with bkm:Ref394992438 and without bkm:Ref394992440 the overt transitive realis prefix. The argument structure frame (Actor-ergative and Undergoer-absolutive) makes it clear that both examples are transitive, and the contexts make it clear that both are realis:

‘She took her child to their house.’ (Her child had died, so she carried her back to their house.) [VAWN-T-20 4.5]

…- Daļa nay sawa din daw sawa Lola Maria na patay … \\

[BCWN-C-04 9.1]

This omission is optional and does not create ambiguity, since context makes the intended form clear; prefixes may also appear in the same environments without a change in meaning, though the grammar suggests a fuller discourse study would be needed to determine the distribution.

Hermit Crab tricks Sea Turtle by having many hermit crabs distributed along the race course, so there is always a hermit crab ahead of Sea Turtle and the one that he was racing is waiting for him at the finish line. But Sea Turtle does not know there are many hermit crabs and he can not understand why Hermit Crab is always ahead of him. The verb kita ‘to see’ can be replaced with nakita, and the verb lambayan ‘to pass by’ can be replaced with palambayan or nalambayan, though palambayan is more appropriate in this story.
