summary: The passage contrasts transitive and detransitive verb frames, showing how different prefixes mark tense, aspect, modality, and event type. In the transitive frame, forms with **pa-**, **are-**, **naa-**, and **maa-** express meanings such as past/perfect, future, accidental/careless action, ability, and completed action; in the detransitive frame, corresponding forms like **ga-**, **mag-**, **mare-**, **naka-**, and **maka-** show similar distinctions but with an absolutive subject and optionally a non-absolutive object.

section: Roots describing non-volitional intransitive situations (Classes I – III)
text:
Root Classes I through III described above consist of verbal roots that express non-volitional semantically intransitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic situations. Roots in Classes I and II additionally involve a change of state in the absolutive arguments. The difference between Class I and Class II is that Class I roots express punctual situations (achievements), whereas Class II roots express durative situations (accomplishments). Both Class I and II roots allow a “zero” form (no inflectional affixation) that describes a state that is the result of the situation expressed in the root, for example, the glass is shattered, the sail is torn. Since Class III roots don’t involve a change in state, there is no resultant state form for these roots.

For Class I and II roots, the happenstantial forms express a semantic perfective aspect, for example, the glass shattered/will shatter, the sail tore/will tear. The dynamic forms ( ga - realis and mag - irrealis) occur in Class II and Class III roots. For Class II roots, the dynamic forms describe an inceptive, the sail began to tear, or an imperfective, the sail is tearing, sense. Because Class I roots describe achievements (i.e., they are punctual), they do not allow the inceptive or imperfective senses.

The dominant pattern for Class III roots is that they only occur in the dynamic forms. These verbs for the most part describe activities, for example, the bells are ringing, the fire is flaring up, the weather is getting better. These do not occur in the zero form nor in the happenstantial forms because they do not describe resultant states, or situations that result in a change in state. Occasionally some of these roots may occur in the irrealis happenstantial form, but we have not investigated the conditions under which this may occur.

As will be seen below, volitional activities (Class IV) take both happenstantial and dynamic affixes, but the dynamic affixes seem to be the default forms in basic intransitive frames, and commonly express a semantic perfective aspect. For these verbs, the happenstantial forms express more subtle aspectual or modal senses such as accidentally/carelessly, ability, happenstance, or opportunitive (see chap:verbstructure, sec:verbinflection ).

Because of the patterns described above and illustrated in bkm:Ref148453300 through bkm:Ref148532215, we conclude that non-volitionality and change of state are the core semantic features that underlie the use of the happenstantial modality. At times these core features may be extended into other domains (e.g. change of state may include change of place, as in to fall off accidentally ). The inherent semantics of Class I roots so strongly favor these features that happenstantial modality is (almost) obligatory. Class II roots, on the other hand, may be interpreted as involving either a change of state, or an activity, depending on the context. Such situations may be expressed in either happenstantial or dynamic modalities, with corresponding differences in meaning. Finally, Class III roots so strongly favor the activity feature that dynamic modality is (almost) required.

tab:rootsexpressingnon-volitionalintransitivesituations lists some of the non-volitional, intransitive verbs that fall into these three classes. While there is individual variation throughout the Kagayanen community, and particular roots may “shift” from one Class to another, depending on the communicative needs and creativity of speakers, the classification given here is our best determination of the default, normal usages of these roots. For an English analogy, one may consider such common assertions as “stative verbs do not occur in the progressive aspect.” However, speakers may certainly use normally stative verbs in non-stative senses by putting them in the progressive, for example, “I’m not understanding what you are saying,” or ``she’s believing more and more that...” Such creative usages on the part of speakers do not negate the general fact that stative verbs in English have distinct grammatical properties from non-stative verbs. Analogous class “shifting” probably occurs in every language. Full examples of a few of these from the corpus follow.

In the following examples, the verbs being illustrated are bolded, in Kagayanen and the English translations.
summary:
The passage explains that Classes I–III are non-volitional intransitive verb roots, with Classes I and II involving a change of state and differing in that Class I is punctual while Class II is durative. Classes I and II can appear in a zero form expressing the resulting state, while Class III roots do not, because they describe activities without resultant states and mainly occur in dynamic forms.  

It further argues that non-volitionality and change of state underlie the happenstantial modality: Class I roots strongly favor happenstantial forms, Class II roots can use either happenstantial or dynamic forms depending on context, and Class III roots almost require dynamic forms. The authors note that roots may shift class in actual usage, but the classification reflects their default patterns.

lk continuously cm drift \\
‘But I was on the back of the boat which had turned over that was continuously now adrift.’ [EFWN-T-11 13.3]

In bkm:Ref149230430 we discuss examples of daeb as a volitional, Class IV, root.
summary: The passage shows that some roots can describe either non-volitional events with an inanimate Undergoer or volitional actions with an animate Actor, and their affixation depends on which participant is absolutive. It illustrates this with examples such as flooding, washing ashore, cracking ground, and a boat turning over, and notes that in narrative contexts the happenstantial modality can express a semantic perfective when the event is on the main event line.

section: Roots describing non-volitional intransitive situations (Classes I – III)
text:
Class III intransitive verbs describe atelic activities that result in no change of state. Therefore, these verbs do not normally occur in the resultant state or happenstantial forms:

* Legļeg apoy an. (‘The fire is flamed.’) (STATE) \\
*Naļegļeg apoy an. (‘The fire flamed.’) (ACHIEVEMENT)

Examples bkm:Ref442966831 through bkm:Ref444436899 illustrate Class III verbs from the corpus:

Mga mata ko na galuag paryo ta apoy na gaļegļeg. \\
Mga mata ko na ga-luag paryo ta apoy na ga-ļegļeg. \\
pl eye 1 s.gen lk i.r -watch like nabs fire lk i.r -flame \\
‘My eyes that were watching were like a fire which is flaming.’ [JCOO-T-11 10.1]

Pagkita nay na apoy an gaubļo na sikad gid bakod dabadaba, dayon kay panaog daw mļagan naan punta ta Sintro. \\
Pag-kita nay na apoy an ga-ubļo na sikad gid bakod dabadaba, dayon kay …-panaog daw m-dļagan naan punta ta Sintro. \\
nr.act -see 1 p.excl.gen lk fire def.m i.r -flare.up lk very int big
big.flames right.away 1 p.excl.abs i.r -go.down and i.v.ir -run spat.def going
nabs Central \\
‘When we saw the fire flaring up with very big flames, we immediately went down and ran going to Central.’ [RZWN-T-02 2.9]

Daw gagilek sikad bakod kagi na taning daw gakereg paryo gid ta naakad blengngan din an.\\
Daw ga-gilek sikad bakod kagi na taning daw ga-kereg paryo gid ta na-akad blengngan din an.\\
if/when i.r -angry very big voice lk high.pitch and i.r -shake like
int nabs a.hap.r -come.apart throat 3 s.gen def.m \\
‘When getting angry, it is a very loud high sound and it shakes really like its throat has come apart.’ (This is a description of the sound of a cat.) [JCWE-T-14 13.2]

Bilang pabugtawen no gid kon anay ittaw an na ganarem bag-o no tuturan lampraan. \\
Bilang pa-bugtaw-en no gid kon anay ittaw an na ga-narem bag-o no -tutod-an lampraan. \\
for.example caus -wake- t.ir 2 s.erg int hsy first/for.a.while person def.m lk
i.r -have.ISP before 2 s.erg t.ir -light- apl lamp \\
‘For example, first wake up the person who has Isolated Sleep Paralysis (ISP) before you light a lamp.’ [ETON-C-07 4.5]

Daw gabagting langganay ta simbaan ta miad, tanda na anen en mga gubat. \\
Daw ga-bagting langganay ta simba-an ta miad, tanda na anen en mga gubat. \\
if/when i.r -ring bell nabs worship- nr nabs well sign lk ext.g cm pl raider \\
‘Whenever the bell of the church was ringing hard, it was the sign that the raiders are here.’ [JCWN-T-20]

Daw may gadagbeng na nuļog, isipen no tak yon nan niog na naipo ko. \\
Daw may ga-dagbeng na na-uļog, isip-en no tak yon nan niog na na-ipo ko. \\
if/when ext.in i.r -thud lk a.hap.r -fall think/count- t.ir 2 s.erg because d 3 abs d 3 abs.pr coconut lk a.hap.r -pick 1 s.erg \\
‘If something falls making a thud sound, count it because that very one is the coconut I have picked.’ (The speaker climbs a tree to get coconuts and he tells the blind guy on the ground to count how many thuds he hears because that will be the coconuts that he picks and lets fall to the ground. But the one who climbs the tree keeps falling out and so the blind guy counts each time the other guy falls out of the tree thinking it is a coconut.) [CBWN-C-15 4.4]
summary: Class III intransitive verbs denote atelic activities that do not involve a change of state, so they normally do not appear in resultant-state or happenstantial forms. The passage illustrates this class with corpus examples of ongoing actions or sounds, such as flaming, flaring up, shaking, ringing, and thudding.

section: Roots describing non-volitional intransitive situations (Classes I – III)
subsection: Class I-III roots in transitive and detransitive frames
text:
Most Class I-III verbs can be used in a transitive frame with no transitivizing stem-forming morphology (applicative or causative). In this case they express direct causation. Example ex:hasdissolved illustrates the Class II root tunaw ‘to dissolve/melt’ in its basic intransitive frame, while example bkm:Ref395126196 illustrates the same root in a transitive, causative, frame:

Natunaw tubuyong an. \\
Na-tunaw tubuyong an. \\
a.hap.r -dissolve manioc.flour def.m \\
‘This manioc flour has dissolved.’

Tunawen no anay tubuyong an para pangmiroļ. \\
Tunaw-en no anay tubuyong an para pang-miroļ. \\
dissolve- t.ir 2 s.erg first/for.a.while manioc.flour def.m for inst -clothes.starch \\
‘ Dissolve please the manioc flour for use as starch.’

Similarly, example bkm:Ref398385527 illustrates the verb tumba ‘to fall over’ in its basic, intransitive frame, while bkm:Ref398385530 illustrates the same verb in a transitive, causative frame:

Natumba kaoy ya naan ta tinanem nay na mga gulay. \\
Na-tumba kaoy ya naan ta t<in>anem nay na mga gulay. \\
a.hap.r -fall.over tree def.f spat.def nabs < nr.res >plant
1 p.excl.gen lk pl vegetables \\
‘The tree fell over on our planted vegetables.’

Patumba din kaoy ya naan ta tinanem nay na mga gulay. \\
Pa-tumba din kaoy ya naan ta t<in>anem nay na mga gulay. \\
t.r -fall.over 3 s.erg tree def.f spat.def nabs < nr.res >plant
1 p.excl.gen lk pl vegetables \\
‘S/he felled the tree (on our planted vegetables).’

Example bkm:Ref119509106 illustrates leddang ‘to sink’ in a transitive form, meaning ‘cause to sink’:

Paleddang ta pirata pambot nay ya. \\
Pa-leddang ta pirata pambot nay ya. \\
t.r -sink erg pirate motor.boat 1 p.excl.gen def.f \\
‘The pirates sank our motor boat.’

We know that the prefix pa - in bkm:Ref398385530 and bkm:Ref119509106 is the transitive, realis pa - rather than the causative for several reasons. First, if pa - in these examples were the causative, the predicates would imply indirect causation, as though the boat retained some responsibility for its own sinking. Second, this pa - is not retained in the irrealis ( bkm:Ref395126196, bkm:Ref123281189 ) or detransitive (Actor voice) form bkm:Ref123281290:

Leddangen nyo lunday an tak sikad bao. \\
Leddang-en nyo lunday an tak sikad bao. \\
sink- t.ir 2 p.erg outrigger.canoe def.m because very odor \\
‘Sink the outrigger canoe because it smells bad.’ (The outrigger canoe probably has the odor of rotten fish and sinking it will wash it out.)

Galeddang mga pirata ta pambot nay ya. \\
Ga-leddang mga pirata ta pambot nay ya. \\
i.r -sink pl pirate nabs motor.boat 1 p.excl.gen def.f \\
‘The pirates sank our motor boat.’

* gapaleddang...

Finally, there is a causative form of this root, expressed with the causative prefix pa - in addition to the transitive inflections (realis in bkm:Ref123281737 and irrealis in bkm:Ref148779410 ):

Papaleddang din ki yaken pambot ya. \\
Pa-pa-leddang din ki yaken pambot ya. \\
t.r - caus -sink 3 s.erg obl.p 1s motor.boat def.f \\
‘S/he caused/let/allowed me to sink the motor boat.’

Paleddangen din ki yaken pambot ya. \\
Pa-leddang-en din ki yaken pambot ya. \\
caus -sink- t.ir 3 s.erg obl.p 1s motor.boat def.f \\
‘S/he will cause/let/allow me to sink the motor boat.’

Most or all verbs that describe transitive situations may occur in an intransitive frame in which the absolutive is the controller of the situation and the Undergoer is either omitted or placed in an oblique role, marked by a pre-nominal particle ta or ki. These are similar in function to English expressions such as Frodo already ate, she drank of the water, he kicked at the ball and so on. These are all grammatically intransitive expressions of semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic situations. In each example the meaning involves an Undergoer, but because of the communicative context, the speaker chooses to “downplay” or omit reference to the Undergoer. Analogous constructions exist in Kagayanen, with the difference being that the verbs are explicitly marked morphologically as intransitive. We have described such constructions as detransitive constructions because they present semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic situations in grammatically intransitive forms (see chap:verbstructure, sec:grammaticaltransitivity, and chap:voice, sec:actorvoice ).

Since Class I, II and III roots may occur in transitive frames, expressing direct causation, they may also occur in detransitive frames, with the causer as the absolutive and the Undergoer either omitted or expressed in the non-absolutive case:

Class I: uļog ‘to fall’: \\
Ta pagpadayon, gauļog a pa gid ta ake na paan daw naylon.\\
Ta pag-pa-dayon, ga-uļog a pa gid ta ake na paan daw naylon.\\
nabs nr.act - caus -continue i.r -fall 1 s.abs inc int nabs 1 s.gen lk
bait and fish.line \\
‘In continuing, I dropped yet again my bait and fish line.’ [EFWN-T-11 6.1]

Class II basa ‘to get wet’ and Class III sablig ‘to splash’ and takļap ‘to get covered’: \\
Duma an gasablig ta waig daw gabasa ta sako daw labyog ki Pedro na takļap ta atep aged mapatay apoy an.\\
Duma an ga-sablig ta waig daw ga-basa ta sako daw …-labyog ki Pedro na …- takļap ta atep aged ma-patay apoy an.\\
others def.m i.r -splash nabs water and i.r -wet nabs sack and t.r -throw obl.p Pedro lk i.r -cover.over nabs roof so.that a.hap.ir -extinguish fire def.m \\
‘Others splashed water and wetted some sacks and threw (them) to Pedro to cover over the roof so that the fire will exinguish.’ [RZWN-T-02 3.14]
summary:
Most Class I–III verbs can appear in a transitive frame without transitivizing morphology, where they express direct causation, as shown by examples of *tunaw* ‘dissolve,’ *tumba* ‘fall over,’ and *leddang* ‘sink.’ The passage also argues that the prefix *pa-* in some of these forms is the transitive realis marker, not the causative, because it is absent in irrealis and detransitive forms; true causatives are formed with *pa-* added to the transitive inflection.

It further notes that many semantically transitive situations can be expressed in grammatically intransitive, detransitive frames, with the absolutive participant controlling the event and the Undergoer omitted or marked obliquely. Class I–III roots can likewise occur in these detransitive constructions, where the causer is absolutive and the Undergoer is non-absolutive or absent.

section: Roots describing volitional intransitive situations (Class IV)
text:
The next major Class of semantically intransitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic verbs involve volition on the part of the only obligatory argument. In other words, the absolutive argument refers to the participant that controls the situation. These include the following:

Note that all of the roots in bkm:Ref120784669 describe activities; that is volitional situations that do not result in a change of state. Therefore, it is not surprising that the basic affixes for these verbs are the dynamic ga - realis and m - or mag - for irrealis modality. In contrast to the non-volitional intransitive verbs, many of these verbs, but not all, can occur with the m - prefix, in which case the root-initial consonant drops out. Another characteristic of these volitional intransitive verbs is that in happenstantial modality, they occur with naka -/ maka -, ka - (and ma - in the hypothetical/polite usage), but do not occur with the ambitransitive forms na- or ma-. Thus we can make the generalization that in happenstantial modality, constructions in which the absolutive is an Actor take naka-/maka - and those in which the absolutive is an Undergoer take na-/ma -.

Dynamic: \\
Gapuay kay uļa nang lugay daw mag-igma. \\
Ga-puay kay uļa nang lugay daw mag-igma. \\
i.r -rest 1 p.excl.abs neg.r only/just long.time and i.ir -lunch \\
‘We were resting/rested for a short time and ate lunch.’ [DBWN-T-24 3.2]

Happenstantial: \\
Nakapuay kay uļa nang lugay. \\
Naka-puay kay uļa nang lugay. \\
i.hap.r -rest 1 p.excl.abs neg.r only/just long.time \\
‘We happened to rest for a short time.’ \\
‘We were able to rest for a short time.’ \\
‘We got to rest for a short time.’ \\
‘We have rested for a short time.’ \\
*Napuay kay uļa nang lugay.

Dynamic: \\
Gatinir a annem buļan ta maistra i. \\
Ga-tinir a annem buļan ta maistra i. \\
i.r -stay 1 s.abs six month nabs teacher def.n \\
‘I stayed for six months with the teacher.’ [DBWN-T-21 2.6]

Happenstantial: \\
Nakatinir a annem buļan. \\
Naka-tinir a annem buļan. \\
i.hap.r -stay 1 s.abs six month \\
‘I happened to stay for six months.’ \\
‘I was able to stay for six months.’ \\
‘I got to stay for six months.’ \\
‘I have stayed for six months.’ \\
*Natinir a annem buļan ta maistra i.

Another grammatical difference between non-volitional and volitional intransitive roots is that non-volitional roots may easily occur in a transitive frame to express direct causation (see bkm:Ref148856716 above). Class IV roots, on the other hand, almost always require explicit transitivizing stem-forming morphology, either causative ( pa -) or applicative (- an, - i ) in order to occur in a transitive frame. This is because the causee is often animate, and therefore retains some control over the situation. However, if the causee is inanimate or otherwise incapable of controlling the situation, some of these roots may express direct causation in a transitive frame without the stem-forming causative prefix. For example, roots such as balik ‘return’, tago ‘hide’ and others that describe motion to a destination (return to a place, hide in a place) when used intransitively describe volitional situations bkm:Ref148946728. When the same roots describe caused situations in which the causee is capable of exercising some control over the situation, the causative prefix is used, as in bkm:Ref148968257. However, the same verbs may occur in a transitive bkm:Ref148946793 or detransitive bkm:Ref148946893 construction with no causative prefix, in which case they imply that the causee is probably inanimate, and therefore has no control or volition. In other words, as with root Classes I-III, this construction expresses direct causation:

Intransitive (volitional): \\
Lugay na tapos kay ipo atis en gabalik kami naan baybay. \\
Lugay na tapos kay ipo atis en ga-balik kami naan baybay. \\
long.time lk finish 1 p.excl.abs pick sugar.apple cm
i.r -return 1 p.excl.abs spat.def beach \\
‘After some time when we finished picking sugar apples, we returned to the beach.’ [DBON-C-06 6.1]

Indirect causative (volitional causee): \\
Papabalik ko kanen an naan ta baļay danen. \\
Pa-pa-balik ko kanen an naan ta baļay danen. \\
t.r - caus -return 1 s.erg 3 s.abs def.m spat.def nabs house 3 p.gen \\
‘I made/let him/her return to their house.’

Direct causation (non-volitional causee):\\
Pabalik ko en kuguran din ya naan ta baļay danen. \\
Pa-balik ko en kugod-an din ya naan ta baļay danen. \\
t.r -return 1 s.erg cm grate.coconut- nr 3 s.gen def.f spat.def nabs house 3 p.gen \\
‘I returned his/her coconut grater to their house.’

Detransitive of causative: \\
Gabalik aren ta kuguran din ya naan ta baļay danen. \\
Ga-balik aren ta kugod-an din ya naan ta baļay danen. \\
i.r -return 1 s.abs nabs grate.coconut- nr 3 s.gen def.f spat.def nabs house 3 p.gen \\
‘I returned his/her coconut grater to their house.’

Other volitional motion verbs of Class IV, such as larga ‘depart’, never take a location as an oblique or Undergoer argument ( bkm:Ref148793705 ). For such verbs, a destination is expressed in a complement clause bkm:Ref148793741, preceded by the linker/complementizer na:

Ambaļ ta rais ya marga gid kon tak galarga kon en duma ya na bļangay. \\
Ambaļ ta rais ya m-larga gid kon tak ga-larga kon en duma ya na bļangay. \\
say nabs captain def.f i.v.ir -depart int hsy because
i.r -depart hsy cm other def.f lk 2.mast.boat \\
‘The captain said to really depart because the other two-mast boats are already departing.’ [VAWN-T-18 3.5]

Galarga kay kan-o na miling Iloilo. \\
Ga-larga kay kan-o na m-iling Iloilo. \\
i.r -depart 1 p.excl.abs previously lk i.v.ir -go Iloilo \\
‘ We departed previously to go to Iloilo.’

The volitional intransitive verb, tago ‘to hide’, may express a location optionally as an oblique ( bkm:Ref148793817 ), but this is not a detransitive of direct causation because it cannot mean ``the younger sibling hid a well":
summary:
The passage describes a class of semantically intransitive verbs whose single absolutive argument is volitional and controls the situation. These roots are typically activity verbs with no change of state, so they take dynamic realis/irrealis affixes and, in happenstantial modality, use naka-/maka- rather than na-/ma-; volitional intransitives also differ from non-volitional ones in that they usually need explicit causative or applicative morphology to appear in transitive frames unless the causee is inanimate and thus non-controlling.

It further notes that some motion verbs in this class can express direct causation without a causative prefix when the causee lacks volition, but with animate causees they require causative marking. Other volitional motion verbs, such as larga ‘depart’, do not take a location as an oblique or Undergoer, instead expressing destination in a complement clause, and tago ‘hide’ can optionally take a location obli

section: Roots describing volitional intransitive situations (Class IV)
text:
Piro mangngod i gatago naan ta bubon para dili makita.\\
Piro mangngod i ga-tago naan ta bubon para dili ma-kita.\\
but younger.sibling def.n i.r -hide spat.def nabs well
for neg.ir a.hap.ir -see \\
‘But the younger sibling hid in the well in order not to be seen.’ [BCWN-C-04 6.8]

The location of hiding may be absolutive, but only with the addition of the applicative - an:

Pataguan din bubon ya. \\
Pa-tago-an din bubon ya. \\
t.r -hide- apl 3 s.erg well def.f \\
‘S/he hid in the well.’

Example bkm:Ref148947015 illustrates the volitional intransitive motion root, iling ‘to go’, with an obligatory destination expressed as an oblique bkm:Ref148947015 or as absolutive with applicative, bkm:Ref148947027 and bkm:Ref148947052:

Kanen i giling ta yi na puļo paagi ta pagsakay ta lunday para manglaya.\\
Kanen i ga-iling ta yi na puļo paagi ta pag-sakay ta lunday para ma-ng-laya.\\
3 s.abs def.n i.r -go nabs d 1 adj lk island by.means nabs nr.act -ride nabs outrigger.canoe for a.hap.ir-pl -cast.net \\
‘He went to this island by means of riding an outrigger canoe in order to cast-net fish.’ [VAWN-T-17 2.2]

Pamiro, first time, ko na pailingan Puerto. \\
Pamiro, first time, ko na pa-iling-an Puerto. \\
first first time 1 s.erg lk t.r -go- apl Puerto. \\
‘First, first time, I went to Puerto.’ [BMON-C-05 1.5]

Kaysan bisan puon ta mga darko na mga kaoy paryo ta baliti, kumpang o bugo pailingan daw ambaļen dya na, “Anen en bata an.”\\
Kaysan bisan puon ta mga darko na mga kaoy paryo ta baliti, kumpang o bugo pa-iling-an daw ambaļ-en dya na, “Anen en bata an.”\\
sometimes even trunk nabs pl large. pl lk pl trees same/like nabs ficus wild.almond or garuga.floribunda t.r -go- apl and say- t.ir d 4 loc lk ext.g cm child def.m \\
‘Sometimes even the trunks of large trees like ficus, wild almond or garuga floribunda (they) go to and say there, “Here is the child.”' [JCWE-T-15 4.4]

Other volitional intransitive, mostly motion+manner roots, may also occur in a transitive frame without valence increasing morphology, but with different semantic effect. For these verbs, the meaning in a grammatically transitive frame is that the Undergoer is the destination of the Actor’s motion, or something retrieved by the Actor. For example luoy ‘to swim’ with transitive inflection, paluoy or luuyon, means ‘to swim to a specific place’ or ‘to swim to get a specific object’. Other verbs that function similarly are daik ‘to crawl’, eseb ‘to go underwater’, panaw ‘to go/walk’, and dļagan ‘to run’.

Di mugpa ka daw luuyon no dya ta Nusa. \\
Di m-tugpa ka daw luoy-en no dya ta Nusa. \\
inj i.v.ir -jump.down 2 s.abs and swim- t.ir 2 s.erg d4loc nabs Nusa \\
`So, what else, won’t you jump down (in the sea) and swim to get them, (shells that were left behind, known from context) there in Nusa?’ [DBWN-T-24 5.2]

Paeseb din sundang an na nuļog na gatebteb ta tilik. \\
Pa-eseb din sundang an na na-uļog na ga-tebteb ta tilik. \\
t.r -go.underwater 3 s.erg machete def.m lk a.hap.r -fall lk i.r -chop nabs sea.urchin \\
‘He went underwater to get the machete that fell when (he was) chopping sea urchin.’

Most Class IV roots can take both happenstantial and dynamic inflections, depending on whether the scene being described involves volition or not. A short list of such roots is given in bkm:Ref148949595:

The following are a few examples of such roots in context. In example bkm:Ref148966154, the root seddep ‘go into a small space’ is used in a transitive frame with happenstantial modality. In this case the ants are presented as a “substance” that happened to enter, was able to enter, or had entered the speaker’s ear. In example bkm:Ref148966156 the same verb occurs in dynamic (volitional) modality. In this case, the ants are presented as “actors”, purposely entering the speaker’s ear:

Naseddepan ta geyem talinga ko i. \\
Na-seddep-an ta geyem talinga ko i. \\
a.hap.r -go.in.small.space- apl nabs ant ear 1 s.gen def.n \\
‘The ant(s) happened to go inside my ear.’

Paseddepan ta geyem talinga ko i. \\
Pa-seddep-an ta geyem talinga ko i. \\
t.r -go.in.small.space- apl nabs ant ear 1 s.gen def.n \\
‘The ant(s) went inside my ear.’

Examples bkm:Ref148966256 and bkm:Ref148965959 illustrate this same root, without the applicative suffix, in dynamic modality:

Ta, ake na duma gaseddep ta baļas an… \\
Ta, ake na duma ga-seddep ta baļas an… \\
so 1 s.gen lk companion i.r -go.in.small.space nabs forest def.m \\
‘So my companion went into the forest…’ [NFWN-T-01 2.10]

Example bkm:Ref148965959 is from a story about a raid on the island of Cagayancillo. A group of Kagayanens were hiding in a cave (referred to as a “hole”), and the attackers set a fire at the entrance to the cave such that everyone inside died except one woman. This was a volitional act on the part of the raiders, though the absolutive argument, the smoke, is not itself volitional:

Aso ta apoy gaseddep en ta lungag… \\
Aso ta apoy ga-seddep en ta lungag… \\
smoke nabs fire i.r -go.in.small.space cm nabs hole \\
‘The smoke of the fire went inside the hole….’ [JCWN-T-25 2.11]

The following are some examples of daeb ‘to turn face down’ expressing volitional intransitive situations:

Gadaeb en bata an. \\
Ga-daeb en bata an. \\
i.r -turn.over cm child def.m \\
‘The child turned over face down.’

Padaeban a din na gatanuga. \\
Pa-daeb-an a din na ga-tanuga. \\
t.r -turn.over- apl 1 s.abs 3 s.erg lk i.r -sleep \\
‘S/He turned over on me when sleeping.’

Nadaeban a din na gatanuga. \\
Na-daeb-an a din na ga-tanuga. \\
a.hap.r -turn.over- apl 1 s.abs 3 s.erg lk i.r -sleep \\
‘S/He happened to turn over on me when sleeping.’
summary:
The passage shows that several motion and posture verbs can appear in transitive frames, often with applicative **-an**, which makes the location or destination absolutive. For volitional intransitive roots like **tago** ‘hide’ and **iling** ‘go,’ the applicative marks the place hidden in or the destination, while some verbs such as **luoy** ‘swim’ can also mean ‘swim to a place’ or ‘swim to get something’ when used transitively.

It also explains that many Class IV roots alternate between happenstantial and dynamic inflections depending on whether the event is nonvolitional or volitional. Examples like **seddep** ‘go into a small space’ and **daeb** ‘turn face down’ show that the same root can describe either something that happened involuntarily or an intentional action, with or without applicative morphology.

section: Roots describing volitional intransitive situations (Class IV)
text:
As evidence that daeb falls into both root Class II and root Class IV, we note that when the absolutive is inanimate, it is possible to use the bare root as a resultative form bkm:Ref149299861 (characteristic of Class II), but when the absolutive is animate, the same form is simply ungrammatical ex:childturnedover (characteristic of Class IV):

Daeb pambot an. \\
daeb pambot an 1cm \\
turn.over motor.boat def.m \\
‘The motor boat is turned over.’

daeb bata an \\
turn.over child def.m \\
(‘The child is turned over.’)
summary: The passage argues that **daeb** shows properties of both root Class II and root Class IV. When the absolutive is inanimate, the bare root can be used as a resultative form, but when the absolutive is animate, the same form is ungrammatical. This contrast is illustrated with a grammatical example involving a motor boat and an ungrammatical example involving a child.

section: Roots describing non-volitional transitive situations (Class V)
text:
The last four classes of verbal roots we will discuss in this chapter can all be characterized as semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic. None of them occur in basic intransitive frames, their only intransitive forms being detransitives. Class V roots describe non-volitional transitive situations. For the most part, these roots do not easily occur in dynamic modality. Many of these describe perception, cognition and emotion. As such they are discussed in more detail in chap:verbclasses-2. There are two subclasses of Class V roots. Subclass Va do not require the applicative -an in the basic transitive form (though

some allow it), while Subclass Vb roots all require the applicative suffix. Example bkm:Ref150247189 lists a subset of these roots. Examples in context follow.

The root agi may take dynamic affixes, in which case it expresses the meaning of ‘to pass somewhere’, and falls into Class IV. However, when occurring with happenstantial affixes, it has the somewhat idiomatic meaning of ‘to experience’, as a sickness (example bkm:Ref150244144 ). In this case the experiencer is expressed as ergative, and the source of the experience as absolutive. Therefore in this usage it falls into Subclass Vb:

Ta buļan na galigad naagian ko a masakit na swalem. \\
Ta buļan na ga-ligad na-agi-an ko a masakit na swalem. \\

The verb igo ‘hit/strike’ describes the non-volitional act of hitting an object, as a tree branch falling on a parked car, or a rock hitting a window. It may or may not be the result of a volitional act of throwing, shooting, etc. (as in bkm:Ref150345606 ), but the event of hitting is presented as happenstantial.

Naigo ko kalilawan i. \\
Na-igo ko kalilawan i. \\
a.hap.r -hit 1 s.erg Philippine.oriole def.n \\
‘I hit the Philippine oriole.’ (He was shooting at it with a slingshot.) [MEWN-T-02 4.1] \\
*paigo *gaigo
summary:
The passage describes the last four classes of verbal roots as semantically transitive and notes that they do not occur in basic intransitive frames, only in detransitive forms. Class V roots express non-volitional transitive situations, often involving perception, cognition, or emotion, and are divided into two subclasses: Va roots may optionally take the applicative -an, while Vb roots require it.

It further explains that some roots have different meanings or class behavior depending on affixation: for example, *agi* can mean ‘to pass somewhere’ with dynamic affixes but ‘to experience’ with happenstantial affixes, and *igo* refers to a happenstantial hitting event rather than a volitional act. Examples show that these Class V meanings are marked by specific affix patterns and argument roles.

section: Roots describing volitional transitive situations (Classes VI-VIII)
text:
Class VI is the majority class of semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic roots. It is distinguished by the use of the suffix - en /- on for the transitive, irrealis inflection. Classes VII and VIII employ the “zero” allomorph of the transitive, irrealis inflection. Semantically, Class VI contains, for the most part, roots that describe transitive volitional accomplishments in which the Undergoer is completely affected by the situation. Classes VII and VIII describe situations in which the Undergoer does not undergo a complete change of state. Class VII for the most part contains roots that involve transfer of a theme (expressed as absolutive in a transitive non-applicative construction) to a recipient or destination. Class VIII is distinguished grammatically by requiring the applicative suffix -an in its basic transitive construction. Roots in this class describe situations in which the Undergoer is only partially, superficially or invisibly affected by the situation.

tab:rootsthattaketwodistincttransitiveirrealisinflections-1 lists several transitive, volitional verbs according to which of these three classes they fall into. \\

Another distinguishing factor among semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic roots has to do with the use of the transitive deontic prefix i-. The roots listed in bkm:Ref447111587 are all Class VI verbs that can occur with i - rather than - en /- on. Notice that the only difference between root+- en and i- +root is that with i- +root there is a deontic meaning. The argument structures are the same—the Actor is ergative and Undergoer (X) is absolutive. Therefore for these, verbs i - may be thought of as the deontic modality replacement for - en /- on:

For Class VI verbs that describe situations that typically involve an instrument, the prefix i - may have an instrumental applicative meaning (see chap:voice, sec:instrumentalvoice ), in addition to deontic modality. That is to say, the roots in bkm:Ref148965668 partially overlap with those in bkm:Ref447111587. For these verbs, i- may be considered the deontic modality “instrumental voice” replacement for - en /- on:

Verbs for which i - selects an Instrument as the absolutive argument: \\
iasod ‘have to pound grain with X \\
iakid ‘have to serve food with X’ \\
ibegkes ‘have to bundle things with X’ \\

igeļet ‘have to cut something with X’ \\

Finally, for another subset of Class VI roots, i - may also function as a deontic modality benefactive applicative marker. We can discern no relevant semantic commonality to this group of roots that is not also shared by many other roots.

Verbs for which i - selects a Beneficiary or Recipient as the absolutive argument: \\
iakid ‘have to serve food to X’ \\
igeļet ‘have to cut something for X’ \\
ikidlas ‘have to cut leaves in long strips for X’ \\
iluto ‘have to cook something for X

Independently of the potential applicative uses of i-, it always expresses deontic modality. Therefore we conclude that deontic modality is its major function.

summary:
Class VI comprises the majority of semantically transitive roots and is marked by the transitive irrealis suffix -en/-on; these roots typically describe volitional accomplishments in which the Undergoer is completely affected. In contrast, Classes VII and VIII use the zero allomorph and describe situations where the Undergoer is not completely changed; Class VII often involves transfer to a recipient or destination, while Class VIII requires the applicative suffix -an and involves only partial, superficial, or invisible affect on the Undergoer.

The prefix i- can replace -en/-on with Class VI verbs, usually adding deontic meaning while keeping the same argument structure. In some verbs it also has instrumental or benefactive applicative functions, but the text concludes that its main function is deontic modality.

section: Roots distinguished by the dynamic, intransitive, irrealis inflections
text:
As mentioned and exemplified in chap:verbstructure, sec:verbinflection, the dynamic, intransitive, irrealis inflections distinguish two groups of verb roots. Verbs in the majority group only allow the prefix mag - while minority group verbs allow either mag - or m-. There are no roots that we are aware of that take only m-. These two groups correlate with the eight root classes discussed in bkm:Ref148856716 through bkm:Ref150248001 in the following way: Classes II, III, and V only allow mag -, while some verbs in classes IV, VI, VII, and, VIII allow m- in addition to mag-. Recall that Class I roots do not take the dynamic affixes, therefore do not fall into either of these groups.

The distinction between verbs that allow m- and those that do not ( tab:twogroupsofverbalroots ) is partly structural, partly semantic, and partly just lexical. On the structural side, verb roots that begin with the syllable li, or nasal consonants ( n or ng ) do not allow m -, regardless of their semantics. On the semantic side, the minority group includes semantically intransitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic motion verbs, and other volitional activity verbs (see ). These verbs take m - as their basic form, and mag - only to express intended/planned or more distant future situations (see below). Many semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic verbs in the minority group are usually expressed in a detransitive frame, and imply a particular Patient or a highly predictable set of possible Patients. For example, bunak ‘to launder’ implies clothing as the Patient, kaan ‘eat’ implies food as the Patient, inem ‘drink’, implies liquid, asod ‘pound (grain)’, and sillig ‘sweep (floor or yard)’. The majority group also includes inherently transitive verbs that impose fewer semantic restrictions on the Patient, and which usually occur with an overt, often human, Patient. These include silot ‘punish’, basoļ ‘scold’, bat-eg ‘choke’, biag ‘capture’, bļebed ‘wrap around’, biak ‘split s.t.’, bilin ‘leave behind’, bitay ‘hang s.t. up’, bugbog ‘hit’, and bugno ‘greet’. Other semantic types that make up the minority group are listed in tab:twogroupsofverbalroots. These include verbs of position ( tindeg ‘to stand’, tuwad ‘to bend over’, taliad ‘to bend backwards’ etc.), verbs of intentional visual perception ( sil-ing ‘to peek inside’, tan -aw ‘to look at’, luag ‘to watch’ etc.), verbs of utterance ( singgit ‘to shout’, isturya ‘to talk’, sugid ‘to tell’ etc.), and others. These semantic characterizations are very general and variable. Apparent “exceptions” exist in both groups. For this reason, we say that the groups are partially “just lexical” — there appear to be no synchronic motivations for some of their members. tab:twogroupsofverbalroots lists a few verbs in each of these groups. It must be kept in mind that any verb root can appear with intransitive affixation (see chap:voice, and chap:verbstructure, sec:grammaticaltransitivity ).

summary: The passage describes two groups of verb roots distinguished by dynamic, intransitive, irrealis inflection: most roots take only the prefix **mag-**, while a smaller group allows either **mag-** or **m-**, and no known roots take only **m-**. This pattern correlates partly with root class, and partly with structure, semantics, and lexical idiosyncrasy: roots beginning with **li**, **n**, or **ng** do not allow **m-**, while the minority group includes various intransitive, motion, volitional activity, and some semitransitive verbs that often imply a predictable patient. The author emphasizes that the grouping is not fully predictable, since there are exceptions and any verb root can appear with intransitive affixation.

‘It has no mouth, it has no nose, it has no eyes, but it’s always teaching/pointing to what others will not see. Answer: finger.’ (The Kagayanen word tudlo can be either a verb meaning to teach or point to something or a noun meaning finger.) [SFWR-L-05 1.1-2]
summary: The passage shows that several Group 2 verbs from Classes IV, VI, VII, and VIII can take either **m-** or **mag-** as the intransitive irrealis form. In some examples the two forms have no clear meaning difference, but **m-** may convey a more immediate or inevitable situation, while **mag-** often appears in more general or habitual contexts, sometimes alongside another clause.

text: In this chapter we describe a few semantically motivated verb classes not mentioned in chap:verbclasses-1. In many cases, these classes have characteristics of the major classes mentioned in chap:verbclasses-1, but all exhibit some distinctive morphosyntactic properties that warrant their separate treatment. Since this chapter takes a “semantics prior” approach, the section headings describe particularly salient situation types, and the content of each section describes the constructions that characteristically express such situations.
summary: This chapter introduces several semantically motivated verb classes that were not discussed earlier, because although they share features with the major verb classes, they also have distinctive morphosyntactic properties that justify separate treatment. Following a “semantics prior” approach, the chapter is organized by salient situation types, and each section describes the constructions typically used to express them.

text:
Meteorological situations are those which describe weather and other natural conditions. They typically have no actor or undergoer participants, and so technically are not semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic or intransitive. In Kagayanen, predicates describing many meterological and other natural phenomena do not require a distinct absolutive argument. Bare roots in such situations are usually inflected with affixes from the intransitive, dynamic set:

Isya na mapon guran ta dakmeļ. \\
Isya na mapon ga-uran ta dakmeļ. \\
one lk afternoon i.r -rain nabs thick \\
‘One afternoon it was raining heavily (lit. thickly).’ [JCWN-L-33 27.1]

Kabay pa na mag-uran. \\
Kabay pa na mag-uran. \\
may.it.be inc cm i.ir -rain \\
‘May it (be that it will) rain.’ (I hope it will rain.)

Mag-alas dos kagaen, gulpi nang galinaw. \\
Mag-alas dos kagaen, gulpi nang ga-linaw. \\
i.ir -o’clock two before.daybreak suddenly just i.r -calm \\
‘It was almost two o’clock before dawn just suddenly the (sea) became calm.’ [VAWN-T-18 5.3]

Naambaļ ta manakem daw magtaliktik gani mian angin an, mian ta mait, magbagyo gid. \\
Na-ambaļ ta manakem daw mag-taliktik gani mian angin an, mian ta mait, mag-bagyo gid. \\
a.hap.r -say nabs older if/when i.ir -light.rain truly northeast.wind wind def.m northeast.wind nabs season i.ir -typhoon int \\
‘The older ones have said when it rains lightly the wind is the northeast wind, the northeast wind season, it will really typhoon.’ [PCON-C-01 2.6]

Happenstantial inflections are normally disallowed with bare roots expressing meteorological phenomena:

Nadlaw en anduni. \\
Na-adlaw en anduni. \\
a.hap.r -day/sun cm now/today \\
(‘It is sunny now/today.’)

Madlaw en kani. \\
Ma-adlaw en kani. \\
a.hap.ir -day/sun cm later \\
(`It will be sunny later.’)

Roots describing meteorological phenomena may take applicative morphology, in which case a typically animate affected participant occurs in the absolutive. The applicative stem is then inflected in happenstantial modality. This is a kind of experiential construction in which the experiencer of the situation is the undergoer (exs. ex:travelling - ex:seaweed ):

Nalinawan kami i ta ame na pagbyai. \\
Na-linaw-an kami i ta ame na pag-byai. \\
a.hap.r -calm- apl 1 p.excl.abs def.n nabs 1 p.excl.gen lk nr.act -travel \\
‘(It) happened to become calm on us during our traveling.’

Naadlawan kay en na munta uma. \\
Na-adlaw-an kay en na munta uma. \\
a.hap.r -adlaw- apl 1 p.excl.abs cm lk toward field \\
‘(It) became sunny on us when going to the field.’

Naadlawan a, tapos nauranan man. Busa, yaken nalagnat aren. \\
Na-adlaw-an a, tapos na-uran-an man. Busa, yaken na-lagnat aren. \\
a.hap.r -adlaw- apl 1 s.abs afterwards a.hap.r -rain- apl also so
1 s.abs a.hap.r -fever 1 s.abs \\
`It was sunny on me, afterwards it rained (on me) also. So, I had become feverish.’ [MBON-T-07 2.12]

While the absolutive in an applicative meteorological construction is typically human, example ex:seaweed illustrates that it need not be. In this example guso ‘agar seaweed’ is the absolutive:

Guso i daw maadlawan ta darwa nang na oras ta takas gayem-ek. \\
Guso i daw ma-adlaw-an ta darwa nang na oras ta takas ga-yem-ek. \\
agar.seaweed def.n if/when a.hap.ir -day/sun- apl nabs two only/just lk hours nabs up.hill i.r -soft \\
`The agar seaweed when in the sunshine for just two hours on the shore it becomes soft.’ [MEWE-T-01 8.2]

Example bkm:Ref149029627 illustrates the root uran ‘rain’ in a dynamic transitive construction, with causative and applicative affixes. Note that the absolutive is the sun-dried corn:

Papauranan ko nang binaļad ya na mais. \\
Pa-pa-uran-an ko nang b<in>aļad ya na mais. \\
t.r-caus -rain- apl 1 s.erg only/just < nr.res >dry.in.sun def.f lk corn \\
‘I just let it rain on the sun-dried corn.’

Example bkm:Ref149030144 illustrates a kind of reflexive construction. This is not an experiential construction (i.e., there is no applicative marker indicating the absolutive is the experiencer of the situation), but the implication is that the speaker “let it rain” on himself while hunting (see chap:voice, sec:causatives for this reflexive use of the detransitive causative ga-pa- or mag-pa- ):

Gapauran a nang gibii. \\
Ga-pa-uran a nang gibii. \\
i.r - caus -rain 1 s.abs only/just yesterday \\
‘I just let it rain (on me) yesterday.’ (Instead of going inside he kept trying to spear a wild pig.) [RCON-L-01 3.9]
summary: Meteorological predicates in Kagayanen typically lack actor or undergoer participants and often do not require a distinct absolutive argument, so bare roots for weather and related natural phenomena are usually marked with intransitive dynamic affixes. Happenstantial inflections are normally not used with these bare roots, but applicative forms can add an affected absolutive participant, often human, creating an experiential construction in which the experiencer is the undergoer. The passage also shows that this absolutive can be nonhuman, and that meteorological roots can appear in causative or reflexive constructions as well.

text:
Situations involving speech (or other types of utterance, such as shouting, whispering, asking or replying) are similar to situations of transfer (Class VII as identified in chap:verbclasses-1 ) in that the content of the utterance (what is said) is presented as a theme that is “transferred” from the Speaker to the Addressee. In Kagayanen predicates that depict utterance situations, the actor is always the speaker, but either the theme or the recipient may be expressed in the absolutive case, as will be described below.

With the root ambaļ ‘to say’ the addressee(s) does not have to be explicitly mentioned if it is obvious in the context. The quote can be either indirect bkm:Ref361243181 or direct bkm:Ref402322324. Notice also that in the first part of the sentence in example bkm:Ref402322324 there is no quote. The quote is in the previous sentence in the text.

Detransitive (Actor = absolutive), indirect quote: \\
Miyirkules sellem gambaļ a ta sawa ko na maglangoy aren inta unduni. \\
Miyirkules sellem ga-ambaļ a ta sawa ko na mag-langoy aren inta unduni. \\
Wednesday morning i.r -say 1 s.abs nabs spouse 2 s.gen
lk i.ir -bathe 1 s.abs opt now/today \\
‘Wednesday morning I said to my husband that I should bathe now.’ [EMWN-T-05 4.6]

Detransitive (Actor = absolutive), direct quote: \\
Na gambaļ ake na papa gatuļo iya na luwa daw ambaļ din, “Malipayen aren daw makita ko ake na mga kabataan daw dayad iran na lawa." \\
Na ga-mbaļ ake na papa ga-tuļo iya na luwa daw …ambaļ din, “Ma-lipay-en aren daw ma-kita ko ake na mga ka-bata-an daw dayad iran na lawa." \\
lk i.r -say 1 s.gen lk papa i.r -drip 3 s.gen lk tears and
t.r -say 3 s.erg ar -joy- ar 1 s.abs if/when a.hap.ir -see
1 s.erg 1 s.gen lk pl nr -child- nr and good 3 p.gen lk body \\
`When my papa was saying (this), his tears were dripping and he said, “I am joyful when I see my children and their bodies are well.”’ [CBWE-C-05 5.5]

Transitive (Theme = absolutive): \\
Dason pambaļ nanay ko, “Man-o kon uļa luag sinayaw Bantayan?" \\
Dason pa-ambaļ nanay ko, “Man-o kon uļa luag s<in>ayaw Bantayan?" \\
next t.r -say mother 1 s.gen why hsy neg.r watch
< nr.res >dance Bantayan \\
`Next my mother said, “Why are (you) not watching the dance in Bantayan?”’ [BMON-C-06 2.29]

Transitive (Theme = absolutive), Deontic modality: \\
Iambaļ no ki kanen daw ino ubraen din. \\
I-ambaļ no ki kanen daw ino ubra-en din. \\
t.deon -say 2 s.erg obl.p 3s if/when what work- t.ir 3 s.gen \\
‘You should say to him/her whatever s/he will work on.’

Applicative (Recipient = absolutive): \\
Pambaļan kay mama na mangamuyo kay nang kon.\\
Pa-ambaļ-an kay mama na m-pangamuyo kay nang kon.\\
t.r -say- apl 1 p.excl.abs mother lk i.ir -pray 1 p.excl.abs only/just hsy \\
‘Mother said to us that we will just pray.’ [VAWN-T-18 4.6]

Occasionally, the recipient may be expressed as the absolutive with no applicative marking. In that case, the implication is the speech is more direct or frank. For example, bkm:Ref402322426 is about a fairy telling a person to go with him to the world of the dead. This is an unusual and momentous direct request, and so the applicative is not used. This emphasizes the usually direct nature of this statement. Example bkm:Ref122516350 is about a woman telling her mother to regret or repent of her sins, which also is an unusually frank thing for anyone to say to their parents.

Pambaļ din yaken i na muyog a mamasyar. \\
Pa-ambaļ din yaken i na m-kuyog a ma-ng-pasyar. \\
t.r -say 3 s.erg 1 s.abs def.n lk i.v.ir -go.with 1 s.abs a.hap.ir-pl -visit \\
‘S/he told me that I will go with (him) to go visiting.’ [EDON-J-01 1.7]

Pambaļ ko kanen an, “Maneļseļ ka ta imo na saļa.\\
Pa-ambaļ ko kanen an, “Ma-neļseļ ka ta imo na saļa."\\
t.r -say 1 s.erg 3 s.abs def.m a.hap.ir -regret/repent 2 s.abs nabs 2 s.gen lk sin/mistake \\
‘I told her (directly), “You may regret/repent of your sins.”' [BMON-C-06 4.11]

The transitive, deontic mood prefix i- may occur with a Beneficiary as absolutive. This may be considered an applicative usage of the i- prefix:

Iambaļ a no naan ta mistro na absint a. \\
I-ambaļ a no naan ta mistro na absint a. \\
t.deon -say 1 s.abs 2 s.erg spat.def nabs teacher lk absent 1 s.abs \\
‘(You must) say for me to the teacher that I am absent.’

Additional examples of utterance predicates from the texts follow:
summary:
The passage explains that utterance predicates in Kagayanen pattern like transfer verbs, with the speech content treated as a theme transferred from speaker to addressee. It shows several constructions: the actor is always the speaker, while either the theme or recipient can be absolutive, with transitive, detransitive, and applicative patterns occurring in direct and indirect quotes.

It also notes that the addressee may be omitted when context makes it clear, and that when the recipient is absolutive without applicative marking, the utterance tends to be especially direct or frank. The deontic prefix i- can also occur with a beneficiary in absolutive case, functioning like an applicative.

Ti, naisturyaan din arey din na danen an Pedro daw Maria dali nang magkasaļ. \\
Ti, na-isturya-an din arey din na danen an Pedro daw Maria dali nang mag-kasaļ. \\
so a.hap.r -converse/talk- apl 3 s.erg friend 3 s.gen lk 3 p.abs def.m Pedro and Maria soon only/just i.ir -wedding \\
`So, he had (previously) conversed with his friend that they, Pedro and Maria, soon will be wed.’ (This is a flashback in the story.) [LGON-L-01 11.2]
summary: The passage describes a story in which Pedro goes spear fishing at Mamaan and meets an older man who asks where he is going, who is with him, and whether he is afraid. Pedro replies that he is going spear fishing alone and is not afraid, saying that anything that might frighten him would instead face his spear. It also notes a flashback explaining that Pedro had previously talked with a friend about Pedro and Maria being soon to marry.

text:
Situations involving perception (as well as emotion and cognition described below) are semantically “somewhat transitive” in that there are two necessary participants involved: an experiencer and a source of the experience, sometimes refered to as a stimulus. For example, in an event of visual perception, the experiencer is the person or animal that sees something, and the stimulus is the thing seen. These situations are different from prototypical transitive situations in that there is little or no activity that is “transferred” from one participant to the other. In the words of the experiencer “attends to” the stimulus, but does not act on it in any way. The stimulus does not undergo a change as a result of being perceived. In some cases the experiencer does act intentionally, as in He listened to the radio, or I looked at the horizon. English expresses the difference between intentional and unintentional perception largely via distinct verb roots, though sometimes the same root can be used either way, for example, He smelled the roses can mean he intentionally sniffed them, or he happened to smell them as he walked by. In Kagayanen this difference is largely expressed via Happenstantial versus Dynamic verbal inflections.

Non-volitional perception, such as seeing, hearing, and smelling something unintentionally, is usually inflected in experiencer modality. This seems to be the norm for roots that express peception. Recall that for non-volitional situations, experiencer modality is neutral with respect to grammatical transitivity – non-volitional verbs inflected in experiencer modality may occur in transitive or intransitive argument structure frames. This is understandable insofar as perception situations are semantically “somewhat transitive”, as mentioned above.

Intentional perception, such as watching, listening and actively tasting, is typically expressed in dynamic modality. Intentional or unintentional Experiential situations may be expressed grammatically in the various “voices” relevant to transitive situations in general, including detransitive (actor voice), and applicative (locative voice) constructions. These are just some of the patterns in which speakers use and adjust roots to express the precise meanings needed, according to specific communicative situations. The following examples from the corpus are of perception predicates that illustrate their various inflectional possibilities and their semantic effects.

We will begin with examples of the common root that expresses visual perception kita ‘to see’. Predicates headed by this root take happenstantial affixes, unless they are the basis of causative or reciprocal stems.

Nakita ko danen dya na sigi kaan. \\
Na-kita ko danen dya na sigi kaan. \\
a.hap.r -see 1 s.erg 3 s.abs d4loc lk continually eat \\
‘I saw them there continually eating.’ [EFOB-J-03 2.9]

Nakita ko na may anen dya na baked na bangkilan, … \\
Na-kita ko na may anen dya na baked na bangkilan … \\

‘I saw that there was some big-tusked wild pig …’ [RCON-L-01 3.11]

Nakita din na gaitem inog an na lumboy. \\
Na-kita din na ga-item inog an na lumboy. \\
a.hap.r -see 3 s.erg lk i.r -black ripe def.m lk Java.plum \\
‘He saw that the ripe Java plums were becoming black.’ [JCWN-L-38 7.3]

Maski makita din ambaw, kanen nang magtan-aw. \\
Maski ma-kita din ambaw, kanen nang mag-tan-aw. \\
even.if a.hap.ir -see 3 s.erg mouse/rat 3 s.abs only/just i.ir -look.at \\
‘Even if s/he (the cat) sees a mouse or rat, s/he will just look at it.’ [JCOO-C-10 8.1]

Iling din makaļa din daw makita din.\\
Iling din ma-kaļa din daw ma-kita din.\\
say 3 s.erg a.hap.ir -know/recognize 3 s.erg if/when a.hap.ir -see 3 s.erg \\
‘He said that he will recognize him if he sees him.' [JCWN-T-26 4.13]

May isya na manakem na ngaran din Tatay Pedro na gasakay ta isya na lunday na manampara. Nakita din ake na mangngod na nalemmes. \\
May isya na manakem na ngaran din Tatay Pedro na ga-sakay ta isya na lunday na ma-ng-tampara. Na-kita din ake na mangngod na na-lemmes. \\

i.r -ride nabs one lk outrigger.canoe lk a.hap.ir-pl -goggles

Ka-kita a unso ittaw na bakod. \\

t.r -call 3 p.abs def.m \\
‘But this older man saw them and straightway called them …’ [PBWN-C-13 4.3]

Paryo ta ayep na kanding, pugya uļa gid kanding banwa i, piro namatian no daw makakita ka ta tai din. \\
Paryo ta ayep na kanding, pugya uļa gid kanding banwa i, piro na-mati-an no daw maka-kita ka ta tai din. \\

‘Like the animal goat, long ago the town really had no goats, but you heard them and you can see their scat.’ (This is a story about a place on Cagayancillo where amazing things happen.) [EFWE-T-05 3.8]

Makakita can also just mean to have the internal ability to see, as when a blind person is healed. Nakakita, nakita, and makita are not used in this way.
summary:
The passage explains that perception events are semantically “somewhat transitive” because they involve an experiencer and a stimulus, but unlike prototypical transitive events, no activity is transferred and the stimulus is not changed. It notes that intentional perception is typically expressed with dynamic modality, while non-volitional perception is usually marked with experiencer modality, and that English and Kagayanen differ in how they signal this distinction.  

Using the root *kita* ‘see’ as an example, the passage shows that perception predicates can appear in several inflectional and voice patterns, including happenstantial, experiencer-modal, detransitive, and applicative forms, with meanings varying accordingly.

Sikad en kon na kalipay danen tak buļag ya makakita en daw buktot ya tanos en.\\
Sikad en kon na ka-lipay danen tak buļag ya maka-kita en daw buktot ya tanos en.\\
very cm hsy lk nr -joy 3 s.gen because blind def.f i.hap.r -see cm and hunchback def.f straight cm \\
‘Their joy was great because the blind one can see and the hunchback is straight.’ [CBWN-C-15 5.18]

The root kita with the meaning of ‘see’ only occurs in happenstantial modality. The causative stem, pakita, may occur in dynamic modality with the meaning of ‘to show’. The reciprocal stem, kitaay ‘to meet together’, may also appear in dynamic modality. There are thirty-eight examples of stems based on kita functioning as predicates in dynamic modality in the corpus, twelve of which are causatives and twenty-six of which are reciprocals. Examples bkm:Ref121468636 and bkm:Ref121468640 illustrate the reciprocal usage:

Gakitaay kay isab ta mga mama nay ya na duma. Lain man iran baļay daen. \\
Ga-kita-ay kay isab ta mga mama nay ya na duma. Lain man iran baļay daen. \\

hermit.crab nabs one lk beach\\

3 s.erg obl.p 2p \\

M-luag gid yan kani ta damag di daw m-panilag di kani nya na mga ittaw. \\

d1loc later d4adj lk pl person \\
`That one will really watch/attend later the wake here and those people will be observing here.’ [CBWN-C-22 13.9]

Paluag ko daw ano na sistema tan na uļa natapat. \\
Pa-luag ko daw ano na sistema tan na uļa na-tapat. \\

`I inspected it (the spear) (to see) what is its position that it (the wild pig) was not mortally wounded.’ (The speaker was spear hunting a wild pig and he hit the pig but the spear fell out of the pig and so he wanted to know why the pig was not mortally wounded.) [RCON-L-01 8.5]

When the happenstantial affixes occur on these roots they express abilitative, optative, or opportunitive modality, or perfect aspect.

Opportunitive: \\
Maluag ko kani sinayaw an daw uļa en ubra. \\
Ma-luag ko kani s<in>ayaw an daw uļa en ubra. \\
a.hap.ir -watch 1 s.erg later < nr.res >dance def.m if/when neg.r cm work \\
‘I will get to watch the dance later if there is no more work.’
summary: The root *kita* ‘see’ occurs only in happenstantial modality, while its causative stem *pakita* can be used in dynamic modality meaning ‘show,’ and the reciprocal stem *kitaay* ‘meet together’ can also appear dynamically. The corpus contains 38 dynamic examples of *kita*-based stems, mostly reciprocals, and the passage illustrates that verbs of intentional visual perception such as *luag* ‘watch’ and *tan-aw* ‘look at’ typically take dynamic affixes without stem-forming morphology. When happenstantial affixes occur on these roots, they express abilitative, optative, opportunitive modality, or perfect aspect.

The root mati ‘to hear/listen’ is of Class V, subclass Vb of non-volitional semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic roots, and Class VIII, volitional transitive roots, depending on the context. Both of these classes are those that take the applicative - an in their basic transitive form (see chap:verbclasses-1, sec:overviewofeightverbclasses ). In happenstantial modality with the applicative, the meaning tends to be unintentional: ‘to hear’ ( bkm:Ref121468755 and bkm:Ref121468759 ), and in dynamic modalities the meaning is more intentional: ‘to listen’ ( bkm:Ref121468840 and bkm:Ref121468843 ):

Transitive, happenstantial (with obligatory applicative): \\

Pag-uļa nang lugay namatian nay en daguno ta iruplano. \\

Nuga in this example is the shortened form of tanuga, which may also be pronounced tinuga and tunuga.
See chap:verbstructure, sec:omissionofprefixes for description of conversational omission of inflectional prefixes.
`When we were asleep around eleven o’clock at night, I heard a call of a male fairy.’ [EDON-J-01 1.6]

Ta pagpangaoy, nakamati kay ta kagi ta isya na yupan na yupan i na gaambaļ na “Kikikiyaw kikikiyaw.” \\

Detransitive, dynamic: \\

1 p.excl.abs two 1 p.excl.abs Pedro i.r -hear nabs drama 3 p.gen Maria \\

With *-luag*, the same root can mean ‘have the opportunity to watch/look at’ or mark perfect aspect, while *mati* ‘hear/listen’ alternates between non-volitional and volitional readings depending on context and class, with the applicative -an required in its transitive forms.

The root mati is unusual in that it allows a detransitive construction in the na - and ma - happenstantial forms (recall that for volitional roots, detransitive happenstantials require naka - or maka -). In such situations, the intentional meaning of the basic root is understood ‘to listen’, though the usual abilitative/opportunitive meanings are also part of the semantics of these constructions.

Detransitive na- and ma - intentional: \\
Namati a ta balita ya kabii kilem. \\
Na-mati a ta balita ya kabii kilem. \\

‘I had the opportunity to hear/listen to the news last night.’

Third, gamati is a dynamic (intentional) usage, and fourth, namatii is the exclamatory form of the happenstantial usage (see chap:stemformingprocesses, sec:exclamatory on the exclamatory suffixes).

`While we were talking, my younger sibling heard something. He said, “Mother, can you hear the singing coming from the mast pole?” We listened. We really became silent for a while. There we (surprisingly) really heard singing, “Halleluja halleluja.”' [VAWN-T-18 5.5-9]

There are two roots that depict situations involving the sense of smell. These are singngot and plamao. These roots are synonymous, but plamao is a borrowing from Hiligaynon. The root singngot is more common, occuring four times in the corpus as an inflected verb, while plamao occurs twice. Though these numbers are small, they accurately represent our impression of the relative frequency of these roots in conversation. With the dynamic affixes the meaning of both roots is intentional ‘to smell/sniff something’. With the happenstantial affixes the meaning is ‘to smell something unintentionally’. As with other sensory roots, the experiencer is the actor and the stimulus, if present, is the undergoer. The root plamao always takes the applicative in its transitive uses (Class Vb for unintentional uses, and Class VIII for intentional uses). For singngot, the applicative is optional (see further below).

Transitive, dynamic with applicative: \\
Paplamauan din buļak an. \\
Pa-plamao-an din buļak an. \\
t.r -smell- apl 3 s.erg flower def.m \\
’S/he sniffed the flower.’
summary: The passage explains that the perception root *mati* ‘hear/listen’ can express abilitative, optative, and opportunitive happenstantial meanings such as ‘may hear’ or ‘get to hear,’ and it gives examples of both transitive and detransitive uses. It also notes that *mati* is unusual because its detransitive *na-* and *ma-* forms can have an intentional meaning ‘to listen,’ though the usual abilitative/opportunitive senses remain. Finally, the excerpt briefly introduces two synonymous smell roots, *singngot* and *plamao*, which differ in frequency and in whether the applicative is optional or required in transitive uses.

text:
Pasingngutan din anay mga pagkaan an bag-o din kan-enen. \\
Pa-singngot-an din anay mga pagkaan an bag-o din kan-en-en. \\
t.r -smell- apl 3 s.erg first/for.a.while pl food def.m before 3 s.erg cooked.rice- t.r \\
‘S/he sniffed first the food before eating it.’

Transitive, dynamic without applicative: \\
Pasingngot ta mga bata ragbi an. \\
Pa-singngot ta mga bata ragbi an.\\
t.r -smell erg pl child rugbi def.m \\
`The children sniffed the rugby.' \\
*Paplamao ta bata ragbi an.

The difference between pasingngutan and pasingngot is that without the applicative, pasingngot implies sniffing up close, for example, holding something up to the nose and deeply sniffing or inhaling. With the applicative, pasingngutan just implies normal sniffing the air and smelling something.

Detransitive, dynamic: \\
Gaplamao en mga ittaw i daw ambaļ danen, “May bui man i na ittaw di en a!” \\
Ga-plamao en mga ittaw i daw …-ambaļ danen, “May bui man i na ittaw di en a!” \\
i.r -smell cm pl person def.n and t.r -say 3 p.erg ext.in
live emph att lk person d1loc cm inj \\
`The people sniffed and they said, “There’s really a live person here now!”’ [CBWN-C-22 10.3]

Gasingngot bata an ta ragbi. \\
Ga-singngot bata an ta ragbi. \\
i.r -smell child def.m nabs rugby \\
‘The child was sniffing some rugby.’

Detransitive, happenstantial: \\
Tak daw naan a agi ta dapit abagat i makasingngot kanen ta bao ko. \\
Tak daw naan a agi ta dapit abagat i maka-singngot kanen ta bao ko. \\
because if/when spat.def 1 s.abs pass nabs direction southwest def.n
i.hap.ir -smell 3 s.abs nabs odor 1 s.gen \\
`Because if I pass in the direction of south he can smell my odor.’ (This is a story about the speaker hunting a wild pig.) [RCON-L-01 2.6]

Detransitive, happenstantial, external motivation: \\
Kaplamao en mga ittaw i ta ammot ta luto ya. \\
Ka-plamao en mga ittaw i ta ammot ta luto ya. \\

‘The people were able to smell the fragance of the cooking.’

As mentioned above, plamao always takes the applicative suffix in a transitive frame, while singngot may or may not occur with an applicative. In happenstantial modality, When the applicative does appear, the meaning is simple non-volitional ‘to sense something by smelling’, whereas without the applicative, the sense is more direct sniffing (as above in dynamic modality), in perfect aspect or abilitative/opportunitive:

Transitive, happenstantial, applicative = non-volitional ‘to sense by smelling’: \\

Na-plamau-an din inog an na nangka. \\
a.hap.r -smell- apl 3 s.erg ripe def.m lk jackfruit \\
‘S/he smelled the ripe jackfruit.’ \\
*Naplamo din inog an na nangka. *Maplamao din inog an na Nangka.

Maplamauan ka tatay no kani na bao ka ta inemen. \\

’Your father will smell you later that you are smelly of alcohol.’

Nasingngutan din bao ya ta durian na pakaan a iya na arey. \\
Na-singngut-an din bao ya ta durian na pa-kaan a iya na arey. \\
a.hap.r -smell- apl 3 s.erg odor def.f nabs durian.fruit lk t.r -eat nabs 3 s.gen lk friend \\
‘S/he smelled the odor of the durian fruit that his/her friend was eating.’

Transitive, happenstantial, no applicative = direct sniffing some specific thing, abilitative/opportunitive: \\
Nasingngot ko bao ta durian. \\
Na-singngot ko bao ta durian. \\
a.hap.r -smell 1 s.erg odor nabs durian.fruit \\
‘I could sniff and smell the odor of the durian fruit.'

Masingngot ko bao ta durian. \\
Ma-singngot ko bao ta durian. \\
a.hap.ir -smell 1 s.erg odor nabs durian.fruit \\
‘I will sniff and smell the odor of the durian fruit.'

Daw mag-inog en gani sikad ammot na maski adyo ka pa nasingngot no an. \\
Daw mag-inog en gani sikad ammot na maski adyo ka pa na-singngot no an. \\
if/when i.ir -ripe cm truly very fragant lk even.if far 2 s.abs inc a.hap.r -smell 2 s.erg def.m \\
`When it (jackfruit) is becoming ripe, truly it is very fragrant that even if you are still far away it is what you can sniff and smell.’ [EFWE-T-04 3.5]

Detransitive, happenstantial, hypothetical/polite meaning: \\
Maplamao ka ta White Flower aged mamang lipeng uļo no. \\
Ma-plamao ka ta White Flower aged ma-kamang lipeng uļo no. \\
i.hap.ir -smell 2 s.abs nabs White Flower so.that a.hap.ir -get/remove dizzy head 2 s.gen \\
‘You should sniff the White Flower so that the dizziness of your head will be removed.’

Masingngot ka ta White Flower aged mamang lipeng uļo no. \\
Ma-singngot ka ta White Flower aged ma-kamang lipeng uļo no. \\
i.hap.ir -smell 2 s.abs nabs White Flower so.that a.hap.ir -get/remove dizzy head 2 s.gen \\
`You should sniff the White Flower so that the dizziness of your head will be removed.’\\
*Nasingngot ka ta White Flower. *Naplamao ka ta White Flower.

There is one root, lasa, that depicts situations of tasting. It usually occurs with happenstantial affixes with a unintentional meaning to sense the taste of something. Like mati ‘to hear/listen’, it belongs to Class V, subclass Vb, which is the class of non-volitional transitive roots that take the applicative - an in their basic, transitive form. The actor is the experiencer, expressed in the ergative case, and the undergoer is the stimulus, expressed in the absolutive. There are no examples of this inflected form in the corpus, though it does occur in conversation.

Nalasaan ko luto din na masin. \\
Na-lasa-an ko luto din na masin. \\
a.hap.r -taste- apl 1 s.erg cook 3 s.gen lk salty \\
‘I tasted his/her cooking that (it is) salty.’
summary:
The passage contrasts the use of the roots *pasingngot/pasingngutan* and *plamao* across transitive and detransitive frames, showing that the applicative suffix changes meaning from direct, close sniffing to more general, non-volitional smelling or sensing by smell. It also notes that *singngot* can occur with or without the applicative, with the applicative marking non-volitional perception and the non-applicative form indicating direct sniffing or abilitative/opportunitive meanings, while in detransitive forms the roots can express dynamic, happenstantial, or polite/hypothetical senses.  

The passage further introduces the taste root *lasa*, which behaves like a non-volitional transitive root taking the applicative in its basic form; the actor is the experiencer and the undergoer is the stimulus.

Kalasa a ta tab-ang tak may trangkaso a. \\
Ka-lasa a ta tab-ang tak may trangkaso a. \\
i.exm -taste 1 s.abs nabs lacking.salt because ext.in flu 1 s.abs \\
‘Everything tastes bland to me because I have the flu.’ (lit. ‘I can taste lacking-salt because I have the flu.’)

The common root that expresses the sense of touch is batyag ‘to feel’. There are sixty (60) examples of batyag used as an inflected verb in the corpus. The meanings of this root in its various possible forms are listed in ex:meaningsofbatyag, along with their frequencies in the corpus. Corpus and conversational examples follow:

enumerate
Transitive frame, happenstantial, with applicative ( nabatyagan/mabatyagan ): non-volitional ‘to physically, emotionally or internally sense or feel something in a permanent, deep, inward way’. This is the most frequent usage of batyag in the corpus (30 examples of nabatyagan and 8 examples of mabatyagan ).
Transitive frame, happenstantial, no applicative ( nabatyag/mabatyag ): Simple non-volitional ‘to physically, emotionally or internally sense or feel something in a momentary, passing way’ (1 example of nabatyag and 1 example of mabatyag used in this way in the corpus).
Detransitive frame, happenstantial ( nakabatyag/makabatyag ): Abilitative/opportunitive ‘to be able to physically, emotionally or internally sense or feel something’ (no examples of nakabatyag and 3 examples of makabatyag in the corpus).
Detransitive frame, external motivation ( kabatyag ): Enablement ‘to be enabled to notice something’ (5 examples).
Detransitive frame, happenstantial ( nabatyag/mabatyag ): Abilitative/opportunitive ‘to be able to take notice of something’, ‘happen to take notice of something’, stimulus often a complement clause (2 examples of nabatyag, 1 example of mabatyag used this way in the corpus).
Transitive frame, dynamic, no applicative ( batyagen only; Realis, pabatyag, is ungrammatical for all speakers consulted): To take notice of something previously talked about (no examples in the corpus).
Transitive frame, dynamic, applicative ( pabatyagan/batyagan ): Volitional ‘to take notice/make note of something’ (no examples of pabatyagan, 3 examples of batyagan ).
Detransitive frame, dynamic, no applicative (gabatyag/magbatyag): Volitional ‘to take notice/make note of something’, stimulus often a complement clause’ (6 examples of gabatyag, no examples of magbatyag ).

When the verb batyag is used in a transitive frame, the experiencer is in the ergative case and the stimulus, the item or sensation felt, is absolutive as in ex:becomingverybig through bkm:Ref123389246, and bkm:Ref122549938. In an intransitive frame, the experiencer is absolutive and the stimulus, if present, is oblique (several examples from ex:willrun through ex:asthmaattack ). Of the sixty examples of batyag used as a inflected predicate in the corpus, thirty-eight are in happenstantial modality plus the applicative - an or its exclamatory equivalent - i (two examples). Twenty are expressed in dynamic modality (usages 6 and 7). There are no examples of batyag with the non-applicative exclamatory suffix - a.

Examples ex:becomingverybig and bkm:Ref122532854 illustrate the difference in meaning between the first two usages of batyag. Both are from the same first person personal experience recounted by a fisherman whose boat overturned in rough seas. While fishing he noticed that he felt hungry, and uses nabatyag ex:becomingverybig (usage 2). Then, after surviving the accident and coming ashore, he was feeling intense hunger and tiredness and used nabatyagan, shown in example bkm:Ref122532854 (usage 1):

Happenstantial, transitive, realis non-applicative (usage 2): \\
Piro nabatyag ko en ļettem daw kaadlek tak baļed gadarko na gadarko. \\
Piro na-batyag ko en ļettem daw ka-adlek tak baļed ga-darko na ga-darko. \\

‘But I felt hungry and afraid because the waves were becoming very big.’ [EFWN-T-11 9.2]

Happenstantial, transitive, realis applicative (usage 1): \\

Naan aren ta baybay Peek nabatyagan ko en ļettem daw kakapoy ta ake na lawa. \\
Naan aren ta baybay Peek na-batyag-an ko en ļettem daw ka-kapoy ta ake na lawa. \\

hunger and nr -tired nabs 1 s.gen lk body \\
`When I was on the beach of Peek I felt hunger and exhaustion of my body.’ [EFWN-T-11 15.1]

Example ex:wholebody illustrates the applicative stem batyagan in happenstantial irrealis modality (usage 1):

Sakit ta kalingking mabatyagan ta bilog na lawa. \\
Sakit ta kalingking ma-batyag-an ta bilog na lawa. \\
pain nabs little.finger a.hap.ir -feel- apl nabs whole lk body \\
‘Pain in the little finger is felt in the whole body.’ [VAWV-J-21 11.1]

Examples bkm:Ref121399507 and bkm:Ref123389246 illustrate the applicative stem batyagan inflected in happenstantial, realis modality, with a complement clause as the stimulus (usage 1):

Uļa nang lugay nabatyagan ko na gabaliskad en dyip na sakayan nay. \\
Uļa nang lugay na-batyag-an ko na ga-baliskad en dyip na sakay-an nay. \\

cm jeep lk ride- nr 1 p.excl.gen \\
`Not a long time I felt that the jeep that we were riding was turning upside down.’ [PMWN-T-02 2.10]

Piro nabatyagan din man na nagayya kanen i ta nubya din … \\

but a.hap.r -feel- apl 3 s.erg too lk a.hap.r -embarrass 3 s.abs def.n
nabs girlfriend 3 s.gen \\
`But he felt too that he was embarrassed to his girlfriend …’ [CBWN-C-12 3.9]

The third usage of batyag is in a detransitive frame in happenstantial modality. In the context of example ex:willrun, the meaning is ‘to be able to sense’: \\
summary: The passage describes the root **batyag** ‘to feel’ and shows that it occurs in 60 corpus examples with several distinct inflected meanings, ranging from involuntary physical or emotional feeling to volitional noticing or taking note of something. It also explains that **transitive** uses mark the experiencer in ergative case and the stimulus in absolutive, while **intransitive/detransitive** uses place the experiencer in absolutive and, if present, the stimulus in oblique case. The corpus data show that the most frequent pattern is the happenstantial transitive form with the applicative, used for deep or persistent sensations, while dynamic and more volitional meanings are less common.

The meaning of ‘to take notice’ can be inferred when batyag is inflected with the intransitive happenstantial external motivation ka -. In this context, the stimulus may be Referring Expression or a complement clause. In bkm:Ref121399400 the stimulus is the nominalization kakulian ‘difficulty’:

Tanan-tanan ki kabatyag ta kakulian ta Cagayancillo … \\
