summary: The passage argues that although *ta* appears in several rows of the tab:cases, the different pronoun sets and uses show that these are distinct cases, and that such multifunctionality is normal in language, as illustrated by English pronouns like *her*, *you*, and *it*. It then contends that in Kagayanen and related Philippine languages, demoted Undergoers are structurally different from ordinary obliques: they cannot usually be fronted without *naan*, unlike some other oblique phrases, and they seem to occupy an intermediate position between core arguments and prototypical obliques.

section: Voice in Philippine languages: An introduction
text:
We’ve seen that the system of organizing grammatical relations in Kagayanen is very different from what is found in European languages; the central grammatical relations in clauses are absolutive and ergative, rather than subject and object. This is a very common system in other Austronesian languages, and in languages of many other parts of the world, though it is often perplexing to speakers and linguists who are used to subject/object systems. In this section we will discuss the notion of “voice” as a grammatical system for adjusting the relationship between grammatical relations and semantic roles in clauses. We will begin with a brief outline of the history of scholarship surrounding voice in Philippine languages, most of which deals with Tagalog.

set the stage for the view of Tagalog verbs as expressing four distinct “voices." Blake used the term “expression of case by the verb" to describe the ways in which verb morphology varies to express different semantic roles of the “subject" (our absolutive) argument. The Tagalog system, according to Blake, represents a more fully developed version of the expression of case by the verb than the two-way active/passive voice systems common in Indo-European and Semitic languages. In other words, for Blake “voice" is a limited variety of case expression in the verb. More recent approaches (e.g.,, and ) have reversed Blake's characterization, instead extending the definition of voice to include Philippine-type systems, rather than extending the definition of case in the verb to include voice in the Indo-European and Semitic traditions. In this grammar, we will use the term voice in the more recent sense to refer to any system of verb (phrase) morphosyntax that specifies the alignment between grammatical relations and semantic roles in a clause.

Ever since, linguists have used various terms to describe the basic clause structure of Philippine languages. treated Tagalog as though it were an Indo-European language with an active/passive voice system. The “active voice” for Bloomfield was what we are calling the detransitive (see above), and the “passive voice” was what we are calling the basic transitive (ergative) construction. By the mid-1960s, however, linguists were beginning to realize that the active/passive perspective didn’t work very well for Tagalog. For example, treated the basic clause structure of Tagalog as a “predicate+topic” system, rather than a voice system. The various verbal categories relating to argument relations represented options for bringing different arguments into the topic position. Of course, this is exactly what a voice system does, but because the Tagalog system seemed so different from familiar active/passive systems, were reluctant to use the term “voice”. were actually inconsistent in their terminology, in that they used the term “topic” when referring to nominal categories, signaled by the pre-nominal particles and certain pronouns, and “focus” when referring to verb forms. Thus, for example, the “Actor-focus” verb forms were ways of indicating that the Actor was the “topic” of the clause. “ Focus is the feature of a verbal predicate that determines the semantic relationship between a predicate verb and its topic.” (, emphasis in the original). This apparent treatment of “topic” and “focus” as the same caused a great deal of confusion, since most linguists consider these categories to be in opposition to each other (see, e.g., inter alia ). Some subsequent work changed the terminology to be more internally consistent, using “Actor-topic”, “Patient-topic” and so on for the verb forms, while others kept the focus terminology for both verbal and nominal categories. The result was a great deal of confusion and sense of mystery among linguists concerning the basic clause structure of Tagalog, and Philippine languages in general.

In 1977 Resty Cena presented arguments for what he called “patient primacy” in Tagalog. Arguing from multiple perspectives, including frequency, syntactic simplicity, psycholinguistic salience, and age of acquisition, Cena showed that Bloomfield’s “passive” voice (Schachter & Otanes’ “goal focus”) construction was the more “basic” or “natural” way of expressing a transitive situation. followed up with morphological evidence for the same claim. Both Cena and De Guzman used the subject/object terminology similar to Bloomfield, but argued that the subject of a transitive clause in Tagalog was a primary patient, rather than an Actor. In other words, the subject for Cena and De Guzman was what we are calling the absolutive in Kagayanen. They independently argued that universally there are two possible primary orientations to a transitive situation, one in which the role of Actor is primary, as in English and many other languages, and the other in which the role of patient is primary, as in Tagalog. Though neither Cena nor De Guzman argued explicitly for an ergative/absolutive analysis of Tagalog, they both recognized and acknowledged the conceptual similarity between patient primacy in Tagalog and indisputably ergative systems.
summary: The passage explains that Kagayanen, like many Austronesian languages, organizes clauses around absolutive and ergative relations rather than the subject/object system familiar from European languages, and it introduces “voice” as the verbal system that aligns grammatical relations with semantic roles. It then reviews scholarship on Tagalog, showing how earlier analysts used active/passive terminology, while later work redefined voice more broadly to cover Philippine-type systems and highlighted confusion between “topic” and “focus” in descriptions of clause structure. Finally, it notes that Cena and De Guzman argued for “patient primacy” in Tagalog, treating the patient-oriented transitive construction as more basic and recognizing its similarity to ergative/absolutive systems.

section: Voice in Philippine languages: An introduction
text: Several linguists in recent years have followed the precedent set by Cena in referring to the absolutive relation in Tagalog as the “subject”, acknowledging that this relation is defined very differently than the subject in a language like English (see, e.g., ). At some level, this may be considered mere terminological variation--whether one chooses to call the case that expresses intransitive S arguments and basic transitive O arguments “absolutive” or “subject” may not seem like a substantive analytic decision. However, in our opinion, using terminology that is common in analyses of nominative/accusative systems for languages like Tagalog and Kagayanen, for which grammatical relations have very different properties, is confusing for speakers and linguists alike in that it may perpetuate the impression that these languages are “mysterious” and fundamentally dissimilar to all other languages of the world. In our opinion, viewing the system for organizing grammatical relations as basically ergative/absolutive, and the voice system as involving various ways of adjusting the relationships between semantic roles and grammatical relations in a clause provides a coherent way of understanding the basic clause structure of most Philippine languages that is consistent with what is known about language in general. The voice system is clearly more elaborate than in most languages commonly studied by linguists, but its fundamental character is well-understood from the extensive body of literature now available on voice and grammatical relations in general, and on ergative/absolutive systems in particular (see, e.g., ).
summary: The passage argues against calling the Tagalog absolutive relation “subject,” even though some linguists do so, because that term is associated with nominative/accusative languages and may obscure how Philippine languages work. The authors prefer analyzing these languages as fundamentally ergative/absolutive, with the voice system understood as shifting the links between semantic roles and grammatical relations in the clause. They claim this provides a more coherent account of Philippine clause structure and aligns it with broader linguistic theory.

text:
In order to understand the role of voice in any language, it may be helpful to start with the fairly simple voice system of a well-known language like English. Consider the sentences in fig:kagayanenchoir. Examples (d) and (e) are marginal or ungrammatical to most English speakers, but they are, we believe, understandable enough to serve as a bridge to understanding voice in Kagayanen:

Using terminology from, we can understand these different syntactic constructions as ways of bringing various parts of a sentence into a “privileged” grammatical status (indicated in the box in fig:kagayanenchoir, and called the “subject” in traditional English grammar). This privileged status is “special” in several ways. In terms of syntax, the Privileged Syntactic Argument (PSA) is the argument that controls various syntactic patterns, like verb agreement, reflexivization, coreference in coordinate structures and others. In terms of pragmatics, the PSA tends to refer to the most “topical” participant. That is, the sentences in fig:kagayanenchoir can be understood as making a comment “about” the Actor ( I in 10.4a), the patient ( fish in 10.4b), the beneficiary ( child in 10.4c), the location ( plate in 10.4d), and the instrument ( spoon in 10.4e) respectively. When these noun phrases are the PSA, they no longer carry any direct marking of their semantic role. In other words, they no longer follow any benefactive, locative or instrumental prepositions. The only overt clues as to the semantic role of the PSA are found in the verb phrase, namely the auxiliary (a form of be ), the past participle form of the main verb, and possible post-verbal particles, such as on, in, or with.

The important feature to notice about the English system is that there are only two grammatical voices, which are traditionally referred to as “Active” and “Passive” active voice passive voice. In these examples, the verb form in the Active voice is served and all the others are in the Passive voice, employing the auxiliary was plus the past participle: was served. However, one could say that the little words on and with following the passive verb forms in fig:kagayanenchoir d and e indicate the semantic role of the PSA -- on indicates that the PSA is a location, and with indicates that the PSA is an instrument. In other words, the verb forms in fig:kagayanenchoir d and e are really was served on and was served with respectively. These little words no longer function as prepositions preceding a noun phrase, but rather as particles in the verb phrase that indicate the semantic role of the PSA.

Constructions analogous to those in fig:kagayanenchoir all occur in Kagayanen, with several important differences. First, the PSA in Kagayanen is the absolutive argument, as described in bkm:Ref482605816. Second, Kagayanen speakers use all the corresponding constructions in Kagayanen fluently, with a wide range of verbs and arguments. While certain verb+argument combinations are limited in the number and type of voices that may be expressed (as discussed at length in chap:verbclasses-1 and chap:verbclasses-2 ), in general the possibilities are much more productive and regular than analogous constructions in English. Third, elements that indicate the semantic role of the absolutive argument are verb forms, differentiated by verbal affixation, rather than by auxiliaries ( was in the English examples), or particles ( on and with ). While all these structural features make voice in English and Kagayanen very different, the voice systems of both languages share one major functional similarity: they are both ways of bringing particular clausal arguments into the Privileged Syntactic Argument position, while “demoting” or “deperspectivizing” other elements. Once an argument is in the PSA position, it is then available for many syntactic functions that are not possible for obliques, or other clausal arguments.

In Kagayanen, verb semantics, grammatical transitivity, and the applicative constructions (see chap:verbstructure through chap:verbclasses-2 ) work together to express the various “voices”. In the following discussion, we will describe the voices semantically according to the semantic role of the absolutive argument. Applicative constructions are used to express Benefactive, Locative, Instrumental, and Adversative voice, depending on the semantics of the predicate.

We hope to show that the voice system of Kagayanen is the result of the interaction between the dimension of transitivity in the inflectional paradigm ( chap:verbstructure ) inflection and applicative applicative morphology processes in the stem-forming stem-forming morphology group ( chap:stemformingprocesses ). These relationships are summarized in ex:voices, and exemplified in the rest of this section:

summary: The passage explains voice as a way of placing a clause’s Privileged Syntactic Argument (PSA) in a special grammatical position that controls syntactic processes and tends to express the most topical participant. It contrasts English, which has a relatively simple active/passive system marked by auxiliaries and particles, with Kagayanen, where analogous voice constructions are more productive and are marked by verbal affixation; in Kagayanen, the PSA is the absolutive argument, and different voice types arise from the interaction of verb transitivity and applicative morphology.

In an intransitive clause, there is only one Referring Expression that has a grammatical relation to the Predicate. Any additional elements are optional. Referring Expressions that have a grammatical relation to the Predicate are called arguments arguments, or sometimes core arguments core arguments. In each of these examples, the absolutive is the only argument of the clause. It is marked as absolutive by either the lack of a prenominal case marker ( bkm:Ref116980651 and bkm:Ref116980654 ), or the absolutive form of a pronoun ( bkm:Ref116980701, bkm:Ref116980703 and bkm:Ref116980658 ). In all the verbal predicates ( bkm:Ref116980651 - bkm:Ref116980703 ), the verb is marked as intransitive, either realis ( bkm:Ref116980651, bkm:Ref116980654 and bkm:Ref116980701 ), or irrealis (twice in bkm:Ref116980703 ). Example bkm:Ref116980658 is a non-verbal predicate. Non-verbal predicates non-verbal predicates are always intransitive, and are not marked for transitivity or modality (see chap:non-verbalclauses ).

In all of these constructions ( bkm:Ref116980651 - bkm:Ref116980658 ), the speaker is making a statement about the absolutive case argument. The absolutive argument is presented as the person or thing that is most relevant or most highly affected by the situation described in the Predicate. It is very common for the absolutive argument of an intransitive clause to be a semantic Actor ( bkm:Ref116980651 - bkm:Ref116980703 ), but this is not always true. Example bkm:Ref116980658 illustrates a clause in which the absolutive does not do anything. It is not an Actor because it does not initiate or control the event. Intransitive verbal predicates in happenstantial modalities happenstantial modality also express situations in which the absolutive argument is not an Actor:... kami naļabo en. \\... kami na-ļabo en. \\
1 p.excl.abs a.hap.r -capsize cm \\
‘... we had capsized.’[VAWN-T-18 6.9]

The absolutive argument of this clause, kami, did not capsize on purpose. The situation is one that happened to the speaker and associates. There is no controlling Actor expressed at all. For this reason, the realis happenstantial mood happenstantial modality prefix is called for (see chap:verbstructure, sec:modality ).

There is a difference between semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic and grammatical transitivity transitivity!grammatical. As mentioned in bkm:Ref482605816, a situation that seems to require an Undergoer and a distinct Controller may be expressed in an intransitive construction, with the Undergoer simply omitted or expressed in a non-absolutive case, preceded by ta or ki. We describe such constructions as detransitive detransitive constructions. They express semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic situations in grammatically intransitive frames. Such constructions are used when there is an Undergoer, but it is less salient in the communicative situation than the Actor in some way. The Actor is presented as the most affected participant in the situation, and the Undergoer, if present at all, is presented as less central in some way, either by being indefinite, non-specific, generic or incompletely affected. Examples of detransitive constructions in the corpus are presented in bkm:Ref125017724v - bkm:Ref117000205 above.

summary: Kagayanen intransitive clauses consist minimally of a predicate and one absolutive referring expression, with any other elements being optional obliques or adverbials. The absolutive is the only core argument and is typically the semantic actor, though it may also be a non-actor or experiencer; verbal predicates are marked as intransitive, while non-verbal predicates are always intransitive and unmarked for transitivity or modality. The passage also notes that some clauses are semantically transitive but grammatically intransitive, with the under- goer omitted or expressed in a non-absolutive case; these are treated as detransitive constructions.

text:
patient voice|( undergoer voice|( transitive constructions|(
In English and other Indo-European languages, almost every complete clause has a subject. Some clauses also have a direct object. Clauses which include a subject (a nominative argument) and no object are considered intransitive, while those that include a subject and a direct object (an accusative argument) are considered transitive (see, e.g., Merriam Webster online 2022, definitions of “transitive” and “intransitive”). These definitions don’t fit Philippine languages very well, since grammatical notions of “subject” and “direct object” do not apply (see, e.g.,, and the discussion above in sec:grammaticalrelations ). Rather, in Kagayanen and most other Philippine languages, it is more accurate to say that almost all clauses include an absolutive argument, either overtly present or strongly implied. Some also include an ergative argument. Intransitive clauses are those that include an absolutive and no ergative argument, as illustrated in the previous section. Transitive clauses are those that include an absolutive and an ergative argument., elaborated in, describes the Indo-european definition of transitivity as the “ transitive model of transitivity ”, and the Kagayanen definition as the “ ergative model of transitivity ". Examples of basic transitive constructions occur throughout this grammar. Here are a few additional examples from the corpus. Notice that all of these examples contain an ergative pronoun that refers to the Actor--the person or persons who control or originate the situation--, in addition to an absolutive argument, either overtly expressed or strongly implied:

Patimod eman danen. \\
Pa-timod eman danen. \\
t.r -pick.up again.as.before 3 p.erg \\
‘They picked (it) up again as before.’ [CBWN-C-10 3.4]

Tapos likid pangdan ya a. Tapos tapa. Diristso no banggod daw likiren isab daw bļaren. \\
Tapos likid-... pangdan ya a. Tapos tapa-... Diristso no banggod-... daw likid-... isab daw baļad-en. \\
then roll.up- t.ir pandan def.f ctr then dry.on.fire- t.ir straight 2 s.erg straighten.out- t.ir and roll.up- t.ir again and dry.in.sun- t.ir \\
Recall from chap:verbstructure, sec:omissionofaffixes that inflectional affixes are often omitted. One common context for such omission is sequences of closely linked events such as this.
`Then roll up the pandan. Then dry (it) on a fire. Right away straighten (it) out and roll (it) up again and dry (it) in the sun.’ [NCOP-C-02 2.2-4]... nakita kon danen sikad tama na kwarta daw bļawan. \\... na-kita kon danen sikad tama na kwarta daw bļawan. \\
a.hap.r -see hsy 3 p.erg very many/much lk money and gold \\
‘... they saw, it is said, much money and gold.’ [CBWN-C-10 6.3]

Constructions such as these are sometimes called “Patient voice” or “Undergoer voice” constructions because they present the Undergoer in the absolutive case. That is, the Undergoer (often patient), is presented as the participant that is the most affected by the situation being expressed, and is the Privileged Syntactic Argument. Like intransitives, these transitive constructions can be understood as statements “about” the absolutive. clearly showed that in Tagalog, transitive constructions such as these are the most common, simplest, and most psychologically salient construction type for expressing situations involving an Undergoer and a separate Actor. This is also the case in Kagayanen. In addition, children acquiring Tagalog as their first language learn to use Patient voice transitive constructions fluently earlier than the corresponding Actor voice constructions. Semantically, the absolutive refers to the referent that is most affected by the event, usually a patient. Pragmatically, the absolutive patient tends to be highly referential, individuated, and specific.

The following examples illustrate transitive patient voice clauses similar to the English clauses illustrated in fig:kagayanenchoir. In these examples, we indicate the absolutive argument by a zero  in the pre-nominal position, though we do not use this convention in other parts of the grammar:

Absolutive = Patient: \\
Paakid ko sidda an naan ta pinggan no. \\
Pa-akid ko sidda an naan ta pinggan no. \\
t.r -serve 1 s.erg abs fish def.m spat.def nabs dish 2 s.gen \\
‘I served the fish on your plate.’

Lutuon ko sidda an para ta mga bisita. \\
Luto-en ko sidda an para ta mga bisita. \\
cook- t.ir 1 s.erg abs fish def.m for nabs pl visitor \\
‘I will cook the fish for the visitors.’

Iluto no sidda an. \\
I-luto no sidda an. \\
t.deon -cook 2 s.erg abs fish def.m \\
‘You must cook the fish.’

summary: In Kagayanen and other Philippine languages, transitivity is better analyzed with an ergative model: clauses are intransitive if they have an absolutive argument and no ergative argument, and transitive if they have both absolutive and ergative arguments. Many basic transitive clauses are “patient voice” or “undergoer voice” constructions, in which the absolutive argument is the participant most affected by the event and functions as the privileged syntactic argument.

subsection: Applicative constructions (Benefactive, Adversative, and Locative voice)
text:
benefactive voice|( adversative voice|( locative voice|( applicative constructions|(
Applicatives are often thought of as "transitivizing" constructions (see inter alia ). This is because applicative morphology on a verb expressing an intransitive situation creates a new verb stem that expresses a transitive situation in which activity is directed to an endpoint, usually a location or a beneficiary. The endpoint introduced by the applicative construction becomes a core argument of the verb--a direct object in a nominative/accusative system or an absolutive in an ergative/absolutive system. However, if the root that accepts applicative morphology already involves activity transferred to an endpoint (i.e., it is “semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic "), the applicative construction redirects the activity to a different endpoint, again usually a location or beneficiary. In such situations, the applicative does not increase transitivity at all--it simply redirects the activity described by the verb to a different endpoint.

This characterization contrasts applicative constructions with causative constructions in that the applicative introduces an endpoint (an “object” in terms used by ), whereas a causative adds a starting point--an initiator, or Actor to a scene (see bkm:Ref500569782 on causatives). In Kagayanen, the verbal suffix - an (and sometimes the prefix i -) normally introduces an endpoint to a scene. That endpoint may be a semantic beneficiary/recipient, maleficiary maleficiary, locative or instrumental participant, depending on the semantics of the verb, its arguments, and the context. If the base clause is intransitive, the applicative is grammatically transitive. If the base clause is transitive, the clause remains transitive and the applicative in effect “replaces" the endpoint of the base clause.

-.2ptApplicative morphology is central to the voice systems of Philippine languages. As mentioned in the introduction to sec:choir, transitivity marking in the inflectional paradigm, plus stem-forming applicative morphology is what gives rise to benefactive, adversative, locative, and instrumental voice in Kagayanen. In each of these construction types, the Actor, if present, appears in the ergative case, the Undergoer/patient, if present, appears in the non-absolutive (demoted Undergoer) case, and a “new" beneficiary, maleficiary, location or instrument appears in the absolutive case.

Benefactive voice often functions to express situations in which something is transferred to a beneficiary, with the beneficiary presented in the absolutive case (examples bkm:Ref500489993 and bkm:Ref500489123 ). However, transfer is not a necessary component of the meaning of this construction (examples ex:thecabinet through ex:thetikling ).

Absolutive = Beneficiary/recipient \\
Paakiran ko kanen an ta sidda. \\
Pa-akid-an ko kanen an ta sidda. \\
t.r -serve- apl 1 s.erg abs 3 s.abs def.m nabs fish \\
‘I served her/him some fish.’

Lutuan ko kanen an ta sidda. \\
-Luto-an ko kanen an ta sidda. \\
t.ir -cook- apl 1 s.erg abs 3 s.abs def.m nabs fish \\
‘I will cook him/her some fish.’

Without the applicative marker on the verb, example bkm:Ref500489123 could only be understood as patient voice, which would be anomalous with these arguments: “I will cook him/her (with/on/by) fish.”

The absolutive of a Benefactive applicative need not be the recipient of a transferred item. In example ex:thecabinet, the absolutive is the pronominal enclitic a, `1 s.abs '. This is understood as the beneficiary of the cleaning event, but not necessarily the recipient of the cleaned item (the cabinet). Similar observations can be made for examples ex:nationalanthem and ex:thetikling:

Palimpyuan a din ta aparador. \\
Pa-limpyo-an a din ta aparador. \\
t.r -clean- apl 1 s.abs 3 s.erg nabs cabinet \\
`S/he cleaned the cabinet for me.' (Meaning I will not have to clean it.)

Pakantaan kay din ta Bayang Magiliw. \\
Pa-kanta-an kay din ta Bayang Magiliw. \\
t.r -sing- apl 1 p.excl.abs 3 s.erg nabs country beloved \\
`S/he sang for us Beloved Country (the National Anthem).'

Pasayawan a danen ta tinikling. \\
Pa-sayaw-an a danen ta tiinkling. \\
t.r -dance- apl 1 s.abs 3 p.erg nabs \\
`They danced for me the tinikling (dance).'

As discussed in chap:verbstructure, sec:modality the Deontic prefix i- may function as an applicative marker, as in bkm:Ref500489008. As such, i - may function as a deontic Benefactive marker:

Absolutive = Beneficiary: \\
Iluto a no ta sidda. \\
I-luto a no ta sidda. \\
t.deon -cook 1 s.abs 2 s.erg nabs fish \\
‘You must cook me some fish.’

Technically, bkm:Ref500489008 is ambiguous between Benefactive and Patient voice. However, pragmatically it can only be understood as Benefactive voice, since people don’t cook other people. We are reminded of English sentences like “I will make you a sandwich” which are similarly “ambiguous”. The usage illustrated in bkm:Ref500489008 has also been described as “conveyance voice” in Cebuano based on the fact that it presents the Undergoer ( sidda ‘fish’) as moving away from the Actor.

Examples bkm:Ref500490084 through bkm:Ref500742432 illustrate Locative voice. Again, these are only understood as locative because of the context. In bkm:Ref500490084, for example, the plate cannot logically be a beneficiary, but rather is a logical location for serving something:

Absolutive = Location: \\
Paakiran ko pinggan no an ta sidda. \\
Pa-akid-an ko pinggan no an ta sidda. \\
t.r -serve- apl 1 s.erg abs plate 2 s.gen def.m nabs fish \\
‘I served on your plate some fish.’

Pakan-anan din pinggan ko an ta sinugba ya na sidda. \\
Pa-kan-en-an din pinggan ko an ta s<in>ugba ya na sidda. \\
t.r -cooked.rice- apl 3 s.erg abs dish 1 s.gen def.m
nabs < nr.res >roast def.f lk fish \\
As mentioned earlier, the verb meaning `to eat' consists of suppletive stems; kaan is the bare form, but when any suffixes are involved, the root changes to kan-en, the nominal root meaning `cooked rice.' When the stem-forming suffix contains an a vowel, such as the applicative - an, vowel harmony applies, resulting in the stem form kan-anan.
‘S/he ate roasted fish in my dish.’

We are calling example bkm:Ref500490264 Locative voice because the younger sibling is presented as the target of laughing. This sentence cannot be understood as Benefactive voice (“He laughed for my younger sibling”), even though the absolutive argument is animate and human.
summary:
Applicative constructions add an endpoint to the event structure of a verb, typically a beneficiary, recipient, location, or instrument, and this new endpoint becomes a core argument in the clause. If the base verb is intransitive, applicative morphology makes it transitive; if the base verb is already transitive, the applicative usually redirects the activity to a different endpoint rather than increasing transitivity.

In Kagayanen, applicative morphology underlies benefactive, locative, and related voice constructions, with the Actor in ergative case and the new endpoint in absolutive case. The passage illustrates that benefactive voice can express transfer but does not require it, while locative voice is used when the absolutive argument is interpreted as the location or target of the action.

subsection: Applicative constructions (Benefactive, Adversative, and Locative voice)
text:
Patawaan din mangngod ko an. \\
Pa-tawa-an din mangngod ko an. \\
t.r -laugh- apl 3 s.erg abs younger.sibling 1 s.gen def.m \\
‘S/he laughed at my younger sibling.’

The following example illustrates a Locative voice construction in Irrealis modality:

Lutuan ko bakod an na kandwagan ta sidda para ta bisita. \\
-Luto-an ko bakod an na kandwagan ta sidda para ta bisita. \\
t.ir -cook- apl 1 s.erg abs big def.m lk skillet nabs fish for nabs visitor \\
‘I will cook in the big skillet some fish for the visitor.’

The following are some additional applicative (Locative or Benefactive/Recipient voice) constructions from the corpus:

Absolutive = Location: \\
Papilitan din kon gantangan ya ta saļeng… \\
Pa-pilit-an din kon gantangan ya ta saļeng… \\
t.r -stick.on- apl 3 s.erg hsy 3.quart.measurer def.f nabs sap \\
‘He stuck the sap on the 3 quart measurer.’ [CBWN-C-22 6.5]

Absolutive = Location: \\
yon nang pakamangan nay ta ame na pangabuian pang-adlaw-adlaw \\
yon nang pa-kamang-an nay ta ame na pangabui-an pang-adlaw-adlaw \\
d 3 abs only/just t.r -get- apl 1 p.excl.erg nabs 1 p.excl.gen lk living- nr inst - red -sun/day \\
`… that only is from where we get our livelihood for daily use.’ (This refers to the salary of the author of this text.) [VPWL-T-03 3.2]

Absolutive = Location (Goal): \\
Pabalikan din pa kwarta ya na bilin ta baļay ya danen. \\
… pa-balik-an din pa kwarta ya na bilin ta baļay ya danen. \\
t.r -return- apl 3 s.erg emph money def.f lk leave.behind nabs house def.f 3 p.gen \\
`…he even returned for the money that he left in their house.’ [BCWN-C-04 6.5]

Absolutive = Beneficiary/recipient: \\
Manang padaļaan a nyo man ta nyo na kudak… \\
Manang - pa-daļa-an a nyo man ta nyo na kudak… \\
Older.sister t.ir- caus -carry/take- apl 1 s.abs 2 p.erg also nabs 2 p.gen lk picture \\
‘Older sister, send me your picture…’ [PBWL-T-10 10.2]

Absolutive = Beneficiary/recipient: \\
Taga-Mampyo daw Nusa pasuļatan na mubos uli ta Sintro tak indyiksyunan. \\
Taga-Mampyo daw Nusa pa-suļat-an na m-ubos uli ta Sintro tak - indyiksyun-an. \\
orig -Mampyo and Nusa t.r -write- apl lk i.v.ir -all go.home nabs Central because t.ir -inject- apl \\
`The ones from Mampyo and Nusa were written to all to come to Central because (they) will be injected.’ (This is about an outbreak of cholera.) [JCWN-T-21 10.1]

Example bkm:Ref118204268 illustrates an applicative construction inside a relative clause. The head is basak ‘land’, which is the location of planting.

Absolutive = Location: \\
Kami may basak nataneman nay ta niog. \\
Kami may basak na-tanem-an nay ta niog. \\
1 p.excl.abs ext.in land a.hap.r -plant- apl 1 p.excl.erg nabs coconut \\
‘As for us (we) have land on which we have planted coconut trees.’ [JCOE-T-06 5.5]

In example bkm:Ref118204368 the composite pronoun ta kaw expresses a first person singular ergative plus second person singular absolutive argument (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:pronouns on the composite pronouns):

Erg.+Abs. = Agent+Addressee: \\
Nay, kisyem nang en sugiran ta kaw. \\
Nay, kisyem nang en - sugid-an ta kaw. \\
mom tomorrow only/just cm t.ir -tell- apl 1 s.erg 2 s.abs \\
The composite pronouns are usually spelled as two words in the Kagayanen orthography, even though they are pronounced as one word.
‘Mom, just tomorrow I will tell you.’ (The content of what she will tell is implied.) [BMON-C-06 3.19]

Example bkm:Ref118204569 illustrates three applicative constructions. The first applicative involves the root ibit ‘hold’, which is a member of the class of roots that always appear in an applicative form when transitive (Class VIII). All such roots involve a patient that does not undergo a change in state, but is only slightly, superficially or invisibly affected by the action of the verb. In this case, the act of holding a child does not change or affect the child in any substantive way, and thus the child shares the semantic feature of “superficial affectedness” with locations. chap:verbclasses-1, sec:volitionaltransitiveroots contains a long list of such roots. In the second applicative in bkm:Ref118204569, the location of the placing of water is the head of the child, which appears in the absolutive. Finally, in the third applicative, the absolutive argument of the stem garayan ‘to chant for’ is ellipted because the child is the main topic in this stretch of text, and in the context it is clear that the midwife chants for the child.

Nanligan i pabitan din bata daw batangan ta waig a ulo ta bata. Tapos pagarayan din.\\
Nanligan i pa-ibit-an din bata daw...- batang-an ta waig a ulo ta bata. Tapos pa-garay-an din.\\
midwife def.n t.r -hold- apl 3 s.erg child and t.r -put- apl nabs water inj head nabs child then t.r -chant- apl 3 s.erg \\
`As for the midwife, she holds the child and puts some water on the head of the child. Then she chants (for the child).’ (This is a naming ceremony for newborn babies similar to baptism.) [VAOE-J-06 1.4]

absolutives in applicative constructions may be “Malefactees", as well as Benefactees. In happenstantial modality without a conscious controller, applicatives almost always imply a “malefactive” or “adversative” sense. Such constructions present an adversely affected participant as the absolutive. For example, ex:thepigdied illustrates a basic intransitive clause, while ex:thepigdiedonus adds an adversely affected participant to the scene:

Absolutive = Patient: \\
Napatay baboy an. \\
Na-patay baboy an. \\
a.hap.r -die abs pig def.m \\
‘The pig died.’
Absolutive = Maleficiary: \\
Napatayan kami i ta baboy. \\
Na-patay-an kami i ta baboy. \\
a.hap.r -die- apl 1 p.excl.abs def.n nabs pig \\
‘The pig died on us (adversely affecting us).’
summary: The passage shows that applicative constructions in Kagayanen can mark a range of absolutive arguments, including locations, goals, beneficiaries/recipients, and even maleficiaries. It also notes that some verbs regularly appear in applicative form with superficially affected patients, that applicatives can occur inside relative clauses, and that composite pronouns may encode combined ergative and absolutive roles.

subsection: Applicative constructions (Benefactive, Adversative, and Locative voice)
text:
The English free translation expresses the approximate sense of ex:thepigdiedonus. Recall that na - is an “ambitransitive” prefix, meaning that it may occur in a transitive or intransitive construction. Example ex:thepigdied is obviously intransitive because there is only one participant, and that participant, the pig, is in the absolutive case. Example ex:thepigdiedonus, on the other hand, is somewhat transitive in that kami ‘us’ is presented as the most saliently affected participant, and the pig, though clearly not an Actor, is the source of the effect. A more literal but non-idiomatic English translation might be “The pig died us” (it died, adversely affecting us).

The following is an example of Adversative voice in irrealis, happenstantial modality:

Absolutive = Maleficiary: \\
Mabadbaran kami ta igot ta katig. \\
Ma-badbad-an kami ta igot ta katig. \\
a.hap.ir -untie- apl 1 p.excl.abs nabs tie nabs outrigger \\
‘The tie of an outrigger will become untied on us (adversely affecting us).’

Example bkm:Ref118208801 illustrates a happenstantial irrealis modality Adversative applicative construction from the corpus. We know the prefix on the bolded verb has been dropped because adlaw `sun/day' used as a verb meaning `become daylight' must take happenstantial modality. The prefix ma - may be added, with no change in meaning, but the dynamic intransitive irrealis prefixes mag - or m - are impossible:

Maria, pilak no duma an na suwa tak kani adlawan ki en. \\
Maria, pilak no duma an na suwa tak kani... -adlaw-an ki en. \\
Maria throw.away 2 s.erg some def.m lk citrus.fruit because later a.hap.ir -sun/day- apl 1 p.incl.abs cm \\
`Maria, throw away some of the citrus fruit because later it will become daytime on us.’ (This is a story about a mother, who is a witch, and her daughter. They were invisible flying home carrying citrus fruit. So the mother tells the daughter to throw away some of the fruit so they will not be seen.) [MBON-T-06 5.8]

In constructions with an Actor in dynamic modality the semantic role of the absolutive argument is sometimes technically ambiguous between beneficiary or maleficiary, though context usually disambiguates:

Pabadbaran kay din ta igot ta katig. \\
Pa-badbad-an kay din ta igot ta katig. \\
i.r -untie- apl 1 p.excl.abs 3 s.erg nabs tie nabs.gen outrigger \\
‘S/he untied the tie of an outrigger on us.’ Adversative \\
Or ‘S/he untied the tie of an outrigger for us.’ Benefactive

Pagubbaan kay din ta pungkuan. \\
Pa-gubba-an kay din ta pungko-an. \\
t.r -ruin- apl 1 p.excl.abs 3 s.erg nabs sit- apl \\
‘S/he ruined the chair on us.’ Adversative \\
Or: ‘S/he ruined the chair for us.’ (They wanted it ruined to use the wood for something else like firewood.) Benefactive

Pataguan kay din ta pagkaan. \\
Pa-tago-an kay din ta pagkaan. \\
t.r -hide- apl 1 p.excl.abs 3 s.erg nabs food \\
‘S/he hid the food from us.’ (So we couldn’t eat it.) Adversative
Or: ‘S/he hid the food for us.’ (So we could eat it and nobody else could eat it first.) Benefactive

Padalukan kay din ta pagkaan. \\
Pa-dalok-an kay din ta pagkaan. \\
t.r -greedy- apl 1 p.excl.abs 3 s.erg nabs food \\
‘S/he was greedy towards us with food.’

The following are some Benefactive and Adversative applicatives from the corpus:

… daw pamisaan ta pari patay an daw pabinditaan din man patay an. \\
… daw pa-misa-an ta pari patay an daw pa-bindita-an din man patay an. \\
and t.r -mass- apl nabs priest die def.m and t.r -bless- apl 3 s.erg also die def.m \\
`…and the priest conducts a mass for the dead one and he also blesses the dead one.’ [CBWE-C-06 6.2]

… daw maimo kon palitan nay daen iran na mga order. \\
… daw ma-imo kon -palit-an nay daen iran na mga order. \\
if/when a.hap.ir -do/make hsy t.ir -buy- apl 1 p.excl.erg 3 p.abs 3 p.gen lk pl order \\
‘... if it is possible they said we will buy for them what they ordered.’ [AFWL-L-01 8.3]

Daw gaduļot kaw ta ittaw na dili makita yaken pa na dili nyo duļutan na bui a i? \\
Daw ga-duļot kaw ta ittaw na dili ma-kita yaken pa na dili nyo 0- duļot-an na bui a i? \\
if/when i.r -food.offering 2 p.abs nabs person lk neg.ir a.hap.ir -see
1 s.abs emph lk neg.ir 2 p.erg t.ir -food.offering- apl lk live 1 s.abs att \\
`If you offer food for unseen people (spirits), even more for me won’t you offer food when I am living?’ [JCWN-T-20 10.5]

… kami napatayan ta makina… \\
… kami na-patay-an ta makina… \\
1 p.excl.abs a.hap.r -die- apl nabs engine \\
‘…the engine (of the boat we were riding) died on us….’ [MMWN-L-01 5.8]

There is also a “partitive” usage of the applicative construction, which may be considered a variation on patient voice. Compare the following two examples:

Absolutive = Patient: \\
Pautod din kaoy an. \\
Pa-utod din kaoy an. \\
t.r -cut 3 s.erg abs tree/wood def.m \\
‘S/he cut the wood.’

Absolutive = Partitive patient: \\
Pauturan din kaoy an. \\
Pa-utod-an din kaoy an. \\
t.r -cut- apl 3 s.erg abs tree/wood def.m \\
‘S/he cut part of the wood.’

The meaning of bkm:Ref500573276 is that the Actor did not cut the wood completely in two parts, but only cut off a small portion. It also notes that with an Actor in dynamic modality, the absolutive role can be ambiguous between beneficiary and maleficiary, though context usually clarifies it. The applicative has this effect for many Class VI verbs that are inherently transitive. Consider the following:

Patient voice (absolutive = patient: roasted fish): \\

As mentioned in chap:verbstructure, one may understand this usage as indicating that the Undergoer is not a prototypical patient. In this case, it is understood that the patient is only partially affected. In other constructions, the applicative indicates that the absolutive is a locative, or beneficiary/maleficiary participant. These are also non-prototypical Patients, in that they are less than completely affected by the activity expressed by the verb.

This observation is corroborated by verbs that always take an applicative suffix in their basic transitive form (Class VIII). In each case, they describe situations in which the patient argument is not prototypical in that it does not undergo a change in state as a result of the event described by the verb. These verbs include amblig ‘to care for’, arek ‘to kiss’, tabang ‘to help’, and many others listed in chap:verbclasses-1, sec:volitionaltransitiveroots.

Instrumental voice constructions are characterized by a grammatically transitive verb form, with the Actor in the ergative case, and an instrumental element in the absolutive. In realis modality, Instrumental and Patient voice constructions are structurally identical; the only way to distinguish the two is by semantics--if the absolutive argument is a semantic instrument, it is Instrumental voice, whereas if the absolutive argument is a patient, it is Patient voice:

Absolutive = Instrument: \\
Paakid ko luag i na bag-o ta sidda. \\
Pa-akid ko luag i na bag-o ta sidda. \\
t.r -serve 1 s.erg abs big.spoon def.n lk new nabs fish \\
‘I used the new serving spoon to serve some fish.’

In irrealis modality, however, instrumental voice is distinguished by the presence of the transitive deontic prefix i -. In such situations, the - i prefix has an instrumental applicative function, as in ex:servesomefish and bkm:Ref500142287:

Iakid ko luag i na bag-o ta sidda. \\
I-akid ko luag i na bag-o ta sidda. \\
t.deon -serve 1 s.erg abs big.spoon def.n lk new nabs fish \\
‘I must use the new serving spoon to serve some fish.’

Without the i - prefix in example ex:servesomefish, the sentence becomes anomalous:

*Akiren ko luag i na bag-o ta sidda. \\
*Akid-en ko luag i na bag-o ta sidda. \\
serve- t.ir 1 s.erg abs big.spoon def.n lk new nabs fish \\
(‘I will serve the new serving spoon to/for fish.’)

Iprito ko bag-o i na mantika ta sidda. \\
I-prito ko bag-o i na mantika ta sidda. \\
t.deon -fry 1 s.erg abs new def.n lk oil nabs fish \\
‘I must use the new oil to fry some fish.’

Again, in transitive irrealis modality without the i- prefix, example bkm:Ref500142287 becomes anomalous (??‘I will fry the new oil for/to/with fish.’). Because the absolutive nominal can be construed as an instrument in each instance, the only possibility is Instrumental voice.

In several other Philippine languages, such as Waray, reflexes of the same verbal prefix i - are more strongly associated with Instrumental voice. However, in Kagayanen i- is essentially a transitive deontic modality marker that occasionally has an irrealis instrumental applicative usage.

summary: Instrumental voice in Kagayanen is a transitive construction with the Actor in ergative case and an instrumental element in the absolutive. In realis modality it is structurally identical to Patient voice, so it can only be distinguished by meaning, while in irrealis modality it is marked by the transitive deontic prefix **i-**, which functions as an instrumental applicative. The passage notes that in Kagayanen **i-** is mainly a transitive deontic modality marker, though it can also mark instrumental voice, especially when the absolutive noun is clearly interpreted as an instrument.

text: To this point, we have characterized voice in Kagayanen as a grammatical system for adjusting the relationship between semantic roles and grammatical relations. In particular, the various voices in the Kagayanen choir highlight different semantic roles by bringing them into the absolutive case. In this section we will describe three additional grammatical phenomena that linguists often view as transitivity increasing or decreasing constructions. These are morphological causatives morphological causatives, reflexives reflexive constructions. and reciprocals reciprocal constructions.
summary: The passage says that Kagayanen voice is a grammatical system that adjusts the relationship between semantic roles and grammatical relations by placing different semantic roles in the absolutive case. It then introduces three other kinds of constructions that linguists often treat as transitivity-increasing or transitivity-decreasing: morphological causatives, reflexives, and reciprocals.

causative constructions|(

A causative construction is one in which an external causal agent is added to the message-world situation described by a clause. Semantically, a causative situation consists of two main parts: the cause and the effect. The effect is the base situation, and the cause is what the external causal agent does in order to bring about the effect. We will call the added agent the causer, and we will call the central participant of the effect the causee. Consider the following English causative construction:

The devil made me do it.

In this example, I did it describes the effect, and the devil made (something happen) describes the cause; the devil is the causer (also known as the agent cause ), and me is the causee. Typically, the notion of cause may involve permission ( allow ), and/or facilitation ( make possible ), as well as strict causation. For example, in the following English sentences, the semantic roles of the participants are given above the referring expressions:.15cm Causer.95cm Causee \\
[ Corelli ] fed [ the horses ]. ‘Corelli made/let the horses eat.’

Causer.7cm Causee \\
[ You ] made [ me ] laugh. \\.15cm Causer 1.45cm Causee 1.8cm Patient \\
[ Meribel ] urged [ Calixto ] to order [ Hawaiian Pizza ]. \\.15cm Causer.9cm Causee 1.2cm Recipient.2cm Theme \\
[ Simeon ] let [ Meribel ] send [
Michael ] [ flowers ]. \\

Grammatically, causation may be accomplished in the lexicon, the syntax, or the morphology of any language. A lexical causative lexical causatives is a single verb that embodies both the notions of cause and effect. For example, the English verb die evokes an inherently intransitive concept. The verb kill, on the other hand, evokes the same intransitive concept as die does, but with the addition of a causer-- kill means cause to die. There are many such non-causative/causative pairs of verbs in English, including learn/teach, see/show, go/send, eat/feed, and so on. Example ex:letthehorseseat is a lexical causative construction ( feed means ‘cause/allow to eat’). Corelli is the participant who does something to cause, allow or make it possible for the horses to eat.

A syntactic causative construction syntactic causative construction causatives!syntactic (also called an “analytic causative” analytic causatives causatives!analytic is one in which the notions of cause and effect are embodied in different verbs. For example, cause to die is a syntactic causative because there are two verbs, one expressing the cause and the other expressing the effect ( die ). Examples ex:youmademelaugh through ex:simeonletmeribelsendmichaelflowers are all syntactic causative constructions because they involve the addition of a main verb, make, urge, or let, which expresses the cause, while the dependent verbs ( laugh, order, and send ) express the effect. The subject of the causative verb is the causer, while the grammatical object of that verb is the causee.

-4.1ptFinally, a morphological causative morphological causatives causatives!morphological (also sometimes called a “synthetic causative” synthetic causatives causatives!synthetic ) is one in which non-causative and causative forms are related morphologically, usually via some kind of affixation. English does not have very productive morphological causatives, though pairs such as dark/darken ( darken ‘cause to be dark’), and mad/madden ( madden ‘cause to be mad’) come close. In other languages, including Kagayanen, morphological causatives are a much more robust and regular part of the grammar.

Kagayanen exhibits many pairs of lexical roots that may be considered non-causative/causative pairs. A few we have encountered to date are given in tab:non-causativeandlexicallycausativeverbs.

In addition to these lexical causative verbs, Kagayanen has several verbs that function as syntactic causatives. These verbs evoke the notion of cause, while the effect is expressed in a separate verb in irrealis modality. We term this use of the irrealis modality “subjunctive” subjunctive (see chap:clausecombining, sec:subjunctiveclauses ). A few of these verbs are listed in bkm:Ref501085954, and some examples from the texts are given below, beginning with bkm:Ref501085964:

ambaļan ‘to warn, advise, speak directly to, order’ The verb ambaļ ‘say’ only means ‘to warn/advise/order’ in the applicative form. In other forms it means simply ‘to say.’

summary:
A causative construction adds an external causer to a clause, with the cause and effect as its two semantic parts: the causer brings about an effect experienced by the causee. Such causation can be expressed lexically in a single verb, syntactically with separate verbs for cause and effect, or morphologically by affixation; English has many lexical and syntactic causatives, but few productive morphological ones.  

The passage then shows that Kagayanen has both lexical causative verb pairs and syntactic causatives, with verbs such as *pwirsa* ‘force,’ *pilit* ‘urge,’ *sugo* ‘order,’ and others taking an irrealis-subjunctive effect clause. It also notes a morphological causative prefix *pa-* in forms like *pa-leges* and *pa-sugo*, which expresses causation such as ‘cause to borrow’ or ‘order to carry water.’

text:
The most productive means of forming a causative construction in Kagayanen is morphologically, morphological causatives expressed with the verbal prefix pa -. This is a very common stem-forming prefix, as discussed in chap:stemformingprocesses, sec:morphologicalcausative. A few common non-causative morphological causative verb pairs are given in bkm:Ref501438581. However, the causative prefix may be added to practically any root to form a transitive, causative verb stem. Meanings expressed by the morphological causative include ‘to cause someone to do something’, ‘to ask someone to do something’, ‘to let someone or something do something’, ‘to make it possible for someone to do something’, or ‘just wait for someone to do something or something to happen.’

As discussed in chap:verbstructure, sec:transitiverealis, the causative prefix pa - is homophonous with the transitive realis Inflectional prefix. Therefore, one transitive verb with pa - can have two meanings: one simple transitive bkm:Ref501092121 and the other causative bkm:Ref329253035.

Pasuot din bayo din ya. \\
Pa-suot din bayo din ya. \\
t.r -wear 3 s.erg clothes/shirt 3 s.gen def.f \\
‘S/he wore his/her shirt.’...-Pasuot din ki yaken bayo din ya. \\
pa-pa-suot din ki yaken bayo din ya. \\
t.r-caus -wear 3 s.erg obl.p 1s clothes/shirt 3 s.gen def.f \\
‘S/he let me wear his/her shirt.’

It is clear, however, that there are two distinct pa - morphemes for at least two reasons. First, example bkm:Ref329253035 is ditransitive--it has three arguments: a causer din '3serg', a causee ki yaken ` obl.p 1s ', and a patient bayo din ya `shirt 3 s.erg def.f '. This can only be understood as causative. The only non-causative interpretation would be “s/he wore his/her shirt to/on me”, which makes no sense. Example bkm:Ref501092121, on the other hand, has only two arguments, and may not be understood as causative (*‘S/he made the shirt wear something’...). Second, it is possible for both pa - morphemes to occur on the same verb:

Papasuot din ki yaken bayo din ya. \\
Pa-pa-suot din ki yaken bayo din ya. \\
t.r-caus -wear 3 s.erg obl.p 1s clothes/shirt 3 s.gen def.f \\
‘S/he made me wear his/her shirt.’

As discussed in chap:verbstructure sec:omissionofprefixes, sequences of double pa - often simplify. However, when a double pa - does occur, it expresses a stronger causative, as roughly reflected in the English free translations of bkm:Ref329253035 and ex:his/hershirt.

With ditransitive verb roots, when there is only one pa - it is the transitive, realis prefix bkm:Ref236213080. For the causative, the shortened form is not normally used, probably for clarity bkm:Ref329253571, but it can be used in fast speech.

Non-causative: \\
Pabligya din ki yaken baboy din an. \\
Pa-bligya din ki yaken baboy din an. \\
t.r -sell 3 s.erg obl.p 1s pig 3 s.gen def.m \\
‘S/he sold his/her pig to me.’

Causative: \\
Papabligya din ki yaken baboy din an. \\
Pa-pa-bligya din ki yaken baboy din an. \\
t.r - caus -sell 3 s.erg obl.p 1s pig 3 s.gen def.m \\
‘S/he made/let me sell his/her pig.’

Some non-volitional intransitive verbs are understood as causative when used in a grammatically transitive frame, even without the causative prefix pa -. These are described as patient-preserving labile patient-preserving labile verbs verbs in chap:verbclasses-1 (Classes I-II), or “P-labile” verbs P-labile verbs:

Non-volitional intransitive (Class II) root: pudpod ‘to crumble to powder’: \\
Gapudpod siminto an tak lugay en. \\
Ga-pudpod siminto an tak lugay en. \\
i.r -crumble.into.powder cement def.m because long.time cm \\
‘The cement is/was crumbling up into powder because it has been a long time.’

Causative: \\

`Crush the medicine into powder so that she can put (it) on her wound.' (lit. `Cause the medicine to crumble to powder...’)

As with all semantically transitive semantic transitivity transitivity!semantic verbs, causative verb stems can appear in a Detransitive (Actor voice) construction. In this case, the pa - causative does appear with some verbs (such as lunot `decay' in example bkm:Ref501112712 ) but not with others (such as pudpod, ‘crumble into powder’ in example bkm:Ref329259219 ):

Detransitive of causative: \\

Ga-pa-lunot kanen ta tampayas. \\

‘S/he let/caused the papaya to decay.’ \\

a.hap.r -crumble.into.powder all lk cement lk t.r -work lk hollow.block \\

Pa-pudpod din buļong an aged -batang din naan ta nina din. \\
t.r -crumble.into.powder 3 s.erg medicine def.m so.that t.ir -put
3 s.erg spat.def nabs wound 3 s.gen \\
`S/he crumbled the medicine into powder so that s/he could put it on his/her wound.’

We know that the pa - in example ex:putitonwound is the transitive realis prefix and not a causative because a) in irrealis modality, pa - does not need to appear even though the frame is transitive, and the meaning is causative ( ex:onthewound ), and b) a double pa - is not possible for this subclass of verbs: * papapudpod.

Detransitive (Actor voice) of causative: \\

Ga-pudpod kanen an ta buļong. \\

summary: The passage explains that Kagayanen most productively forms causatives with the prefix **pa-**, which can be added to almost any root and expresses meanings such as causing, asking, letting, or enabling someone to do something. It also shows that **pa-** is homophonous with a transitive realis prefix, so some forms are ambiguous, but true causatives can be identified by their argument structure and by the possibility of double **pa-**, which yields a stronger causative meaning. The text further notes that some non-volitional intransitive verbs can be interpreted causatively in transitive frames without **pa-**, and that whether **pa-** appears in detransitive constructions depends on the verb class.

text:
We know that bkm:Ref329259219 is a detransitive of a causative construction and not a simple intransitive construction because a) the absolutive pronoun refers to a person, and persons don’t (normally) crumble into powder, and b) the understanding is that the medicine is what crumbles, with the absolutive argument referring to a causal agent.

The reason verbs like lunot ‘to decay/disintegrate’ require an overt causative morpheme in the detransitive may be that they describe processes that are not accomplished by an external agent--there is nothing one can do to “decay something”. Rather, one can only wait or allow it to happen on its own. On the other hand, verbs like pudpod ‘to crumble into powder’ can be construed as the result of someone’s act.

Causative constructions may also take the applicative suffix to express Locative, Benefactive, or Adversative voice. With P-labile roots, such causatives may be expressed without an overt causative prefix.

‘S/he caused/let the small boat wash ashore.’

1 s.erg spat.def nabs yard 1 p.excl.gen \\
`S/he kept alive for me the banana that I planted in our yard.’

Magpalunot ka ta tampayas ki kanen. \\
Mag-pa-lunot ka ta tampayas ki kanen. \\
i.ir - caus -decay 2 s.abs nabs papaya obl.p 3s \\
‘You will cause him/her to let the papaya decay.’

Double causative and applicative (Locative voice). P-Labile verb: \\
Papadagsaan din ki yaken baybay an ta mga batang. \\
Pa-pa-dagsa-an din ki yaken baybay an ta mga batang. \\
t.r - caus -wash.ashore- apl 3 s.erg obl.p 1s beach def.m nabs pl driftwood \\
`S/he made me let some driftwood wash ashore on the beach.’

Padagsaan din ki yaken baybay an ta mga batang. \\
- Pa-dagsa-an din ki yaken baybay an ta mga batang. \\
t.ir-caus -wash.ashore- apl 3 s.erg obl.p 1s beach def.m nabs pl driftwood \\
`S/he will make me let some driftwood wash ashore on the beach.’

We know that the pa - prefix is a causative, and the modality is irrealis in bkm:Ref501176811 because of the argument structure. The presence of an oblique argument, ki yaken, makes it clear that this is a double causative. The absence of an overt transitivity marker on the verb indicates that this must be irrealis modality (recall that the presence of the applicative - an precludes the use of the transitive irrealis suffix - en, thus leaving “zero” as the only indicator of transitivity). If the pa - in this example were the transitive realis pa -, the only possible reading would be “You brought the driftwood to the beach at me,” and such a meaning is impossible.

The following are examples of causatives of semantically volitional intransitive verbs. In contrast to non-volitional P-labile verbs, these verbs must occur with the causative prefix in order to be understood as causative:

Papalarga din bata din ya aged mangita ta ubra.\\
Pa-pa-larga din bata din ya aged ma-ng-ita ta ubra.\\
t.r - caus -depart 3 s.erg child 3 s.gen def.f so.that a.hap.ir - pl -search nabs work \\
‘S/he caused his/her child to depart in order to search for work.’

Palargaen a ta mga ginikanan ko tak adlek na mangasawa. \\
Pa-larga-en a ta mga ginikanan ko tak adlek na ma-ngasawa. \\
caus -depart- t.ir 1 s.abs nabs pl parent 1 s.gen because afraid lk a.hap.r -get.married \\
`My parents will send me away (cause me to depart) because (they) are afraid I will get married soon.’

Detransitive (Actor voice) of causative, absolutive = agent cause: \\
Gapalarga kanen an ta mga lansa tak uļa en bagyo. \\
Ga-pa-larga kanen an ta mga lansa tak uļa en bagyo. \\
i.r - caus -depart 3 s.abs def.m nabs pl launch because neg.r cm typhoon \\
‘S/he is/was causing/letting the launches (to) depart because there was no more typhoon.’

Magpalarga kanen an ta mga lansa daw linaw en. \\
Mag-pa-larga kanen an ta mga lansa daw linaw en. \\
i.ir - caus -depart 3 s.abs def.m nabs pl launch if/when calm cm \\
‘S/he will cause/let the launches (to) depart when it is calm.’
summary:
The passage explains that certain verbs are analyzed as detransitives of causative constructions rather than simple intransitives, based on argument semantics and event interpretation: for example, some verbs imply an external causer or allow a reading where the absolutive argument is the causal agent. It also shows that causatives can combine with applicative suffixes for Locative, Benefactive, or Adversative voice, and that with P-labile roots these combinations may appear without an overt causative prefix.

It further distinguishes non-volitional intransitives, which require a causative prefix to get a causative meaning, from semantically volitional intransitives, which must also appear with the causative prefix when causativized. The examples illustrate double causatives, detransitive causatives, and how argument structure and the presence or absence of applicative and transitivity markers determine whether forms are interpreted as realis or irrealis.

text:
Applicative (Locative voice) + Causative: \\
Papailingan din ki yaken baļay din an na pagpayag. \\
Pa-pa-iling-an din ki yaken baļay din an na pag-payag. \\
t.r - caus -go- apl 3 s.erg obl.p 1s house 3 s.gen def.m lk red -nipa.house \\
‘S/he caused/let me go to his/her house that is a rest house.’

The following examples illustrate causatives of inherently transitive and ditransitive verbs. Again, with these verbs the causative prefix is required in order to express the causative sense:

Patient = Absolutive: \\
Papatangtang ko ki kanen igot an ta lunday. \\
Pa-pa-tangtang ko ki kanen igot an ta lunday. \\
t.r - caus -remove 1 s.erg obl.p 3s tie def.m nabs outrigger.canoe \\
‘I had him/her remove the tie from the outrigger canoe.’

Causee = Absolutive: \\
Papatangtang ko kanen an ta igot ta lunday. \\
Pa-pa-tangtang ko kanen an ta igot ta lunday. \\
t.r - caus -remove 1 s.erg 3 s.abs def.n nabs tie nabs outrigger.canoe \\
‘I made him/her remove the tie from the outrigger canoe.’

Causer = Absolutive (detransitive): \\
Gapatangtang a ki kanen ta igot ta guso. \\
Ga-pa-tangtang a ki kanen ta igot ta guso. \\
i.r - caus -remove 1 s.abs obl.p 3s nabs tie nabs seaweed \\
`I am/was causing/allowing him/her to remove the tie of the agar-agar seaweed.’

Magpatangtang ka nang ki kanen ta igot ta lunday. \\
Mag-pa-tangtang ka nang ki kanen ta igot ta lunday. \\
i.ir - caus -remove 2 s.abs just obl.p 3s nabs tie nabs outrigger.canoe \\
‘You just cause/let him/her remove the tie of the outrigger canoe.’

Instrument = Absolutive (Instrumental voice): \\
Iparabas no ki kanen ļangkaw an na sundang. \\
I-pa-rabas no ki kanen ļangkaw an na sundang. \\
t.deon - caus -clear.land 2 s.erg obl.p 3s long def.m lk machete \\
‘You must cause/let him/her clear the land with the long machete.’

Paparabas ko ki kanen ļangkaw an na sundang. \\
Pa-pa-rabas ko ki kanen ļangkaw an na sundang. \\
t.r - caus -clear.land 1 s.erg obl.p 3s long def.m lk machete \\
‘I caused/let him/her clear the land with the long machete.’

Theme = Absolutive (causative of ditransitive): \\
Paatag no kani ki kanen kwarta i naan ta tatay din. \\
- pa-atag no kani ki kanen kwarta i naan ta tatay din. \\
t.ir - caus -give 2 s.erg later obl.p 3s money def.n spat.def nabs father 3 s.gen \\
`Let him/her later give the money to his/her father.’

Ipaatag no kani ki kanen kwarta i naan ta tatay din. \\
I-pa-atag no kani ki kanen kwarta i naan ta tatay din. \\
t.deon - caus -give 2 s.erg later obl.p 3s money def.n spat.def
nabs father 3 s.gen \\
`You must later let him/her give the money to his/her father.’

Patient as absolutive (Patient voice): \\
Papasabligan din ki yaken mga ittaw an ta waig. \\
Pasablig no ki kanen waig an naan ta mga ittaw. \\
- Pa-sablig no ki kanen waig an naan ta mga ittaw. \\
t.ir - caus -splash 2 s.erg obl.p 3s water def.m spat.def nabs pl people \\
‘Cause/let him/her splash the water on people.’

Ipasablig no ki kanen waig an naan ta mga ittaw. \\
I-pa-sablig no ki kanen waig an naan ta mga ittaw. \\
t.deon - caus -splash 2 s.erg obl.p 3s water def.m spat.def nabs pl people \\
‘You must cause/let him/her splash the water on people.’

No example has been found of Benefactive or Adversative voice in a deontic causative construction ( i- + pa -) in the corpus.

Applicative of a causative (Locative voice): \\
Pa-pa-sablig-an din ki yaken mga ittaw an ta waig. \\
t.r - caus -splash- apl 3 s.erg obl.p 1s pl people def.m nabs water \\
‘S/he caused/let me splash at the people with water.’

Applicative of a causative (Benefactive voice): \\
Papabunakan ka din ki yaken ta mga bayo no. \\
Pa-pa-bunak-an ka din ki yaken ta mga bayo no. \\
t.r - caus -laundry- apl 2 s.abs 3 s.erg obl.p 1s nabs pl clothes 2 s.gen \\
‘S/he caused/let me wash your clothes for you.’

Applicative of a Causative (Adversative voice): \\
Papalagpukan din ki yaken mga ittaw an ta baril. \\
Pa-pa-lagpuk-an din ki yaken mga ittaw an ta baril. \\
t.r - caus -explode- apl 3 s.erg obl.p 1s pl people def.m nabs gun \\
‘S/he caused/let me fire off a gun on the people.’ (This does not mean the people were being shot at, but just being scared or intimidated by the firing of the gun.)

The detransitive causative of some verbs has a reflexive sense, since the causer and the patient may be coreferential ( bkm:Ref329267348 ). The meaning is ‘to let oneself have something done to oneself.’ A distinct causee can occur optionally in an oblique phrase, as in bkm:Ref329267373 and bkm:Ref329267376.

Magpasagod ka nang en daw manakem ka. \\
Mag-pa-sagod ka nang en daw manakem ka. \\
i.ir - caus -take.care 2 s.abs just cm if/when older 2 s.abs \\
‘Just have yourself taken care of when you are elderly.’

Gapabuļong a naan ta duktor. \\
Ga-pa-buļong a naan ta duktor. \\
i.r - caus -medicine 1 s.abs spat.def nabs doctor \\
‘I am/was having myself medicated by the doctor.’

Gapaluko ka nang imo ta yo na ittaw. \\
Ga-pa-luko ka nang imo ta yo na ittaw. \\
i.r - caus -trick 2 s.abs just emph nabs d4adj lk person \\
‘You just let yourself be tricked by that person.'

Example bkm:Ref108689939 illustrates two instances of this “reflexive/causative” usage for two other verbs, kita ‘to see’ and kasaļ ‘to marry’:
summary:
The passage shows that the causative prefix **pa-** is required to express causative meaning with several verb types, including transitive, ditransitive, and causativized intransitive verbs, and that it can combine with applicative morphology to yield locative, benefactive, adversative, and other voice patterns. It also notes that no examples were found of benefactive or adversative voice in **deontic causatives** with **i- + pa-** in the corpus.  

In addition, some **detransitive causatives** can have a **reflexive** interpretation, where the causer and patient are the same person, meaning ‘let oneself have something done to oneself,’ with an optional separate causee in an oblique phrase.

Sabat ta pangka ya, “ Mag-pa-kita a ta imo na mga ginikanan daw ambaļ-en ko danen na mag-pa-kasaļ ki." \\
