text:
Reflexive and Reciprocal constructions

express the idea that two main participants in a scene are “the same” in some way. A reflexive reflexives construction is one in which the Actor (A) and an Undergoer (O) are the same entity, as in She saw herself. All true reflexive constructions reduce the semantic transitivity of a transitive clause by specifying that there are not two separate entities involved. Rather, one entity fulfills two semantic roles and/or grammatical relations. A prototypical reciprocal reciprocal clause is one in which two participants equally act upon each other, for example they saw each other.

Certain verbs can be described as “lexical reflexives” in that, when they occur in an intransitive construction, they are automatically understood as reflexive. These are mostly ``grooming” verbs, such as langoy ‘bathe’ and arbas ‘shave’:

Galangoy kanen an. \\
Ga-langoy kanen an. \\
i.ir -bathe 3 s.abs def.m \\
‘S/he bathed (him/herself).’

Gabarbas kanen an. \\
Ga-barbas kanen an. \\
i.ir -shave 3 s.abs def.m \\
`He shaved (himself).’

Except for these lexical reflexives, and the extended use of causative morphology to express a kind of reflexive described in the previous section, most reflexive constructions in Kagayanen are syntactic. They consist of a transitive or detransitive construction with a possessed Referring Phrase headed either by kaugalingen ‘self’ or lawa ‘body’ occurring in the Undergoer role. These may either be transitive ( bkm:Ref118617763 ), or detransitive ( bkm:Ref118617766 ):

Panina din lawa din an. \\
Pa-nina din lawa din an. \\
t.r -wound 3 s.erg body 3 s.gen def.m \\
‘S/he wounded him/herself.’ (lit. ’S/he wounded her/his own body.’)

Gaugas kanen ta kaugalingen din. \\
Ga-ugas kanen ta kaugalingen din. \\
i.r -wash 3 s.abs nabs self 3 s.gen \\
‘S/he washed her/himself.’

These examples must be understood as reflexive; the possessor of the Undergoer may not refer to a distinct person. In other words, bkm:Ref118617763 cannot mean `S/he wounded someone else's body’. Kaugalingen is the dedicated reflexive nominal. Lawa ’physical body’ is sometimes used in place of kaugalingen, possibly because it is shorter.

Examples bkm:Ref118617763 and bkm:Ref118618251- bkm:Ref118618196 show that ergative case Actors may antecede absolutive case reflexive RPs. Examples bkm:Ref118617766 and bkm:Ref501865097 illustrate that an absolutive Actor ( ka ‘you’) may be the antecedent for a reflexive Referring Phrase in a detransitive construction:

Dili ka gid dyan magpabaya ta imo na kaugalingen. \\
Dili ka gid dyan mag-pa-baya ta imo na kaugalingen. \\
neg,ir 2 s.abs int d 4 loc i.ir - caus -ignore nabs 2 s.gen lk self \\
‘Do not just ignore yourself there.’ [VBWL-T-06 2.4]

The following are some additional examples of syntactic reflexives from the corpus:

Reflexive RP = Absolutive (theme): \\
Iran nang na kaugalingen isip ya danen. \\
Iran nang na kaugalingen isip ya danen. \\
3 p.gen only lk self think def.f 3 p.erg \\
‘Themselves only is what they think about.’ [MOOE-C-01 189]

Reflexive RP = Non-absolutive (addressee): \\
Yon ambaļ ko ta ake na kaugalingen... \\
Yon ambaļ ko ta ake na kaugalingen... \\
d 3 abs say 1 s.erg nabs 1 s.gen lk self \\
‘That is what I said to myself...’ [EMWN-T-05 7.4]

Reflexive RP = Absolutive (theme): \\
Piro gusto ko gid anay ipakilala ko ake na kaugalingen. \\
Piro gusto ko gid anay i-pa-kilala ko ake na kaugalingen. \\
but want 1 s.erg int first/for.awhile t.deon - caus -know 1 s.erg 1 s.gen lk self \\
‘But I really want to first have to introduce myself.’ ( kilala is code switching from Tagalog.) [EMWL-T-04 4.5]

Reflexive RP = Absolutive (patient): \\
… pirmi a nang en na pangamuyo ta Dios, "Daw anen ka pa man gapamati, tagan no ta dayad na disisyon para malibri ko pambot, malibri ko lawa ko."\\
… pirmi a nang en na …-pangamuyo ta Dios, "Daw anen ka pa man ga-pa-mati, -atag-an no ta dayad na disisyon para ma-libri ko pambot, ma-libri ko lawa ko." \\
always 1 s.abs only/just cm lk i.r -pray nabs
God if/when ext.g 2 s.abs inc also i.r - caus -hear t.ir -give- apl 2 s.erg nabs good lk decision for a.hap.ir -free 2 s.erg motorboat a.hap.ir -free 2 s.erg body 1 s.gen \\
`… I kept on praying to God, “If you are still here listening, give (me) a good decision that I may free the motorboat, I may free myself."’ (This is a story about a fisherman whose boat was turned upside down and he was riding on the bottom of the boat still holding on to his hook and line with a big fish on it.) [EFWN-T-10 4.7]

Reflexive RP = Non-absolutive (patient) \\
Nang Maria, mag-amblig ka ta imo na lawa para dili ka magmasakit daw dili man malik imo na sakit. \\
Nang Maria, mag-amblig ka ta imo na lawa para dili ka mag-ma-sakit daw dili man m-balik imo na sakit. \\
older.sister Maria i.ir -be.careful/take.care 2 s.abs nabs 2 s.gen lk body for
neg.ir 2 s.abs i.ir - adj -sick and neg.ir also i.v.ir -return 2 s.gen lk pain \\
`Older sister Maria, take care of (your) self so that you will not become sick and your pain will not return.’ [BCWL-C-02 6.1]

Though kaugalingen is the dedicated reflexive nominal, there is evidence that the meaning of lawa is also becoming a dedicated reflexive itself. Example bkm:Ref118699324 shows that lawa does not always refer literally to someone’s physical body.
summary: The passage explains that reflexive constructions identify the Actor and Undergoer as the same entity, while reciprocal constructions involve two participants acting on each other equally. In Kagayanen, some verbs are lexical reflexives, but most reflexives are syntactic and use a possessed phrase headed by **kaugalingen** ‘self’ or sometimes **lawa** ‘body’ in the Undergoer role, with the possessor obligatorily referring to the same participant as the Actor. The text also notes that **kaugalingen** is the dedicated reflexive nominal, though **lawa** may be developing a similar specialized reflexive use.

text:
Reflexive RP = Non-absolutive (figure of speech) \\
Yi ni isya na liksyon ta isya na ittaw na sali ta bansag ta iya na lawa na dili man kasarang. \\
Yi ni isya na liksyon ta isya na ittaw na sali ta bansag ta iya na lawa na dili man ka-sarang. \\
d1abs d1pr one lk lesson nabs one lk person lk always nabs nickname 3 s.gen
3 s.gen lk body lk neg.ir also i.exm -able \\
`This very thing is a lesson for a person who always is boasting of him/herself (lit. nicknaming him/herself) when (s/he) is not capable (of doing what s/he boasts about).’ [DBWN-T-26 12.1]

Example bkm:Ref118618209 illustrates the Tagalog borrowing sarili ‘self’ used in place of kaugalingen or lawa:

… dili ki magbugal ta ate na sarili na kiten mabiskeg… \\
… dili ki mag-bugal ta ate na sarili na kiten ma-biskeg… \\
neg.ir 1 p.incl.abs i.ir -proud nabs 1 p.incl.gen lk self lk 1 p.incl.abs
ar -strong \\
`….let’s not be proud of ourselves that we are strong…’ [BCWN-T-05 12.19]

Kagayanen employs morphological reciprocal constructions. The morphological reciprocal reduces semantic and grammatical transitivity by expressing a multi-argument situation in a grammatically intransitive clause. As described in chap:stemformingprocesses, sec:reciprocals, there are two verb suffixes that express reciprocal constructions, - anay and - ay.

Examples bkm:Ref414723974 through bkm:Ref414775243 illustrate several prototypical examples of the reciprocal suffixes from the text corpus. Following this, some extended usages are described. A prototypical reciprocal construction involves an inherently transitive verb in a grammatically intransitive construction, with a reciprocal suffix on the verb and an Actor understood or explicited expressed as plural. The plural Actor may appear as a plural pronoun ( bkm:Ref414723974 ) or full RP ( bkm:Ref414775363 ):

Dimalas na gasugatay danen i naan ta Puerto. \\
Dimalas na ga-sugat-ay danen i naan ta Puerto. \\
bad.luck lk i.r -meet- rec 3 p.abs def.n spat.def nabs Puerto \\
‘(It was) bad luck that they met each other in Puerto.’ [BEWN-T-01 5.3]

The plural Actor can also be expressed in coordinated noun phrases:

Pagkitaay danen na tama en na mga umang, pasugiran en na kanen an daw Pwikan kisyem sellem maglumbaay dļagan.\\
Pag-kita-ay danen na tama en na mga umang, pa-sugid-an en na kanen an daw Pwikan kisyem sellem mag-lumba-ay dļagan. \\
nr.act -see- rec 3 p.abs lk many cm lk pl hermit.crab t.r -tell- apl cm lk 3 s.abs def.m and sea.turtle tomorrow morning i.ir -race- rec run \\
`When he and many hermit crabs met, (he) told (them) that he and Sea-turtle tomorrow morning would race each other running.’ [JCON-L-08 19.4]

Notice the first word in example bkm:Ref414775363 carries the reciprocal suffix - ay and also the action nominalization prefix pag - (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:pag ). The sense of this action nominalization is “seeing each other”, or “meeting together”. Examples bkm:Ref501776847 and bkm:Ref501776849 illustrate the same verb with the reciprocal suffix as the main predicator of the clause:

Uyi kitaay danen ta iya na sawa paagi man ta kaļat nang. \\
U-yi...- kita-ay danen ta iya na sawa paagi man ta kaļat nang. \\
emph-d 1 abs i.r -see- rec 3 p.abs nabs 3 s.gen lk spouse by.means too nabs rope only \\
`These ones, he and his spouse met/saw each other by means of just a rope…’ (His wife lowered a rope out her window and they eloped.) [MBON-T-07a 13.1]

Mam, taan sadya kaw pirmi tak gakitaay kaw ta inyo na mga utod daw arey. \\
Mam, taan sadya kaw pirmi tak ga-kita-ay kaw ta inyo na mga utod daw arey. \\
Ma’am maybe happy 2 p.abs always because i.r -see- rec 2 p.abs nabs
2 p.gen lk pl sibling and friend \\
`Ma’am, maybe you are always happy because you and your siblings and friends are seeing each other.’ [AFWL-L-014.2]

Reciprocal constructions are very productive and common. The following are some additional examples from the corpus:

Dili mag-agaway ta mga pagkaan. \\
Dili mag-agaw-ay ta mga pagkaan. \\
neg.ir i.ir -grab- rec nabs pl food \\
‘Don’t grab food from each other.’ [ETOP-C-10 2.4]

Paambaļ na tangkeban, sura din, may darwa na bato na gatubangay na may kulor na gainog-inog. \\
Pa-ambaļ na tangkeb-an, sura din, may darwa na bato na ga-tubang-ay na may kulor na ga-inog-inog. \\
t.r -say lk close- nr looks 3 s.gen ext.in two lk rock lk i.r -facing- rec lk ext.in color lk i.r - red -red \\
The usual root meaning ‘red’ is minog. Sometimes the form is inog, especially when reduplicated, as in this example, in which case it means ‘reddish’ or ‘getting red’ as a red fruit when ripening.
`What is called tangkeban, it looks like two rocks that have a reddish color facing each other.’ [EFWE-T-05 3.1]

Reduplication may co-occur with a reciprocal suffix:

Daw danen gampang dili magtangayaw-tangayaway … Dili makagat-kagatay. \\
Daw danen ga-ampang dili mag-tangayaw-tangayaw-ay … Dili ma-kagat-kagat-ay. \\
if/when 3 p.abs i.r -play neg.ir i.ir - red -say.bad.things- rec neg.ir a.hap.ir-red -bite- rec \\
`When they are playing together, (they) will not keep saying bad things to each other … (They) will not keep biting each other.’ [LBOP-C-04 1.2-3]

Gaampang danen daw galagas-lagasay danen naan ta suba … \\
Ga-ampang danen daw ga-lagas-lagas-ay danen naan ta suba … \\
i.r -play 3 p.abs and i.r-red -chase- rec 3 p.abs spat.def nabs river \\
‘They were playing and they kept chasing each other in the river …’ [CBWN 6.2]

The following are two non-prototypical usages of the reciprocal suffix. These uses do not occur in the corpus, but are often heard in conversation. First, the suffix - ay can express “mutual action”, that is, a group of people doing an action together over a period of time, though not necessarily acting on each other:

Gasayaway mga bai naan ta balkon. \\
Ga-sayaw-ay mga bai naan ta balkon. \\
i.r -dance- rec pl woman spat.def nabs porch \\
‘The women danced together (as a group but not as dance partners) on the porch.’
summary:
The passage first gives examples of reflexive expressions, including forms where Tagalog *sarili* ‘self’ is borrowed to mean ‘self’ in place of native forms. It then explains that Kagayanen has productive morphological reciprocal constructions, marked by the verb suffixes *-anay* and *-ay*, which reduce transitivity by placing a multi-participant event in an intransitive clause with a plural actor.

The text shows prototypical reciprocal uses like “meet each other,” “see each other,” and “grab from each other,” and notes that reduplication can co-occur with the reciprocal suffix. It also mentions a non-prototypical use, where *-ay* can express mutual action done together as a group, such as dancing together without necessarily acting on one another.

text:
Gainemay mga mama naan ta balkon. \\
Ga-inem-ay mga mama naan ta balkon. \\
i.r -drink- rec pl man spat.def nabs porch \\
‘The men drank together for some time on the porch.’

Ta buļan ta Nobyembre 1988 ta mga bagyo na gasunod-sunuray alos galibeg uļo ta mga ittaw di tak naubusan kay ta beggas.\\
Ta buļan ta Nobyembre 1988 ta mga bagyo na ga-sunod-sunod-ay alos ga-libeg uļo ta mga ittaw di tak na-ubus-an kay ta beggas.\\
nabs month/moon nabs November 1988 nabs pl typhoon lk i.r - red -follow- rec almost i.r -worry head nabs pl person d 1 loc because a.hap.r -use.up- apl 1 p.excl.abs nabs milled.rice \\
`In the month of November, 1988, because of typhoons that kept following one after another, mostly people here were worried because we ran out of rice.’ [EMWL-T-03 7.2]

Gaeļes-eļesay kami ta kanta. \\
Ga-eļes-eļes-ay kami ta kanta. \\
i.r - red -take.turns- rec 1 p.excl.abs nabs sing \\
‘We keep taking turns singing.’

Gaeļes-eļesay kami ta bayo. \\
Ga-eļes-eļes-ay kami ta bayo. \\
i.r-red -borrow- rec 1 p.excl.abs nabs clothes \\
‘We keep borrowing each other’s clothes.’ (lit. ‘We keep on taking turns with clothes.’)

Finally, the reciprocal may be used in a special sense when only one participant is acting ( bkm:Ref402683617 - bkm:Ref118453570 ). The free translations of these examples somewhat capture the sense of what this construction expresses, though they are not very literal. A literal translation of bkm:Ref402683617 would be something like “That is dancing of the woman with each other.” The idea is that the woman is dancing so well or vigorously that it seems as though there are several women dancing together. This is a very productive construction that can involve all kinds of actions and participants.

Nyan na sayaway ta bai an! \\
Nyan na sayaw-ay ta bai an. \\
d2abs lk dance- rec nabs woman def.m \\
‘Wow! Look at the woman dance!’

Nyan na ampangay ta bata an! \\
Nyan na ampang-ay ta bata an. \\
d2abs lk play- rec nabs child def.m \\
‘Wow! Look at the child play!’

Nyan na layugay ta yupan an! \\
Nyan na layog-ay ta yupan an. \\
d2abs lk fly- rec nabs bird def.m \\
‘Wow! Look at the bird fly!’

Nyan na kantaay ta mama an na ingaw! \\
Nyan na kanta-ay ta mama an na ingaw. \\
d2abs lk sing- rec nabs man def.m lk drunk \\
‘Wow! Look at the drunk man sing!’

Nyan na kantaay ta bata an! \\
Nyan na kanta-ay ta bata an. \\
d2abs lk sing- rec nabs chld def.m \\
‘Wow! Look at the child sing!’

Nyan na basaay ta libro bata an! \\
Nyan na basa-ay ta libro bata an. \\
d2abs lk read- rec nabs book chld def.m \\
‘Wow! Look at the child reading books!’
voice|)
summary: The passage shows that the reciprocal suffix can express repeated or mutual action, as in examples meaning “drink together for some time,” “keep following one another,” or “keep taking turns singing/borrowing clothes.” It also notes a special productive use where only one participant is involved, but the action is presented as if multiple actors were doing it, giving meanings like “look at the woman dance” or “look at the child play/sing/read.”

text: Up to this point we have been concerned primarily with Kagayanen constructions whose prototypical function is to express affirmative assertions in compact information packages (see, e.g., on information packaging in discourse). In this chapter we will describe several constructions that deviate from this prototype in one way or another, and so may be characterized as “pragmatically marked” pragmatically marked constructions. First we will describe various types of negation ( bkm:Ref445900201 ). Then we will discuss non-declarative speech acts ( bkm:Ref445900286 ), that is, constructions whose functions are to elicit information ( interrogative constructions, bkm:Ref445900289 and bkm:Ref445900292 ), and those whose primary function is to encourage or direct other people to act ( imperative constructionss, bkm:Ref445900361 ). Next, we will discuss several pragmatically marked construction types that are used to ascribe different types of special prominence to parts of a clause ( bkm:Ref445900433 ). These include argument fronting ( bkm:Ref445900436 ), special discourse particles ( bkm:Ref118460437 ), and cleft constructions ( sec:cleftconstructions ). Finally, we discuss certain interjections ( bkm:Ref113971883 ) and the general pro-form kwa ‘thingamajig’ ( bkm:Ref113971891 ).
summary: The passage introduces a chapter on Kagayanen constructions that depart from the language’s prototypical affirmative, information-packaging pattern and are therefore described as pragmatically marked. It says the chapter will cover negation, non-declarative speech acts such as interrogatives and imperatives, constructions that give special prominence to parts of a clause, and finally certain interjections and the pro-form kwa ‘thingamajig.’

negation|(
There are two particles in Kagayanen that express clausal negation negation!clausal clausal negation. Uļa negates existential clauses and clauses in realis modalities ( bkm:Ref80510883 ). Dili negates non-verbal clauses other than existentials, individual words, and clauses in irrealis modalities ( bkm:Ref446684276 ). These particles may be considered adjunct adverbs, as discussed in chap:modification, sec:adjunctadverbs. Like all adjunct adverbs, both negative particles attract second-position enclitics and clitic pronouns.

Realis negative: uļa
negation!realis|(
The adjunct adverb uļa negates verbal clauses in realis moods (examples bkm:Ref446045407 -- bkm:Ref373140065 ). Like other preverbal adjunct adverbs, uļa attracts second position adverbs and enclitics. In examples bkm:Ref230081554 and bkm:Ref80941165, the ergative enclitic pronouns din and ko follow uļa. In example bkm:Ref80941209 both din and the referential expression kami i follow uļa:

Mangngod din ya a uļa din gid tagi. \\
Mangngod din ya a uļa din gid...-atag-i. \\
younger.sibling 3 s.erg def.f ctr neg.r 3 s.erg int t.r -give- xc.apl \\
‘His younger sibling he did not give (him anything)!’ [RBWN-T-02 2. 8]

… nademdeman ko inay daw amay ko na uļa ko pamatian iran na ambaļ. \\
… na-demdem-an ko inay daw amay ko na uļa ko pa-mati-an iran na ambaļ. \\
a.hap.r -remember- apl 1 s.erg mother and father 1 s.gen lk
neg.r 1 s.erg t.r -hear- apl 3 p.gen lk say \\
‘… I remembered my mother and father, that I did not obey what they said.’ [PMWN-T-02 2.13]

Salamat nang man ta Dios tak uļa din kami i patandega. \\
Salamat nang man ta Dios tak uļa din kami i pa-tandeg-a. \\
thank only emph nabs God because neg.r 3 s.erg 1 p.excl.abs def.n t.r -touch- xc \\
‘Thanks to God also because he did not touch us!’ (This is a text about an attack by pirates.) [BCWN-C-04 5.4]

Examples bkm:Ref80941234 through bkm:Ref373140065 illustrate various second-position adverbs following uļa:

Duma an uļa man gatanem ta guso. \\
Duma an uļa man ga-tanem ta guso. \\
some def.m neg.r emph t.r -plant nabs seaweed \\
‘Some do not really plant agar-agar seaweed.’ [ETOP-C-08 3.12]

… daw uļa din en nakita yo na mga kabaw daw mga lengngessa. \\
… daw uļa din en na-kita yo na mga kabaw daw mga lengngessa \\
and neg.r 3 s.erg cm a.hap.r -see d4abs lk pl water.buffalo
and pl blood \\
‘…and he did not see those water buffalo and blood.’ [PBWN-C-13 11.5]

Tapos asta anduni uļa pa man danen pakamang iran na mga order tak uļa kon danen kwarta… \\
Tapos asta anduni uļa pa man danen pa-kamang iran na mga order tak uļa kon danen kwarta … \\
then until now/today neg.r inc emph 3 p.erg t.r -get 3 p.erg lk pl order
because neg.r hsy 3 p.abs money \\
‘Then even until now/today they did not yet get what they ordered because they say they have no money …’ [AFWL-L-01 5.13]

Tama a man nailingan na mga lugar na uļa ko pa nailingan. \\
Tama a man na-iling-an na mga lugar na uļa ko pa na-iling-an. \\
many 1 s.abs emph a.hap.r -go- apl lk pl place lk neg.r 1 s.erg inc a.hap.r- go -apl \\
‘There are many places I have gone (lit. I have many gone-to places) that I had not yet gone to.’ [SLWN-C-01 10.3]

When a noun or pronoun is replaced with the existential may (see chap:non-verbalclauses, sec:existentialconstructions ), the clause contains both uļa and may:

Pila kon bisis tilipunuan danen piro uļa may gasabat. \\
Pila kon bisis tilipuno-an danen piro uļa may ga-sabat. \\
few hsy times telephone- apl 3 p.erg but neg.r ext.in i.r -answer \\
‘A few times they telephoned (him/her) but no one answered.’ [PBWL-T-07 3.3]

Uļa replaces the existential particles may and anen (see chap:non-verbalclauses, sec:existentialconstructions ) in negative existential clauses:

Uļa kan-en gid tak uļa ittaw dya i. \\
Uļa kan-en gid tak uļa ittaw dya i. \\
neg.r cooked.rice int because neg.r person d 4 loc att \\
‘There is really no cooked rice because there are no people there.’ [MOOE-C-01 5]
negation!realis|)

Irrealis negative: dili
negation!irrealis|(
The form dili negates all types of irrealis clauses (examples bkm:Ref373243062 - bkm:Ref446617639 ):

Daw balikiren ko kanen ya, dili ko man nya makita. \\
daw balikid-en ko kanen ya, dili ko man nya ma-kita \\
if/when look.back- t.ir 1 s.erg 3 s.abs def.f neg.ir 1 s.erg also d 4 abs a.hap.ir -see \\
‘If I look back at him/her, I will not be able to see that one.’ [JCON-T-08 42.4]

Dili kay gid magsagbak, Sir. \\
dili kay gid mag-sagbak, sir \\
neg.ir 1 p.excl.abs int i.ir -noisy sir \\
‘We really will not be noisy, Sir.’ [SFOB-L-01 3.4]

Piro daw kapatay ka man dili a makatabang ki kaon. \\
Piro daw ka-patay ka man dili a maka-tabang ki kaon.' \\
but if/when i.exm -kill 2 s.abs also neg.ir 1 s.abs i.hap.ir -help obl.p 2s \\
‘But if you happened to kill someone, I cannot help you.’ [RBON-T-01 2.7]

Nyan en ambaļ ko lecture ko ta mga bataan ko na dili nyo gid labien duma na ittaw daw labien nyo gid utod nyo. \\
Nyan en ambaļ ko lecture ko ta mga bata-an ko na dili nyo gid labi-en duma na ittaw daw labi-en nyo gid utod nyo. \\
d 2 abs cm say 1 s.erg lecture 1 s.erg nabs pl child- nr 1 s.ge lk neg.ir 2 p.erg int favor- t.ir other lk person if/when favor- t.ir 2 p.erg int sibling 2 p.gen \\
`That is what I say, I lecture to my children that you do not ever favor other people and you really favor your own sibling(s).’ [RBON-T-01 7.1]
summary:
Kagayanen has two particles for clausal negation: **uļa** for existential clauses and clauses in realis modalities, and **dili** for non-verbal clauses other than existentials, individual words, and clauses in irrealis modalities. Both are treated as adjunct adverbs, so they attract second-position enclitics and clitic pronouns.

The passage further shows that **uļa** negates realis verbal clauses and can appear with second-position adverbs, while in negative existential clauses it replaces existential particles like **may** and **anen**. **Dili** is used for all irrealis clauses, as illustrated by several examples.

text:
Tama na mga ittaw na gambaļ na dili gid kon madayon ame na kasaļ tak basi dili a kon kapanaw. \\
Tama na mga ittaw na ga-ambaļ na dili gid kon ma-dayon ame na kasaļ tak basi dili a kon ka-panaw. \\
many lk pl person lk i.r -say lk neg.ir int hsy a.hap.ir -continue
1 p.excl.gen lk wedding because maybe neg.ir 1 s.abs hsy i.exm -go/walk \\
`Many people said that our wedding should not really continue because maybe I could not walk.’ [VAWN-T-163.4]

Ambaļ ko, “Daw may tirador ka dyan dili no tiraduron tak yan, yupan i, yan gatabyang ta ate na uma daw tanto na danen i makakaan ta luod.” \\
Ambaļ ko, “Daw may tirador ka dyan dili no tirador-en tak yan, yupan i, yan ga-tabyang ta ate na uma daw tanto na danen i maka-kaan ta luod.” \\
say 1 s.erg if/when ext.in slingshot 2 s.abs d 2 loc neg.ir 2 s.erg slingshot- t.ir
because d 2 abs bird def.n d 2 abs i.r -help nabs 1 p.incl.gen lk field and reason.why lk 3 p.abs def.n i.hap.ir -eat nabs worm \\
`I said, “If you have a slingshot there, do not shoot (it) with the slingshot because that one, the bird, that one helps our fields and for the reason they can eat worms.”' [MEWN-T-02 3.2]

The form dili also negates predicate nominal and other non-verbal predicates, except existentials (see the functions of uļa above). With non-verbal clauses the negative marker occurs before the Predicate, in both Predicate+Argument (exs. bkm:Ref80941751 through bkm:Ref80941878 ) and Argument+Predicate structures (exs. bkm:Ref113700006 and bkm:Ref80941881 ).... dili man kon pelles angin an. \\... dili man kon pelles angin an. \\
neg.ir also hsy strong wind def.m \\
‘... the wind was not even strong, they say.’ [EMWN-T-06 5.3]

Dili maklaro agi din ya daw indi gagi. \\
Dili ma-klaro agi din ya daw indi ga-agi. \\
neg.ir adj -clear path 3 s.gen def.f if/when where i.r -path \\
‘His path is not clear where he went.’ [RCON-L-01 5.5]

Dili keļeng buok din an. \\
Dili keļeng buok din an. \\
neg.ir curly shair 3 s.gen def.m \\
‘Her hair is not curly.’ [CBOE-C-01 1.13]

Isya din na mari a maļbaļ daw isya ya a dili maļbaļ. \\
Isya din na mari a maļbaļ daw isya ya a dili maļbaļ. \\
one 3sgen lk godmother inj witch and one def.f inj neg.ir witch \\
‘One of her godmothers is a witch and the (other) one is not a witch.’ [CBWN-C-13 3.2]

Paryo ta makay ta lunday, “manaog” dili man igo. \\
Paryo ta m-sakay ta lunday, “m-panaog” dili man igo. \\
like nabs i.v.ir -ride nabs outrigger.canoe i.v.ir -go.down.stairs neg.ir also right \\
‘Like riding an outrigger canoe, “ manaog ” (going down stairs) is not right.’ (This is about the words makay ta lunday, which do not collocate with manaog ‘go down stairs’ because the verb should be mawas ‘disembark’.) [RCON-L-03 21.12]

Like other adjunct adverbs, dili attracts enclitic pronouns bkm:Ref446051860 and second-position adverbs enclitics ( bkm:Ref373229895 ).

Dayon a ambaļ, “Pedro, dili a lain na ittaw.” \\
Dayon a ambaļ, “Pedro, dili a lain na ittaw.” \\
right.away 1 s.abs say Pedro neg.ir 1 s.abs different lk person \\
‘Right away I said, “Pedro, I am not a different/another person.”' [EFWN-T-11 15.5]

… dili pa yaken sagad. \\
… dili pa yaken sagad. \\
neg.ir inc 1 s.abs skillful \\
‘… I am not yet skillful.’ [MAWL-C-03 8.1]
negation!irrealis|)
summary: The passage explains that **dili** is the main irrealis negator and is used not only with verbal predicates but also with **predicate nominals and other non-verbal predicates**, though not with existentials. In non-verbal clauses it appears **before the predicate** in both predicate-plus-argument and argument-plus-predicate structures, and it also behaves like an adjunct adverb by attracting enclitic pronouns and second-position adverbs.

text:
negation!constituent|( constituent negation|(
Constituent negation is a clause type in which a constituent of a clause is negated, rather than the clause itself. Examples in English include:

No-one arrived. \\
Not many people attended the party. \\
She planted no trees. \\
None of our students received an award.

Examples of constituent negation in Kagayanen can always be interpreted as cleft constructions (see sec:cleftconstructions ). This is because Kagayanen employs no copula in predicate nominal constructions. Thus a sentence like “She planted no trees” can always be understood literally as “No trees are what she planted”. Not surprisingly, then, dili is used in such contexts, since clefts are a kind of predicate nominal construction:

Yi dili nyog tanem din. Iya a mangga. \\
Yi dili nyog tanem din. Iya a mangga. \\
d1abs neg.ir coconut plant 3 s.erg 3 s.gen ctr mango \\
‘These ones (the parents), what they planted was not coconut. As for them, (what they planted was) mango.’ In this narrative, the speaker uses singular pronouns ( din, iya ) to refer to two people, parents, who acted together. This is a common discourse usage. [SFOB-L-01 5.2]

Anduni uļa gapati mga ittaw tak dili Apo Kagiyaw gibit ta angin i daw dili, ate na Maal na Dios. \\
Anduni uļa ga-pati mga ittaw tak dili Apo Kagiyaw ga-ibit ta angin i daw dili, ate na Maal na Dios. \\
now/today neg.r i.r -believe pl person because neg.ir Apo Kagiyaw
i.r -hold nabs wind/air def.n
if/when neg.ir 1 p.incl.erg lk beloved lk God \\
Daw dili is an idiomatic expression translated freely in English as “but rather.” The following elliptical clause is affirmative in every respect.
`Now/today people do not believe (it) because it is not Ancestor Kagiyaw holding the wind but rather, our Beloved God (holds the wind).’ [VAWN-T-17 5.2]

Dili magtakaw ta dili imo na ampangan. \\
Dili mag-takaw ta dili imo na ampang-an. \\
neg.ir i.ir -steal nabs neg.ir 2 s.gen lk play- nr \\
‘Do not steal what is not your play thing.’ [LBOP-C-04 1.4]

Pakaan danen iran dili iling na beggas daw dili bunga ta kaoy na mga kan-enen na dili makilo. \\
Pa-kaan danen iran dili iling na beggas daw dili bunga ta kaoy na mga kan-en-en na dili ma-kilo. \\
t.r -eat 3 p.erg 3 p.gen neg.ir like lk milled.rice if/when neg.ir
fruit nabs tree lk pl cooked.rice- t.ir lk neg.ir a.hap.ir -kilogram \\
`What they ate was not like rice but rather, fruit of trees which was food that cannot be weighed.’ [PTOE-T-01 3.5]

The following is a riddle containing two negative predicate nominal constructions:

Dili ittaw. Dili ayep. Naļam mambaļ ta maskin ino. Radyo. \\
Dili ittaw. Dili ayep. Na-aļam m-ambaļ ta maskin ino. Radyo. \\
neg.ir person neg.ir animal a.hap.r -know i.v.ir -say nabs even what radio \\
‘(It is) not a person. (It is) not an animal. (It) knows how to say anything. Radio.’ [MRWR-T-01 22.1]

Adverbs may be negated, even if the main predicate is not negated. This is also a context for the use of dili:

Tapos uļa din tuturi lampraan tak ambaļ ta mga manakem dili kon anay tuturan lampraan daw narem. \\
Tapos uļa din...-tutod-i lampraan tak ambaļ ta mga manakem dili kon anay -tutod-an lampraan daw narem. \\
then neg.r 3 s.erg t.r -light- xc.apl lamp because say nabs pl
older neg.ir hsy first/for.a.while t.ir -light- apl lamp if/when sleep.paralysis \\
‘Then he did not light the lamp because the older people say do not first light the lamp if/when (someone) has sleep paralysis.' [ETON-C-07 4.4]

In this example, dili in the second clause negates the adverb anay ‘first/for awhile’. The older people do say to light the lamp when someone has sleep paralysis, but you are not supposed to light the lamp first. You must wake the person up first, then light the lamp.

Dili nay gid pirmi buat na iling tan. \\
Dili nay gid pirmi buat na iling tan. \\
neg.ir 1 p.excl.erg int always make/do lk like d3nabs \\
‘We really do not always do like that.’ (elicited – a variation of example bkm:Ref118463113 )

Dili ko enged naisturbuan ka ta imo na pagtunuga… \\
Dili ko enged na-isturbo-an ka ta imo na pag-tunuga… \\
neg.ir 1 s.erg intentionally a.hap.r -disturb- apl 2 s.abs nabs 2 s.gen lk nr.act -sleep \\
‘I did not intentionally disturb you in your sleeping….’ (The mouse passed by the lion waking him up, though the mouse didn't intend to disturb him.) [BCWN-T-05 1:4]

… ingkantado i dili gulpi mag-atag ta masakit. \\
… ingkantado i dili gulpi mag-atag ta masakit. \\
fairy def.n neg.ir suddenly i.ir -give nabs sick \\
‘… fairies do not suddenly give sickness.’ (It is believed that fairies can give sickness but it is gradual not sudden) [CBWE-T-07 4.1]

Yon buat nay kaysan piro dili gid man pirmi. \\
Yon buat nay kaysan piro dili gid man pirmi. \\
d 3 abs do/make 1 p.excl.erg sometimes but neg.ir int emph always \\
‘That is what we do sometimes but not really always.’ [EMWE-T-01 3.6]

A time phrase may also be negated with dili. This is similar to constituent negation in that such clauses may always be considered a kind of predicate nominal. In the following examples, the negated time phrase is bolded in the English free translation:

Gambaļ danen na pagtakaw tak beet ambaļen dili pa pwidi lungien tak ilaw pa o dili pa oras ta lungi. \\
Ga-ambaļ danen na pag-takaw tak beet ambaļ-en dili pa pwidi lungi-en tak ilaw pa o dili pa oras ta lungi. \\
i.r -say 3 p.abs lk nr.act -steal because means say- t.ir neg.ir inc
can harvest- t.ir because unripe inc or neg.ir inc time/hour nabs harvest \\
`They said ‘stealing’ because it means to say that (the corn) can’t yet be harvested because (it is) not yet ripe or (it is) not yet time for harvesting corn.’ [VAOE-J-07 4.5]
summary: Constituent negation in Kagayanen negates a clause constituent rather than the whole clause, and such cases are often interpretable as cleft or predicate nominal constructions because the language lacks a copula in predicate nominal sentences. As a result, dili is used to negate nouns, adverbs, and time phrases, including expressions that are best understood as “not X” or “not yet time,” and some idiomatic uses like daw dili mean “but rather.”

text:
Magbata kanen ta dili iya na oras. \\
Mag-bata kanen ta dili iya na oras. \\
i.ir -child 3 s.abs nabs neg.ir 3 s.gen lk time/hour \\
‘She gave birth when (it was) not yet her time.’ [VAOE-J-05 1.3]

Piro dili man tanan-tanan na oras makailing ka na danen an miad iran na isip daw dili kaysan masinawayen gid man. \\
Piro dili man tanan-tanan na oras maka-iling ka na danen an miad iran na isip daw dili kaysan ma-s<in>away-en gid man. \\
but neg.ir also red -all lk time/hour i.hap.ir -say 2 s.abs lk
3 p.abs def.m good/kind 3 p.gen lk think if/when neg.ir sometimes
adj - <nr.res>correct- adj int also \\
`But not all the time can you say that as for them their thinking is good/kind but rather sometimes (their character) really is to be corrected.’ [EMWE-T-01 3.2]

Prepositional phrases (bolded in the free translations) may also be negated with dili:

A yan, dili nang para ki kiten anduni. \\
A yan, dili nang para ki kiten anduni. \\
inj d 2 abs neg.ir only for obl.p 1 p.incl now/today \\
‘(Expression of dismay) as for that, (it is) not just for us now/today.’ [EFOB-C-01 6.8]

Magtanem ki ta kaoy na dili para nang ki kiten anduni. \\
Mag-tanem ki ta kaoy na dili para nang ki kiten anduni. \\
i.ir -plant 1 p.incl.abs nabs tree lk neg.ir for only obl.p 1 p.incl now/today \\
‘Let’s plant trees not just for us now/today.’ (elicited, variation of bkm:Ref373356719 )

It is also possible to negate one constituent within a noun phrase. For example, in bkm:Ref446156832, only the modifier segeng ‘extreme’ is negated. The assertion is that the Actor indeed had asthma attacks in former years but they weren’t as extreme as the current one.

Piro duma ya na galambay ya na tinaon dili pa gid segeng na pag-ataki ta apo. \\
Piro duma ya na ga-lambay ya na t<in>aon dili pa gid segeng na pag--ataki ta apo. \\
but other def.f lk i.r -pass.by def.f lk < <nr.res> year
neg.ir inc int
extreme lk nr.act -attack nabs asthma \\
`But in other past years (they were) not yet very severe attacks of asthma.’ [JCWN-T-22 2.2]

Sakit mata minog na daon i na giting-giting na dili gid ļapad. \\
Sakit mata minog na daon i na giting giting na dili gid ļapad. \\
pain eye red lk leaf def.n lk scalloped lk neg.ir int wide \\
‘For painful eyes, (use) the red leaf that is scalloped, that is not very wide.’ [DBOE-C-04 11.1]

One constituent in an attributive clause can also be negated with dili. In example bkm:Ref446664253 the meaning is that the governing is very bad:

Iya na panggubirno ta mga ittaw sikad gid na dili usto. \\
Iya na pang-gubirno ta mga ittaw sikad gid na dili usto. \\
3 s.gen lk nr- governor nabs pl person very int lk neg.ir well/right \\
‘His governing of people was very much not right.’ [BEWN-T-01 2.8]

Example bkm:Ref373243525 is a variation of bkm:Ref446664253, in which dili is placed at the beginning of the predicate modifier. In this case, the meaning is ‘not very good’, that is, not as bad as in example bkm:Ref446664253.

Iya na panggubirno ta mga ittaw dili sikad gid na usto. \\
Iya na pang-gubirno ta mga ittaw dili sikad gid na usto. \\
3 s.gen lk nr- governor nabs pl person neg.ir very int lk well/right \\
‘His governing of people was not really very right.’

Negated hypothetical assertions and assertions that are negative for all times are also often expressed with the predicating verb in an action nominal form with pag - (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:pag ) and sometimes with the nominalizing suffix - én or the applicative suffix - an.

Daw gaumaw isya na manakem dili pagsabatén na ee tak magilek. \\
Daw ga-umaw isya na manakem dili pag-sabat-én na ee tak ma-gilek. \\
if/when i.r -call one lk older neg.ir nr.act -answer- nr lk yes
because a.hap.ir -angry \\
`When an older person calls (you) do not answer ‘yes’, because (s/he) will become angry.’ (lit. (Your) answering is not “yes”) [LBOP-C-04 1.6]

Rhetorical confirmation, di ba
rhetorical confirmation|(
The expression di ba (a short form of dili ‘ neg.ir’ plus the common Philippine question particle ba ) can occur clause-initially to indicate rhetorical confirmation (exs. bkm:Ref441346257 - bkm:Ref441346278 ). As mentioned in sec:interjections, in Kagayanen ba alone is a marker of rhetorical questions rhetorical questions, irony, or sarcasm. By using di ba the speaker asserts something that s/he thinks is true or maybe not completely sure about and wants the addressee to consider it carefully or to confirm it as true. The assumed response to such expressions is “yes.” Di ba may also occur in second position, or clause finally with approximately the same effect – a full discourse study would be needed to fully understand any nuances associated with the different possible positions for di ba. Examples of tag questions with di ba are given below in sec:yesnoquestions.

Di ba, gambaļ ka na dumaan a no? \\
Di ba, ga-ambaļ ka na -duma-an a no? \\

text: The term “declarative” in traditional grammar refers to clause types that speakers use to express information. Often the term “declarative mood” will be found in the literature. In this grammar, and in linguistics in general, this sense of the word “declarative” does not describe a mood at all (see chap:verbstructure, sec:modality on the expression of modality in Kagayanen). Rather, in the tradition of speech act theory, the term assertion assertion:speech act type! most closely approximates the traditional notion of declarative mood. An assertion is a kind of speech act speakers perform when they want to express information to other people (see e.g. ). This is a very common task that people perform using language, therefore assertions are usually the most common construction types in any language. Up to now, most of the examples and discussion in this grammar have dealt with declarative assertions. In this section we will describe some grammatical construction types that are used primarily to accomplish other, non-declarative, speech acts. These speech acts include requesting information ( interrogative constructions interrogative constructions ), and requesting or commanding action ( imperative constructions imperative constructions ).
summary: In traditional grammar, “declarative” refers to clause types used to express information, but in this grammar the term is not treated as a mood; instead, the closest speech-act concept is an assertion. Assertions are common because speakers frequently use language to convey information. The passage also introduces non-declarative construction types used for other speech acts, especially interrogatives for requesting information and imperatives for requesting or commanding action.

Polar, or “yes/no”, questions are interrogative clauses for which the expected answer is either ‘yes’ or ‘no’. In Kagayanen, polar questions have the same syntax as assertions. The only difference between an assertion and a yes/no question is that assertions typically have falling intonation at the end of the sentence and yes/no questions have rising intonation at the end. This rising intonation is indicated in the orthography, and in this grammar, with a question mark:

Pagtapos, guli kanen i daw painsaan ta manakem i na, “ Guli ka man dayon?” \\
Pag-tapos, ga-uli kanen i daw pa-insa-an ta manakem i na, “ Ga-uli ka man dayon?” \\

older def.n lk i.r -go.home 2 s.abs emph immediately \\
`Afterwards, he went home and the older person asked (him), “Did you come home immmediately?”' (The older man was surprised that he came back home so soon.) [NEWN-T-07 6.3]

Isya man na ga-tindir ta yi na pa-lumba, pa-ambaļ-an din, “Pwikan, anda ka en? ” Sabat ta Pwikan, “Ee.” Dason pa-insa-an man Umang i, “Umang, anda ka en ta inyo na pa-lumba-anay? ” Sabat man ta Umang, “Ee, anda aren en.” \\

The passage also notes that such questions can be identified by context, may optionally include the tag *di ba* as a genuine confirmation question or in sarcastic/ironic uses, and can sometimes begin with *ino* ‘what’ even though it does not refer to anything in the clause.

text:
Questions that expect a more elaborate response than simply an affirmation or disaffirmation are called question-word questions question-word questions!, content questions content questions!, information questions or WH- questions information questions!. In this grammar we will use the term “question-word questions.”

The question words in Kagayanen consist of three interrogative pronouns, and four interrogative adverbs. The three interrogative pronouns are kino ‘who’, ino ‘what’, and pila ‘how many.’ These only occur in the absolutive case, and are described in the context of a general discussion of pronouns in chap:referringexpressions, sec:interrogativepronouns. The four interrogative adverbs are kan-o ‘when’, indi ‘where’, indya ‘which’, and man-o tak ‘why’. The interrogative pronouns and adverbs can also be used as modifiers within RPs (see ex:atthewindow and ex:restroom ). In this section we will discuss all of these forms and their functions in the formation of question-word questions.

summary:
The passage explains that Kagayanen “question-word questions” are questions requiring more than yes/no answers, and it outlines the interrogative forms used to form them. Kagayanen has three interrogative pronouns—kino ‘who,’ ino ‘what,’ and pila ‘how many’—and four interrogative adverbs—kan-o ‘when,’ indi ‘where,’ indya ‘which,’ and man-o tak ‘why’; these forms can also function as modifiers within noun phrases.

It further notes that the pronouns occur only in the absolutive case, while indi normally means ‘where’ and indya ‘which,’ though indya can sometimes also express ‘where’ because of its form. The passage illustrates each question word with examples showing its use in questions and, in some cases, in noun phrase modification.

summary:
The passage describes how interrogative forms in the language function as adverbs, modifiers, and verbal inflections. It notes that forms like *man-o* and *man-o tak* are used for “why” questions, often rhetorically in scolding, while interrogative pronouns such as *kino*, *ino*, *pila*, and *indya* can modify nouns with the linker *na* or, in some cases, occur with verbal inflection to ask about actions, events, or manner.

It also states that the adverbs *kan-o*, *indi*, *man-o*, and *man-o tak* cannot be used as noun modifiers, unlike the interrogative pronouns. Finally, the passage mentions that there is one content question construction without an explicit question word, though only one example of this type appears in the corpus.

‘What is (the name of) your sickness?’ (lit. ‘name of that your sickness’) [ETWC-C-03 3.1]

Grammatically, this is a simple RP (Referring Phrase) meaning “name of your sickness.” However, because of intonation and context, it is obviously intended to be a question. This may be an example of omission of a question word, as in interview questions in English: “Name? Address? Place of birth?”
summary: The passage explains that the phrase *ngaran tan masakit no an?* is grammatically a simple referring phrase meaning “name of your sickness,” even though intonation and context show that it functions as a question. It may therefore illustrate the omission of a question word, similar to English interview-style questions like “Name? Address? Place of birth?”

Imperative construction is the term linguists use to refer to a type of sentence that is uniquely adapted to the speech act of directing someone to do something. While most languages have special forms for this type of construction, Kagayanen does not. Rather than having a special imperative construction, Kagayanen speakers use the plain declarative irrealis construction with a second person Actor. The examples in bkm:Ref113955378 illustrate some simple imperatives. Note that some of these are grammatically transitive and some are grammatically intransitive. Thus, the second person Actor may be absolutive or ergative. Following bkm:Ref113955378 are some examples from the corpus:

text: All languages provide special grammatical constructions, particles, or affixes that draw attention to particular parts of communicative acts. For example, English places elements at the beginning of a clause when they merit various kinds of focus according to the communicative intentions of the speaker. For example, “Coffee I like”, “It’s coffee I like”, “Coffee is what I like”, “As for coffee, I like it” are all pragmatically marked variations on the basic assertion “I like coffee.” In this section we describe three ways of ascribing special pragmatic statuses to elements in a clause. These are constituent order variation ( bkm:Ref445900436 ), grammatical particles ( bkm:Ref118460437 ), and cleft constructions ( bkm:Ref122603009 ). We have done our best to characterize the discourse functions of these constructions as they appear in the corpus, but a full discourse study is still needed to precisely evaluate the pragmatic effects of each of them.
summary: Languages commonly have grammatical devices that highlight particular elements of an utterance, and English often does this by placing focused material at the beginning of a clause, as in pragmatically marked variants of “I like coffee.” The passage identifies three such ways of assigning special pragmatic status to clause elements: constituent order variation, grammatical particles, and cleft constructions, while noting that their discourse effects are only partially characterized and need fuller study.

text:
The basic unmarked constituent order in Kagayanen intransitive clauses is V ABS, that is, a predicating word (usually a verb) followed by an absolutive RP referring to the single argument (S) of the intransitive clause. There are two basic orders of core arguments in transitive clauses, depending on the relative position of the arguments on the following saliency hierarchy:

Pronoun.5cm Full RP \\
1 > 2 > 3 > human > animate > inanimate

Of the two core arguments, A and O (see chap:voice, sec:grammaticalrelations ), whichever one is higher (further to the left) on this hierarchy usually occurs first. This may be considered a word order direct/inverse construction word order direct/inverse construction (see on Cebuano ). The direct form occurs when A and O are equal on this hierarchy (example bkm:Ref113973502 ), or when A outranks O (example bkm:Ref113973505 ). The inverse form occurs when O outranks A (example bkm:Ref113973507 ):

1.1cm V 2cm A 2.1cm O \\
… daw patigbas man ta amay ta bata manakem ya na bai. \\
… daw pa-tigbas man ta amay ta bata manakem ya na bai. \\
and t.r -chop also erg father nabs child older.person def.f lk woman \\
‘… and the father of the child chopped the older woman.’ [YBWN-T-01 5.11]

When O outranks A on the hierarchy, the O appears first. In example bkm:Ref113973507 the 1 s.abs pronoun precedes the full RP referring to the ergative constituent:

4.4cmV.4cm O.1cm A \\
Na gapanaw kay ta daļan, kagat a ta sitsipit. \\
Na ga-panaw kay ta daļan, kagat a ta sitsipit. \\
lk i.r -walk/go 1 p.excl.abs nabs road bite 1 s.abs erg scorpion \\
‘When we were walking on the road, a/the scorpion bit (stung) me.’ [LSWN-T-01 2.8]

There are no examples in the corpus in which both A and O are third person pronouns, and such examples are difficult for speakers to contextualize. However, A and O can both be pronouns if one is a different person category than the other. In such cases, the pronoun that is higher on the hierarchy occurs first, whether it is A or O. In examples bkm:Ref113973505 and bkm:Ref113973510 the first person pronoun occurs first, though it is A in bkm:Ref113973505, and O in bkm:Ref113973510:.4cmV.8cmA.3cmO \\
… nakita ko danen dya na sigi kaan. \\
… na-kita ko danen dya na sigi kaan. \\
a.hap.r -see 1 s.erg 3 p.abs d 4 loc lk continue eat. \\
‘…I saw them there continuing to eat.’ [RCON-L-01 2.9].4cmV 1.4cmO.1cmA \\
… pakamang a danen na magduma ta iran na bata na gaiskwila man ta Iloilo. \\
… pa-kamang a danen na mag-duma ta iran na bata na ga-iskwila man ta Iloilo. \\
t.r -get 1 s.abs 3 p.erg lk i.ir -companion nabs 3 p.gen lk child
lk i.r -school also nabs Iloilo \\
`… they got me to companion their child who was attending school in Iloilo.’ [DBWN-T-21 4.6]

There are no examples in the corpus of VOA order occurring when both core arguments are full RPs. However, such examples do occur in conversation, and speakers agree they are grammatically correct. A full discourse study of the function of VOA order in this circumstance would require a much larger corpus, since it is so rare. The following are perfectly grammatical elicited examples. Note that “my child” bkm:Ref113974691 and “our house” bkm:Ref113974693, though both in the grammatical function of O (undergoer), are likely to be more highly salient than the corresponding A arguments by virtue of being definite and possessed by the speaker. This may explain why these examples are easy to imagine, but again, a full discourse study would be needed to confirm or disconfirm this hypothesis..2cmV 1.5cmO 1.8cmA \\
Napattikan bata ko an ta sitsipit. \\
Na-pattik-an bata ko an ta sitsipit. \\
a.hap.r -sting- apl child 1 s.gen def.m nabs scorpion \\
‘A/The scorpion stung my child.’.2cmV 1.2cmO 2cmA \\
Nasunog baļay nay ya ta apoy. \\
Na-sunog baļay nay ya ta apoy. \\
a.hap.r -burn house 1 p.excl.gen def.f nabs fire \\
‘A/the fire burned our house.’ or ‘Our house was burned with fire.’

Though the above generalizations hold in the majority of situations, it is not uncommon for these patterns to vary for special emphasis or when the speaker is in some heightened emotional state. For example, when someone is frightened or excited by the content of the utterance, a marked word order may occur. With the marked word order, free emphatic absolutive pronouns occur instead of enclitic pronouns (see chap:referringexpressions, sec:personalpronouns ). In example bkm:Ref447287658 the speaker was describing a very fearful time when in a dream a fairy was forcing her to go away with him. It is believed that such dreams can result in one’s death..1cmV.8cm A.5cm O \\
Pambaļ din yaken i na muyog a. \\
Pa-ambaļ din yaken i na m-kuyog a. \\
t.r -say 3 s.erg 1 s.abs def.n lk i.v.ir -go.with 1 s.abs \\
‘He told me that I will go with (him).’ [EDON-J-01 1.7]

Since this is a clause in which the O argument (the speaker) is higher in the salience hierarchy than the Actor (the fairy) the unmarked word order would be VOA, with the enclitic absolutive enclitic pronoun a, instead of the free pronoun yaken referring to the speaker:.1cmV.7cm O.2cmA.5cm (Expected, common order) \\
Pambaļ a din na muyog a. \\
Pa-ambaļ a din na m-kuyog a. \\
t.r -say 1 s.abs 3 s.erg lk i.v.ir -go.with 1 s.abs \\
‘He said to me that I will go with (him).’

The use of the emphatic pronoun, and the unusual word order in bkm:Ref447287658 signals that the speaker was strongly affected emotionally by this frightening event.

Because the basic constituent order is predicate-initial, the pre-predicate position is a very powerful signal of special pragmatic importance. describe the functions of the pre-predicate element in expository discourse as follows:
summary:
Kagayanen intransitive clauses have a basic predicate-initial order, with the verb followed by the absolutive argument. In transitive clauses, the order of A and O is governed by a saliency hierarchy, so the higher-ranking argument normally comes first, yielding direct order when A is equal to or higher than O and inverse order when O outranks A.  

The text also notes that marked orders can occur for special emphasis or emotional states, often with free emphatic absolutive pronouns instead of enclitic forms; because pre-predicate position is highly salient, it signals special pragmatic importance.

modquote
Fronted RPs mark sentences that: 1) introduce new themes, 2) signal changes in theme, 3) summarize themes, 4) present results or reasons that are peaks, 5) signal selective focus, and 6) signal contrastive focus.
modquote

In this section we summarize the findings of using new examples from the corpus for the present study. The same or similar observations can be made regarding the functions of pre-predicate position in genres other than expository as well.

The primary function of fronted RPs in Kagayanen expository discourse is to mark the kinds of information that are most important for developing an expository text, namely global and lower level themes, Not to be confused with “Theme” as a semantic role as discussed in other parts of this grammar. result, and contrast. A “global theme”, or the main idea being explained in an expository text, is usually introduced in a fronted RP in the first paragraph. In a text explaining the traditional belief about lunar eclipses bkm:Ref372792644, the global theme is introduced in the first fronted RP in the first sentence of the paragraph. It is stated again in the second part of the same sentence:

Kaanlao, pagpati ta mga ittaw di ta Cagayancillo na daw buļan an, kaan ta lao, kaanlao, bakod kon an bekkessan palam-ed din buļan an. \\
Fronted RP1 \\
Kaanlao, pagpati ta mga ittaw di ta Cagayancillo\\
lunar.eclipse nr.act -believe nabs pl person d 1 loc nabs Cagayancillo\\

1.8cmFronted RP2 \\
na daw buļan an, kaan ta lao, kaanlao, \\
lk if/when moon/month def.m eat nabs sky.snake lunar.eclipse \\

Fronted RP3 \\
bakod kon an bekkessan pa-lam-ed din buļan an. \\
big hsy def.m snake t.r -swallow 3 s.erg moon/month def.m \\
` Lunar eclipse, a belief of people here on Cagayancillo is that when as for the moon, the sky snake eats (it), lunar eclipse, as for the big snake s/he swallowed the moon.’ [JCOE-C-03 2.1]

Notice that the sentence-initial fronted RP and its repeated form later in the sentence are not arguments of any clause in the sentence. There are, however, two fronted RPs that are arguments of a clause. The verb pati ‘believe’ takes a long complement clause which is made up of a conditional clause and a main clause. Both the conditional clause and the main clause have fronted RPs. In the conditional clause, the O argument, buļan ‘moon’, is fronted to the initial position of its clause. In the main clause the A argument, bakod an na bekkessan ‘the big snake’, is fronted to a position following the fronted RP that states the global theme. In this text, the moon and the snake are participants that have important roles in the global theme.

In the same text two sentences later bkm:Ref113975815, a lower-level theme is introduced-- people trying to frighten the snake (which is eating the moon). The theme, partially represented by the phrase mga ittaw ‘people’, is expressed in the fronted RP. Notice that the fronted RP is an argument of the immediately following dependent clause and of the main clause.

Ta, mga ittaw an, tak nakita danen na buļan ya naduwad en tak palam-ed ta bekkessan na bakod, magpukpok danen an ta mga lata, mga drum o daw ano man na makaatag ta sikad sagbak aged na bekkessan an, maadlek ilua din buļan ya, ig bekkessan an, mļagan ya en. \\.5cm Fronted RP1 5.2cm Fronted RP2 \\
Ta, mga ittaw an, tak na-kita danen na buļan ya na-duwad en tak pa-lam-ed ta bekkessan na bakod, mag-pukpok danen an ta mga lata, mga drum o daw ano. \\

7.8cm Fronted RP3 \\
man na maka-atag ta sikad sagbak aged na bekkessan an, \\
also lk i.hap.ir -give nabs very noise so.that lk snake def.m \\

Fronted RP4 \\
bekkessan an, m-dļagan ya en. \\
snake def.m i.v.ir -run att cm \\
The word ig is a Cuyunon word meaning ‘and’ and is used sometimes in more formal types of oral speeches.
The word ano is a Tagalog word meaning ‘what’.

`So, the people, because they saw that as for the moon (it) happened to disappear because the big snake swallowed it, they will beat on cans, drums and whatever else that can give out very noisy (sound) so that when the snake will be afraid, s/he will have to spit out the moon and the snake will run away.’ [JCOE-C-03 2.3]

Fronted RPs also mark sentences that signal a change of theme. An expository text of any significant length usually has more than one lower-level theme. When the speaker changes from one lower-level theme to another, the first mention of theme 2 occurs in a fronted RP, and this usually marks the beginning of a new paragraph. Theme 2 is not necessarily a brand new theme, but may be a previously mentioned theme that is being reintroduced. For example, the following three examples are from a text in which the global theme is the speaker’s family, introduced with a series of fronted RPs in the first paragraph. The second paragraph introduces the speaker and her husband as a secondary theme bkm:Ref372873939, with the fronted pronoun kami. In the third paragraph, the first-born daughter is introduced as another secondary theme, with the fronted RP panganay na bata ‘firstborn child’ bkm:Ref122614214. Finally, in the fourth paragraph the speaker returns to the secondary theme of herself and her husband bkm:Ref372873998, using another fronted RP kami na magsawa ‘my husband and I’:

Second paragraph, second sentence: \\
Kami, may kabataan na limma buok. \\
Fronted RP \\
Kami, may ka-bata-an na limma buok. \\
1 p.excl.abs ext.in nr- child- nr lk five piece \\
‘ As for us, we have five children.’ [CDWE-T-01 2.2]
summary: Fronted RPs in Kagayanen expository discourse primarily mark the information most important for developing a text: global and lower-level themes, results, and contrast. They often introduce a main theme in the first paragraph, introduce or reintroduce lower-level themes at paragraph boundaries, and can also signal theme change, selective focus, or contrastive focus.

Fronted RPs also mark sentences that summarize themes. These summaries occur at the ends of paragraphs, sections, and texts. Example bkm:Ref372876159 is from the eclipse text. It is the last sentence in a paragraph explaining the belief that a pregnant woman should not look at an eclipse. Here the deictic yon ‘that’ is the fronted RP.

Yon, isya man na pagpati ta mga inay na gabagnes. \\
Fronted RP \\
Yon, isya man na pag-pati ta mga inay na ga-bagnes. \\
d 3 abs one also lk nr.act -believe nabs pl mother lk i.r -pregnant \\
‘ That, it is another belief of mothers who are pregnant.’ [JCOE-C-03 5.2]

One might argue that bkm:Ref372876159 is a cleft construction; however, fronted RP constructions and cleft constructions differ in two ways. First, fronted RPs are always followed by a phonological pause (as indicated by the comma in bkm:Ref372876159 ), while head RPs of cleft constructions are never followed by a pause. Second, in cleft constructions, the head RP is the absolutive of a following nominalized clause (see sec:cleftconstructions below), whereas the clause that follows a fronted RP is not necessarily nominalized. The following are some additional examples of fronted RPs from the corpus.

Ta daw may sabid ittaw an na nagamasakit na gainay-inay ta luya, yon na masakit nan o sabid naan galin ta mga ingkantado, tak ingkantado i, dili gulpi mag-atag ta masakit. \\
Ta daw may sabid ittaw an na naga-masakit na ga-inay inay ta luya, yon na masakit nan o sabid naan ga-alin ta mga ingkantado, \\
so if/when ext.in sickness.from.spirits person def.m lk i.r -sick lk
i.r - red slow nabs weak d 3 abs lk sick d 3 abs.pr or sickness.from.spirits spat.def i.r -from nabs pl fairy \\

1.4cmFronted RP \\
tak ingkantado i, dili gulpi mag-atag ta masakit. \\
because fairy def.n neg.ir suddenly i.ir -give nabs sick \\
The prefix naga- in this example is another borrowing from Ilongo. The form in Kagayanen would be simply ga -.
`So if the sick person has a sickness from a spirit in which he gradually becomes weak, that very sickness or sickness from a spirit, it came from fairies because the fairy, it does not give sickness suddenly.’ [CBWE-T-07 4.1]

Finally, fronted RPs mark sentences that signal contrastive focus, another type of pragmatic focus. For this type of focus, one item is selected from a presupposed set in which the correct values are restricted. In the eclipse text, the speaker talks about the beliefs of the older generation concerning the eclipse. Then in bkm:Ref372890039, he contrasts the old generation with the new generation of young people who do not hold those beliefs. The new generation is the selected item and occurs in a fronted RP which is followed by a second fronted RP mga ittaw ‘the people’ which also refers to the same people, the new generation.

Piro anduni ta mga bag-ongtubo, mga ittaw i uļa en gapati ta iling tan. \\
3.4cmFronted RP1 1.3cm Fronted RP2 \\
Piro anduni ta mga bagongtubo, mga ittaw i uļa en ga-pati ta iling tan. \\
but now/today nabs pl new.generation pl person def.n neg.r cm i.ir -believe
nabs like d 3 nabs \\
`But now regarding the new generation, the people, they do not believe (in things) like that.’ [JCOE-C-03 4.2]

In example bkm:Ref122614892 the “other boats” are contrasted with kami the first person plural pronoun, both of which are fronted.

Duma ya na bļangay ubos balik ta Cagayancillo. Kami i nang gadiritso ta Anini-y. \\
Fronted RP1 \\
Duma ya na bļangay ubos balik ta Cagayancillo. \\
other def.f lk 2.masted.boat all return nabs Cagayancillo \\

Fronted RP2 \\
Kami i nang ga-diritso ta Anini-y. \\
1 p.excl.abs def.n only i.r -straight nabs Anini-y \\
` The other two-masted boats all returned to Cagayancillo. We only went straight to Anini-y.’ [VAWN-T-18 6.4]

Question words in information questions occur preverbally (see bkm:Ref445900292 ). In answers to such questions, the focused element occurs in either the normal word order or preverbally. In the following example the answer has two clauses; the first is a nonverbal clause and the second is a verbal clause. In the nonverbal clause the topic gadaag ya ‘the one who won’ is fronted before the comment umang ‘hermit crab’ which is also the focus item. The verbal clause has normal word order.

Q: Kino gadaag ya ta lumba ya? \\
A: O, gadaag ya umang. Gadaag umang ya. \\

Q: Kino ga-daag ya ta lumba ya? \\
who i.r -win def.f nabs race def.f \\

A: O, ga-daag ya umang. Ga-daag umang ya. \\
oh i.r -win def.f hermit.crab i.r -win hermit.crab def.f \\

Q: ` Who was the one who won the race?' \\
A: 'Oh, the one who won was hermit crab. Hermit crab won.’ [JCON-T-08 55.3-4]

Q: Man-e tak gadaag umang ya? \\
A: Gadaag umang ya tak pausar din utok din an. \\
Q: Man-e tak ga-daag umang ya? \\
why because i.r -win hermit.crab def.f \\
summary: Fronted RP constructions in this passage are shown to mark a range of discourse functions: they can introduce theme summaries at paragraph or text boundaries, express contrastive focus, and appear in answers to information questions. The text also distinguishes fronted RPs from cleft constructions, noting that fronted RPs are followed by a phonological pause and are not necessarily followed by a nominalized clause.

text:
A: Ga-daag umang ya tak pa-usar din utok din an. \\
i.r -win hermit.crab def.f because t.r -use 3 s.erg brain 3 s.gen def.m \\

Q: ` Why did hermit crab win?' \\
A: 'Hermit crab won because he used his brain.' [JCON-T-08 55.5-6]

Painsaan din isab gasukot ya ki kanen, “ Ino baba ta sidda ya na gautang ki kaon?” Ambaļ ta gasukot, “ Mļangkaw iya na baba.” \\
Pa-insa-an din isab ga-sukot ya ki kanen, “ Ino baba ta sidda ya na ga-utang ki kaon?” ambaļ ta ga-sukot, “ Mļangkaw iya na baba.” \\
t.r -ask- apl 3 s.erg again i.r -collect.payment def.f obl.p 3s what mouth nabs fish def.f lk i.r -debt obl.p 2s say nabs i.r -collect.payment long 3 s.gen lk mouth \\
`He asked again the one who was collecting money from him, “ What was the mouth of the fish who was borrowing money from you?” The one collecting the payment said, “His mouth was long.”' [EMWN-T-08 3.4-5]
summary: The passage gives examples of clauses with the prefix **ga-** and related forms, showing how they are used in questions and answers. In the first example, the hermit crab wins because he “used his brain,” and in the second, a speaker asks a follow-up question about “the mouth of the fish who was borrowing money,” with the response that “his mouth was long.”

text:
Discourse particles are small words that are used by speakers to guide the addressee through the structure of the discourse. For example, they may signal points of transition (e.g., paragraph and episode boundaries), points of heightened tension, climax, and contrast. They also may suggest how ideas are related to one another. In English, words such as therefore, so and OK may be considered discourse particles. Here we discuss only three common discourse particles in Kagayanen, a, gani, and ta. There are undoubtedly others, but a full discourse study is needed to elucidate all of their usages. Some of the words we have described as adjunct adverbs in chap:modification, sec:adjunctadverbs may also qualify as discourse particles. As with most distinctions proposed by linguists, the differences among discourse particles, adjunct adverbs, and interjections may not be absolute.

When the particle a occurs after a noun or noun phrase, it indicates contrast bkm:Ref372900695. For this reason, we call it a contrast particle contrast particle. However, when it occurs at the end of a sentence, it indicates truth value focus bkm:Ref372900724. It also appears utterance initially to mark special discourse functions, as discussed in bkm:Ref113971883.

Buli i daw imo na bitan paryo ta tama pantad na gasapļa daw gabiskeg bitan no tak may bekkeg na gaduma. Pandan i a paryo ta isya na lima na uļa ubra na daw bitan no sikad na yem-ek daw mapino. \\
Buli i daw imo na -ibit-an paryo ta tama pantad na ga-sapļa daw ga-biskeg -ibit-an no tak may bekkeg na ga-duma. Pandan i a paryo ta isya na lima na uļa ubra na daw -ibit-an no sikad na yem-ek daw ma-pino. \\
buri def.n if/when 2 s.gen lk t.ir -hold- apl same nabs many sand lk i.r -rough and i.r -strong t.ir -hold- apl 2 s.erg because ext.in bone lk i.r -with pandan def.n ctr same nabs one lk hand lk neg.r work lk if/when t.ir -hold- apl 2 s.erg very lk soft and adj -fine \\
`Buri (leaf), if you feel it (it is) like much sand that is rough, and hard is what you feel because there is a rib with it. Pandan (leaf), (it is) like a hand that has no work, that if you feel it (it is) very soft and fine.’ [DBWE-T-18 8.1]

Lain man nyan, bao san na agas a. \\
Lain man nyan, bao san na agas a. \\
bad emph d 2 abs odor d 2 nabs lk kerosine truly \\
‘That is truly very bad, the odor of that kerosene.’ [RZWN-T-02 4.10]

Examples bkm:Ref441496729 and bkm:Ref441496733 compare two rituals. The contrast particle a is homophonous with the first person singular pronoun and two interjections (see bkm:Ref113971883 on interjections). The difference is that the contrast particle occurs after the noun phrase it is contrasting, and has a level intonation that is held longer than for ordinary words.

a Contrast \\
Duļot i a isya na buaten ta isya na surano daw may mag-umaw ki kanen na gamasakit. \\
Duļot i a isya na buat-en ta isya na surano daw may mag-umaw ki kanen na ga-masakit. \\
food.offering def.m ctr one lk make/do- t.ir nabs one lk healer
if/when ext.in i.ir -call obl.p 3s lk i.r -sick \\
` Duļot food offering is one thing a healer does when someone who is sick calls him/her.’ [VAOE-J-04 1.1]’

Mikaw i a iya man ta surano na ubra ni sise nang dipirinsya ta duļot. \\
Mikaw i a iya man ta surano na ubra ni sise nang dipirinsya ta duļot. \\
food.offering def.n ctr 3 s.gen also nabs healer lk work d1abs
little only difference nabs food.offering \\
` Mikaw food offering, this is also the work of the healer, with only a little difference from duļot food offering.’ [VAOE-J-04 2.1]’

The word gani when it occurs in second position indicates truth value focus of the whole sentence. It is usually used to counter what another person assumes. Example bkm:Ref373133996 is part of a conversation about where the ancestors of the Kagayanen people originated. The one telling the story says that some people came to Cagayancillo on a boat from another island in the south called Cagayan de Sulu. The one who asks the question below assumes they were going to a certain destination. The one telling the story corrects that wrong assumption by saying they were just fleeing from Cagayan de Sulu island.

Piro indi danen inta punta? Galayas gani danen Cagayan Sulu tak adlek na tulien. \\
Piro indi danen inta punta? Ga-layas gani danen Cagayan Sulu tak adlek na tuli-en. \\
but where 3 p.abs opt going i.r -flee truly 3 p.abs Cagayan Sulu because afraid lk circumcision- t.ir \\
‘But, where were they going? They were truly fleeing from Cagayan Sulu because (they) were afraid to be circumcised.’ [MOOE-C-01 16-17]

The form ta in sentence-initial position, followed by a pause often expresses a conclusion to what has been said earlier. It sometimes follows a flashback, background information, digression or quotation, and brings the text back to the main point of the story or conversation.

ta ‘so’ (return to main topic of discussion after a quote) \\
Ta, gapanaw en darwa i na mag-utod. \\
Ta, ga-panaw en darwa i na mag-utod. \\
so i.r -walk/go cm two def.n lk rel- sibling \\
‘So, the two siblings left.’ (This follows a conversation between the two siblings.) [CBWN-C-22 9.1]

Ta, gadiritso kay ame so Barrio. \\
Ta, ga-diritso kay ame so Barrio \\
so i.r -straight 1 p.excl.abs 1 p.excl.gen d4abs.pr Barrio \\
So, we ourselves went straight there to Baryo.’ (Previous to this sentence was a digression about some people fishing with dynamite.) [DBON-C-09 2.9]

Ta, utod din ya pasikway din. \\
Ta, utod din ya pa-sikway din. \\
so sibling 3 s.gen def.f t.r -reject 3 s.erg \\
‘So, his brother rejected (him).’ [RBON-T-01 1.12]
summary: The passage explains that discourse particles are small words that help guide the addressee through discourse by marking transitions, tension, contrast, climax, and relations among ideas. In Kagayanen, three common discourse particles are described: **a**, which marks contrast after a noun phrase and truth-value focus at sentence end; **gani**, which in second position marks truth-value focus for the whole sentence and often corrects an assumption; and **ta**, which sentence-initially often signals a conclusion or a return to the main topic after a digression or quotation.

A cleft construction in Kagayanen consists of a clause with a noun phrase fronted before the verb and no resumptive pronoun left in situ. This same construction can function either as topicalization or as focal prominence construction ( bkm:Ref329967612 - bkm:Ref113976722 ).

Pedro ya gaatag ki yaken ta kwarta. \\
Pedro ya ga-atag ki yaken ta kwarta. \\
Pedro def.f i.r -give obl.p 1s nabs money \\
‘Pedro is the one who gave me money.' Or 'It was Pedro who gave me money.’

Kwarta i paatag din ki yaken. \\
Kwarta i pa-atag din ki yaken. \\
money def.n t.r -give 3 s.erg obl.p 1s \\
‘The money is what s/he gave me.' Or 'It was the money that s/he gave me.’

Yaken i paatagan din ta kwarta. \\
Yaken i pa-atag-an din ta kwarta. \\
1 s.abs def.n t.r -give- apl 3 s.erg nabs money \\
‘I was the one s/he gave money to.’ Or ‘It was me whom s/he gave money to.’

A different kind of cleft construction consists of a nominalized clause followed by a RP as in bkm:Ref329967818. The nominalized clause has the regular verbal affixes and a demonstrative determiner i, an, or ya after the verb. The RP has no determiner. When the verb in the nominalized clause is inflected as intransitive, the meaning is ‘the one who did the action’. The examples in bkm:Ref329968346 show that the determiner cannot occur in other positions than after the verb, including at the end of the nominalized clause ( bkm:Ref329968346 a, b, c), and the RP must occur in clause-final position ( bkm:Ref329968346 d, e).

Gaatag an ki yaken ta kwarta Pedro. \\
Nominalized clause 2cm RP \\
Ga-atag an ki yaken ta kwarta Pedro. \\
i.r -give def.m obl 1s nabs money Pedro \\
‘The one who gave me money was Pedro.’

Gaatag ki yaken an ta kwarta Pedro. \\

Gaatag ki yaken ta kwarta an Pedro. \\

Gaatag an ki yaken ta kwarta Pedro i. \\

Pedro gaatag an ki yaken ta kwarta. \\

Pedro an gaatag an ki yaken ta kwarta.

When the verbal inflection is transitive, the verb is followed by a clitic ergative pronoun indicating the Actor and the demonstrative determiner occurs after the clitic pronoun. Any oblique phrases occur after the determiner (exs. bkm:Ref329968477 and bkm:Ref329968698 ). The determiner cannot occur at the end of the nominalized clause as in ( bkm:Ref235676492 a, b) and ( bkm:Ref329968619 a, b). After the nominalized clause is the RP that cannot take a determiner. It also cannot occur before the nominalized clause (exs. ex:kiyaken and ex:takwarta ).

Patag din an ki yaken kwarta. \\
Nominalized clause 2.5cm RP \\
Pa-atag din an ki yaken kwarta. \\
t.r -give 3 s.erg def.m obl.p 1s money \\
‘What s/he gave to me was money.’

Paatag din ki yaken an kwarta. \\

Paatag din an ki yaken kwarta i. \\

Kwarta paatag din an ki yaken. \\

Paatagan din an ta kwarta yaken. \\
Nominalized clause 3.6cmRP \\
Pa-atag-an din an ta kwarta yaken. \\
t.r -give- apl 3 s.erg def.m nabs money 1 s.abs \\
‘The one s/he gave money to was me.’

Paatagan din ta kwarta an yaken. \\

Paatagan din an ta kwarta yaken i. \\

Yaken paatagan din an ta kwarta.

Cleft constructions with a demonstrative initially usually occur as a summary sentence for a paragraph, section or text.

Yon na isturya na inagian ko na sise a pa. \\
Yon na isturya na <in>agi-an ko na sise a pa. \\
d 3 abs lk story lk < nr.res >pass- nr 1 s.gen lk small 1 s.abs inc \\
‘ That was the story which was my experience when I was small.’ [BMON-C-02 1.17]

Galebbeng an ta mga patay mga seed nang na mga utod. \\
Ga-lebbeng an ta mga patay mga seed nang na mga utod. \\
i.r -bury def.m nabs pl dead pl close only lk pl sibling \\
‘The ones burying the dead are only the close relatives.’ [JCWN-T-21 13.7]

Another way clefts are structured is with a definite referring phrase followed by another referring phrase, which is the normal way of constructing predicate nominal constructions (see chap:non-verbalclauses, sec:predicatenominals ).

Sakayan an di batil, bļangay daw lansa. \\
[ 1.1cmRP1 1.1cm].5cm [ 2.6cmRP2 2.6cm] \\
Sakay-an an di batil, bļangay daw lansa. \\
ride- nr def.n d 1 loc 1.masted.boat 2.masted.boat and launch \\
‘The transportation here is one-masted boats, two-masted boats and launches.’ [SAWE-T-01 2.4]

Patugtog an ta banda mga tukar an kingmanakem en pugya a. \\
[ 1cmRP1 1cm].4cm [ 3.5cmRP2 3.5cm] \\
Pa-tugtog an ta banda mga tukar an king-manakem en pugya a. \\
t.r -play.music def.m nabs band pl music def.n style-older cm long.ago truly \\
‘What the band played was music of the style of older people long ago truly.’ [PBON-T-01 6.17 edited for naturalness]

Sakit en an namatian ko ya. \\
Sakit en an na-mati-an ko ya. \\
pain cm def.n a.hap.r -hear- apl 1 s.erg def.f \\
‘What is hurtful now is what I hear.’ (In the context others were laughing and so the speaker felt emotional pain that they were laughing at him.) [JCON-L-07 10.3]

Tape nang gaambaļ an piro sikad dayad man. \\
Tape nang ga-ambaļ an piro sikad dayad man. \\
tape only/just i.r -say def.m but very good also \\
‘Just a tape was what was speaking, but it was very good also.’ [BMON-C-05 16.4]
summary:
Kagayanen has cleft constructions in which a noun phrase is fronted before the verb with no resumptive pronoun, and this form can express either topicalization or focal prominence. A separate cleft type uses a nominalized clause followed by a resumptive phrase; the clause contains the normal verbal affixes plus a demonstrative determiner in a fixed position after the verb, while the resumptive phrase must appear clause-finally and cannot take a determiner.  

With intransitive nominalized clauses, this construction means ‘the one who did the action,’ and with transitive clauses the ergative clitic marks the Actor while the postverbal determiner and following oblique phrases are strictly ordered. Clefts with an initial demonstrative are often used as summary sentences, and another pattern uses a definite referring phrase followed by another referring phrase, matching the normal structure of predicate nominals.

friend 3 s.gen def.f d 3 abs t.r -favor 3 s.erg \\
‘It was his friend, that one he favored.’[RBON-T-01 1.13]

Ittaw ya na galabyog gasinggit, “Apo Kagiyaw, anen pagkaan no i en." \\
Ittaw ya na ga-labyog ga-singgit, “Apo Kagiyaw, anen pagkaan no i en." \\

2 s.gen def.n cn \\
